chunks.heading: PRD lifecycle diagram
chunks.body:
## PRD lifecycle diagram

```
PRD CREATED
  │
  ├─ memory_seed.from_archives=[prior_id]  ←── import archived memories
  ├─ memory_seed.from_prds=[live_id]       ←── inherit live prd-shared
  │
  ▼
DECOMPOSE
  │  Decomposer queries project-shared → injects top-15 as prior-context
  ▼
STORY 1
  ├─ TASK 1.1 spawned
  │    └─ [auto-seed] project-shared + prd-shared + story-shared → session-local
  │    └─ task runs → writes session-local + explicit scopes
  │    └─ [harvest] session-local learning → story-shared
  │
  ├─ TASK 1.2 spawned (sees task 1.1's story-shared memories)
  │    └─ [auto-seed] + task 1.1's harvested memories in story-shared
  │    └─ ...
  │
STORY 2
  ├─ TASK 2.1 spawned (sees story 1's prd-shared memories)
  │    └─ [auto-seed] prd-shared includes learnings from story 1
  │    └─ ...

ALL COMPLETE
  ├─ [auto-report] memory_prd_report generated
  └─ PRD deleted (strategy=archive)
       ├─ learnings → project-shared
       └─ prd-shared + story-shared purged

NEW PRD
  └─ memory_archive_import source_prd_id=<old> → new prd-shared
```

chunks.heading: Verifier feedback loop
chunks.body:
## Verifier feedback loop

When a task fails verification, retries automatically see the failure reason:

```
Task fails verification
  └─ Verifier writes to prd-shared:
       role=verifier-finding
       text="Missing null check in handler.go:45; test TestHandlerNil fails"

Task retried (auto-seeded from prd-shared)
  └─ Session sees: "Verifier finding: Missing null check..."
  └─ Session fixes the issue
  └─ Task passes verification
  └─ No new verifier-findings → harvest skips role=verifier-finding
```

No operator intervention needed. The verifier-finding memories persist
in `prd-shared` until the PRD is deleted or archived.

chunks.heading: Archive and delete strategies
chunks.body:
## Archive and delete strategies

When deleting a PRD, choose what happens to its memories:

| Strategy | Command | When to use |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `keep` (default) | `autonomous prd delete <id>` | Memories stay as orphaned scopes; searchable but no longer part of any hierarchy |
| `purge` | `autonomous prd delete <id> memory_strategy=purge` | Hard delete all memories; irreversible |
| `archive` | `autonomous prd delete <id> memory_strategy=archive archive_role_filter=learning,decision` | Promote qualifying memories to project-shared, then purge scopes |

**Archive is recommended** for any PRD that ran successfully — it
preserves institutional knowledge in project-shared where all future
PRDs and sessions can see it.

After archiving, the memories carry a breadcrumb:
```
_(archived from prd/0fb4e302 at 2026-09-15T14:22:00Z)_
```

A new PRD can import them with `memory_archive_import`.

---

chunks.title: How-to: Automata memory workflow
chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.body:
## Troubleshooting

**"My memories aren't visible to the next task"**
→ Check `memory_seed.enabled=true` and `memory_harvest.enabled=true` on the PRD.
→ Check `role_filter` — if it's set to `["learning"]` but the task only wrote
   `role=finding`, the harvest skips it. Use `memory_scope_inventory` to see counts.

**"I wrote to prd-shared but recall doesn't return it"**
→ Verify the `prd_id` you passed matches the PRD the session was spawned for.
→ Run `memory_scope_inventory project=<dir>` to confirm the scope has entries.
→ Check the recall query — semantic search may not match; try a broader query.

**"archive-import returned seeded=0"**
→ Check the source PRD was deleted with `memory_strategy=archive`, not `purge` or `keep`.
→ Confirm `role_filter` matches roles that were actually written. Check with
   `memory_scope_inventory` before and after archive — project-shared count should have increased.

**"The decomposer isn't using project-shared memories"**
→ Decomposer enrichment requires v8.32.0+. Verify version with `get_version`.
→ Check project-shared has entries: `memory_scope_inventory project=<dir>`.

**"Subprocess session can write to global scope"**
→ Should not happen. In subprocess mode, `memory_remember` with no `scope=` always
   goes to session-local. If you see global writes, check that `--caller-session-id`
   was passed at spawn time (`subprocessMode()` requires it).

---

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton-DAG orchestrator
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

An Automaton-DAG is a YAML spec that names Automata (existing or to-be-created),
declares dependencies between them (`depends_on:`), and attaches
guardrails. The executor:

1. Picks the next Automaton with all dependencies satisfied + status
   `approved`.
2. Spawns its tasks (per [`autonomous-planning.md`](autonomous-planning.md)).
3. Runs declared guardrails on completion.
4. If guardrails pass → marks Automaton `completed`; checks for the next
   eligible Automaton.
5. If guardrails fail → marks Automaton `blocked`; pauses the graph for
   operator action.

States: `draft` → `planning` → `needs_review` → `approved` → `running`
→ `paused` / `completed` / `failed`.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton-DAG orchestrator
chunks.heading: 4a. Happy path — CLI
chunks.body:
### 4a. Happy path — CLI

```sh
# 1. Author a graph spec.
cat > /tmp/auth-graph.yaml <<'EOF'
name: auth-refactor-graph
goal: Refactor auth from cookies to JWT in 3 phases
prds:
  - id: audit
    name: auth-audit
    title: Audit current auth flow
    backend: claude-code
  - id: implement
    name: jwt-implementation
    title: Implement JWT issuance + middleware
    backend: claude-code
    depends_on: [audit]
  - id: migrate
    name: migrate-cookies
    title: Migrate live sessions from cookies to JWT
    backend: claude-code
    depends_on: [implement]
guardrails:
  - rules
  - security
  - release-readiness
  - docs-integrity
EOF

# 2. Create the graph.
GRAPH_ID=$(datawatch orchestrator create --spec /tmp/auth-graph.yaml 2>&1 \
  | grep -oP 'id=\K[0-9a-f]+')

# 3. Inspect.
datawatch orchestrator get $GRAPH_ID
#  → name: auth-refactor-graph  status: draft
#    prds:
#      audit       (status: draft)
#      implement   (depends: [audit])  (status: draft)
#      migrate     (depends: [implement])  (status: draft)
#    guardrails: rules, security, release-readiness, docs-integrity

# 4. Decompose all child Automata (LLM-driven; async per Automaton).
datawatch orchestrator decompose $GRAPH_ID
sleep 90

# 5. Approve the graph (or per-Automaton via the autonomous CLI).
datawatch orchestrator approve $GRAPH_ID

# 6. Run.
datawatch orchestrator run $GRAPH_ID

# 7. Watch.
watch -n 5 "datawatch orchestrator get $GRAPH_ID | jq '{status, prds: .prds|map({id,status,n_completed_tasks})}'"

# 8. If an Automaton blocks on a guardrail:
datawatch orchestrator unblock $GRAPH_ID --prd implement \
  --reason "Security finding accepted: SAST false-positive in legacy file"
```

chunks.heading: 4b. Happy path — PWA
chunks.body:
### 4b. Happy path — PWA

1. Settings → Automate → **Automata Orchestrator** card → click
   **+ New Graph**.
2. Editor opens with a starter YAML template; fill in name + Automata +
   `depends_on` + guardrails. **Save**.
3. The new graph appears in the Orchestrator card list with status
   `draft`. Click into it.
4. Detail view shows a graph visualization (nodes = Automata; edges =
   `depends_on`) and a control toolbar:
   - **Plan all** — kicks off LLM planning for every child
     Automaton in parallel.
   - **Review** — opens the per-Automaton review pane (same UI as
     [`autonomous-review-approve.md`](autonomous-review-approve.md)).
   - **Approve graph** — marks all Automata approved when you've reviewed.
   - **Run** — start execution in topological order.
5. While running, nodes color: gray (waiting), blue (running), green
   (completed), red (blocked). Click a blocked node for the guardrail
   verdict.
6. To unblock: per-node action menu → **Unblock with rationale** →
   modal asks for the rationale text. Recorded in the audit log.

### 5b. REST

```sh
# Create.
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @/tmp/auth-graph.yaml \
  $BASE/api/orchestrator/graphs

# Get.
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  $BASE/api/orchestrator/graphs/$GRAPH_ID

# Decompose / Approve / Run / Cancel.
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  $BASE/api/orchestrator/graphs/$GRAPH_ID/decompose
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  $BASE/api/orchestrator/graphs/$GRAPH_ID/approve
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  $BASE/api/orchestrator/graphs/$GRAPH_ID/run
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  $BASE/api/orchestrator/graphs/$GRAPH_ID/cancel

# Unblock an Automaton inside the graph.
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"prd":"implement","reason":"Accepted SAST FP"}' \
  $BASE/api/orchestrator/graphs/$GRAPH_ID/unblock
```

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton-DAG orchestrator
chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Cyclic depends_on.** Daemon refuses with a clear error; remove
  the cycle.
- **Decompose timeout on a large graph.** Kicks off N decomposes in
  parallel; if all use the same backend you may rate-limit. Stagger
  with `orchestrator decompose --concurrency 2`.
- **Approve graph without reviewing children.** Same risk as
  per-Automaton. The graph view's per-node click opens the per-Automaton review
  modal — use it.
- **Unblock without rationale.** API requires a `reason`; the audit
  log entry is permanent.
- **Mid-run spec edits.** Editing a child Automaton spec while its graph
  is running is allowed but only the next-spawned task picks up the
  edit. In-flight tasks complete under the old spec.

chunks.title: Automata progress: how far along, and when will it be done
chunks.body:
# Automata progress: how far along, and when will it be done

The progress dashboard answers two questions about the Automata you run:
**how much is finished**, and **roughly when will the rest be**. It counts
Automata and their tasks by kind (feature, bug, other), measures how fast
work really finishes, keeps the work you know about apart from the work you
can only estimate, and turns that into a **range of days**, never a single
promised date.

It is read-only. Nothing on the card or in the commands starts, stops or
changes an Automaton; the only thing you can set from here is an
Automaton's *kind* (see [Setting an Automaton kind](#setting-an-automaton-kind)).
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [autonomous, progress, estimate, throughput, backlog, snapshots, trend]
exec_steps:
  - tool: autonomous_progress
    description: Read the progress numbers - counts by kind, rates, utilization, work left (known and estimated) and the completion range
    args: {}
    read_only: true
  - tool: autonomous_progress_trend
    description: Read how the completion range moved over the saved daily snapshots (last 30 days)
    args: {days: 30}
    read_only: true

chunks.title: Automata progress: how far along, and when will it be done
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

- **Counts by kind.** Every Automaton is a *feature*, a *bug* or *other*.
  Each kind gets a row with the number of Automata, how many are done,
  running, waiting and blocked, the tasks they hold, and how many tasks are
  done and left. A *total* row sums them. The *other* row only shows when it
  has something in it.
- **Rates, per active day.** How many Automata and tasks finish per day of
  **active time** (below), the worker time used per day, and how much of the
  lane capacity that is (utilization).
- **Work left, in two parts.** *Known* work is Automata that exist and the
  tasks they still hold. *Estimated* work is what does not exist yet: backlog
  rows not filed as Automata, and Automata with no tasks yet. The two are
  never blended into one figure without saying so.
- **A completion range.** Four ways of dividing the work left by a measured
  rate, shown as a low to high number of active days, with the sentence of
  assumption behind each and what is widening the range.
- **Lead time.** How long Automata sit in each stage between creation and the
  last finished task. It is shown for information only.
- **Inactive windows.** Every stretch of time left out of the rates, listed,
  never hidden.
- **A trend.** Once a day the numbers are saved; the trend says whether the
  completion range is converging, widening or flat.

chunks.title: Automata progress: how far along, and when will it be done
chunks.heading: Active time
chunks.body:
### Active time

Rates are measured per **active** day, not per calendar day. An *inactive
window* is a stretch where nothing was happening, so including it would make
the rates look slower than the workers really are. Two sources feed it:

- **Inferred gaps.** Any gap between two consecutive task starts or
  completions that is at least `autonomous.progress.inactive_gap_hours`
  (default 3 hours) counts as an inactive window.
- **The explicit waits file** (see [The waits file](#the-waits-file)), for
  stretches you know about: a weekend away, a quota reset, a host that was
  down.

Windows that overlap or touch are merged first, so no stretch is subtracted
twice. Active days are the calendar days since the start date minus the
merged windows. Inferred windows are marked *inferred* on the card.

Active time is why a pause you took does not wreck the estimate, and why the
card still shows the pause: the WAITS line gives the number of windows, the
hours left out, their share of calendar time, and **what the finish would be
in calendar days if the same share of idle time recurs**.

chunks.title: Automata progress: how far along, and when will it be done
chunks.heading: Why lead time never feeds the estimate
chunks.body:
### Why lead time never feeds the estimate

Lead time (created to approved, approved to first task, run time, created to
last task done) includes everything an Automaton waited on: your approval, a
full capacity pool, a back-off. Those waits are real, but they are not how fast
the workers go, and they overlap between Automata running side by side. Using
them to predict the finish would count the same waiting time again for each
Automaton. So lead time is **tracked, shown, and kept out of every estimate**.
Look at it to see where Automata spend their life; do not read a finish date
from it.

chunks.title: Automata progress: how far along, and when will it be done
chunks.heading: Known versus estimated remaining
chunks.body:
### Known versus estimated remaining

The LEFT block has three lines:

- **known** - Automata not done (how many are running, how many wait or are
  blocked), the tasks still open in them, and how many have not been
  decomposed into tasks yet.
- **estimated** - backlog rows not filed as Automata (a row marked
  `{phases=3}` counts as three), plus the Automata with no tasks yet, times
  the **mean tasks per Automaton** measured over Automata that do have tasks.
- **combined estimate** - known plus estimated, always labelled an estimate.

If something could not be measured (no backlog file was read, no Automaton
has tasks to average), the card says **not measured**. It never shows a zero in
place of an unknown. A missing backlog file is not an error; the estimated
part just excludes the rows.

chunks.title: Automata progress: how far along, and when will it be done
chunks.heading: Reading the range and the drivers
chunks.body:
### Reading the range and the drivers

The ETA line gives a **low to high** number of active days. The four methods
behind it each divide the combined work left by one measured rate:

| Method | Assumes |
|---|---|
| Automaton rate | Automata finish at the rate of the last three active days. |
| Task rate | Tasks finish at the average rate over all active days so far. |
| Task rate, last 24 h | Tasks finish at the rate of the last 24 hours of active time. |
| Worker hours | Each task takes the average worker time of a finished task, and workers stay as busy as they have been per active day. |

A method with no rate yet reads *not measured* and is left out; the low and
high are the smallest and largest of those that were measured. A wide range
means the methods disagree. The **drivers** line says why:

- *Workers were idle much of the time, so the rate may rise* - utilization is
  under half.
- *A few large Automata pull the average task count up* - the mean task count
  is well above the median.
- *Much of the remaining work is estimated because it has no tasks yet* - more
  than 30% of the work left is estimated.
- *Few Automata have finished, so every rate is thin* - fewer than five done.

Treat the range as a planning aid. It is an estimate; it narrows as more work
finishes and as Automata are decomposed.

chunks.heading: Setting an Automaton kind
chunks.body:
## Setting an Automaton kind

The kind decides which row an Automaton is counted in and which tasks-per-Automaton
average is used for it. It is resolved in this order:

1. the kind you set on the Automaton;
2. the kind of the backlog row that links the Automaton (`{kind=...}`);
3. a guess from the title and the start of the spec: *bug* when it contains a
   whole word such as fix, regression, crash or leak, else *feature*.

Set it explicitly when the guess is wrong. An empty kind clears your setting
so the guess applies again.

```bash
# CLI: set, and set at creation
datawatch autonomous prd-set-kind a1b2c3d4 bug
datawatch autonomous prd-create "Fix the stall on reconnect" --kind bug

# REST
curl -sk -X POST https://localhost:8443/api/autonomous/prds/a1b2c3d4/set_kind \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"kind":"bug"}'
```

Other channels:

- **Web UI:** Automaton settings > *Kind* (feature, bug, other, or "Derived from
  title and spec").
- **MCP:** `autonomous_prd_set_kind` (`id`, `kind`), and the `kind` argument of
  `autonomous_prd_create`.
- **Chat channels:** `autonomous set-kind a1b2c3d4 bug`.

An unknown kind is refused (HTTP 400, or an error from the CLI before anything
is sent).

chunks.title: Automata progress: how far along, and when will it be done
chunks.heading: Backlog markers
chunks.body:
## Backlog markers

The estimated part counts the open rows of the backlog table that no Automaton
is linked to yet. Two optional markers in a row's item cell steer it:

```markdown
| 41 | Rework the export pipeline {kind=feature} {phases=3} | not filed |
| 42 | Fix the reconnect stall {kind=bug} | not filed |
| 43 | Tidy the docs index | `a1b2c3d4` running |
```

- `{kind=feature}`, `{kind=bug}` or `{kind=other}` sets the kind of the row,
  and of the Automata linked to it that have no kind of their own. Without it
  the kind is guessed from the item text.
- `{phases=N}` says the row will become *N* Automata (a whole number, at least
  1). An unfiled row adds *N* to the estimate. A row that already has linked
  Automata adds only the phases beyond the ones linked, so a row is never
  counted twice.

A row is **linked** when its cells hold the Automaton's 8-character id in
backticks. A row is **open** while its status reads as open work (not started,
draft, running, approved, blocked, queued, merge pending, and so on) and is not
done, shipped, superseded or deferred past the next major release. The markers
are removed from the text shown to you.

chunks.title: Automata progress: how far along, and when will it be done
chunks.heading: The waits file
chunks.body:
## The waits file

A file named `operator-wait-windows.tsv`, **in the same folder as the backlog
file**, lists stretches to leave out in addition to the inferred ones. One line
per window, tab separated:

```text
# start<TAB>end<TAB>kind<TAB>reason
2026-10-14T18:00:00Z	2026-10-15T08:00:00Z	operator	away overnight
2026-10-18T00:00:00Z	2026-10-18T06:30:00Z	quota	provider quota reset
```

- Timestamps are ISO 8601; with no zone they are read as UTC. A bare date means
  midnight UTC.
- `kind` is a short label shown on the card; `reason` is optional free text.
- Lines starting with `#`, blank lines, lines with fewer than three fields, a
  bad timestamp, or an end that is not after the start are skipped silently.
- Overlaps with inferred windows (or each other) are merged, not double counted.

A missing file means no explicit windows. The file is read on every request, so
an edit shows up on the next refresh.

chunks.title: Automata progress: how far along, and when will it be done
chunks.heading: Daily snapshots and the trend
chunks.body:
## Daily snapshots and the trend

Once a day (UTC) the numbers are saved to `progress-snapshots.jsonl` in the
Automata data folder, first checked about 30 seconds after the daemon starts and re-checked hourly. A
**milestone** snapshot is also saved each time an Automaton completes.
Snapshots older than `autonomous.progress.snapshot_retention_days` (default 90)
are dropped.

`progress trend` reads them back: each point carries the date, the reason
(daily or milestone), the completion range low and high in days, the known and
estimated tasks, the 3-day throughput, utilization and completed count. The
**direction** says how the range width moved from the first point to the last:
*converging* (narrower by more than 10%), *widening* (wider by more than 10%),
*flat* (within 10%), or *unknown* with fewer than two points that have a range. Converging is what you want to see as
the work is decomposed and finished.

chunks.heading: Setup
chunks.body:
## Setup

The defaults need no setup. To tune them:

```yaml
autonomous:
  progress:
    lanes: 5                      # parallel lanes used for utilization (0 = 5)
    inactive_gap_hours: 3         # gap without activity that makes an inactive window (0 = 3)
    backlog_path: docs/plans/README.md   # relative paths resolve against autonomous.worktree_base_repo
    since: "2026-10-01"           # first day counted; empty = the first Automaton's creation date
    snapshot_retention_days: 90   # days snapshots are kept (0 = 90)
```

All five keys apply live; no restart. A bad value is rejected and nothing is
written.

chunks.heading: The five access methods
chunks.body:
### The five access methods

| What you want | YAML | CLI | Web UI | REST | Chat |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Read the numbers | - | `datawatch autonomous progress [--automation ID] [--tag ID] [--since D] [--until D] [--json]` | Automation sub-tab > *Overview* > *Progress* card, beside the *Capacity* card | `GET /api/autonomous/progress` | `progress [automation=ID] [tag=ID] [since=D] [until=D]` |
| Read the trend | - | `datawatch autonomous progress-trend [--days N] [--json]` | *Trend* section of the card | `GET /api/autonomous/progress/trend?days=N` | `progress trend [days]` |
| Set an Automaton kind | - | `datawatch autonomous prd-set-kind ID KIND` | Automaton settings > *Kind* | `POST /api/autonomous/prds/{id}/set_kind` | `autonomous set-kind ID KIND` |
| Change a setting | `autonomous.progress.*` | `datawatch config set autonomous.progress.lanes 5` | Settings > General > Autonomous > *Progress ...* | `PUT /api/config` `{"autonomous.progress.lanes": 5}` | `configure autonomous.progress.lanes=5` |

MCP agents use `autonomous_progress`, `autonomous_progress_trend`,
`autonomous_prd_set_kind`, and `config_set` (or the `progress_*` arguments of
`autonomous_config_set`). The commands and tools print or return the **same
object** as the REST route, so every surface shows the same figures.

`since` and `until` are dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`); `until` includes the whole day.
`automation` narrows the count to the Automata of one Automation, `tag` to the
Automata carrying one tag. A bad date is refused (HTTP 400).

chunks.title: Automata progress: how far along, and when will it be done
chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Everything reads "not measured".** No Automaton has finished yet, or the
  start date is later than all of them. Lower `autonomous.progress.since` or
  wait for the first completions.
- **The estimated part is zero.** No backlog file was read. Check
  `autonomous.progress.backlog_path`; a relative path resolves against the
  Automata base repository when one is set, else the daemon's working directory.
- **A bug is counted as a feature.** The guess missed it. Set the kind.
- **The range is very wide.** Read the drivers line. Decomposing the Automata
  with no tasks and filing the backlog rows narrows it.
- **A pause made the finish look late.** Add the stretch to the waits file so
  it stays out of the rates.

chunks.title: How-to: how the Automata tab loads
chunks.body:
# How-to: how the Automata tab loads

The **Automata** tab in the web app loads a short, paged summary of your
Automata instead of every record in full. A long-running daemon can hold
thousands of Automata with a lot of story and task text each; the list only
needs enough to draw one card per Automaton, so that is all the tab asks for
first. This page explains what you see while it loads, what **Load more** does,
what happens when you open a row, and how the tab behaves when the connection
drops and comes back.

For the API behind it (`limit`, `cursor`, ETag / 304, gzip) see
[list-endpoints-and-paging.md](list-endpoints-and-paging.md). For the chains
tab next to it see [automation-tab.md](automation-tab.md).
chunks.frontmatter_raw:

  index: true
  topics: [automata, pwa, loading, performance]

chunks.title: How-to: how the Automata tab loads
chunks.heading: What loads when you open the tab
chunks.body:
## What loads when you open the tab

Opening the Automata tab requests one **summary page of 50 rows**, newest
activity first. A summary row carries the identity of the Automaton (id,
title, status, revision), its story and task counts, its status counts, cost
totals, tags, type, backend, priority and its parent, but none of the story or
task text. The size of a row does not depend on how much text an Automaton
holds, so the first page stays small even when one Automaton is many
megabytes in full.

By default the tab shows the active Automata. The status filters, the search
box and the history toggle narrow the list on the server, so a filtered tab
also fetches only one page of matching rows.

Next to the list the tab loads the capacity and queue card, the list of LLM
backends and the tag list. Each one has its own request and its own error
handling, so a failure in one never blanks the list.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [automata, pwa, loading, performance]

chunks.title: How-to: how the Automata tab loads
chunks.heading: Load more
chunks.body:
## Load more

When more Automata match than the 50 shown, a **Load more** button appears
under the last card with the count, for example **Load more (50/273)**.

- Tap it to fetch the next 50 rows. The button shows **Loading…** and is
  disabled while the request runs.
- Rows already on screen stay where they are; the new rows are added below.
  A row that arrived twice is shown once.
- If the request fails, the rows you have stay, and the message **Could not
  load this list** with the reason appears beside the button. Tap **Load
  more** again to retry from the same place.
- The button disappears when there is nothing left to load.

The Sessions and Alerts tabs page the same way and use the same control.

chunks.title: How-to: how the Automata tab loads
chunks.heading: Loading, cached, stale and failed
chunks.body:
## Loading, cached, stale and failed

The tab always shows something and tells you where the data came from.

| You see | It means |
|---|---|
| Three grey placeholder rows and **Loading…** | First load, with nothing saved on this device yet. |
| The list with a **Cached** label and **Last updated N s ago**, and a small **Loading…** beside it | The list from your last visit, drawn immediately from this browser's storage while a fresh request runs. |
| The list with **Last updated N s ago** | A fresh copy. The age counts up while you look at it. |
| The list with **Data may be out of date** | The copy is older than the 30 second refresh interval and no load is running, for example because the last refresh was slow. The rows are still shown. |
| A red **Could not load this list: <reason>** banner with a **Retry** button | The request failed or took longer than 15 seconds (the reason then reads `timeout (15 s)`). Any cached rows stay visible below the banner. |
| **No automata. Launch one with ⚡.** | The load succeeded and there is nothing to show. It never appears while loading or after a failure. |

Stale is not failed: a slow refresh keeps the old rows on screen. **Retry**
sends the same request again. A late answer to an older request cannot replace
a newer one.

The tab refreshes itself every 30 seconds while it is on screen. A tab you are
not looking at does not poll, and the browser's own background throttling for a
hidden page is respected, so a phone is not kept busy. When you come back to
the tab it refreshes if the data is older than 30 seconds.

  index: true

chunks.title: How-to: how the Automata tab loads
chunks.heading: Opening a row
chunks.body:
## Opening a row

A row on the list holds counts only, so its stories and tasks are not there
yet. Open a row and the tab fetches the **full record for that one Automaton**
(one request), then its **children**. The text **Open to load stories and
tasks** is what a closed row stands for. While the record is loading the row
shows a loading line; if the request fails the row shows the error and you can
close and open it again.

The full record is kept for the row and fetched again only when the
Automaton's revision changes, so opening and closing a row does not re-download
it, and a running Automaton you are watching updates when it changes.

Very long text inside a record (verifier transcripts, task output) is capped
in the record shown on the card and marked as cut. The complete text is one
more request away through the outputs route described in the paging guide.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [automata, pwa, loading, performance]

chunks.title: How-to: how the Automata tab loads
chunks.heading: Children
chunks.body:
## Children

A child is an Automaton spawned by a task of another Automaton. A child row
shows a purple **parent** badge with the parent's id.

- On the list the children are ordinary rows. A child that is on a page you
  have already loaded shows up on its own card and in its parent's **Children**
  section.
- When you open a parent, the tab asks the server for that parent's children
  once, whether or not they are on a loaded page. The section lists each child
  with its id, status and counts; tap a child's id to jump to its row when it
  is loaded.
- When none of the parent's tasks spawned a child, the section says so:
  "no children".

So you never have to press **Load more** just to see the children of an
Automaton you have opened.

chunks.title: How-to: how the Automata tab loads
chunks.heading: What happens when the connection drops and returns
chunks.body:
## What happens when the connection drops and returns

The web app keeps a live socket to the daemon. When it drops and then
reconnects (a phone going through a tunnel, a Tailscale route changing, the
daemon restarting), the app does **not** reload the tabs.

- It sends **one small request**: the first summary page of sessions (50 rows),
  with the same row-only shape as the list. Several reconnect events in a row
  share that one request.
- If you have a session open, its full record is fetched once more only when
  the summary row for it was cut.
- Every other list refreshes only if its tab is on screen and its data is older
  than the refresh interval, and then it reloads the **first page only**. Open
  rows and the rows you already loaded by **Load more** stay on screen.
- Retries of the socket back off, up to about 30 seconds between attempts, so a
  long outage does not create a burst of requests.

A drop that is repeated again and again stays inside the same small request
and byte budget each time.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [automata, pwa, loading, performance]

chunks.title: How-to: how the Automata tab loads
chunks.heading: Troubleshooting a slow tab over a phone or Tailscale link
chunks.body:
## Troubleshooting a slow tab over a phone or Tailscale link

1. **Look at the label first.** **Cached** with a ticking age means the list
   on screen is real but old and the new one is on its way. **Data may be out
   of date** means a refresh is overdue. Neither is a failure.
2. **Wait for the 15 second timeout before assuming it is stuck.** On a slow
   link the tab shows **Loading…** and then, if the request cannot finish, the
   red banner with **Retry**. Your cached rows stay visible under it. Tap
   **Retry** once the link is better.
3. **Check the path, not just the tab.** Over Tailscale, check that the route
   to the daemon is direct and not relayed: `tailscale ping <daemon-host>`
   prints whether the path is direct or through a relay. A relayed path is much
   slower than a direct one.
4. **Measure the request.** Set `DW` to the daemon base URL, then time the first
   page and look at its size:

   ```bash
   export DW="http://<host>:<port>"
   curl -sS --compressed -o /dev/null \
        -w 'status %{http_code}  bytes %{size_download}  total %{time_total}s\n' \
        "$DW/api/autonomous/prds?limit=50&active=1"
   ```

   A healthy first page is tens of kilobytes at most, and a repeat that sends
   the ETag back answers **304 Not Modified** with no body. A very large
   response here means something is asking for the full form; see the last
   item.
5. **Narrow what the tab asks for.** Use the status filters or the search box;
   the server filters first, so a narrower list is a smaller first page.
6. **Keep the tab visible.** A hidden browser tab stops polling to save
   battery and refreshes when you return. Switching apps on a phone and back
   triggers that one refresh.
7. **If a page is huge, find the full form.** The only requests that return
   whole records are `full=1` on the Automata routes and an `/api/sessions`
   call with no `view=summary` or `limit`. The web app does not send these.
   A script or an older client that does is the likely cause.
8. **Clear the saved copy if the tab shows something odd.** The cached list
   lives in this browser's storage and is replaced by the next successful
   load. Clearing site data for the daemon's address removes it.

  topics: [automata, pwa, loading, performance]

chunks.heading: Checking it yourself
chunks.body:
## Checking it yourself

The load scenarios run a throttled slow-4G profile against a daemon holding
thousands of sessions and hundreds of Automata:

```bash
cd scripts/test-stories/pwa
env -u TMUX -u TMUX_TMPDIR node run-all.mjs --group load
```

One scenario checks that the first load of the Automata and Sessions tabs makes
no full-form list request and stays inside a byte budget. Another drops the
connection, holds it down, restores it, and checks that the refresh stays
inside a small request and byte budget, twice in a row. The same checks run in
release smoke against the smoke daemon.

chunks.body:
# How-to: Share one tag registry across federated daemons

Several daemons in a federation can share one set of Automata tags. The same
tag names, parents, colors and descriptions then appear on each of them, so a
tag browser on any daemon shows the same tree. This how-to covers how the
shared registry is set up, what happens when the keeper is unreachable, and
how to read and dismiss the notes a merge leaves behind.

Read [automata-tags](automata-tags.md) first for the tag tree itself. The
sync rules are in [flow/tag-registry-sync-flow](../flow/tag-registry-sync-flow.md).

chunks.title: How-to: Share one tag registry across federated daemons
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

- One daemon is the **keeper**. It holds the registry.
- The other daemons are **peers**. A peer keeps a cached copy of the keeper's
  tags on disk, pulls the keeper's copy on a timer, and sends its own tag edits
  to the keeper.
- A daemon with **no keeper** is **standalone**. It keeps its own tags, and
  nothing syncs. This is the default, and what a daemon did before the shared
  registry existed.
- The roles follow from one setting, `autonomous.tags.registry_keeper`. It is
  a federation peer name, and it is **chosen by the operator**, not inferred:
  you set it on each peer to the keeper's name, and on the keeper to its own
  name.

chunks.title: How-to: Share one tag registry across federated daemons
chunks.heading: Base requirements
chunks.body:
## Base requirements

- At least two daemons that are federation peers of each other. The keeper's
  name must be the name of a federation peer on each peer daemon (see
  [federated-observer](federated-observer.md) for adding a peer).
- The federation grants on the keeper must allow the peer's autonomous read
  (to pull the registry) and autonomous write (to forward edits). A peer
  without a write grant can still read, but its edits are refused the way
  any federated write is refused.
- A tag a peer creates while the keeper is unreachable is pushed to the keeper
  when it returns, and merged if the keeper already has the same name under
  the same parent (see steps 4 and 5).

chunks.heading: 1. Name the keeper on every daemon
chunks.body:
### 1. Name the keeper on every daemon

Set the keeper on each peer and on the keeper. Each change applies at once; no
restart is needed.

- **On the keeper:** `autonomous.tags.registry_keeper` = the keeper's own name.
- **On each peer:** `autonomous.tags.registry_keeper` = the keeper's name.
- Optional: `autonomous.tags.registry_sync_seconds` (a whole number of
  seconds, minimum 5, default 30) sets how often a peer pulls the keeper's
  copy.

The settings are listed with every channel in [the settings table](#the-settings-and-the-five-ways-to-set-them).

chunks.title: How-to: Share one tag registry across federated daemons
chunks.heading: 3. Edit on a peer
chunks.body:
### 3. Edit on a peer

Create, rename, move, recolor, describe or delete a tag on a peer as you
would on the keeper. The peer forwards the edit to the keeper, and the reply
shows the **keeper's** value, so what you see is what the keeper holds.

Each field of a tag has its own revision on the keeper. Two edits to
**different** fields of one tag both apply. Two edits to the **same** field,
made while apart, produce a conflict:

- The keeper keeps its own value.
- The peer shows a notice in the form *The keeper's version won: `<field>` is
  now `<value>`*, and the registry panel shows the keeper's value.

chunks.heading: 4. When the keeper is unreachable
chunks.body:
### 4. When the keeper is unreachable

A peer keeps working from its last copy and says so.

- **Stale copy.** The tag browser shows the banner *Showing the last copy from
  `<time>`; the keeper is unreachable*. Every tag count carries a *stale*
  mark, and the tag count is the count from that copy.
- **Refused writes.** Rename, move, recolor, describe and delete are disabled,
  with the reason as the tooltip. Over the API they return `503`, and nothing
  changes.
- **Creates still work.** A tag created on the peer is marked *pending sync*
  until the keeper takes it. The registry status counts these tags in
  `pending_sync_count`.

When the keeper answers again, the next sync (within `registry_sync_seconds`)
pulls its copy, pushes the pending tags, and clears the stale mark.

> **Current gap.** The PWA *pending sync* badge is not drawn yet in this
> build: the tag list the browser reads does not carry the per-tag pending
> flag. The count is correct in the registry status, on the API, in the CLI
> and in the comm channel. Until the badge is drawn, read the pending count
> from `tag-registry` or `pending_sync_count` instead of the browser.

chunks.title: How-to: Share one tag registry across federated daemons
chunks.heading: 5. Read and dismiss the merge notes
chunks.body:
### 5. Read and dismiss the merge notes

A tag created on two nodes while they were apart is **merged** when it reaches
the keeper, if the keeper already has a tag with the same name (ignoring case)
under the same parent. The peer rewrites its assignments to the keeper's tag,
and both nodes record a note, so the merge is never silent:

> Tag `<name>` was created on two nodes while they were apart and has been merged

A tag the keeper **deletes** while a peer still has Automata or sessions under
it leaves a note as well:

> Tag `<name>` was deleted on the keeper while this node still had Automata under it

Click **Dismiss** to remove a note on this node. Dismissing changes no tag and
no assignment, and a dismissed note stays dismissed when later snapshots
arrive. Each daemon keeps its own notes, so dismissing one on the keeper does
not clear the note on a peer.

chunks.heading: The settings and the ways to set them
chunks.body:
## The settings and the ways to set them

Each setting below is changed the same way from every runtime channel. An invalid
value is refused on every channel with the same message, and nothing is written.

| Setting | Values | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `autonomous.tags.registry_keeper` | a federation peer name, or empty | empty (standalone) | This daemon's own name makes it the keeper. |
| `autonomous.tags.registry_sync_seconds` | whole seconds, minimum 5 | 30 | How often a peer pulls the keeper's copy. |

Channels for the settings (the five ways to set a value, plus the YAML file):

| Channel | How to set `autonomous.tags.registry_keeper` |
|---|---|
| **REST** | `PUT /api/config` with `{"autonomous.tags.registry_keeper": "<name>"}`; read back with `GET /api/config` under `autonomous.tags` |
| **PWA** | Settings → General → Automata → **Tag browser** group, the *Tag registry keeper* field |
| **CLI** | `datawatch config set autonomous.tags.registry_keeper <name>`; read with `datawatch config get autonomous.tags.registry_keeper` |
| **MCP** | `config_set` with the key `autonomous.tags.registry_keeper` (the MCP server needs `mcp.allow_self_config=true`) |
| **Comm channel** | `configure autonomous.tags.registry_keeper=<name>` |
| **YAML** | `autonomous.tags.registry_keeper:` in `config.yaml`, with the comment in [config-reference](../config-reference.yaml) |

Set `registry_sync_seconds` the same way, with the key
`autonomous.tags.registry_sync_seconds`.

## Same thing from every other surface

| Task | REST | MCP | CLI (`datawatch autonomous …`) | Comm channel (`autonomous …`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Registry status (role, keeper, stale, pending, notes) | `GET /api/autonomous/tags` (the `registry` object) | `autonomous_tag_registry_status` | `tag-registry` | `tag-registry` |
| Dismiss a note | `POST /api/autonomous/tags/registry/notes/{id}/dismiss` | `autonomous_tag_registry_dismiss_note` | `tag-registry-dismiss <note-id>` | `tag-registry-dismiss <note-id>` |

`POST /api/autonomous/tags/registry/write`) are for daemons, not operators. A
peer asked for the keeper's snapshot answers `409`, because only the keeper
holds the registry.

chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Edits refused on a peer with `503`.** The keeper is unreachable. Check
  the federation peer's address and the keeper's health; creates still work
  in the meantime.
- **The peer shows a stale copy from the start.** The keeper name must be the
  name of a federation peer on that daemon. When it is not, the peer treats the
  keeper as unreachable: it serves its cached copy, `stale` is true, and
  `last_error` names the keeper as not a federation peer. Fix the name, or add
  the peer.
- **A tag appears twice across nodes.** A same-name, same-parent tag created on
  a peer while apart is merged into the keeper's tag when the peer syncs. If
  the names differ, both tags stay; rename one.
- **Expecting an instant pull.** A peer pulls on its interval (default 30 s).
  Changing `registry_keeper` triggers an immediate reconfiguration; an ordinary
  tag edit on the keeper reaches a peer on the next interval.
- **Expecting a per-tag pending badge in the browser.** Not drawn in this
  build; see the gap note in step 4.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

- A **tag** is a named object with an `id` (8 hex characters), a `name`,
  an optional `parent_id`, an optional `color` and `description`.
- Tags form a **tree**: `Work` → `Mobile App` → `iOS`.
- An Automaton carries **several tags** (`tag_ids` on its JSON). One
  tagged both `Mobile App` and `Q4 Security` shows up under both.
- An Automaton may have one **primary tag**. It orders the Automaton inside a
  tag branch and never hides a membership. It defaults to none.
- A **session** carries its own tags. A session started by an Automaton also
  **inherits** that Automaton's tags. Inherited tags are read-only on the session.
- The **attention group** holds the Automata that need you: blocked, needing
  review, paused, or holding a task for review.
- Tags are stored in `tags.jsonl` in the autonomous data directory, so
  they survive a daemon restart. When several daemons share a registry, the
  tags are shared too; see [automata-tag-registry](automata-tag-registry.md).
- Tags only organise. They never start, stop or schedule anything.

### 1. Create a tag tree

1. Open **Settings → Automata → Tag Registry**.
2. Type a name (`Work`), leave **Parent** at *— top level —*, pick a

3. Create `Mobile App` with **Parent** = `Work`, then `iOS` with
   **Parent** = `Mobile App`.

Use **Rename**, the **Parent** dropdown and the color swatch on a row to
edit a tag later. Renaming or moving a tag updates it everywhere it is
used, because Automata store the tag's ID, not its name.

chunks.heading: 3. Browse by tag
chunks.body:
### 3. Browse by tag

The Automata list opens on the **attention view** or the **tag browser**
(see [step 6](#6-the-attention-group-and-the-landing-view)). Switch between
them with the **List** and **Tags** buttons above the list. The tag browser
shows the tag tree, and each tag shows a **subtree count**.

- **Subtree count.** The number of distinct Automata under the tag, including
  every tag below it. An Automaton under two children of `Work` is counted once
  under `Work`.
- **Several tags, one Automaton.** An Automaton with several tags appears under
  each of them, with an *also in:* line naming its other tags. It is counted once
  per tag branch.
- **Untagged.** Automata with no tag at all are listed in an *Untagged* section
  at the end of the tree.
- **Direct count.** Set `autonomous.tags.direct_counts_visible` to show the count
  of Automata tagged with exactly that tag as a tooltip beside the subtree count.

chunks.heading: Selecting tags and the match mode
chunks.body:
#### Selecting tags and the match mode

Pick one or more tags in the **Tags** filter (on a phone, the **Filters** button
opens a sheet). The default match mode is **match ANY**:

- **match ANY** (default): an Automaton matches when it carries at least one
  selected tag. Selecting a second tag **widens** the list.
- **match ALL**: an Automaton must carry every selected tag. Press the
  match-mode control to switch. Selecting a second tag **narrows** the list.

While a filter is active the browser shows a flat grid of the matches. If none
match, the browser says *No matches. Clear N filters*; press it to clear the
selection.

**Sub-tags are always included in the tag browser.** Choosing `Work` matches
Automata tagged `Work` **or any tag below it**, and the counts roll up. Tagging
an Automaton only at the leaf (`iOS`) is enough. There is no switch to match
exact tags only in the browser yet; the Automata-by-tag route
(`GET /api/autonomous/prds?tag=<id>`) takes `include_sub=false` for that.

The tag selection and the match mode are remembered in the browser between
visits. The match mode is a browser setting, and its starting value comes from
`autonomous.tags.default_match_mode`. REST, MCP, the CLI and the comm channel
do not take a match mode.

On a phone the tree drills down one level at a time with a breadcrumb trail and
a **Back** row; the URL hash follows the drill-down.

chunks.heading: The header Tags dropdown
chunks.body:
### The header Tags dropdown

The page header has an icon button showing a tag icon, with no visible word.
The tag is a solid tag filled in the theme accent color, with a lighter hole and a
subtle darker edge, so it reads clearly on both the dark and the light theme.
It looks brighter when the dropdown is open or a tag filter is on, it carries a
count badge while filters are active, and it shows a visible focus ring for
keyboard users. Its accessible name and its tooltip read **Tags**. It opens a dropdown that
holds the session list's filters and the actions for the session you have open.

- **Active-filter count.** A small number on the tag icon button counts the
  filters in force: one for **Watched only**, plus one for each ticked tag.
  It is empty when no filter is on.
- **Watched only.** A checkbox at the top. Tick it to list only the sessions
  you watch.
- **Tags.** One checkbox per tag, in tree order. Tick several to filter the
  session list by them. The match button switches between **match ANY**
  (default) and **match ALL**, and **Clear** appears once a tag is ticked.
  With no tags yet, the list reads *No tags yet*.
- **This session.** Shown only while a session is open. **Watch this session**
  (or **Stop watching this session**) replaces the watch eye the session
  header used to carry, and **Edit tags of this session** opens the session
  tag editor described in [step 7](#7-tag-a-session).

Press Escape, the button again, or click outside the dropdown to close it.

chunks.heading: 4. Primary tag (sorting only)
chunks.body:
### 4. Primary tag (sorting only)

A primary tag orders an Automaton inside each branch it appears in. It is
optional and defaults to **No primary tag**.

1. Open the Automaton's **Tags** dialog and tick its tags.
2. Pick a **Primary tag** from the choices; the choices are the tags you ticked.
3. Press **Save**.

The primary tag changes only the order. It never hides an Automaton from a
branch, and it is cleared when its tag is removed from the Automaton.

chunks.heading: 6. The attention group and the landing view
chunks.body:
### 6. The attention group and the landing view

The **attention group** is the set of Automata that need you. It holds an
Automaton when:

- its status is one of the statuses in `autonomous.tags.attention_statuses`.
  The default is **blocked, needs_review and paused**. A paused Automaton is in
  the group so that every paused item is in one place; or
- it has a task held for operator review. Its card reads *N task(s) held for
  review*.

The list shows the group as a pinned **Needs attention** section above the tag
browser. The view switch shows its count, as **Attention (N)**. When nothing
needs attention the section reads *Nothing needs attention right now.*

A pinned **Running** strip sits beside it and shows the Automata that are
running, with *+N more* when there are more than fit.

**The landing view** is set by `autonomous.tags.default_view`:

- `auto` (default): the attention view when at least one Automaton needs
  attention, otherwise the tag browser.
- `attention`: always the attention view.
- `tags`: always the tag browser.

The landing view is decided once per page load. Any viewer can switch views
afterwards; that choice is remembered in the browser for that viewer.

Counts stay current without a reload. A status change, a tag change or a tag
rename sends a live event, and the list updates. If the event stream drops, the
list catches up on its next poll.

chunks.heading: 7. Tag a session
chunks.body:
### 7. Tag a session

A session carries its own tags, and shows the tags of the Automaton that
started it.

- **On the list.** Each session card, and each node of the session tree,
  shows its own tags as normal chips. Tags inherited from its Automaton are
  drawn as dashed chips with a small *inherited* label.
- **Inherited tags are read-only.** They change when you change the
  Automaton's tags, not on the session. The session editor never sends them.
- **Edit a session's own tags.** Open the session and choose **Tags → This
  session → Edit tags of this session** in the header (see
  [the header Tags dropdown](#the-header-tags-dropdown)). The session detail
  itself shows only the session's tag chips, with inherited ones marked
  read-only; it has no edit control of its own. Tick the tags and press **Save**.
  The editor lists every tag and names the inherited ones below the list. If
  the server refuses a tag, the toast shows its reason.
- **Start a session with tags.** The New Session form has a **Tags
  (optional)** picker; the ticked tags are sent with the start request.
  The picker is hidden when you start from a project profile.
- **Bulk tag.** Press the select button on the sessions list, tick finished
  sessions and press **Tag** in the bar. The picked tags are added to every
  selected session and the tags each already has are kept.
- **Counts.** A session counts under a tag through its own tags **and** through
  the tags it inherits from its Automaton, so the session totals in the tag tree
  include both.

A tag renamed, recolored, deleted or assigned elsewhere updates the chips
on its own; no reload is needed.

chunks.heading: 8. The two refused deletes
chunks.body:
### 8. The two refused deletes

Deleting a tag is refused, with nothing changed, when:

1. **It still has child tags.** Move the children to another parent or
   delete them first. The REST response is `409` and the UI shows
   *Tag has child tags — move or delete them first*.
2. **It is still in use.** The refusal carries a `count` of the Automata and
   sessions that carry the tag (the UI shows *Tag is used by N Automata —
   unassign it first*, and the count includes sessions). Remove the tag from
   them, then delete it.

A third refusal protects the tree: moving a tag under itself or under one
of its own sub-tags is rejected as a cycle.

chunks.heading: Settings
chunks.body:
## Settings

Six keys under `autonomous.tags` control the tag browser. Each one is set the
same way from every channel, and an invalid value is refused on every channel
with the same message, with nothing written.

| Setting | Values | Default | PWA field |
|---|---|---|---|
| `autonomous.tags.default_view` | `auto`, `attention`, `tags` | `auto` | Settings → General → Automata → Tag browser: *Default view* |
| `autonomous.tags.attention_statuses` | a comma list of Automaton statuses | `blocked, needs_review, paused` | *Attention statuses* |
| `autonomous.tags.default_match_mode` | `any`, `all` | `any` | *Default tag match mode* |
| `autonomous.tags.direct_counts_visible` | `true`, `false` | `false` | *Show the direct count as a tooltip* |
| `autonomous.tags.registry_keeper` | a federation peer name, or empty | empty (standalone) | *Tag registry keeper* |
| `autonomous.tags.registry_sync_seconds` | whole seconds, minimum 5 | `30` | *Tag registry sync interval* |

The five ways to set any of them at runtime:

| Method | How |
|---|---|
| **REST** | `PUT /api/config` with `{"autonomous.tags.default_view": "attention"}`; read back with `GET /api/config`, under `autonomous.tags` |
| **PWA** | Settings → General → Automata → **Tag browser** group |
| **CLI** | `datawatch config set autonomous.tags.default_view attention`; read with `datawatch config get autonomous.tags.default_view` |
| **MCP** | `config_set` with the key `autonomous.tags.default_view` (the MCP server needs `mcp.allow_self_config=true`) |
| **Comm channel** | `configure autonomous.tags.default_view=attention` |

The YAML file takes the same keys under `autonomous.tags:`; the annotated
template is in [config-reference](../config-reference.yaml). Changes apply
without a restart.

## Same thing from every other surface

| Task | REST | MCP | CLI (`datawatch autonomous …`) | Comm channel (`autonomous …`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| List the tag tree | `GET /api/autonomous/tags[?include_sub=true&counts=true]` | `autonomous_tag_list` (`include_sub`, `counts`) | `tag-list [--include-sub] [--counts]` (alias `tags`) | `tags [counts]` |
| Create | `POST /api/autonomous/tags` | `autonomous_tag_create` | `tag-create <name> [--parent <id>] [--color <hex>]` | `tag-create <name> [parent=<id>] [color=<hex>]` |
| Rename | `PATCH /api/autonomous/tags/{id}` | `autonomous_tag_rename` | `tag-rename <id> <new-name>` | `tag-rename <id> <new-name>` |
| Move | `PATCH /api/autonomous/tags/{id}` (`parent_id`) | `autonomous_tag_set_parent` | `tag-move <id> --parent <id\|root>` | `tag-move <id> <parent-id\|root>` |
| Color | `PATCH /api/autonomous/tags/{id}` | `autonomous_tag_set_color` | `tag-color <id> <color>` | `tag-color <id> <color>` |
| Delete | `DELETE /api/autonomous/tags/{id}` | `autonomous_tag_delete` | `tag-delete <id>` | `tag-delete <id>` |
| Set an Automaton's tags | `POST /api/autonomous/prds/{id}/set_tags` | `autonomous_prd_set_tags` | `prd-set-tags <prd-id> --tags <id1,id2>` | `set-tags <prd-id> <id1,id2>` |
| Set an Automaton's primary tag | `POST /api/autonomous/prds/{id}/set_tags` (`primary_tag_id`) | `autonomous_prd_set_tags` (`primary_tag_id`) | `prd-set-tags <prd-id> --primary <tag-id>` | `set-primary <prd-id> <tag-id\|none>` |
| The attention group | `GET /api/autonomous/attention` | `autonomous_attention_list` | `attention` | `attention` |
| A session's own tags | `POST /api/sessions/tags` (`{id, tag_ids}`) | `session_set_tags` | `session tags <session-id> --tags <id1,id2>` | `session-tags <session-id> <id1,id2>` |
| List Automata under a tag | `GET /api/autonomous/prds?tag=<id>[&include_sub=false]` | — | — | — |

An empty tag list clears an Automaton's or a session's own tags.

chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Delete refused with a count.** Unassign the tag from those Automata and
  sessions first (`set_tags`, or `session_set_tags` for a session), then delete.
- **Expecting a tag to hide an Automaton.** A primary tag only sorts. Membership
  comes from the tag set.
- **Selecting a second tag and getting more results.** That is ANY, the default.
  Press the match-mode control for ALL.
- **Inherited tags on a session do not change.** Change the Automaton's tags
  instead.
- **`include_sub` defaults differ.** The Automata-by-tag route includes sub-tags
  by default (`include_sub=false` turns it off). The plain tag list
  (`GET /api/autonomous/tags`, `autonomous_tag_list`) counts only exact tags unless
  you ask for `include_sub`. The tag browser always rolls up sub-tags.
- **Tags across daemons.** Tags are federated only when the daemons share a
  registry (`autonomous.tags.registry_keeper`). Otherwise each daemon has its own
  tags; see [automata-tag-registry](automata-tag-registry.md).

chunks.title: How-to: Automation chains
chunks.heading: 1. What an Automation is
chunks.body:
## 1. What an Automation is

An **Automation** is a named chain of Automatons. An **Automaton** is one unit
of work: a goal that is decomposed, approved, run and verified. An Automation
does not do the work itself. It decides which Automaton runs next, using one
edge per outcome on every member: `on_complete`, `on_blocked` and `on_failed`.
An empty edge means "stop here"; the Automation then becomes `blocked` and an
alert is raised.

Once an Automation is **active**, datawatch starts the next Automaton by
itself, with no chat session or operator call in between. Members can also be
a **fork** and **join** (run branches in parallel) or another Automation
(nesting). The lifecycle is `draft → active → paused → completed / blocked /
cancelled`. The hand-off itself is described in
[automation-queue-advance.md](automation-queue-advance.md).

Base requirements: a daemon with `autonomous.enabled: true`, and approved
Automatons that no other Automation owns.

Read what exists first:

```bash
datawatch automation list
datawatch automation get <id>
```

MCP: `automation_list`, `automation_get`. REST: `GET /api/automations`,
`GET /api/automations/{id}`.

chunks.heading: 2. Create a chain of three Automatons
chunks.body:
## 2. Create a chain of three Automatons

Members go in as a JSON array, inline or as a file path. Each member has an
`id`, the `prd_id` of its Automaton, and its edges. Here A leads to B leads to
C:

```bash
datawatch automation create --name nightly \
  --entry-member a \
  --members '[
    {"id":"a","prd_id":"<automaton-1>","on_complete":"b","added_reason":"build"},
    {"id":"b","prd_id":"<automaton-2>","on_complete":"c","added_reason":"test"},
    {"id":"c","prd_id":"<automaton-3>","added_reason":"publish"}
  ]'
datawatch automation activate <id>
```

MCP: `automation_create` (`name`, `entry_member_id`, `members`), then
`automation_activate`. REST: `POST /api/automations`, then
`POST /api/automations/{id}/activate`. The Automation stays a draft, and does
nothing, until you activate it. Activation validates the whole graph (unknown
members, cycles, ownership) and refuses with the reason when it is wrong.

To route a failure somewhere else, add `on_blocked` or `on_failed` pointing at
a fix-up member, for example `"on_failed":"fixup"`. You can change a draft with
`datawatch automation update <id> --members <file>`.

chunks.heading: 3. Fork and join
chunks.body:
## 3. Fork and join

A **fork** starts several branch members together. A **join** waits for those
same branches, then continues. This diamond runs `left` and `right` in
parallel between `start` and `finish`:

```bash
datawatch automation create --name diamond --entry-member start --members '[
  {"id":"start","prd_id":"<automaton-1>","on_complete":"split"},
  {"id":"split","kind":"fork","fork_members":["left","right"]},
  {"id":"left","prd_id":"<automaton-2>","on_complete":"merge"},
  {"id":"right","prd_id":"<automaton-3>","on_complete":"merge"},
  {"id":"merge","kind":"join","join_members":["left","right"],
   "on_branch_failure":"all_must_succeed","on_complete":"finish"},
  {"id":"finish","prd_id":"<automaton-4>"}
]'
```

A fork needs at least two branches, and the join's `join_members` must equal
the paired fork's `fork_members`. Set only the fields that belong to a
member's kind. `on_branch_failure` on the join decides what a failed branch
means:

| Choice | Result |
|---|---|
| `all_must_succeed` (default) | Every branch must complete; one failure is a failure of the join |
| `any_one_is_enough` | The join passes as soon as one branch completes |
| `continue_anyway` | The join passes once all branches have finished, whatever their outcome |

While branches run, the Automation has several active cursors. Pause, resume
and cancel act on the whole Automation; skip and edge edits name one member.
Same call over MCP: `automation_create` with the same `members` array.

chunks.heading: 4. Nest an Automation inside another
chunks.body:
## 4. Nest an Automation inside another

A member with `kind` `automation` runs a whole child Automation as one step of
the parent. Create the child first, then name it with `automation_id`:

```bash
datawatch automation create --name release-checks --entry-member x --members '[...]'
datawatch automation create --name release --entry-member build --members '[
  {"id":"build","prd_id":"<automaton-1>","on_complete":"checks"},
  {"id":"checks","kind":"automation","automation_id":"<child-id>","on_complete":"ship"},
  {"id":"ship","prd_id":"<automaton-2>"}
]'
```

The child completes, is blocked or fails like any member, and the matching
edge on the parent member is followed. A child can be nested by only one
unfinished parent, and an Automation cannot reach itself through its
children; activation refuses either with the reason. MCP: `automation_create`.
REST: `POST /api/automations`.

chunks.heading: 5. Budget
chunks.body:
## 5. Budget

A budget policy caps the spend of one Automation, or of one member, with a
ceiling narrower than any global one. The tightest ceiling always wins; a
policy never widens a global limit.

```bash
datawatch automation set-budget <id> \
  --ceiling-type dollar --ceiling-value 40 --window week \
  --pacing even --on-breach pause --reset-weekday monday --reset-time 00:00
datawatch automation set-budget <id> --member b --estimated-cost-usd 6
datawatch automation set-budget <id> --clear
```

MCP: `automation_set_budget`. REST: `POST /api/automations/{id}/set_budget`.
`--window` is `automation` (lifetime), `day`, `week` or `month`;
`--ceiling-type` is `dollar` or `allocation_pct` (an estimate only).
`--pacing even` holds spend to the share of the ceiling that matches the
elapsed part of the window.

On a breach, `--on-breach` chooses the response, and an alert is raised either
way:

- **pause** (default): the Automation becomes `paused`. Where the reset time is
  known (a day, week or month window, or a reset time read from a rate-limit
  message) it resumes by itself at the reset. If the reset time is not known it
  waits for you.
- **block**: the Automation becomes `blocked` and never resumes by itself. You
  raise the ceiling or clear the policy, then resume.

chunks.heading: 6. Control operations
chunks.body:
## 6. Control operations

Every control call is checked against the Automation's current `version`
(CLI: `--expected-version`). Left out, the CLI reads the Automation's
current version first and uses it, retrying the call once if the version
moved in between. A `--expected-version` you supply yourself is sent as is,
and a stale one is still refused with HTTP 409 either way. `--actor` and
`--reason` are recorded in the audit trail.

| Operation | CLI | MCP | REST (`/api/automations/{id}/...`) | Allowed when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pause | `automation pause <id>` | `automation_pause` | `pause` | Active. Running members finish; nothing new starts |
| Resume | `automation resume <id>` | `automation_resume` | `resume` | Paused or blocked |
| Skip | `automation skip <id> <member> --edge on_complete` | `automation_skip_member` | `skip_member` | The member is stuck or not started; follows the edge you choose |
| Insert | `automation insert <id> <automaton> --reason "..." [--urgent] [--after <member>]` | `automation_insert_member` | `insert_member` | Not finished; a reason is required; one urgent insert at a time |
| Remove | `automation remove <id> <member>` | `automation_remove_member` | `remove_member` | The member has not started |
| Reorder edges | `automation edges <id> <member> --on-complete <m> --on-blocked <m> --on-failed <m>` | `automation_reorder_edges` | `reorder_edges` | The member has not started, or is the running member (its own outgoing edges) |
| Cancel | `automation cancel <id> --cancel-in-flight true\|false` | `automation_cancel` | `cancel` | Draft, active, paused or blocked |

`edges` rewrites all three edges: one you leave out becomes "stop", so name
every edge you want to keep. A member that has already completed, been
blocked or been skipped is history and cannot be removed or rewired.

**Cancel makes you choose.** `--cancel-in-flight` has no default. `true` ends
the sessions of members running now; `false` lets them finish while nothing
new starts. Cancelling cannot be undone, so the call is refused without the
choice.

```bash
datawatch automation pause <id> --reason "deploy freeze"
datawatch automation skip <id> b --edge on_failed --reason "known flaky"
datawatch automation insert <id> <automaton> --urgent --reason "hotfix first"
datawatch automation cancel <id> --cancel-in-flight false
```

An insert made by an agent can be held for your approval. `datawatch
automation get` and `datawatch automation status` list each pending insert
with its member id, its `prd_id`, and the reason it was held, and show the
command that approves it —
`datawatch automation approve <automation id> <member id>`
(MCP `automation_approve_insert`).

chunks.heading: 8. Move from an old orchestrator graph
chunks.body:
## 8. Move from an old orchestrator graph

An orchestrator graph can be turned into a draft Automation. Always preview
first; `--dry-run` stores nothing and prints the Automation that would be
created, plus any warnings:

```bash
datawatch automation import-graph <graph-id> --dry-run
datawatch automation import-graph <graph-id>      # prints the new Automation ID
```

MCP: `automation_import_graph` with `graph_id` and `dry_run`. REST:
`POST /api/automations/import-graph/{graph_id}` with `{"dry_run": true}`.
Automaton nodes become members, fan-out and fan-in become a paired fork and
join, and guardrail nodes are dropped with one warning each (per-Automaton
guardrails cover them now).

A graph that an Automation cannot express is **refused** with the reason and
a non-zero exit (HTTP 422), because guessing would change what runs. That
covers a node with an empty or duplicate ID, an unknown node kind, a node that
depends on an unknown node, an Automaton node with no Automaton ID, a graph
with no Automaton nodes, a graph in several disconnected pieces (import each
separately), and a shape that cannot be placed in a chain.

The source graph is only read. It is **never deleted or changed**, so it keeps
working beside the new draft. Review the draft, activate it, and retire the
graph yourself when you are satisfied.

# How-to: The Automation decision assistant

The **decision assistant** is an optional, off-by-default setting that lets an
Automation (or one of its members) hand a bounded judgment call to a configured
local model instead of a hardcoded default or an operator stop. It picks among
options the Automation already allows. It never widens them.

chunks.heading: 2. Where it can decide: the four hook points
chunks.body:
## 2. Where it can decide: the four hook points

Each hook point is enabled on its own. A hook that is not listed never consults
the model.

| Hook | Question put to the assistant | Options it can pick |
|---|---|---|
| `empty_edge` | A member blocked or failed and has no edge for that outcome. Stop, as today? | pause the Automation, skip along an existing edge, or "needs the operator" |
| `skip_member` | A member is stuck. Should it be skipped? | skip along an existing edge, or keep waiting |
| `insert_member` | A corrective member would help. Insert one? | insert a named Automaton, or do nothing |
| `budget_breach` | The budget ceiling was hit. Pause or block? | `pause` or `block`, whichever the budget policy already allows |

It reads a bounded evidence packet (failure reason, verdict, progress, spend),
with every text field cut to a fixed size.

## 3. Turn it on

Set it on the whole Automation, or on one member with `--member`. A member's
setting wins over the Automation's. The flags replace the whole setting.

```bash
datawatch automation set-decision-assistant <id> \
  --backend ollama --model <model> \
  --hooks empty_edge,skip_member

`POST /api/automations/{id}/set_decision_assistant`, and the chat verb
`automation set-decision-assistant <id> backend=<b> model=<m> hooks=<a,b>`.
It is allowed while the Automation is draft, active, paused or blocked.

Turn it off again with `--clear` (or an empty backend).

## 5. Start in shadow mode

`--mode` is `shadow` by default. In shadow mode the assistant is asked, and what
it **would have** done is recorded, but the Automation behaves exactly as it
did without it. Run in shadow until the recorded decisions match what you would
have chosen, then switch:

datawatch automation set-decision-assistant <id> \
  --backend ollama --model <model> --mode live \
  --hooks empty_edge,skip_member
```

In `live` mode a decision at or above the hook's threshold is acted on.

## 6. Thresholds and conservative defaults

Each hook has its own confidence threshold. Below it the assistant must
escalate rather than decide.

| Hook | Default threshold |
|---|---|
| `empty_edge` | 0.9 |
| `skip_member` | 0.9 |
| `insert_member` | 0.9 |
| `budget_breach` | 0.95 |

Override one with a number in (0, 1]; for example `--threshold skip_member=0.97`
(repeatable). A hook without an override keeps its default.

chunks.heading: 7. Read assistant decisions in history
chunks.body:
## 7. Read assistant decisions in history

Every assistant outcome is a normal decision entry in the Automation's history
and a normal audit record, with the actor `assistant:<model>`. It reads the same
as an operator decision. Each note carries the hook, the outcome, the option,
the confidence, a short evidence line and the model's reason.

- **Web:** open the Automation. The detail view shows the setting (backend,
  model, mode, hooks, thresholds), an edit control, and the history. A shadow

  confidence and evidence.

chunks.title: Lane fill
chunks.body:
# Lane fill

**Lane fill** is the daemon's own check that every execution lane stays busy.
Before it, a person had to notice that a lane was idle and start the next
queued Automaton by hand. Now, on every poll, the planner looks at the lanes
and the queue and decides what each idle lane should take. In the default
**shadow** mode it only records those decisions. In **on** mode it starts the
work it has decided on, through the same start path a person uses.

chunks.title: Lane fill
chunks.heading: The lanes
chunks.body:
## The lanes

| Lane | What it is | Default count | Backend it runs |
|---|---|---|---|
| GPU lane | A channel on the local model pool. Two machines can share one pool, and which machine serves a given session is not fixed per lane. A GPU lane costs no Claude usage. | 2 | `pi-prompt` by default (`gpu_backend`), with the model in `gpu_model` |
| Claude lane | A channel that runs one Automaton at a time on the Claude backend. | 3 (0 means none) | `claude-code` (`claude_backend`) |

A lane is **occupied** when an Automaton is running on it, or when a session is
using the GPU pool that belongs to no Automaton. A lane is **idle** otherwise.
An idle lane with nothing it can take shows a **blocker**: the reason the lane
must not be called idle or the reason no eligible work fits it.

chunks.title: Lane fill
chunks.heading: The three modes
chunks.body:
## The three modes

| Mode | What the planner does | Starts anything? |
|---|---|---|
| `off` | Does not run. Records nothing. | No |
| `shadow` (default) | Runs on every poll. Records every decision it would make, with its inputs and the pool evidence it used. | No |
| `on` | Runs on every poll and carries out the decisions. | Yes |

**Why shadow comes first.** The rules for what counts as eligible and which
lane suits which work are decisions for the operator. Shadow mode lets you check
those rules against what the supervisor actually did, for about a day, before
the daemon acts on them. A decision recorded in shadow mode shows
`executed: false`. Clients must show it as "would start", not "started".

Switching mode takes effect on the next poll. No restart is needed.

chunks.heading: Reading the status
chunks.body:
## Reading the status

The status shows the same facts on every surface:

- the mode, and when the last poll ran;
- each lane, with its type, whether it is occupied or idle, its occupant (the
  Automaton title and backend) or its blocker;
- the eligible work queued for each lane type (GPU and Claude);
- the pool evidence: how many sessions are using the GPU pool, which models are
  loaded on the pool hosts, or the error if a host could not be read;
- the newest decisions, newest first, each with its action (`start_prd`,
  `decompose`, `decompose_ahead`, `report_merge`, `blocked` or `idle`; the PWA and
  the comm reply show them as plain words), its reason, whether it was executed,
  and any error;
- the recent idle-lane alerts.

| Surface | How |
|---|---|
| REST | `GET /api/autonomous/lane-fill?limit=50` (`limit` is a whole number from 1 to 1000; default 50) |
| MCP | `autonomous_lane_fill_status` with an optional `limit` |
| CLI | `datawatch autonomous lane-fill [--limit N] [--json]` (`--json` prints the REST body unchanged) |
| Comm channel | `autonomous lane-fill [limit]`: one line per lane, the queued counts and the newest five decisions |
| PWA | Automata tab, **Automation** sub-tab: the **Lane fill** card sits beside the capacity card. It reloads on its own every five seconds. |

An example from the CLI:

```bash
datawatch autonomous lane-fill --limit 20
```

chunks.title: Lane fill
chunks.heading: Setting a lane preference
chunks.body:
## Setting a lane preference

Every Automaton has a **lane preference**:

- `gpu`: it may take only a GPU lane;
- `claude`: it may take only a Claude lane;
- `any`: it may take whichever lane type is idle. This is the default.

The planner honours `gpu` and `claude` exactly. It never reads a spec and
decides that the work is hard or easy, or needs design. Choosing a preference
is a decision for a person, and it is recorded on the Automaton.

| Surface | How |
|---|---|
| REST | `POST /api/autonomous/prds/{id}/set_lane_preference` with `{"lane_preference": "gpu" \| "claude" \| "any"}` |
| MCP | `autonomous_prd_set_lane_preference` with `id` and `lane_preference`; an empty value means `any` |
| CLI | `datawatch autonomous prd-set-lane-preference <id> gpu\|claude\|any` |
| Comm channel | `autonomous set-lane-preference <automaton-id> gpu\|claude\|any` |
| PWA | The **Lane preference** select in the Automaton settings form. An Automaton with nothing stored shows **Any lane**. |

A value other than the three above is refused. The CLI and the comm channel refuse
it before they send anything, and the daemon answers 400 to any other caller. The
preference only affects which lane the planner picks. It does not change the
Automaton's status or its plan.

## Setting the lane fill options

| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `autonomous.lane_fill.mode` | `shadow` | `off`, `shadow` or `on` |
| `autonomous.lane_fill.gpu_lanes` | `2` | How many GPU lanes exist |
| `autonomous.lane_fill.claude_lanes` | `3` | How many Claude lanes exist; `0` means none |
| `autonomous.lane_fill.idle_alert_minutes` | `30` | How long a lane may sit idle with eligible work waiting before an alert; `0` turns the alert off |
| `autonomous.lane_fill.decompose_ahead_min` | `2` | The minimum number of decomposed Automata kept ready per lane type |
| `autonomous.lane_fill.poll_seconds` | `60` | Seconds between planner polls; a value below 5 is raised to 5 |
| `autonomous.lane_fill.gpu_backend` | `pi-prompt` | The backend the GPU lanes run |
| `autonomous.lane_fill.gpu_model` | empty | The model the GPU lanes run; empty means the backend's own model |
| `autonomous.lane_fill.claude_backend` | `claude-code` | The backend the Claude lanes run |

Every key is settable at runtime with no restart:

| Channel | How |
|---|---|
| Config file | the `autonomous.lane_fill` block in `config.yaml` |
| CLI | `datawatch config set autonomous.lane_fill.mode shadow` |
