chunks.title: Lane fill
chunks.heading: The day-long shadow comparison
chunks.body:
## The day-long shadow comparison

Run shadow mode for about one day while the supervisor still fills lanes by
hand. Then compare:

1. **Start on the default mode.** Confirm the status shows `mode: shadow`. Each
   poll adds decisions; none show `executed: true`.
2. **Read the status at the end of the day.** Use `--limit 1000`, the largest
   the status returns, so the whole day is in view:

   ```bash
   datawatch autonomous lane-fill --limit 1000 --json > lane-fill-day.json
   ```

   Keep the file outside the repository.
3. **Compare each `start` and `decompose ahead` decision** with what the
   supervisor did in the same window: which Automaton went to which lane, and
   when.
4. **List the differences**: decisions the supervisor did not make; supervisor
   starts the planner did not propose; lanes the planner called idle while the
   supervisor had a reason to leave them that way; and any decision that named a
   held or sequenced Automaton.
5. **Check the criteria before switching**:
   - no decision named a held or sequenced Automaton;
   - every difference is explained, and either accepted or fixed;
   - the pool evidence never reported a busy pool as idle, and an unreadable
     host always appeared as an error or a blocker, never as an idle lane;
   - the idle alert fired only when a lane was idle with eligible work waiting;
   - the operator has answered the open questions on switching (below).

If any criterion fails, stay in shadow mode, fix the cause, and run another day.

chunks.title: Lane fill
chunks.heading: Switching to on
chunks.body:
## Switching to on

Once the criteria pass, set the mode:

```bash
datawatch config set autonomous.lane_fill.mode on
```

The change takes effect on the next poll. To go back, set it to `shadow` or
`off`; no restart is needed either way. `off` stops the planner. Work already
running keeps running.

In `on` mode, each decision goes through the existing start path:

- A **start** sets the Automaton's worker backend to the lane's backend, if the
  Automaton's current status allows that change. It approves the Automaton if
  it still awaits review, using the same approve call a person would make. The
  plan-coverage gate and the plan-review gate still apply to that approval. A
  refused approval is recorded on the decision. Then it runs the
  Automaton through the normal admission path, so capacity limits, quality gates
  and the stuck-task rules apply exactly as they do to a manual start.
- A **decompose** or **decompose ahead** starts a decomposition of a draft in the
  background, with the planning settings the draft already has, so a poll does
  not wait for it. A failed decomposition is recorded on the decision.
- A **report merge** is recorded and nothing else. Lane fill never merges.
- A **blocked** or **idle** decision is recorded only.

A failed start is recorded with its error. It is tried again no sooner than five
minutes later, not on every poll.

Before switching, the operator should have answered these:

- Whether the routing pattern list in the plan (`docs/plans/2026-10-24-lane-fill-shadow-mode.md`)
  is confirmed or amended.
- Whether `on` mode may approve a review-pending Automaton through the approve
  call, as it does now, or may start only Automata that are already approved.
- The default Claude lane count and the default idle alert minutes.
- Whether an Automaton on a backend that is neither the GPU backend nor the
  Claude backend counts toward lane occupancy.

chunks.heading: The idle alert

## The idle alert

When a lane has sat idle for longer than `idle_alert_minutes` while eligible
work waits for it, lane fill raises one alert:

- it names the lane, how long the lane has been idle, and the first eligible
  Automaton it could have started;
- it is raised once per idle period, not on every poll;
- it clears when the lane takes work, so a later idle period alerts again;
- it goes through the normal alert path, at warning level, and is listed in the
  status under the idle lane alerts.

`idle_alert_minutes: 0` turns the alert off. The alert is read live, so a change
needs no restart.

chunks.title: Lane fill
chunks.heading: Restart behaviour
chunks.body:
## Restart behaviour

- **Decision history survives a restart.** The decisions are kept, up to 1000,
  in a file beside the other autonomous stores.
- **Nothing is decided before boot recovery has finished.** Automata that were
  running before the restart are not read as idle lanes.
- **An Automaton that was started is never started twice.** Lane fill remembers
  the starts it made until the store shows the Automaton as running, so the next
  poll neither starts it again nor reads its lane as idle. An Automaton started
  before the restart already shows as running in the store, so it is left alone.
- **Idle timers begin again.** The idle alert counts from the restart, so a lane
  that was idle before the restart alerts after the full threshold, not earlier.
- **Mode and thresholds are read live.** A changed mode or threshold applies on
  the next poll with no restart.

chunks.title: Lane fill
chunks.heading: What lane fill never does
chunks.body:
## What lane fill never does

- **It never merges.** Finished work that needs a merge is reported, and merging
  stays a supervisor or operator act.
- **It never judges design or difficulty.** It starts an Automaton only from its
  lane preference, its status, its priority and its age.
- **It never holds GPU work because of Claude usage limits.** GPU lanes cost no
  Claude usage. Claude usage limits and budget pace are not inputs to the
  planner, so they never keep a GPU lane idle. The existing admission path still
  applies its own rules to a Claude-lane start.
- **It never starts a held Automaton.** A held Automaton is one whose spec has a
  line starting with `HOLD`, says "do not run" or "sequenced last", or is
  "sequenced after" an Automaton that has not completed. Held work is listed
  with its reason and is never silently dropped.
- **It never bypasses the normal start rules.** Lane fill adds no second way to
  start work. Admission, approval gates, quality gates and the stuck-task rules
  all still run.
- **It never moves work onto a lane it cannot run.** A GPU lane takes an
  Automaton only when its backend is already the GPU backend, or when its status
  still allows the backend to change.
- **It never acts in shadow mode.** Shadow mode starts nothing and approves
  nothing.

chunks.title: Automation queue advance
chunks.heading: Walkthrough: activate → advance → idle alert
chunks.body:
## Walkthrough: activate → advance → idle alert

1. **Create** a draft Automation `nightly` with members A then B (A's
   `on_complete` points at B). A draft does nothing.
2. **Activate** it. The entry member (A) is validated and started through the
   normal approval gate:

   ```
   datawatch automation activate <id>
   ```

   The Automation becomes `active` and A is `running`. If A is not approved, the
   Automation becomes `blocked` with the reason and an alert is raised.
3. **Advance.** When A completes, the coordinator takes A's `on_complete` edge
   and starts B. Watch it in the status array:

   ```
   curl -s $BASE/api/autonomous/status | jq .automations
   ```

   Each row shows the current member and Automaton, pending members, idle time
   and any blocked reason. A duplicate or racing completion event starts B once.
4. **Blocked.** If B is not approved when its turn comes, the Automation becomes
   `blocked` and you get a "Automation blocked" alert naming the reason.
   Approve B so it is ready; the Automation stays blocked until a later release
   adds the pause, resume and skip controls. A paused B is resumed automatically
   when its turn comes. An empty edge (for example A is blocked and has no
   `on_blocked` target) also blocks the Automation.
5. **Idle alert.** With `idle_alert_minutes: 30`, if an active Automation has no
   member running for 30 minutes, one "Automation idle" alert is raised for that
   idle episode. When a member starts again the episode ends; a later idle spell
   alerts again.
6. **Finish.** When the last member completes, the Automation is `completed`,
   an info alert is raised and its members are free to join another Automation.

If the daemon restarts mid-chain, it reconciles once its normal resume has
finished: a member that finished while the daemon was down advances the chain, a
member still running is left alone, and a start that had not happened yet is
retried without starting it twice. A **failed** member is not advanced on the
live event; it waits for the restart-time recovery, so a restart that kills a
task never routes the chain by mistake.

chunks.title: Automation queue advance
chunks.heading: Give an Automation its own model defaults
chunks.body:
## Give an Automation its own model defaults

By default every member Automaton runs and is verified on the daemon's global
backend and model. If a whole chain should use something else, for example a
stronger model for a risky nightly job, set the defaults once on the
Automation instead of editing each Automaton.

The Automation's defaults sit between the Automaton and the global default.
For the execution backend, model and effort, and for the verification LLM,
the first level that sets a value wins: task, then story, then Automaton, then
Automation, then global. Backend and model are taken from the same level;
effort is resolved on its own. So an Automaton or task that names its own
backend keeps it, and the Automation default only fills what they leave open.

1. **Set the execution default** (while the Automation is draft, active,
   paused or blocked):

   ```bash
   datawatch automation set-llm <id> --backend claude-code --model claude-opus-5-5 --effort high
   ```

   Chat: `automation set-llm <id> backend=claude-code model=claude-opus-5-5 effort=high`.
   REST: `POST /api/automations/{id}/set_llm` with the same names in the body.
   MCP: `automation_set_llm`.

2. **Set the verification default** the same way:

   ```bash
   datawatch automation set-verification-llm <id> --backend claude-code --model claude-sonnet-5-5
   ```

3. **Optionally pick a planner.** `--planning-backend` and `--planning-model`
   on `set-llm` choose the LLM that decomposes a member into stories and tasks.
   Leave them unset and the global planning backend is used. They only affect
   decomposing; they never change which LLM runs or verifies the work.

4. **Clear a field** by sending it empty, for example `--model ""` or `model=`
   in chat. A field you leave out is kept as it is. Name at least one field.

`expected_version` is optional on both operations: leave it out (or send `0`)
to skip the check, or send the version you read to be told with a 409 if
someone else changed the Automation first.

A change applies to members that start afterwards; a task already running is
not touched. To see which level supplied the backend for a task, read its
`executor_source` (and, after verification, `verifier_source`), which can be
`task`, `story`, `prd`, `automation`, `global` (or `pool` for the verifier).
The PWA shows `executor_source` as an **Executor** line on the task and on the
session status card; there is no Automation view in the PWA yet, so setting the
defaults is API, MCP, CLI and chat only for now.

chunks.title: Repo CI watch
chunks.body:
# Repo CI watch

The **repo CI watch** is the daemon's standing watch over your repository's CI. On
every poll it looks at the head of `main` and the newest release tags across
**every workflow** in the repository you listed, keeps one record per CI run,
classifies each one, and — in `on` mode — takes the small, budgeted set of
actions it is allowed to take: one rerun of an infra-broken run, one cancel of
a run that hung, and the retention cleanup of runs that were superseded.

It is off by default (`mode: off`). The middle mode, **shadow**, is the
comparison mode: the pass runs, classifies, and records every action it *would*
take as explicit `would-do` lines — but writes nothing, cancels nothing and
alerts nothing. You read those would-dos next to what you (or the supervisor
loop) actually did for the same runs, and only switch to `on` once the two
agree over several episodes.

chunks.heading: What the watch sees
chunks.body:
## What the watch sees

For each repository in `repos`, one poll reads:

| What | How | Default |
|---|---|---|
| The head of `main` | `git rev-parse origin/main` (or the default branch) and then the CI runs on that SHA | always, for listed repos |
| The newest release tags | the newest `tag_count` tags in the repository, each of the shape `v\u003cmajor\u003e.\u003cminor\u003e.\u003cpatch\u003e` (`v2` does not count as a release tag) | 5 (0 = no tags) |

For every one of those refs the pass lists the runs on that ref's head commit — every workflow that ran on that SHA — not a fixed workflow name. So a poll covers the head of `main` plus the newest `tag_count` release tags, each across every workflow that ran there. A run belongs to the (repository, ref, workflow) triple it ran on, and each one gets at most one watch record.

chunks.title: Repo CI watch
chunks.heading: The record states
chunks.body:
## The record states

Each record keeps one watch state. The pass records four of them — `green`, `failing`, `pending` and `hung` — and the read view's status filter accepts all six vocabulary values, so it can also filter on the two records the pass marks — `rerunning` (its own rerun is recorded on the record's rerun log) and `superseded` (a later green run names it in its `superseded_run_ids`); any other value is a 400 that names the allowed values.

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `green` | The run finished cleanly (success, skipped or neutral). For retention it still matters: when the ref moves on and a later run on the same ref/workflow goes green, this run is named **superseded** by the newer green record and becomes a retention-cleanup candidate. |
| `failing` | The run finished red (a failure conclusion or action-required) and carries the classification the pass reached for it. |
| `pending` | The run is still in flight. It is not `hung` until it has been in flight longer than `hung_after_minutes`. |
| `hung` | A `pending` run that outlived `hung_after_minutes` (default 60, minimum 1). In `on` mode it is cancelled once. |
| `rerunning` | Vocabulary value: the pass's rerun of this run was posted; the record's rerun log names it and the pass waits for the new attempt. |
| `superseded` | Vocabulary value: this run was preceded by a later run on the same ref/workflow, named on the green record that superseded it; it is a retention candidate, and the record keeps its run id so the pass can address it. |

chunks.title: Repo CI watch
chunks.heading: The classification and what each one means
chunks.body:
## The classification and what each one means

After a poll, the pass classifies every run. The classification is what decides what the pass may do with that run, and the value you read on every surface is one of seven:

| Classification | What it means | What the pass may do with it |
|---|---|---|
| `none` | Unclassified — the state a record carries until the pass classifies it, and the one a green or pending run stays at. | Nothing; it is the default, not a verdict. |
| `infra` | The run broke because of the CI infrastructure, not the code: it finished by cancellation, timeout, a pre-start failure, or staleness (a pipeline abort, not a red test). One automatic rerun is safe and expected. | In `on` mode, **one rerun** of the recorded run — at most once per run id — and only while the infra retry budget still has reruns left. In shadow mode the rerun is recorded as a would-do and never executed. |
| `security` | A run on a workflow named in `security_workflows` finished without a green or infra outcome (its conclusion is a failure or action-required). The default list is `CodeQL`, `dependency-review`, `owasp-zap`, `secret-scan`, `security-scan`. **Record-only by design.** | Nothing is rerun or acted on. The pass does not emit a would-rerun either — a security failure is information for the operator plus whatever the operator's own security process says to do, and the watch's job is to keep the record visible, not to touch it. |
| `policy` | A failed non-security run whose **judge verdict** is a policy-gate refusal (the pass spends at most one LLM judge call per poll, on the first non-green run it meets, and never re-judges a run that already carries a verdict). Like `security`, **record-only** — the watch does not rerun or waive it. | Nothing beyond the record. The operator's policy process owns the disposition. |
| `code_or_test` | A failed non-security run the judge cleared of policy: the verdict's other category, meaning the defect is in the code or the test and only the owner of the change can fix it. Not an infrastructure fault, not a policy gate. | Nothing automatic — no rerun, no cancel. The record and the alert name it so the owner can look. |
| `judging` | A failed non-security run the pass could not reach a verdict on in this poll — the pass's single judge call was already spent, or the judge call itself failed. **A pending state, not a verdict**: a later poll reuses the cached verdict if the run has one, or re-judges it. | Nothing; it settles to `policy` or `code_or_test` once a verdict exists. |
| `hung` | The run is in flight and outlived `hung_after_minutes`. | In `on` mode it is cancelled once. |

**Why `security` is record-only.** A failed security run is evidence, not a
flake. Rerunning it is a decision: it can legitimately rerun green (the finding
was real and the rerun hid it), or it can be re-baselined in a process the
watch does not own. The pass therefore never puts a security run in its
rerun queue — not in `on` mode, and not even as a would-do in shadow mode.
The record carries the classification and the run URL so the operator can see
exactly which security workflows are failing, on which ref, and for how long.
That is the whole contract. `policy` and `code_or_test` share the same shape: the
watch records the verdict and the run URL; the disposition belongs to the
policy process or the change owner.

chunks.title: Repo CI watch
chunks.heading: The alert
chunks.body:
## The alert

Once a run has been non-green — `failing`, `pending` or `hung` — for longer
than `alert_minutes` (default **30**; `0` turns the alert off), measured from
the run's first-seen stamp, the pass raises **exactly one alert per episode**.
The alert names the repository, the ref, the workflow, the run, its
classification, the first-seen stamp and the run URL — enough for one action
per line. The alert is stamped onto the record as `alerted_at`, which is what
makes it once-per-episode: a later pass that sees the same episode does not
re-alert, and the watch will not touch that run further until it is resolved,
superseded, or the budget changes.

The alert raises in `on` mode only — in `shadow` mode nothing is raised at
all: shadow records would-dos and never interrupts. Turning `alert_minutes`
to `0` turns the alert off in any mode (the reported threshold then reads 0).

chunks.heading: The automatic actions in `on` mode
chunks.body:
## The automatic actions in `on` mode

The pass takes three kinds of action, and only these three, and only in `on`
mode. Each one is budgeted or one-shot so the pass cannot loop:

| Action | When | How many times |
|---|---|---|
| **Infra rerun** | The record is classified `infra` and the infra retry budget — the Manager's `RetryPolicy["infra"]`, read as `0` when unset (no automatic reruns at all) — still has a rerun for that repository·ref·workflow. | One rerun per run id, shared across the repository·ref·workflow. A rerun that errors is not counted as spent — the record stays unresolved and the later pass may retry. A rerun whose new attempt is itself red is not re-re-run automatically: it needs the operator again, or a re-classification. |
| **Hung cancel** | The record is `pending` and older than `hung_after_minutes`. | Once per run id. The pass checks the run is not already cancelled before it posts the cancel, so a hung run that has already resolved is never cancelled twice. |
| **Superseded deletion** | The green record names the superseded runs in its `superseded_run_ids`. | One deletion per run, addressed by the run ID recorded on the record — not by re-deriving the ref, so a tag that moved on after the record was written does not break the delete. A run named by this very poll is deleted on the **later** pass, never on the pass that named it; and it is never rerun while it is a deletion candidate. See the deletion policy below. |

chunks.heading: The deletion policy (`delete_superseded`)
chunks.body:
### The deletion policy (`delete_superseded`)

| Value | What the pass does with superseded runs |
|---|---|
| `report` (default) | The pass names the superseded runs on the green record and stops there. Deleting is the operator's explicit act. This is the safe default: retention cleanup is a repository-management decision, and the pass should propose it, not make it. |
| `delete` | In addition to recording, the pass issues the deletion — but only in `on` mode, and the pass that names the runs does not also delete them: the deletion is picked up on the **later** pass, after the green record is durably written, so a crash between "decide" and "issue" costs nothing. In `shadow` mode `delete` behaves exactly like `report` — recording only, no deletion call. |

There is no `delete` that fires in `shadow`: shadow never issues any call that
changes state, and the deletion policy's `delete` value is not a write switch,
it is a declaration of what the pass is allowed to do once `mode` is `on`.

chunks.title: Repo CI watch
chunks.heading: Shadow mode — and how to compare it with the supervisor's actions
chunks.body:
## Shadow mode — and how to compare it with the supervisor's actions

**Shadow** is the mode you run first. On every poll the pass does everything
it would do in `on` mode, except the write:

- it polls the refs, classifies every run the same way an `on` pass would,
- it records the would-rerun for each `infra` run (with the budget it would
  spend), the would-cancel for each hung run, and the would-delete for each
  superseded run,
- it does **not** post a rerun, does **not** post a cancel, does **not** issue
  a deletion, and does **not** raise the alert.

Every would-do is written into the record in a form that names the action, the
target (repository, ref, workflow, run) and the policy that would have gated
it, so reading the record is reading the decision. The actor for every such
line is `repo_ci_watch`, explicitly, so a later read of the audit trail or the
read view cannot mistake a would-do for a did-do.

**The comparison you owe before `on`.** For a handful of episodes — one red
`main`, one hung run, one run you reran yourself, and one tag that got
superseded — put the two sides side by side:

1. **What the watch would have done.** Read the records for the episode (any
   surface below; the would-do lines are in the record body). Note the
   classification, the action, the budget it would have spent and the order.
2. **What actually happened.** The supervisor loop's actions for the same runs
   — the rerun it posted, the cancel it allowed, the tag it superseded — from
   the CI UI, the audit trail, or whatever process owned that work.
3. **Judge the three things that matter here** — classification (did the watch
   call `infra` what you called `infra`, and `security` what you called
   `security`? did a `code_or_test` verdict match what you saw?),
   budget (would the watch have rerun something you would have
   left alone, or left alone something you would have rerun?), and order
   (would the watch have cancelled a run you were still debugging, or rerun one
   you wanted to hold for evidence?).

When those agree over several episodes — including at least one `security`
episode you deliberately left alone, and one superseded run you deliberately
deleted or kept — `on` is a reasonable next step. When they disagree, the
disagreement is the finding: fix the policy (`security_workflows`,
`hung_after_minutes`, the infra retry budget) and re-shadow.

chunks.heading: Reading the state on every surface
chunks.body:
## Reading the state on every surface

The watch is readable from all five operator surfaces, all of them reads of
the same stored state (mode, threshold, repos, last poll, records newest
first). None of them changes anything.

| Surface | Read the state | Filter it |
|---|---|---|
| REST | `GET /api/autonomous/repo-ci-watch` | `?repo=<repository>` and/or `?status=<state>` (one of `green`, `failing`, `pending`, `hung`, `rerunning`, `superseded`; anything else is a 400 that names the allowed values; a filter that matches nothing is 200 with an empty list) |
| MCP | `autonomous_repo_ci_watch` (read-only, same body) | `repo` and `status` parameters, same vocabulary |
| CLI | `datawatch autonomous repo-ci-watch` (a table: repository, ref, workflow, status, classification, first seen, alerted) | `--repo <repository>`, `--status <state>`, `--json` for the unfiltered body |
| Comm channel | `autonomous repo-ci-watch` (alias `repo_ci_watch`) — the mode on the first line, then one line per record: repository, ref, workflow, status, classification, run URL | the read takes no arguments; to narrow, use the CLI, MCP or REST filters |
| PWA | Automata tab → the **Repo CI watch** status line on the tab: the mode in effect, the `failing` and `pending` counts, and how long ago the coordinator last polled — refreshed every 30 s, or immediately when the tab renders | the line itself is the summary; the full records are the REST/MCP/CLI reads |

chunks.title: Repo CI watch
chunks.heading: Configuration
chunks.body:
## Configuration

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `autonomous.automation.repo_ci_watch.mode` | `off` | `off` (the pass does not run and nothing is recorded), `shadow` (everything runs, nothing writes, no alert) or `on` (the actions above are taken, budgeted, and the alert raises). |
| `autonomous.automation.repo_ci_watch.repos` | empty | Comma-separated absolute paths of the repositories to watch. Empty means nothing is watched. |
| `autonomous.automation.repo_ci_watch.poll_seconds` | `300` (unset or `0` reads `300`) | Seconds between polls. Values below 60 are **refused on write** by every path — the minimum is 60; nothing is ever clamped up for you. |
| `autonomous.automation.repo_ci_watch.alert_minutes` | `30` | How long a non-green run may sit before the once-per-episode alert. `0` turns the alert off (in which case the reported threshold reads 0); negative values are refused. |
| `autonomous.automation.repo_ci_watch.tag_count` | `5` | How many of the newest release tags (shaped `v\u003cmajor\u003e.\u003cminor\u003e.\u003cpatch\u003e`) are covered per poll. `0` means no tags; negative values are refused. |
| `autonomous.automation.repo_ci_watch.hung_after_minutes` | `60` | How long a run may be `pending` before it is `hung`. Minimum 1; below that is refused. |
| `autonomous.automation.repo_ci_watch.security_workflows` | `CodeQL, dependency-review, owasp-zap, secret-scan, security-scan` | Workflow names that classify a non-green run as `security` (record-only). Empty list means nothing classifies as `security` — set it deliberately before turning `on`. |
| `autonomous.automation.repo_ci_watch.delete_superseded` | `report` | `report` (name the superseded runs, do not delete them) or `delete` (in `on` mode, the pass issues the deletion for the runs a green record names, on the later pass). |
| infra retry budget — the Manager's `RetryPolicy["infra"]` (`retry_policy.infra`) | unset reads `0` — no automatic reruns at all | The cap on automatic infra reruns shared per repository·ref·workflow. A budget of 0 means the pass never reruns an `infra` run; set it to allow one rerun per run id while it holds. |

Every key is read live from `config.yaml`. Changing `mode`, `poll_seconds`,
`alert_minutes`, `tag_count`, `hung_after_minutes`, `security_workflows` or
`delete_superseded` takes effect on the next poll — no restart. A bad value is
refused on write by every path — an unknown `mode`, a non-absolute repository
path, a `poll_seconds` below 60, a negative `alert_minutes` or `tag_count`, a
`hung_after_minutes` below 1 — and nothing is written. The `repos` list and
the classification vocabulary are read on every poll, so adding a repository
mid-episode starts being watched on the following pass, and removing one stops
it on the following pass without erasing its records (the records stay readable
on every surface).

chunks.title: Repo CI watch
chunks.heading: What the watch never does
chunks.body:
## What the watch never does

It never merges, never judges design or difficulty, and never holds or starts
Automata — the watch is about the repository's CI runs, not about the
Automation queue. It never reruns a `security` or `policy` run, in any mode,
and never as a `would-do`. It never posts a second cancel for a run that is
already resolving, and never spends infra budget on a run it named for
deletion. It never issues a deletion in `shadow`, in `off`, or in
`report` — and never a deletion on the same pass that named the run. It never
re-judges a run that already carries a verdict, and it never re-alerts an
episode that already alerted. It never spends retry budget it does not have —
a rerun that comes from a zero budget is not a rerun, it is the operator
deciding. And in `shadow` it never writes anything at all: the record and the
would-do text are the entire surface — no action, no alert.

chunks.title: Repo CI watch
chunks.heading: Operations
chunks.body:
## Operations

**Turning it off.** Set `mode` to `off`. The pass stops, the alert stops, and
every record already written stays readable on every surface — turning the
watch off does not delete history.

**Restarting the daemon.** The records are persisted to
`<data-dir>/autonomous/repo_ci_watch.jsonl` and reloaded at startup, so the
watch resumes with its full history. A run that was `pending` across the
restart is still `pending` when the next pass runs, and its hung age is read
from the CI run's own start time — the restart does not reset the hung
timer — and a rerun or cancel already in flight before the restart is not
re-issued after it (the record's state is what the pass acts on, not a
queue that survives the process).

**Audit.** Every would-do, rerun, cancel and deletion the pass makes is
recorded on the record itself — the `would-do` lines, the rerun log, the
failure notes and the `alerted_at` stamp — so the read view is the durable
trace. In `on` mode the alert goes through the daemon's alert sink with the
run's identity, classification, first-seen stamp and URL in the body. The
`alerted_at` stamp on the record is the once-per-episode proof; the `would-do`
lines in shadow mode are the comparison evidence.

**The deletion is irreversible.** `delete_superseded: delete` in `on` mode
issues real deletions of real CI runs on the ref the record names. Before you
set it, confirm the repository's retention expectations with the process that
owns them — once a run is deleted it is gone from the CI UI, and the record
keeps the run ID but not the run's output.

chunks.title: How-to: the Automation view
chunks.body:
# How-to: the Automation view

The **Automation** view is the place in the web app where you build, watch and
steer chains of Automata. It is the first sub-tab of the **Automata** tab: open
Automata in the bottom navigation and Automation is selected on the sub-tab bar,
left of **Automata** and **Templates**. It shows every Automation as a card, draws the chain
of the one you open as a strip, and puts the controls (pause, resume, cancel,
skip, insert, remove, edit edges) next to the members they act on. Inside the
Automation sub-tab, a second row of sub-tabs splits the view: **Overview**, with
the Progress card, the Capacity and queue card, and the other summary cards that
sit with them; and **Chains**, with the status badges, the search and filter
bar, the list of Automations, and the open Automation with its pipeline strip
and controls. Chains is the one open by default. A **Questions** sub-tab will
join the second row when the question queue lands; no Questions sub-tab exists
today.

chunks.title: How-to: the Automation view
chunks.heading: What an Automation is
chunks.body:
## What an Automation is

An **Automation** is a named chain of Automata. An **Automaton** is one unit of
work; an Automation is the chain that decides which Automaton runs next when the
current one completes, is blocked, or fails. Once an Automation is active,
datawatch starts the next Automaton by itself. See
[automation-queue-advance.md](automation-queue-advance.md) for how the hand-off
works behind the scenes.

The bottom navigation has no Automation button of its own. Inside the Automata
tab, the sub-tab bar reads **Automation**, **Automata**, **Templates**. The
Automata sub-tab lists single Automata; the Automation sub-tab lists the chains
that connect them.

chunks.title: How-to: the Automation view
chunks.heading: Opening it, the remembered sub-tab and saved links
chunks.body:
## Opening it, the remembered sub-tab and saved links

- **First visit.** Tapping Automata in the bottom navigation opens on the
  Automation sub-tab, on its Chains sub-tab. Tap **Automata** or **Templates**
  on the sub-tab bar, or **Overview** or **Chains** on the second row under it,
  to switch. There is no New Automation button in the bar: an Automation is
  created with the round button at the bottom right, or with **＋ Create
  Automation** on the empty state, both opening the same form. The action
  buttons at the right of the bar (select, filter, history, watch) change with
  the sub-tab, and so does the round button; on the Automation sub-tab, filter
  and history show on Chains, because both act on the list.
- **Remembered sub-tab.** While the web app stays open, the sub-tab you chose
  stays selected when you leave the Automata tab and come back. The same rule
  holds on the second row: the sub-tab you chose is kept while the page stays
  open, and a fresh load of the page starts the view on Chains again. Storing a
  chosen sub-tab across loads is switched off until the operator decides how it
  should behave.
- **Saved links.** A link to `#automation` opens the Automata tab on the
  Automation sub-tab, on Chains, and shows its list. `#automation/<id>` and
  `?automation=<id>` land the same way and open that Automation. Older links and
  history entries that name the Automation view land in the same place, and the
  back control on a member's Automaton page returns to the Automation that holds
  it, on Chains.
- **Subsystem off.** When the autonomous subsystem is not enabled, the
  Automation sub-tab is not offered and every one of these links lands on the
  Automata sub-tab.
- **Phone width.** On a narrow screen the two rows of sub-tabs fit at 360 px
  without scrolling or clipping, and every sub-tab in both rows is at least
  40 px tall and wide enough to tap.

- A running daemon with `autonomous.enabled: true`.

chunks.title: How-to: the Automation view
chunks.heading: The pipeline strip
chunks.body:
## The pipeline strip

The detail page draws the Automation as a strip of member cards joined by
connectors, starting at the entry member and following each member's
"on complete" edge.

- **Status dots.** Every member card has a dot: grey for pending, amber for
  approved, a pulsing dot for running, a tick for completed, yellow for
  blocked, red for failed.
- **Active ring.** Members that are running or are the current position of the
  chain are drawn with a ring. When several branches are live, each has its own
  ring.
- **Branch outcomes as sub-rows.** A member can say what happens when it is
  blocked or when it fails, as well as when it completes. Those extra outcomes
  are drawn as sub-rows below the main row, labelled "If blocked →" or
  "If failed →", and a ⑂ mark on the card tells you the member has more than
  one outcome. A member that already appeared earlier in the strip is shown as
  a short reference rather than drawn again, so a loop cannot run away.
- **Dashed untaken edges.** Once a member has finished, the connector it took is
  drawn solid and the connectors it did not take are dashed. Before the member
  finishes, all its connectors look the same.
- **Fork lanes.** A **fork** starts several members at once. Its branches are
  drawn side by side as lanes under the fork, between the fork and its join.
- **Joins and the join rule.** A **join** waits for the branches of its fork.
  Its **join rule** decides what a failed branch means:
  - *All branches must succeed*: one failed branch stops the join from
    succeeding.
  - *One branch is enough*: the join succeeds as soon as one branch does.
  - *Continue anyway*: the chain carries on after the branches finish,
    whatever happened to them.

  While a join is waiting, the detail page says "Join waiting: N of M branches
  finished".
- **Nested Automations.** A member can be a whole other Automation. It is drawn
  as one card with a **Show nested Automation** button; tap it to expand the
  nested chain as another level underneath, and **Hide nested Automation** to
  fold it away again.
- **Inserted markers.** A member that was added after the Automation was first
  built shows an **inserted** marker. Hover it to see who added it and why. The
  **Details** button on any card opens a drawer with its ID, kind, status,
  outcome, the edge it took, and start and finish times.

Below the strip the page lists any **pending inserts** waiting for approval and
the most recent **decisions** (what changed, who did it and when).
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [automation, automata, pipeline, pwa]

chunks.title: How-to: the Automation view
chunks.heading: Creating and editing
chunks.body:
## Creating and editing

Create an Automation with the round button at the bottom right, or with
**＋ Create Automation** on the empty state; both open the same form. The same
form edits an existing Automation.

1. Give it a **name** and, if you like, a description.
2. **Add Automaton** to pick members. The picker lists your Automata and greys
   out the ones you cannot use, with the reason: it is a template, it is a
   child Automaton, it already belongs to another Automation, or it is already
   in this one.
3. **Linear wiring.** Members are chained in the order you add them: each
   member's "on complete" points at the next one and the last one stops. The
   first member is the entry member.
4. **Edge selects.** Each member also has "On complete", "On blocked" and "On
   failed" selects. Each lists the other members, plus **Stop and alert**. Change
   one to send a blocked or failed member somewhere else.
5. **Fork and join.** **Add fork and join** asks for at least two branch
   Automata and a join rule, then adds a fork, its lanes and the paired join
   into the chain.
6. **Nested.** **Add nested Automation** lets you pick another Automation to run
   as a single member. An Automation cannot contain itself, and one that is
   already inside another Automation cannot be nested again.
7. **Default models.** Under **Default models** you can set an execution,
   planning and verification backend, model and effort for the whole chain.
   Members that name their own backend keep it; the Automation default fills
   what they leave open.
8. **Budget policy.** Under **Budget policy** choose a ceiling type, a ceiling,
   a window (lifetime, daily, weekly or monthly), pacing (spend freely or pace
   evenly), what to do on breach (pause or block) and an optional backend. The
   ceiling must be above zero, and at most 100 when it is a percentage.
   **Share of allocation** is marked **estimated** in the form and on the
   card, because a share of a plan allocation is an estimate rather than an
   exact figure.
9. **Save.**

Only a **draft** lets you change its members in the form. Once an Automation has
started, the form shows the members as they are and asks for a **reason** for
the change; to change the chain itself, use the member buttons described below.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:

  index: true
  topics: [automation, automata, pipeline, pwa]

chunks.heading: Control buttons
chunks.body:
## Control buttons

The row of buttons above the strip depends on the status:

| Button | When it shows | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Pause** | Active | Pauses the chain so it starts nothing new until you resume |
| **Resume** | Paused or blocked | Carries on |
| **Cancel Automation** | Draft, active, paused or blocked | Ends the Automation |

An Automation is activated from the CLI, REST, MCP or chat; see
[automation-queue-advance.md](automation-queue-advance.md).

chunks.title: How-to: the Automation view
chunks.heading: Cancel always asks
chunks.body:
### Cancel always asks

Cancel opens a dialog with two choices and **neither is preselected**. You must
pick one before **Cancel Automation** will go through:

- **Stop advancing; let the running member finish.** Nothing new starts; work
  already running carries on to its end.
- **Also cancel the member that is running now.** The running work is stopped
  as well.

It always asks because cancelling cannot be undone and the two choices have very
different effects on work that is already in flight.

chunks.title: How-to: the Automation view
chunks.heading: Member buttons
chunks.body:
### Member buttons

Each member card carries its own buttons, and each dialog names the member it
acts on in its title.

- **Skip member.** Choose which outcome the skipped member takes (on complete,
  on blocked or on failed) and, optionally, a reason. The chain carries on along
  that edge. Available on a member that is pending, approved or running.
- **Insert before / Insert after.** Pick an Automaton to splice into the chain
  next to this member. A **reason is required**: the dialog will not continue
  without one, and the reason is kept on the new member's inserted marker. The
  **Insert urgently** box takes the next slot. The entry member has no slot
  before it once the Automation has started, so only **Insert after** is offered
  there.
- **Remove.** Takes out a member that has not started, after a confirmation.
- **Edit edges.** Reorder where the member's on complete, on blocked and on
  failed outcomes lead. Each select offers the other members or **Stop and
  alert**.
- **Approve insert.** An insert made by an agent or session can be held until
  you approve it, depending on the agent insert policy. Held inserts appear
  under **Pending inserts** with who asked and why; **Approve insert** lets one
  in.

chunks.heading: When several branches are active
chunks.body:
### When several branches are active

With a fork running, several members are live at once. The control row then
shows an **Acting on branch** selector. Pause, resume and cancel always apply to
the **whole Automation**, and the row says so. When only one branch is live the
row simply names it. The member buttons never guess: each one acts on the card
it sits on, and its dialog title names that member.

chunks.title: How-to: the Automation view
chunks.heading: When someone else changed the Automation
chunks.body:
## When someone else changed the Automation

Every change you make carries the version you loaded. If someone else (another
operator, an agent or the CLI) changed the Automation in the meantime, the
daemon refuses your change with a conflict (409) and the page shows **Out of
date: This Automation was changed elsewhere. Reload it before making changes.**
Tap **Reload** to load the current version, then make the change again. Nothing
is retried for you, so a change is never applied on top of something you have
not seen.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:

  topics: [automation, automata, pipeline, pwa]

make alone, and you, the operator, **answer it** the way you like best. For now
the question channel is on REST only: the in-PWA queue, the CLI subcommands,
the MCP tools and answering from a comm channel all come after and build on

chunks.title: How-to: the Automation view
chunks.heading: Turn the channel on
chunks.body:
### Turn the channel on

The channel is **off by default** behind the switch
`autonomous.questions.enabled`. While it is off, every endpoint under
`/api/questions` answers with a 503 that names the switch. Turn it on by
setting the switch to `true` — the PWA Settings toggle (labeled in English,
German, Spanish, French and Japanese), `configure` from chat, or REST:

```bash
env -u TMUX -u TMUX_TMPDIR rtk curl -sS -X PUT http://127.0.0.1:8787/api/config \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"autonomous.questions.enabled": true}'
```

The switch takes effect on the next request — no restart. Reads need the
`autonomous:read` capability, writes (raise, answer, withdraw) need
`autonomous:write`; local operators always pass.

chunks.title: How-to: the Automation view
chunks.heading: Raise a question
chunks.body:
### Raise a question

`POST /api/questions` raises one. A question carries a label, risk, a context
(`none` when it has no work of its own), its text, a set of options (2 to 20),
an optional recommendation, and a **required `default`** — the fallback option,
or the word `hold`. It is required precisely so that a question always has
some position attached and no choice is ever left silent.

```bash
env -u TMUX -u TMUX_TMPDIR rtk curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8787/api/questions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "label": "decision",
    "risk": "low",
    "context": "none",
    "text": "Should the retry keep using the free backend, or should it move to the paid one?",
    "options": [
      {"id": "stay-free",  "label": "Stay on the free backend"},
      {"id": "move-paid",  "label": "Move to the paid backend now"}
    ],
    "recommendation": {"id": "stay-free", "rationale": "The task is close to done and the free backend is idle"},
    "default": "stay-free"
  }'
```

The response is the stored question with its generated id and state `open`.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:

  index: true
  topics: [automation, automata, pipeline, pwa]

chunks.title: How-to: the Automation view
chunks.heading: Answer — option, words, or both
chunks.body:
### Answer — option, words, or both

An answer is an **option**, your own **words** (the quote), **or both**.
Answers are **immutable**: nothing about the question can be edited after the
fact, and your quote is stored **verbatim, byte for byte** (no trims, no
normalization) with its SHA-256 over exactly those bytes, so any reader can
check later that it was never altered.

```bash
# Pick the option and add words
env -u TMUX -u TMUX_TMPDIR rtk curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8787/api/questions/q-0195c8e2a4b6d7f81c/answer \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "chosen_option_id": "move-paid",
    "quote": "Move it — the deadline is tomorrow and the free backend has been thrashing",
    "surface": "rest"
  }'

# Words alone work too; so does the option alone.
```
chunks.frontmatter_raw:

  index: true
  topics: [automation, automata, pipeline, pwa]

one stays in the log, marked as superseded. Superseding an answer that is not
the currently standing one is refused, as is answering a withdrawn question.

```bash
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "chosen_option_id": "stay-free",
    "quote": "Actually, hold — the paid backend has the same backlog today",
    "supersedes": "a-0195c8e3b5c7e8a92d"
  }'
```

chunks.title: How-to: the Automation view
chunks.heading: What the channel does not do
chunks.body:
### What the channel does not do

- **No clock expiry.** A question does not time out. It sits in the channel
  until it is answered or withdrawn; `expired` only ever appears as an
  explicit terminal move recorded in the log, never as a timer firing.
- **A secret answer is refused, not stored.** If your words look like a
  credential, the answer is refused with a 422 that names the two safe routes
  — put the value in the datawatch secrets store and reference it as
  `${secret:name}`, or in a session-facing file — and it is never stored, the
  audit line for the refusal never carries the text, and nothing of it is
  echoed back to you.
- **Every state change is audited.** Raise, answer, supersede, withdraw and
  expire each write one line to the single audit log under its own CEF name
  (`QuestionRaised`, `QuestionAnswered`, `AnswerSuperseded`,
  `QuestionWithdrawn`, `QuestionExpired`, `QuestionAnswerRefused`).

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle event subscriptions
chunks.body:
# How-to: Automaton lifecycle event subscriptions

Automata emit lifecycle events as they move — PRD and task status
changes (`prd.blocked`, `task.completed`, …), worker session
start/clear (`task.session_started`, `task.session_cleared`), and PRD
updates (`prd.updated`). A **subscription** is one persisted rule:
*when this event fires, deliver it there*. Register it once and the
daemon handles the rest — no session-list polling, no racing your
scripts against the worker pane.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [autonomous, lifecycle, subscriptions, events]

  - {name: kinds, required: false, default: "task.session_started", description: "Comma-separated lifecycle event kinds to watch"}
  - {name: level, required: false, default: "task", description: "Event level: prd or task"}
  - {name: sink, required: false, default: "topic", description: "Sink type: comm | session | topic | alert | mcp_queue"}
  - {name: target, required: false, default: "lifecycle-howto", description: "Sink target (session id, topic, router or alert name, or the mcp_queue queue name)"}
exec_steps:
  - tool: autonomous_subscriptions
    description: List the currently persisted lifecycle event subscriptions
    args: {}
    read_only: true
  - tool: autonomous_subscribe
    description: Register a one-shot subscription for the chosen kinds (it self-deletes after its first delivery)
    args:
      kinds: "{{params.kinds}}"
      level: "{{params.level}}"
      sink_type: "{{params.sink}}"
      sink_target: "{{params.target}}"
      one_shot: true
    read_only: false
  - tool: autonomous_subscriptions
    description: Confirm the new subscription is registered
    args: {}
    read_only: true

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle event subscriptions
chunks.heading: What it solves: the watch-and-inject polling script
chunks.body:
## What it solves: the watch-and-inject polling script

The classic pattern: a task spawns its worker session, and you want
text typed into that session the moment it exists. Before:

```sh
# old: poll and race — the pane may not be ready when you inject
while ! datawatch sessions list | grep -q "$TASK_ID"; do sleep 5; done
datawatch session-ops send "$SESSION" "Start with the Setup section of TASK.md"
```

After — one rule, registered ahead of time:

```sh
datawatch autonomous subscribe \
  --task "$TASK_ID" --on session_started \
  --send "Start with the Setup section of TASK.md" \
  --sink session --target "$SESSION" --one-shot
```

When the task's worker session starts, the daemon delivers the text to
the session and the subscription deletes itself (one-shot). If you
missed the window and the one-shot is already gone, register it again
from the *next* event boundary — the rule is declarative, not
positional.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle event subscriptions
chunks.heading: The subscription model
chunks.body:
## The subscription model

Every subscription is **filter → sink → optional action**:

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Filter** | `kinds` (event kinds; repeatable) and/or `level` (`prd` or `task`), plus optional scope to one Automaton (`prd_id`) or one task (`task_id`). At least one of `kinds` / `level` is required. |
| **Sink** | One of: `comm` (router fan-out), `session` (a datawatch session), `topic` (SSE / mobile-push topic bus), `alert` (in-app alert store), `mcp_queue` (a named pending-events queue that a client polls). Each has a `target`; for `mcp_queue` it is the queue name. |
| **Action** *(optional)* | `send_input` with text (max 4096 chars), only with a `session` sink — the text is typed into the target session on every match. |
| **Flags** | `one_shot` (delete after first *successful* delivery), `expires_at` (TTL), `coalesce` (batch human-facing deliveries in quiet windows). |

Event kinds are a closed set: every PRD status kind (`prd.draft`,
`prd.planning`, `prd.needs_review`, `prd.completed`, `prd.blocked`,
…), every task status kind (`task.pending`, `task.queued`,
`task.in_progress`, `task.completed`, `task.failed`, `task.blocked`,
…), plus the non-status kinds `task.session_started`,
`task.session_cleared` and `prd.updated`. The daemon rejects unknown
kinds at creation (`"filter kind %q is not a known event kind"`), so a
typo fails fast instead of silently never firing.

Note: the CLI/comm shorthand `prd_updated` currently resolves to
`task.prd_updated`, which is **not** in the known-kind set — use the
full form `--on prd.updated` for PRD-update notifications.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle event subscriptions
chunks.heading: Quickstart (CLI)
chunks.body:
## Quickstart (CLI)

```sh
# One-shot watch-and-inject (the polling-script replacement):
datawatch autonomous subscribe \
  --task "$TASK_ID" --on session_started \
  --send "Pick up the brief in TASK.md — Start with its Setup section." \
  --sink session --target "$SESSION" --one-shot
```

Notes:

- `--on` is repeatable; shorthand words map to task kinds
  (`session_started` → `task.session_started`,
  `session_cleared` → `task.session_cleared`); full kinds containing a
  dot pass through (`prd.blocked`, `prd.updated`).
- `--task` implies `--one-shot` by default (that is the
  watch-and-inject shape); pass `--one-shot=false` to keep it.
- `--send` requires `--sink session` and sets the action text.
- `--target` for a session sink may be a session id; if omitted the
  CLI falls back to `$DATAWATCH_SESSION_ID` (subscribe *from* the
  target session).
- `--expires <seconds>` sets a TTL (`0` = never).
- `--coalesce` batches human-facing sink deliveries in quiet windows.

Other examples:

```sh
# Notify a comm router whenever any Automaton reaches blocked (kept
# forever, delivery batched):
datawatch autonomous subscribe --on prd.blocked --sink comm --target my-router --coalesce

# One Automaton's completions to the alert store:
datawatch autonomous subscribe --on prd.completed --prd <prd-id> --sink alert --target system

# Park matching events in a queue a generic MCP client can poll:
datawatch autonomous subscribe --on task.failed --on prd.blocked --sink mcp_queue --target ops-watch

# List, change, test, then delete by id:
datawatch autonomous subscriptions [--owner operator]
datawatch autonomous subscription-update <subscription-id> --on prd.blocked --sink comm --target my-router
datawatch autonomous subscription-test <subscription-id>
datawatch autonomous unsubscribe <subscription-id>
```

`subscription-update` takes the same flags as `subscribe` and **replaces**
the whole configuration: anything you leave out is cleared, so pass
everything you want to keep. Unlike `subscribe`, `--task` does not imply
`--one-shot`.

chunks.heading: Test a subscription before you rely on it
chunks.body:
## Test a subscription before you rely on it

A subscription that never fires is hard to tell from one that has
nothing to fire on. **Test-fire** sends one labelled event to just that
subscription's sink, now:

```sh
datawatch autonomous subscription-test <subscription-id>
```

The message text starts with `[test] ` and describes a synthetic
`prd.updated` event, so you can see it arrive in the comm channel,
session, topic, alert list or queue (in a queue it appears as an event
with `"test": true`). A test never types the
subscription's `send_input` action text and never uses up a one-shot, so
it is safe on a live rule. The answer is `ok` with the sink type, or an
error such as `sink not available` when that delivery path is not wired
in this daemon.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle event subscriptions
chunks.heading: PWA walkthrough
chunks.body:
## PWA walkthrough

Open an Automaton in the PWA (**Automata** → the Automaton) and choose the
**Subscriptions** tab.

1. **Read the list.** The tab shows every subscription that applies to this
   Automaton: rules scoped to it, plus unscoped rules that fire for every
   Automaton ("all automata"). Each row shows the event kinds or level, the
   sink and target, and badges for one-shot, coalesce, expiry and owner.
2. **Add.** Choose **Add subscription**. Tick at least one event kind (they
   are grouped as Automaton status, Task status and Other) or pick a level.
   Choose the scope (this Automaton or all automata), an optional task id,
   the sink type and its target, and optionally send-input text (session
   sink only), one-shot, coalesce and an expiry in hours. The form checks
   the same limits as the daemon (queue name characters and length, 4096
   characters of action text) before it saves.
3. **Test.** Choose **Test** on a row. A line under the tab header reports
   "Delivered via <sink>" or why the test failed.
4. **Edit.** Choose **Edit**, change what you need and save. The edit
   replaces the rule's configuration; the id is kept.
5. **Delete.** Choose **Delete** and confirm.

If the tab says "Lifecycle subscriptions are disabled on this server.",
the daemon's subscription engine is not wired (see Troubleshooting). The
tab is loaded when you open it and after each change; it does not poll.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle event subscriptions
chunks.heading: A generic MCP client: the pending-events queue
chunks.body:
## A generic MCP client: the pending-events queue

An MCP host that cannot receive pushes (no session to type into, no
comm channel) can still follow Automaton events by **polling a queue**.

1. **Register a queue subscription** (once). The sink target is the
   queue name — letters, digits and `. _ : -`, at most 64 characters:

   ```sh
   datawatch autonomous subscribe --on task.completed --on task.failed \
     --on prd.blocked --sink mcp_queue --target ops-watch
   ```

   From an MCP client: `autonomous_subscribe(kinds="task.completed,task.failed,prd.blocked", sink_type="mcp_queue", sink_target="ops-watch")`.

2. **Poll with a cursor.** The first call uses cursor 0:

   `autonomous_events_pending(queue="ops-watch", since_cursor=0)`

   returns

   ```json
   {"events":[{"cursor":1,"event":{"kind":"task.completed","prd_id":"…"}}],"next_cursor":1,"dropped":false}
   ```

   (shape abbreviated). Handle the events, then pass `next_cursor` back as
   `since_cursor` on the next call. `limit` defaults to 50 and is capped at
   200. The same data is available over REST
   (`GET /api/autonomous/events?queue=ops-watch&since=1`), the CLI
   (`datawatch autonomous events --queue ops-watch --since 1 [--json]`) and a
   comm channel (`autonomous events queue=ops-watch since=1`).

3. **Watch for `dropped`.** Each queue is bounded
   (`autonomous.notify.pending_events_max`, default 500) and evicts the
   oldest events first. `dropped: true` means events you had not read yet
   were evicted — re-read the Automaton's state instead of assuming the
   history is complete. Queues live in memory only, so after a daemon
   restart the queue is empty and cursors start again from 1; the
   subscription itself survives. Deleting the last subscription that
   feeds a queue discards the events it still held.

Poll no faster than you need; there is no push. For immediate delivery
use a `session`, `comm` or `topic` sink instead.

chunks.heading: MCP
chunks.body:
## MCP

The MCP tools proxy the daemon's REST surface on loopback — the daemon
store is the source of truth, so nothing is lost when an MCP host
restarts:

- `autonomous_subscribe(kinds, level, prd_id, task_id, sink_type,
  sink_target, action_text?, one_shot?, coalesce?,
  expires_in_seconds?)` — `kinds` accepts a comma-separated string or a
  JSON array; returns the stored record (with its `id`).
- `autonomous_unsubscribe(id)`
- `autonomous_subscriptions()` — list everything (filterable by owner
  on the REST route).
- `autonomous_subscription_update(id, …)` — same optional fields as
  `autonomous_subscribe`; replaces the configuration and returns the
  updated record.
- `autonomous_subscription_test(id)` — test-fire; returns
  `{"ok","sink","error"}`.
- `autonomous_prd_set_notify_events(id, notify_events)` — set the
  Automaton's own notify-event kinds (a non-empty list), or clear them
  (empty/omitted — the Automaton then inherits its guardrail profile or
  the global default set). See *Choosing which events notify* below; the
  response carries the resolved set with its source tier.
- `autonomous_events_pending(queue, since_cursor?, limit?)` — poll an
  `mcp_queue` queue (see above).

chunks.heading: Comm channel (owner-scoped)
chunks.body:
## Comm channel (owner-scoped)

From any configured comm channel:

```
autonomous subscribe task.session_started prd=<prd-id>
autonomous subscriptions
autonomous subscription-update <id> kinds=prd.blocked,prd.failed coalesce=true
autonomous subscription-test <id>
autonomous events [queue=<name>] [since=<cursor>]
autonomous unsubscribe <id>
autonomous set-notify-events <prd-id> <kind,kind,...|inherit>
```

A guardrail profile's own list travels under the `guardrail` verb
namespace: `guardrail profile notify-events <id> <kind,kind,...|inherit>`
(`inherit` clears it).

In `subscription-update`, fields you do not name keep their stored value
(keys: `kinds`, `level`, `prd`, `task`, `coalesce`, `one_shot`, `expires`;
`prd=`, `task=` and `expires=0` clear). `events` defaults the queue to one
derived from the calling channel.

The calling channel is **both the owner and the sink target**. That is
deliberate: a channel can only list and un-subscribe *its own*
subscriptions — it can never see, change, test or remove another
channel's, and it can only read queues its own subscriptions feed.

## REST

```
GET    /api/autonomous/subscriptions[?owner=<owner>]   (autonomous:read)
POST   /api/autonomous/subscriptions                    (autonomous:write) → 201 + record
PUT    /api/autonomous/subscriptions/{id}               (autonomous:write) → 200 + record
POST   /api/autonomous/subscriptions/{id}/test          (autonomous:write) → 200 {"ok","sink","error"}
DELETE /api/autonomous/subscriptions/{id}               (autonomous:write)
GET    /api/autonomous/events?queue=<name>[&since=<cursor>][&limit=<n>]   (autonomous:read)
POST   /api/autonomous/prds/{id}/set_notify_events      (autonomous:write) → 200 + record (with notify_events_effective)
```

`503` when the lifecycle engine is not wired (bare daemon / unit test
contexts). `400` on a malformed or unknown-kind payload (or a missing
`queue`, non-numeric `since` / `limit` on events), `404` on an unknown id.

Example create body:

```json
{
  "owner": "operator",
  "filter": {"kinds": ["task.session_started"], "level": "task", "task_id": "task_7"},
  "sink": {"type": "session", "target": "5a9e0c41"},
  "action": {"type": "send_input", "text": "Start with the Setup section of TASK.md."},
  "one_shot": true,
  "expires_at": "2026-10-21T23:59:59Z"
}
```

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle event subscriptions
chunks.heading: Delivery to a session: bridge preferred, SendInput fallback
chunks.body:
## Delivery to a session: bridge preferred, SendInput fallback

When a subscription with a `session` sink fires, the daemon:

1. **Bridge first** — if the target session has a channel bridge with a
   local port (a live Signal/Telegram/etc. bridge for that session),
   it POSTs the message to the bridge's `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/send`
   (5 s timeout).
2. **Fallback** — port 0, POST error, or no bridge at all: it types the
   text into the session's input via `SendInput`, tagged with source
   `lifecycle-sub` (visible in the session's input history so you can
   tell daemon-typed text from operator-typed text).

A failed one-shot delivery is retried once; after that the
subscription is dropped and the failure is logged (the daemon never
holds a one-shot hostage to a dead target).

## One-shot, expiry, coalesce

- **`one_shot`** — deleted only after *successful* delivery; see above
  for the failure behavior.
- **`expires_at`** — a janitor prunes expired subscriptions
  continuously; they stop matching as soon as the timestamp elapses.
- **`coalesce`** — for human-facing sinks (comm/alert) deliveries are
  batched within a quiet window instead of firing one message per
  event.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle event subscriptions
chunks.heading: Choosing which events notify
chunks.body:
## Choosing which events notify

A subscription filter decides which *matching* events a subscriber gets;
the **notify set** decides which event kinds an Automaton notifies for at
all. A subscription for a kind that is not in its Automaton's resolved
set never fires — the filter can only *narrow* what the set already
allows, a subscription can never *widen* it.

The resolved set has three tiers, highest first:

1. the Automaton's own `notify_events` list;
2. the `notify_events` list of its assigned guardrail profile;
3. the global default `autonomous.notify.default_events` — unset means
   the shipped five-kind baseline:
   `prd.needs_review, prd.blocked, prd.failed, prd.completed,
   prd.cancelled`.

The first **non-empty** tier wins. At tiers 1–2 an empty (or missing)
list means *inherit*, never *off*; only the global tier can resolve to
"no kinds" (explicit `default_events: []`). Each resolved answer also
names its **source**: `automaton`, `profile` or `global` — that is
what the surfaces show as `notify_events_effective`.

`task.session_started`, `task.session_cleared`, `scope_warning` and
`guardrail_warn` are **opt-in** kinds and are not in the default set: a
subscription on one of them fires only on Automata whose resolved set
includes that kind (add it to the per-Automaton, profile or global
default list). `scope_warning` (a task touched files outside its declared
scope; the event lists the files) and `guardrail_warn` (a guardrail
returned a warn outcome; the event names the guardrail and carries the
level: task, story or Automaton) are bare kind names with no `prd.` or
`task.` prefix. They are informational only and never block or change any
task, story or Automaton. The usable closed set is every known
lifecycle event kind except `prd.updated`, which is deliberately not a
notify kind. Unknown or blank kinds are rejected (400 / a tool error).

**Per-Automaton** (one Automaton, everything else unchanged):

```sh
# CLI — list wins; `inherit` (or omitting the kinds) clears the list
datawatch autonomous prd-set-notify-events <id> prd.blocked,task.session_started
datawatch autonomous prd-set-notify-events <id> inherit

# Comm
autonomous set-notify-events <prd-id> prd.blocked,prd.failed
```

plus MCP `autonomous_prd_set_notify_events(id, notify_events)`, REST
`POST /api/autonomous/prds/{id}/set_notify_events` with a
`{"notify_events": [...]}` body (an absent key, `null` or `[]` is a
clear), and the PWA settings on the Automaton view — the
"Notification events" panel with an inherit toggle, grouped
kind checkboxes and the resolved set + source shown after save.

**Per guardrail profile** (every Automaton assigned to it):

```sh
# CLI
datawatch guardrail profile create --name ops-watch \
  --guardrails ci-watch --notify-events prd.blocked,prd.failed
datawatch guardrail profile update <id> --notify-events prd.failed,task.session_started

datawatch guardrail automaton set <automaton-id> --profile ops-watch

# Comm
guardrail profile notify-events <id> prd.blocked,prd.failed
guardrail profile notify-events <id> inherit
```

plus the `notify_events` field in the profile create/update body on
REST, the `guardrail_profile_create` / `guardrail_profile_update` MCP
tools, and the profile editor in PWA **Settings → Automate → Guardrail
Profiles**.

**Globally** (every Automaton; the lowest tier, and the only tier that can
express *no kinds*):

```yaml
autonomous:
  notify:
    # adds guardrail_warn to the five-kind baseline for every Automaton
    default_events: [prd.needs_review, prd.blocked, prd.failed, prd.completed, prd.cancelled, guardrail_warn]
```

under `autonomous.notify` in the config file (annotated example in
[config-reference.yaml](../config-reference.yaml)), or without touching the
file: REST `PUT /api/config` with `{"autonomous.notify.default_events": [...]}`
(JSON array; read back via `GET /api/config`), MCP `config_set`, CLI
`datawatch config set autonomous.notify.default_events <kinds>`, comm channel
`configure autonomous.notify.default_events=<kinds>`, or the PWA settings
field (Settings → General → Automate). Changed once, applies at daemon start;
an explicit empty list (`default_events: []`) turns the global tier off.

chunks.heading: Enabling warning kinds from every surface
chunks.body:
#### Enabling warning kinds from every surface

| What you want | YAML | CLI | Web UI | REST | comm channel |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| One or both warning kinds for one Automaton | — (the per-Automaton list is data, set through the other surfaces) | `datawatch autonomous prd-set-notify-events <id> prd.blocked,guardrail_warn` | Automaton settings → *Notification events* panel: tick the opt-in kinds, toggle *Inherit* off | `POST /api/autonomous/prds/{id}/set_notify_events` with `{"notify_events": ["prd.blocked", "guardrail_warn"]}` | `autonomous set-notify-events <id> prd.blocked,guardrail_warn` (`inherit` clears it back to the profile/global tier) |
| Warning kinds for all Automata on one guardrail profile | — (the profile's list is data, set through the other surfaces) | `datawatch guardrail profile update <id> --notify-events prd.failed,scope_warning` | Settings → Automate → Guardrail Profiles → the profile's notify list | `PUT /api/autonomous/guardrail_profiles/{id}` with `{"notify_events": ["scope_warning"]}` | `guardrail profile notify-events <id> prd.failed,scope_warning` (or `inherit`) |
| Warning kinds globally (lowest tier) | `autonomous.notify.default_events` (example above) | `datawatch config set autonomous.notify.default_events "prd.blocked,prd.failed,guardrail_warn"` | Settings → General → Automate → the default-events field | `PUT /api/config` with `{"autonomous.notify.default_events": ["prd.blocked", "prd.failed", "guardrail_warn"]}` | `configure autonomous.notify.default_events=prd.blocked,prd.failed,guardrail_warn` |

MCP joins every row: `autonomous_prd_set_notify_events(id, notify_events)` for
the Automaton tier, `guardrail_profile_update(id, notify_events_json="[\"scope_warning\"]")`
for the profile tier, and `config_set` / `autonomous_config_set` for the
global tier. Every surface validates the kinds, reports the effective set on
read, and rejects a typo'd kind with a near-miss hint.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle event subscriptions
chunks.heading: Worked example: a guardrail `warn` into a queue
chunks.body:
#### Worked example: a guardrail `warn` into a queue

1. **Allow the kind** on the Automaton (any tier — the highest non-empty tier wins):

   ```sh
   datawatch autonomous prd-set-notify-events a1b2c3d4 prd.blocked,guardrail_warn
   ```

2. **Subscribe** the kind to the sink you want:

   ```sh
   # a named queue a generic MCP client polls:
   datawatch autonomous subscribe --on guardrail_warn --prd a1b2c3d4 --sink mcp_queue --target warn-watch
   # or a datawatch session (the event is typed in when it fires):
   datawatch autonomous subscribe --on guardrail_warn --prd a1b2c3d4 --sink session --target "$SESSION"
   ```

3. **When a guardrail judge returns `warn`**, the event is delivered to that
   sink: the Automaton, and (for a task- or story-scoped warning) its task and
   story; `guardrail` names the guardrail; `verdict` carries the outcome,
   summary and issues; `decision` is the verdict decision the same check
   recorded; and `link` is the PWA alert deep-link when the same check also
   raised an alert. In a queue it looks like:

   ```json
   {"kind":"guardrail_warn","level":"task","prd_id":"a1b2c3d4","story_id":"story_2","task_id":"task_9","guardrail":"ci-watch","verdict":{"outcome":"warn","summary":"re-run flake","issues":["flaky re-run"]},"link":"?alert=alert_171"}
   ```

   A `scope_warning` event is the same shape with `level` always `task` and
   `files` listing what the task touched outside its declared scope (including
   pre-existing foreign files swept into the task's commit), and, only when the
   finding did raise an alert, the same `link`. The full field list and the
   closed kind set are in the [lifecycle reference](../api/autonomous.md#lifecycle-event-kinds).

Two things stay fixed regardless of the notify set: **the PWA still shows the
warning either way** — the alert and the inline scope-drift marker appear for
every operator no matter what the tiers say — and **the warnings never block
or alter anything**: the task keeps running, the verdict does not fail the
work, and no status changes. The notify events only add delivery destinations
on top of the PWA warning.

Check where an Automaton stands at any tier with
`datawatch autonomous prd-get <id>` (`notify_events`,
`notify_events_effective`) or the `notify` block of
`GET /api/autonomous/status` (the global `default_events` plus the
per-Automaton overrides, capped at 100, each with its source). Turning notifications off for one Automaton,
replacing the global baseline, or restoring a cleared list is covered
in `operations.md` under *Managing Automata lifecycle event
subscriptions*.

Every set/clear is audit-logged (action `autonomous_notify_events_changed`)
with the old and new lists; the Automaton entry also records which tier
the resolved set came from after the change.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle event subscriptions
chunks.heading: Storage, audit & restart behavior
chunks.body:
## Storage, audit & restart behavior

- Persisted at `<data_dir>/lifecycle_subscriptions.json`, encrypted at
  rest with the daemon's secfile key (same treatment as channel
  routing rules). It survives daemon restarts — re-apply after
  migrating the data dir.
- Create/update/test/delete are audit-logged. Per-event delivery is intentionally
  not audited (high-frequency, same as discussion `subscribe`
  deliveries) — inspect the daemon log (`lifecycle-sub` lines) for
  delivery failures.
- **No daemon restart needed** to apply changes: the engine
  re-attaches to the store immediately on any add/remove
  (`OnChanged`), and the REST/MCP/CLI/comm surfaces all hit the same
  store.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle event subscriptions
chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.body:
## Troubleshooting

- **`503` from the REST route** — this daemon build's engine isn't
  wired (unit-test or stripped-down context); use a normal daemon.
- **`filter kind "…" is not a known event kind`** — use the full kind
  (`prd.updated`, `task.session_started`); check the closed set above.
- **Session sink never fires** — the event kind or task scope doesn't
  match what actually happens (e.g. subscribed to
  `task.session_cleared` instead of `session_started`), or the
  one-shot already consumed its event. List with
  `datawatch autonomous subscriptions` and re-register for the next
  boundary if needed.
- **Text arrived but looks wrong** — verify the `lifecycle-sub`
  source tag in the session input history; `send_input` types verbatim,
  4096-char cap.
- **`webhook` sink is refused** — by design in this release; outbound
  webhooks arrive in a later phase.
- **Polling a queue returns nothing** — confirm a subscription with sink
  `mcp_queue` and the *same* queue name exists
  (`datawatch autonomous subscriptions`), that the events you expect match
  its filter, and that the `since` cursor is not from before a daemon
  restart (cursors restart at 1).
- **Test says `sink not available`** — that delivery path is not wired in
  this daemon (for example no comm router is configured for a `comm`
  sink).

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle webhooks and peer forwarding
chunks.body:
# How-to: Automaton lifecycle webhooks and peer forwarding

The lifecycle subscriptions described in
[Automata lifecycle subscriptions](automaton-lifecycle-subscriptions.md)
deliver events to a chat channel, a session, a topic, the alert store or a
polling queue. This guide covers two more sinks that send events **out of
this daemon**:

- **Outbound webhook** — each matching event is an HTTPS `POST` to a
  receiver you run. Every request is signed with HMAC-SHA256 so the
  receiver can prove who sent it and that it was not changed.
- **Peer forwarding** — each matching event is sent to another datawatch
  daemon that you have registered as a federation peer. The receiving
  daemon re-emits it to its own subscriptions.

> **Both features ship disabled.** Until you turn them on, a webhook or peer
> subscription is refused when you create it, and any such subscription that
> is already stored delivers nothing. Subscriptions with the other sink types
> are not affected.
>
> The retry counts, the signature format and the payload shape in this guide
> are the proposed defaults in the
> [lifecycle webhook and forwarding proposal](../plans/2026-10-23-lifecycle-outbound-webhook-and-forwarding-proposal.md).
> They are pending the operator's confirmation. Keep both features off until
> that confirmation is recorded.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle webhooks and peer forwarding
chunks.heading: What happens to an event
chunks.body:
## What happens to an event

1. An Automaton emits a lifecycle event (for example `task.completed` or
   `prd.blocked`).
2. The subscription engine checks every stored subscription against it. A
   webhook or peer subscription that matches is handed to its sink.
3. The sink builds one JSON envelope for the event, signs it and sends it.
   A failed send is retried with a growing delay. A send that is still
   failing after the last attempt is dropped, raises one alert, and writes
   an audit record.

Every attempt, and the final outcome, is written to the audit log (see
[Retries, failures and audit records](#retries-failures-and-audit-records)).
