chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle webhooks and peer forwarding
chunks.heading: Enable the sink and set the allow-list
chunks.body:
## Enable the sink and set the allow-list

A webhook can only reach a host that is on the **allow-list**. The list is
the operator's decision about where events may go, and it is checked when a
subscription is created and again on every delivery.

The allow-list entries are:

- an exact host, such as `hooks.example.net` (matches that host on any port), or
- an exact host and port, such as `hooks.example.net:8443` (matches only that
  port).

Entries are case-insensitive. An entry must not contain a scheme, a path, a
query, a wildcard or a user name. An **empty list means nothing can receive
an event**.

The keys are:

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `autonomous.notify.webhook.enabled` | `false` | Master switch for the webhook sink |
| `autonomous.notify.webhook.allow_hosts` | `[]` | Hosts allowed to receive a webhook |
| `autonomous.notify.forwarding.enabled` | `false` | Master switch for peer forwarding, in both directions |

Set the same values on every surface below. The other retry and limit keys
are listed in the [configuration reference](../config-reference.yaml).

| Surface | How to turn the sink on and set the allow-list |
|---|---|
| YAML | In `config.yaml`, under `autonomous.notify.webhook`, set `enabled: true` and `allow_hosts: ["hooks.example.net", "hooks.example.net:8443"]`. Under `autonomous.notify.forwarding`, set `enabled: true` for peer forwarding. The file is read when the daemon starts. |
| CLI | `datawatch config set autonomous.notify.webhook.enabled true` then `datawatch config set autonomous.notify.webhook.allow_hosts hooks.example.net,hooks.example.net:8443` |
| Web UI | **Settings → Comms → Notifications**: the **Outbound webhook sink: enabled** toggle and the **Webhook allow-list (host or host:port)** field. Peer forwarding has its own toggle in the same card. |
| REST | `curl -sk -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"autonomous.notify.webhook.enabled": true, "autonomous.notify.webhook.allow_hosts": ["hooks.example.net", "hooks.example.net:8443"]}' https://localhost:8443/api/config` |
| Comm channel | `configure autonomous.notify.webhook.enabled=true` then `configure autonomous.notify.webhook.allow_hosts=hooks.example.net,hooks.example.net:8443` |

The Web UI, REST, CLI and comm channel changes take effect on the next event,
with no restart. A value that is refused leaves the stored settings unchanged.

chunks.heading: Store the signing secret in the vault
chunks.body:
## Store the signing secret in the vault

The signing key is never typed into a subscription. Store it in the secrets
vault and refer to it by name:

```sh
# Generate a random key, then store it. Keep the value; the receiver needs it too.
openssl rand -hex 32
datawatch secrets set lifecycle-hook-prod "<the value you generated>"
```

A webhook subscription then carries the reference `${secret:lifecycle-hook-prod}`.

- The reference must be exactly one `${secret:name}`. A literal value is
  refused when you create the subscription, so the value is never stored in
  the subscription.
- The daemon resolves the reference on **every delivery**. A rotated secret
  applies to the next event, with no restart. The receiver must be given the
  new value at the same time.
- The resolved value is never written to a subscription, a log line, an audit
  record, an alert or any API response.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle webhooks and peer forwarding
chunks.heading: Create a webhook subscription
chunks.body:
## Create a webhook subscription

A webhook subscription needs a filter, the sink type `webhook`, the HTTPS URL
as the target, and the secret reference. The examples below watch for three
event kinds.

**MCP** (any MCP host connected to the daemon):

```text
autonomous_subscribe(
  kinds="task.completed,task.failed,prd.blocked",
  sink_type="webhook",
  sink_target="https://hooks.example.net/datawatch",
  secret_ref="${secret:lifecycle-hook-prod}")
```

**CLI:**

```sh
datawatch autonomous subscribe \
  --on task.completed --on task.failed --on prd.blocked \
  --sink webhook --target https://hooks.example.net/datawatch \
  --secret-ref '${secret:lifecycle-hook-prod}'
```

**REST:**

```sh
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "owner": "operator",
    "filter": {"kinds": ["task.completed", "task.failed", "prd.blocked"]},
    "sink": {"type": "webhook",
             "target": "https://hooks.example.net/datawatch",
             "secret_ref": "${secret:lifecycle-hook-prod}"}
  }' \
  https://localhost:8443/api/autonomous/subscriptions
```

**Comm channel:**

```text
autonomous subscribe task.completed,task.failed,prd.blocked sink=webhook target=https://hooks.example.net/datawatch secret_ref=${secret:lifecycle-hook-prod}
```

**PWA:** open an Automaton, choose the **Subscriptions** tab, then
**Add subscription**. Choose the event kinds, set the scope to all Automata
if the rule should cover every one, choose **Webhook** as the sink, enter the
**Webhook URL** and the **Secret reference** (`${secret:lifecycle-hook-prod}`),
and save. The form does not show the secret's value.

Creation is refused, with a message that names the cause, when:

- webhook delivery is disabled (`webhook delivery is disabled; set autonomous.notify.webhook.enabled to true …`);
- the URL is not `https` (plain `http` is accepted only for an allow-listed host);
- the URL contains a user name or password, or has no host;
- the host is not on the allow-list;
- no secret reference is given, or the value is a literal rather than a `${secret:name}` reference.

Test a rule before you rely on it:

```sh
datawatch autonomous subscription-test <subscription-id>
```

The test sends one signed event labelled `[test]` through the same path a real
event takes. It does not use up a one-shot rule.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle webhooks and peer forwarding
chunks.heading: What the receiver gets
chunks.body:
## What the receiver gets

Every delivery is one `POST` to the URL with these headers:

| Header | Value |
|---|---|
| `Content-Type` | `application/json` |
| `User-Agent` | `datawatch-lifecycle/1` |
| `X-Datawatch-Signature` | `t=<unix seconds>,v1=<lowercase hex>` |
| `X-Datawatch-Delivery` | The delivery id: 32 hex characters. The same value on every retry of one delivery. |
| `X-Datawatch-Event` | The event kind, such as `task.completed` |

The body is a JSON envelope. The `event` object is the same lifecycle event the
other sinks receive:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "delivery_id": "0f3c9a6e1b7d4c2a8e5f9b0d6a1c3e7f",
  "sent_at": "2026-10-25T12:30:00Z",
  "host": "build-01",
  "subscription_id": "<subscription-id>",
  "event": {
    "id": "<event-id>",
    "at": "2026-10-25T12:29:58Z",
    "kind": "task.completed",
    "level": "task",
    "prd_id": "<automaton-id>",
    "task_id": "<task-id>",
    "old_status": "running",
    "new_status": "completed",
    "host": "build-01"
  }
}
```

The envelope fields are:

- `version` — the envelope version. It is `1` today; a new version adds fields
  and keeps the existing ones.
- `delivery_id` — the same value as `X-Datawatch-Delivery`.
- `sent_at` — when the first attempt was made. It is the same on every retry.
- `host` — the name of the daemon that sent the event.
- `subscription_id` — the subscription that matched.
- `event` — the lifecycle event itself.
- `truncated` — present and `true` only when the event's `decision` and
  `verdict` were removed to keep the body under the size cap (64 KiB).
- `forward` — present only on an event that arrived through peer forwarding
  (see [Peer forwarding](#peer-forwarding)).

**Signature.** The signed string is the timestamp, a full stop, and the raw
request body. The value is `hex(HMAC-SHA256(secret, "<t>" + "." + body))`.
Each attempt is signed with its own timestamp; the body does not change
between attempts.

**Verify it on the receiver.** Check the signature over the raw bytes you
received, before any JSON parsing. Then check the timestamp and de-duplicate
on the delivery id. This Python snippet is a complete check:

```python
import hashlib
import hmac
import time

TOLERANCE_SECONDS = 300  # autonomous.notify.webhook.signature_tolerance_seconds


def verify(secret: bytes, signature_header: str, raw_body: bytes) -> bool:
    fields = dict(part.split("=", 1) for part in signature_header.split(","))
    ts = fields["t"]
    if abs(time.time() - int(ts)) > TOLERANCE_SECONDS:
        return False  # too old or too far in the future: a replay, or clock skew
    expected = hmac.new(secret, ts.encode() + b"." + raw_body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, fields.get("v1", ""))
```

Pass the shared secret as bytes (UTF-8 encoded), and pass the body exactly as
it was received, not re-serialised JSON. Then:

1. Store the `X-Datawatch-Delivery` value and skip any delivery you have
   already handled. A retry after a lost response arrives a second time.
2. Answer with any `2xx` status once the event is stored. Answer quickly; a
   slow receiver is cut off after the attempt timeout and retried.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle webhooks and peer forwarding
chunks.heading: Retries, failures and audit records
chunks.body:
## Retries, failures and audit records

| Setting | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Attempts | 5 in total | `autonomous.notify.webhook.max_attempts` |
| Delays between attempts | 1 s, 4 s, 16 s, 64 s | Each delay has ±20 % random jitter. `backoff_seconds` and `jitter_percent` change them. |
| Time limit per attempt | 10 s | Connect, request and response together |
| Retried | Network errors, timeouts, `408`, `429`, any `5xx` | A `429` `Retry-After` is honoured when it is longer than the next delay, up to 120 s |
| Not retried | Any other `4xx`, any `3xx`, a payload over the cap, a refused host, an unresolvable secret | These fail at once |
| Payload cap | 64 KiB | An over-size event first loses its `decision` and `verdict`. If it is still too large, it is dropped without being sent. |

Redirects are never followed. A `3xx` is a permanent failure, so point the
URL at the final address.

A subscription's own retries run on that subscription's delivery worker. A
slow or failing receiver delays only its own subscription.

**When a delivery is dropped:**

- The subscription is kept. The next matching event tries again.
- A one-shot subscription is kept too. It is removed only after a successful
  delivery.
- One **alert** is raised, titled *Lifecycle webhook delivery failed*, at the
  error level. It appears in the alert list described in
  [Alerts and notifications](alerts-and-notifications.md).

**Audit records.** The audit log is `<data_dir>/audit.log`, one JSON object per
line. When the CEF mirror is enabled (`audit.cef_mirror_enabled`), the same
records are written to `audit.log.cef`, for a SIEM. The action names are:

| Record | JSON-lines action | CEF name | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| Each attempt | `autonomous_lifecycle_webhook_delivery` | `AutonomousLifecycleWebhookDelivery` | After every attempt, and for a refused or skipped delivery. `outcome` is `delivered`, `retry`, `failed`, `refused` or `skipped`. |
| Dropped delivery | `autonomous_lifecycle_webhook_failed` | `AutonomousLifecycleWebhookFailed` | Once, after the attempt records, when a delivery is dropped |

The fields are `subscription_id`, `delivery_id`, `attempt`, `max_attempts`,
`host` (host and port only), `status_code`, `outcome`, `error` and
`duration_ms`. The signing secret, the signature, the body, any user name in
the URL and the URL's query string are never recorded. A subscription that is
created, changed, tested or deleted is also audit-logged.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle webhooks and peer forwarding
chunks.heading: SSRF rules and the allow-listed private host
chunks.body:
## SSRF rules and the allow-listed private host

The daemon will not make a request to an address it should not reach. These
rules run when the subscription is created, on every attempt, and again at
the moment the connection is made, so a name that changes its address later
is still caught.

- **Scheme.** `https` only. Plain `http` is accepted only for a host that is on
  the allow-list.
- **Address classes refused by default:** loopback (`127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`),
  link-local (`169.254.0.0/16`, `fe80::/10`), unspecified, multicast, private
  ranges (RFC 1918 `10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/16`), IPv6 unique-local
  (`fc00::/7`) and Tailscale CGNAT (`100.64.0.0/10`).
- **Allow-listed private host.** The address classes above are allowed only
  when the host is on the allow-list, written as a name or as a literal IP. A
  receiver on your LAN is reachable this way:

  ```sh
  datawatch config set autonomous.notify.webhook.allow_hosts receiver.lan:8443
  ```

  Allow-listing a name trusts that name's DNS. Do not allow-list a name that
  you do not control.
- **Cloud metadata addresses stay refused.** `169.254.169.254` and
  `fd00:ec2::254` are refused even when their host is on the allow-list. This
  is the proposed behaviour, pending the operator's confirmation.
- **Obfuscated IP spellings are refused.** Decimal, octal, hex and short forms
  such as `2130706433`, `0177.0.0.1`, `0x7f.1` and `::ffff:127.0.0.1` are not
  accepted. Write the address in dotted-quad form, or use a name.
- **Proxies are ignored.** The request does not use the proxy environment
  variables.
- **Response size is capped.** The daemon reads only the first part of the
  receiver's response, which is used for diagnostics only.

chunks.title: How-to: Automaton lifecycle webhooks and peer forwarding
chunks.heading: Peer forwarding
chunks.body:
## Peer forwarding

Peer forwarding sends a matching event to another datawatch daemon. You
register that daemon as a federation peer; the subscription names the peer,
and no address or token is stored in the subscription.

**Set up the two daemons:**

1. **On the sending daemon**, register the receiving daemon as a peer. Use the
   token that the receiving daemon issued for this daemon, and grant the
   `autonomous-operator` group (or a capability set that includes
   `autonomous:write`):

   ```sh
   datawatch federation peer add --name hub-east \
     --url https://hub-east.example.net:8443 \
     --token "<token issued to this daemon>" \
     --capabilities autonomous-operator
   ```

2. **On both daemons**, turn on forwarding (`autonomous.notify.forwarding.enabled`
   set to `true`). The sending daemon needs it to create a peer subscription.
   The receiving daemon needs it to accept forwarded events.
3. **On the receiving daemon**, register the sending daemon as a peer with the
   same token and the `autonomous-operator` group. Its token must be the one the
   sending daemon uses, or every forward is refused with `401`.

**Subscribe with the peer sink.** The target is the registered peer name. Letters,
digits, `.`, `_` and `-` are allowed, up to 64 characters. A peer subscription
carries no secret.

```sh
datawatch autonomous subscribe --on task.failed --on prd.blocked \
  --sink peer --target hub-east
```

```text
autonomous subscribe task.failed,prd.blocked sink=peer target=hub-east
```

In the PWA, choose **Federation peer** as the sink and pick the peer from the
list. Creation is refused, and the refusal names the failed condition, when the
peer is not registered, is not enabled, is not a federation peer, or does not
grant `autonomous:write`. The same checks run again on every delivery.

**What the sender sends.** The sender posts the same envelope as the webhook
sink to `<peer base URL>/api/autonomous/events/forward`. The request carries:

- `Authorization: Bearer <token>` for the peer;
- the same `X-Datawatch-Signature`, `X-Datawatch-Delivery` and `X-Datawatch-Event`
  headers, with the peer's token as the signing key;
- an `X-Datawatch-Hop-Chain` header that names the origin and the hops taken.

The envelope has a `forward` block: `origin_host` (the daemon the event started
on), `hops` (how many daemons have handled it, counting the sender) and
`visited` (the host names it has passed through).

**What the receiving daemon sees.** A forwarded event that is accepted is
answered with `202` and then:

- re-emitted to its own subscriptions. Local subscriptions of every sink type
  (comm, session, topic, alert, `mcp_queue` and webhook) see it like any other
  event;
- shown in human-readable sinks with the words `(forwarded from <origin host>)`;
- carried in `mcp_queue` events and in webhook envelopes with its `forward`
  block, so the origin is visible to your code;
- never written to the receiving daemon's Automaton state, and never used to
  drive an Automaton. It is a notification only.

**Loop prevention.** A forwarded event does not go out again.

- A daemon never forwards an event that it received as forwarded. The peer sink
  refuses it.
- A receiving daemon answers `409` and does not accept the event when:
  - its own name is the origin host;
  - its own name is already in the `visited` list;
  - the hop count has reached the cap (`autonomous.notify.forwarding.max_hops`,
    default `3`).
- A `409` is never retried by the sender. Every refusal is audited.

**When the peer is offline.** The sender retries with the same schedule as the
webhook sink (five attempts, 1 s, 4 s, 16 s and 64 s, with jitter). If the
peer is still unreachable after the last attempt, the event is dropped for that
peer, one alert is raised (*Lifecycle peer forward failed*), and the attempts
are audited. There is no outbox: forwarding is best-effort. The sending
daemon's own Automaton state is still the record, and the peer can read it
through the API once it is back. A daemon restart forgets any retry that is in
progress.

**Audit records for forwarding.** The sending side writes
`autonomous_lifecycle_forward_delivery` (CEF name
`AutonomousLifecycleForwardDelivery`) for each attempt and the final outcome.
The receiving side writes `autonomous_lifecycle_forward_receive` (CEF name
`AutonomousLifecycleForwardReceive`) for every forwarded request it answers,
accepted or refused. Neither record contains the bearer token, the signature or
the body.

chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.body:
## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Creation refused: `host … is not on the webhook allow-list` | The receiving host is missing from the allow-list, or the entry has a scheme, path or port that does not match the URL | Add the exact host, or `host:port`, to `autonomous.notify.webhook.allow_hosts` on any surface. Check the URL's port. |
| Creation refused: `the webhook host allow-list is empty` | Nothing has been allow-listed yet | Add the receiving host. An empty list means no host can receive. |
| Creation refused: `webhook delivery is disabled` | The master switch is off | Set `autonomous.notify.webhook.enabled` to `true`. |
| Subscription exists but nothing arrives | The switch is off, or the host was removed from the allow-list after the subscription was created. Both are checked on every event. | Turn the switch on, or add the host back. A `refused` record in the audit log names the host. The subscription needs no change. |
| Alert and audit: `the signing secret could not be resolved` | The vault entry is missing, the name is misspelled, or the vault is locked | Run `datawatch secrets list`, check the name in `${secret:name}`, and set the entry again. |
| Creation refused: `a literal value is refused` | A secret value was typed in place of a reference | Store the value in the vault and reference it as `${secret:name}`. |
| Receiver rejects the signature | A different secret from the vault, a body that was parsed and re-serialised before checking, or clocks more than 300 s apart | Use the same secret value, check the raw body, and check the time on both hosts (NTP). |
| Receiver gets the same event twice | A retry after a lost response | Skip a delivery id you have already handled. |
| Audit shows `refused` with `refusing to connect to a private …` or `is a loopback` | The host resolves to a blocked address class | Use a public name, or allow-list the private host explicitly. Metadata addresses are never allowed. |
| Audit shows `host … did not resolve` | The name does not resolve from the daemon | Check DNS from the daemon's host. |
| Peer subscription refused: `is not a registered, enabled federation peer` | The peer is missing or disabled | Check `datawatch federation peer list` and enable the peer. |
| Peer subscription refused: `does not grant the autonomous:write capability` | The peer's capabilities do not include `autonomous:write` | Set the peer's capabilities to `autonomous-operator`. |
| Peer answers `401` | Missing or wrong bearer token, or a signature made with a different token | Make the token the same on both daemons. Re-issue it if it has been lost. |
| Peer answers `403` | The sending daemon's token is not granted `autonomous:write` on the receiver | Grant the `autonomous-operator` group to that peer on the receiving daemon. |
| Peer answers `409` | A loop rule: the origin is the receiver, the receiver is already in `visited`, or the hop cap was reached | Look for a loop of forwarding peers and remove one link. Raise `max_hops` only if the topology needs it. |
| Peer answers `400` | The envelope is malformed, or it is over the size cap | Check that both daemons use the same `max_body_bytes`. |
| Peer answers `503` | Forwarding is off on the receiver, or its lifecycle engine is not wired. The sender treats `503` as temporary and retries. | Turn forwarding on at the receiver. A permanent `503` ends in a dropped delivery and an alert. |
| Alert: `payload … over the … byte cap` | The event is still too large after its `decision` and `verdict` are removed | Raise `autonomous.notify.webhook.max_body_bytes` (on both daemons when forwarding). |
| Peer offline, events missing on the peer | Forwarding has no outbox. A dropped event is not replayed. | Read the Automaton state through the API. Watch the forward alert and audit to see which events were dropped. |

Describe a feature in plain English; datawatch **plans** it into a
structured hierarchy of stories + tasks, queues it for review, then
runs the approved tasks under verification.
This howto walks the spawn → plan → review → run loop.

chunks.title: How-to: Autonomous planning
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

An Automaton is a structured spec that the daemon's autonomous
executor walks through: each story has tasks; each task spawns a
session against a configured backend; per-story Evals + scan
guardrails verify output before advancing. Operator-gated approval
(per-story or whole-automaton) keeps the human in the loop.

States: `draft` → `planning` → `needs_review` → `approved` → `running`
→ `blocked` / `completed` / `failed` / `rejected` / `cancelled` /
`archived`.

## Base requirements

- `datawatch start` — daemon up.
- A configured LLM backend (claude-code, opencode-acp, ollama, etc.).
  See [`llm-registry.md`](llm-registry.md) for registering and managing

  the daemon's host runs each task directly. See
  [`profiles.md`](profiles.md) for Cluster Profile setup.
- (Optional) An Evals suite per story for graded verification. See
  [`evals.md`](evals.md).
- (Optional) A Project Profile pre-baked with workspace + skills. See
  [`profiles.md`](profiles.md) and [`skills-sync.md`](skills-sync.md)
  for Skills setup.

chunks.title: How-to: Autonomous planning
chunks.heading: Setup
chunks.body:
## Setup

No setup beyond a backend + (optional) profile.

```sh
# Confirm autonomous subsystem is on (default: yes).
datawatch config get autonomous.enabled
#  → true
```

Optional YAML to pin a planning backend (v7 config key):

```yaml
# ~/.datawatch/datawatch.yaml
autonomous:
  enabled: true
  planning_backend: claude-code   # was "decomposition_backend" before v7.0
  planning_effort: high           # was "decomposition_effort"
  planning_model: ""              # was "decomposition_model" — empty = LLM default
  max_concurrent_tasks: 1         # tasks of one Automaton run at once; 1 = sequential
```

`max_concurrent_tasks` is the daemon-wide default for how many independent
tasks of one Automaton run at the same time. An Automaton's own
`max_concurrent_tasks` overrides it, and tasks of different Automata are not
limited by it. The old `max_parallel_tasks` key is deprecated: it never had
any effect, is accepted and ignored with a startup warning for one release,
and will then be removed.

The old keys (`decomposition_backend` / `decomposition_effort` /
`decomposition_model`) are still accepted on read for backward
compatibility.

chunks.title: How-to: Autonomous planning
chunks.heading: 4a. Happy path — CLI
chunks.body:
### 4a. Happy path — CLI

```sh
# 1. Submit a free-form spec.
PRD_ID=$(datawatch autonomous create \
  --name "auth-refactor" \
  --title "Refactor auth to use JWT-only sessions" \
  --goal "Replace cookie+CSRF with JWT-only; deprecate the cookie middleware" \
  --backend claude-code \
  --profile prod-audit 2>&1 | grep -oP 'id=\K[0-9a-f]+')

# 2. Trigger planning (LLM-driven; async).
#    "prd-plan" is the canonical command; "prd-decompose" is a back-compat alias.
datawatch autonomous prd-plan $PRD_ID
sleep 60
datawatch autonomous get $PRD_ID
#  → status: needs_review
#    stories:
#      - "Audit current auth flow" (3 tasks)
#      - "Implement JWT issuance" (4 tasks)
#      - "Migrate session middleware" (5 tasks)
#      - "Update tests + docs" (3 tasks)

# 3. Review (see autonomous-review-approve.md for the full review flow).
#    Quick approve all if it looks good:
datawatch autonomous approve $PRD_ID

# 4. Run.
datawatch autonomous run $PRD_ID

# 5. Watch progress.
watch -n 5 "datawatch autonomous get $PRD_ID | jq '{status, stories: .stories|map({title, status, completed_tasks})}'"

# 6. Inspect a specific story / task on completion.
datawatch autonomous get $PRD_ID --story 1 --task 2

# 7. Cancel mid-run if needed.
datawatch autonomous cancel $PRD_ID

# 8. Clean up after archival.
datawatch autonomous delete $PRD_ID
```

chunks.title: How-to: Autonomous planning
chunks.heading: 4b. Happy path — PWA
chunks.body:
### 4b. Happy path — PWA

1. Bottom nav → **Automata** tab.
   The list is **active-first sorted**: waiting-input / needs-review →
   blocked → running → planning → completed/archived. Each card shows
   the automaton name, status badge, and last-activity timestamp.
   - **Pin** (📌) any card to lock it at the top regardless of state.
     Pin state persists across reloads.
   - **Inline actions** on each card: Open / Pause / Resume / Cancel /
     Approve (Approve is highlighted yellow when the automaton needs
     your attention).
2. Click the **⚡** FAB → wizard:
   - Top strip: **Start from template** (if you have any saved).
   - Intent: free-text spec.
   - Inferred: type / workspace (auto-derived from intent).
   - Execution: backend / effort.
   - Advanced (collapsed): guided mode, scan, rules, story-approval.
   - **Start**.
3. The automaton appears in the list with status `planning`. Click it to
   open the detail view.
4. Detail view 4-tab layout:
   - **Overview** — spec + status + persistent toolbar.
   - **Stories** — per-story state + Edit / Profile / Files /
     Approve / Reject. Click the ▶ triangle to expand a story's
     tasks inline; click again to collapse. First click works
     immediately — no navigation required.
   - **Decisions** — every state-changing event with expandable
     `details` payload.
   - **Scan** — Run Scan + history.
   The detail header also shows the **initial spec** (expandable —
   click "show full" if the spec exceeds 280 characters).
5. When `status: needs_review`, click **Approve** in the toolbar (or
   per-story approve in the Stories tab — see
   [`autonomous-review-approve.md`](autonomous-review-approve.md)).
6. Click **Run** in the toolbar. The status transitions to `running`.
   While running or decomposing the header shows **status graphs**:
   a ✓/✗ decompose indicator, total story + task counts, and a
   per-story progress bar (X/Y tasks, %) with async CPU%/RSS data
   from active compute envelopes.
7. To cancel mid-run: **Cancel** is always visible in the toolbar for
   non-cancelled automata (including while running). To archive when
   complete: **Archive**.

### 5b. REST

```sh
# Create.
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"auth-refactor","title":"...","goal":"...","backend":"claude-code"}' \
  $BASE/api/autonomous/prds

# Plan (canonical endpoint; /decompose is a back-compat alias).
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  $BASE/api/autonomous/prds/$PRD_ID/plan

# Get.
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $BASE/api/autonomous/prds/$PRD_ID

# Approve / Run / Cancel / Archive.
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $BASE/api/autonomous/prds/$PRD_ID/approve
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $BASE/api/autonomous/prds/$PRD_ID/run
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $BASE/api/autonomous/prds/$PRD_ID/cancel
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $BASE/api/autonomous/prds/$PRD_ID/archive

# Hard delete.
curl -sk -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "$BASE/api/autonomous/prds/$PRD_ID?hard=true"
```

```yaml
  - rules
```

chunks.title: How-to: Autonomous planning
chunks.heading: Declaring files for write tasks
chunks.body:
## Declaring files for write tasks

The plan-coverage check expects a task that writes to say which files it
changes. A task whose title starts with a write verb (`Write`, `Add`, `Update`,
`Create`, `Fix`, `Bump`, `Implement`, `Document`, `Register`, `Wire`, `Make`,
`Move`, `Replace`, `Rename`, `Extend`, `Remove`) must list those files in its
`files` list. A task with no files gets the `write_task_without_files` finding,
which blocks approval in the default `block` mode. See the
[coverage gate](../operations.md#plan-requirement-coverage-gate-autonomousplan_coverage_check)
for the modes and the acknowledge path.

When a task changes nothing, make the **first line of its spec** `READ-ONLY:`
followed by a reason. Only the first non-empty line counts, and the case does
not matter. The check looks only at the marker, so the reason is for the people
reading the plan and is not enforced:

```text
READ-ONLY: audits the retry paths and reports what it finds; no file is edited.
List every call site of the retry helper and note which ones skip the backoff.
```

A task that does change files needs no marker; it lists them instead, for
example `internal/config/config.go` and `internal/config/config_test.go` for a
task titled "Add the retry setting to the config loader".

These are exempt without a marker:

- a task of kind `smoke` or `final_gate`;
- a task whose title contains one of the phrases `final gate`, `stability gate`,
  `suite run`, `eval`, `install` or `investigation` as whole words. Only the
  title is matched, never the spec, so a doc task that mentions a test suite in
  its body is still checked.

chunks.heading: Choose the verifier per task, story or Automaton
chunks.body:
## Choose the verifier per task, story or Automaton

After a task runs, a verifier LLM judges the work. By default every
task uses the global `autonomous.verification_backend` /
`verification_model` / `verification_effort` (or the
`verification_backends` pool). Since v9.0.67 you can override that per
task, per story or per Automaton while the Automaton is in review
(`needs_review` / `revisions_asked`) or cancelled.

When to use it:

- **Routine tasks** (docs, renames, test fixtures): point the story or
  Automaton at a cheaper, faster verifier, such as a local Ollama model.
- **Risky tasks** (auth, migrations, anything touching data): give the
  one task a stronger verifier and higher effort.
- **Independence:** use a different backend for verifying than for
  doing the work.

Most specific wins: task → story → Automaton → Automation → global. Set a
**backend** at the level you want; a model or effort without any
per-unit backend leaves the verifier on the global path. An explicit
backend also skips the `verification_backends` pool. Send `""` (or an
empty field in the PWA) to clear and inherit again.

```bash
# Stronger verifier for one risky task.
datawatch autonomous prd-set-task-verification-llm <id> --task <task-id> \
  --backend claude-code --model opus --effort high

# Cheaper verifier for a routine story.
datawatch autonomous prd-set-story-verification-llm <id> --story <story-id> \
  --backend ollama --model qwen3:8b

# Clear the task override.
datawatch autonomous prd-set-task-verification-llm <id> --task <task-id> \
  --backend "" --model "" --effort ""
```

PWA: task **Edit**, story **LLM** or Automaton **Set LLM** →
*Verification LLM* row. MCP: `autonomous_prd_set_task_verification_llm`
/ `_set_story_verification_llm` / `_set_verification_llm`. Chat:
`autonomous set-task-verification-llm <id> <task-id> backend=claude-code model=opus`.
REST: `POST /api/autonomous/prds/{id}/set_task_verification_llm`
(see [`../api/autonomous.md`](../api/autonomous.md)).

**Read which verifier actually ran.** After verification, the task's
`verification` object in `datawatch autonomous prd-get <id>` (or
`GET /api/autonomous/prds/{id}`) carries `verifier_backend`,
`verifier_model`, `verifier_effort` and `verifier_source`. The source
tells you where the choice came from: `task`, `story`, `prd` (the
Automaton level), `automation` (the default set on the Automation the
Automaton belongs to), `global`, or `pool`. In the PWA the verification
result shows a **Judged by** line. If you set an override and still see
`global` or `pool`, check that a backend (not just a model) was set.

**Read which backend ran the work.** The same way, each task carries an

chunks.title: How-to: Autonomous planning
chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Planning hangs.** Backend slow or unreachable. `datawatch
  autonomous get $PRD_ID` shows `status: planning` for >5 min →
  check backend health (`datawatch llm test <name>`).
- **Approve without review.** Easy to fall into; for non-trivial
  Automata always at least read the Stories tab. Per-story approve gives
  finer control.
- **Run without approve.** Returns 400 (`approval required`). Approve
  first.
- **Story blocks on Evals failure.** That's the safety net working —
  inspect the failed grader, fix or accept-with-rationale.
- **Spec changes mid-run.** Edit-Spec + Run-Continue is supported,
  but the LLM only sees the new spec on the next task spawn; in-flight
  tasks finish under the old spec.
- **Duplicate session for the same task after a retry or daemon
  restart.** Fixed — the executor now kills a task's previous session
  before spawning its replacement, on every path (retry, boot-resume).
  See [`task-session-reconcile-flow.md`](../flow/task-session-reconcile-flow.md).

- **Tasks fail with `scope: ...`, or the Overview shows Scope warnings.**
  Workers and the planner are confined to the project directory (the
  PRD's *writable* directories) plus any *read-only* directories. A plan
  that names a path outside them (for example "work in another repo")
  is flagged at planning time and its tasks are refused at start rather
  than wandering. Fix the task text, or open Settings and add the
  directory under Read-only or Writable directories (REST:
  `POST /api/autonomous/prds/{id}/set_dirs`). Put a research
  Automaton's output folder in the project directory, not elsewhere.
- **Tasks show "waiting for capacity".** The host, a compute node or an LLM is full; the task starts when a slot frees and is not failed. See [`automata-capacity.md`](automata-capacity.md).
- **A story shows failed although its files exist.** A story is marked
  completed only when none of its tasks failed. Reset the failed task
  after fixing the cause and the story rolls up again.

## Live progress in the Status tab

While an Automaton is running, open any of its worker sessions and switch to
the **Status** tab to see a live task tree updated in real time via WebSocket.
Each story in the Automata detail view also shows a "● Status" quick-link to
jump directly to that worker session's Status tab.

carries its own live progress strip (removed in 9.31.3 — it took a lot of
room and once showed another session's stale pi log numbers on a non-pi
session); for pi sessions the data is still available at

# How-to: Recover a stuck, failed, or incorrectly-terminal Automaton

[`autonomous-planning.md`](autonomous-planning.md) covers the normal
spawn → plan → run → complete loop. This howto covers the unhappy paths:
a task fails or gets stuck, a story gets cancelled and never restarted,
or an Automaton reaches `completed` while a story inside it is still
`cancelled`. It also covers `repair_depends_on`, a one-time fix for
Automata whose stories/tasks were created before v8.36.5.

chunks.title: How-to: Recover a stuck, failed, or incorrectly-terminal Automaton
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

Three operator-facing repair tools, all scoped to a single story or task
so you never have to discard a partially-completed run:

- **`reset_task`** — puts one task back to pending so the run picks it
  up again. Without `force`, only `failed`/`blocked` tasks qualify. With
  `force: true`, it also requeues a `completed` or `cancelled` task —
  and, as of v8.36.6, this works even when the *Automaton* itself has
  already reached `completed`, and correctly reopens the task's story if
  that story was `cancelled` (previously only `completed`/`failed`
  stories reopened — a cancelled one had no recovery path at all).
- **`cancel_story`** / **`cancel_task`** — stop an individual story or
  task without cancelling the whole Automaton. The most common cause of
  the "completed Automaton with a cancelled story inside it" scenario
  below is cancelling a story mid-run to fix something, then forgetting
  to `reset_task` it back — the run then proceeds around the gap.
- **`repair_depends_on`** — resolves `depends_on` entries against real
  story/task IDs. Decompose can only reference a sibling by its title
  (IDs don't exist until stories are saved), and versions before v8.36.5
  never translated those titles to IDs afterward — so on an Automaton
  planned before that fix, `depends_on` still holds raw titles and was
  never actually enforced. Safe to call on any Automaton; a no-op if
  everything already resolves.

A fourth path, `rejudge` (covered below), is for the opposite stuck
state: an Automaton whose tasks are all already `completed` but which
ended `blocked` on its completion guardrail — it re-runs that guardrail
as a fresh judgment without resetting anything.

chunks.title: How-to: Recover a stuck, failed, or incorrectly-terminal Automaton
chunks.heading: Fixing it
chunks.body:
## Fixing it

`reset_task`, `cancel_story`, `cancel_task`, and `repair_depends_on` are
REST + MCP only — there's no `datawatch autonomous` CLI subcommand for
any of them yet (the CLI has `prd-get` and whole-Automaton `prd-cancel`,
but nothing per-story/per-task). Use `datawatch autonomous prd-get <id>`
to confirm the diagnosis, then the REST or MCP calls below to fix it:

1. Confirm the diagnosis — look for a cancelled story next to a
   completed one that depends on it (`prd-get`, or the REST/MCP reads
   below).
2. If this Automaton predates v8.36.5, resolve `depends_on` titles to
   real IDs first, so dependency ordering is actually enforced on the
   retry below (no-op if already resolved).
3. Force-requeue the cancelled story's tasks, in dependency order
   (oldest task ID first is a safe proxy for creation order if you'd
   rather not read the `depends_on` graph by hand).
4. Once the skipped story's tasks complete for real, force-requeue any
   downstream tasks that ran without them, so they redo their work
   using the now-real prerequisite output.

Each `reset_task` call restores the Automaton to `running` and reopens
its story to `pending` automatically; the daemon's executor picks the
newly-pending task back up without any separate "resume" step.

chunks.heading: Re-judging a blocked Automaton whose guardrail verdict was lost (`rejudge`)
chunks.body:
## Re-judging a blocked Automaton whose guardrail verdict was lost (`rejudge`)

A different stuck state from the ones above: every task completed fine, but
the Automaton ended `blocked` because the completion guardrail's verdict was
lost or in doubt. The **rejudge** action asks for that same completion
guardrail to run again — as a fresh judgment — without resetting or retrying
any task:

- The Automaton must be `blocked`; re-judging one that isn't is refused.
- **Every task in every story must be `completed`.** If any task is pending,
  running, failed, or cancelled, the call is refused and names the first such
  task and its status — fix that one first (`reset_task` above) and re-judge
  once the genuine work is done.
- It never resets anything: no task goes back to pending, no story reopens.

Outcome, in every case written to the Automaton's decision log (attributed
to the acting operator) **before** any status change:

- **Pass** — the blocked reason is cleared and the Automaton becomes
  `completed` in the same step.
- **Block** — the Automaton stays `blocked`, and its blocked reason is
  updated from the new verdict.
- **No verdict** (the judge failed or returned nothing) — the Automaton
  stays `blocked` with its previous blocked reason, and an error is
  returned so you see the re-judge produced no judgment.

Reading the judge's verdict:

- **Issues come back normalized to strings, whatever the judge emitted.**
  The guardrail judge and the per-task verifier may return `issues` as
  plain strings or as objects (with `description`/`message`/`file`/`line`/
  `severity` keys); objects are rendered into one readable line (for
  example `[high] pkg/file.go:42: description / message`) before the
  verdict is stored, so an object-shaped or mixed issues value never
  drops the verdict.
- **The raw judge text is kept on the verdict** in `raw_judge` (truncated
  to 16 KiB), so you can inspect exactly what the judge wrote even when
  its format was off.
- **A PRD that was blocked earlier by
  `json: cannot unmarshal object into GuardrailVerdict.issues.0 of type
  string` now passes when rejudged** — the lenient decoder accepts the
  object-shaped issues that previously failed the whole verdict, so the
  re-judge surfaces the real judgment instead of a decode failure.

chunks.title: How-to: Recover a stuck, failed, or incorrectly-terminal Automaton
chunks.heading: What happens to Automata when the daemon restarts
chunks.body:
## What happens to Automata when the daemon restarts

When the daemon starts, it looks at every Automaton that was in flight and decides whether to pick it back up. Two kinds are considered:

- a **running** Automaton, and
- a **failed** Automaton whose failed tasks were all killed by the restart itself (as opposed to tasks that failed on their own merits).

Each is checked against two things: its age, compared with `autonomous.resume_max_age_seconds`, and whether its project directory still exists.

| `autonomous.resume_max_age_seconds` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `3600` (default) | Resume only Automata that were active within the last hour |
| `0` | Never auto-resume; every candidate is parked |
| `-1` | No age limit (a missing project directory still parks it) |

What happens next:

- **Fresh** (within the limit, directory present): the Automaton is recovered and continues.
- **Stale** (older than the limit, or directory missing): the Automaton is parked as `blocked` with a plain-English reason, an operator alert is raised, and an entry is added to the boot-resume report (`Status().BootResume`). Nothing runs on its own; review it and resume it with the resume action if you still want it.
- **Live worker**: a worker session that is still alive on an `in_progress` task counts as activity, and so does its recent output. An Automaton with a live worker is never treated as stale just because its stored timestamps are old.
- **Resuming a parked Automaton**: use the resume action, which is available everywhere. Approval is not the right action, because a parked Automaton is already approved. REST: `POST /api/autonomous/prds/{id}/resume` with an optional `note`. MCP: `autonomous_prd_resume`. CLI: `datawatch autonomous prd-resume <id> [--note "..."]`. Chat: `autonomous resume <id> [note]`. PWA: the Resume button on the parked Automaton, which shows the park reason. Only an Automaton parked by the boot-resume gate can be resumed this way; any other state is rejected with an error naming the allowed state. A live worker is re-adopted rather than respawned.
- **Cancelled**: an Automaton you cancelled is never recovered.

chunks.heading: Reading the boot-resume report
chunks.body:
### Reading the boot-resume report

Each decision is an entry in `Status().BootResume` with an `outcome` of `resumed`, `parked` or `resumed_by_operator`, the age in seconds and a reason. A `parked` entry that also has `live_sessions` means the Automaton was parked (for example its project directory was missing, or auto-resume is off) while a worker session was still alive. Nothing was killed: resuming it re-adopts those sessions instead of starting new ones. A `resumed_by_operator` entry records your resume action and lists the sessions that were adopted.

Old failed Automata are therefore no longer re-launched at every restart.

chunks.heading: Restarting the daemon while a task is in progress
chunks.body:
## Restarting the daemon while a task is in progress

Restarting the daemon no longer wastes a task that was already `in_progress`
with a live worker session. On boot, the resumed run looks at each
`in_progress` task and does one of three things:

- **Adopts the live worker** (the common case, when the worker's session
  survived the restart and its agent had started). The task stays `in_progress` on the *same* session
  id, keeps holding its capacity slot, and the resumed run simply waits for
  the worker to finish and then verifies its result. No second worker is
  spawned and no duplicate session appears for the same task.
- **Sends the task straight to verification** when the worker session is
  gone but its output already recorded a completion marker — the work
  finished in the shutdown window, so verifying the existing output is
  faster than re-running it.
- **Resets the task to `pending`** only when the session is dead *and* no
  completion marker exists, or when the live session is a bare shell whose
  agent never started (see the next section). The old behavior was to reset unconditionally
  and kill the worker; that is no longer the case.

This applies to every worker backend (`claude-code`, `opencode` and
`pi-prompt`). claude-code workers are adopted too: completion detection after
a restart ignores the task text the daemon typed into the session and the
input placeholder, so a restart does not make a running claude-code worker
look finished. The Automaton itself also stays `running` across the restart:
boot-resume recreates its executor under the same lock a manual run uses, so
there is no gap in which another run request could start a second executor
for the same Automaton.

As operator this needs no action. If a restart happens mid-run, watch the
Automaton with `prd_get`: an adopted task keeps its `session_id` and
surfaces an `adopted_session` marker, and the session list shows the same
worker session continuing to run. A reset task is the one to question —
check the session's log for why it died (crash, OOM, operator kill) before
resetting it again.

chunks.heading: A launch that was held at restart
chunks.body:
### A launch that was held at restart

If the daemon restarts while a worker's first launch is still held, the pane
holds only a bare shell with no agent in it. The daemon does not adopt that
shell as the task's session:

- At boot the shell is ended and the task goes back to `pending` with the
  error `session never started`. No retry is counted, and the task is launched
  once more on a new session. A task that was `verifying` on such a session is
  requeued the same way.
- An adopted claude-code worker is held to the same start-confirm bound as a
  launched one, `autonomous.session_start_confirm_seconds` (default 120
  seconds). The bound is measured from the worker's last evidence of life, so a
  worker that was active just before the restart is not ended early. A launched
  worker has no evidence of life until its first sign of work, so its clock
  starts at the first check that finds it silent. A worker that sits in
  `waiting_input` with no sign of work past the bound is ended as a start
  failure. The first two such failures requeue the task and the third fails
  it. A bare shell found at boot does not count toward that budget, and neither
  does the normal retry budget.

What you see: after a restart the task's error reads `session never started`
and it runs again on a new session id. If a task fails on its start budget, its
last pane lines are kept on the task. Check the agent install and any startup
dialog in that pane before you retry the task.

chunks.heading: Launches still running at shutdown
chunks.body:
### Launches still running at shutdown

On a stop the daemon waits up to 6 seconds for the HTTP server to finish, so
no new launch arrives over HTTP. It then refuses new session launches and
gives each launch still in progress a fixed 15 seconds to finish. A launch that
finishes inside that time is adopted by the next boot like any other live
session. A launch still running after it is rolled back: its session is ended,
the next boot does not adopt it, and the daemon logs
`[session] rolled back launch <id>: still running at shutdown` for each one.
When every launch finishes in time, nothing is logged. The 15 seconds is a
fixed value, not a config key.

chunks.heading: How a task stays tied to its worker session
chunks.body:
### How a task stays tied to its worker session

- **The link is saved at launch.** The link between a task and its worker
  session is written to disk when the session is created, before the first
  prompt is delivered. A restart at any point after launch therefore still
  knows which session belongs to the task.
- **Boot reconcile adopts an unlinked live session.** If the link is empty
  (for example the daemon stopped between creating the session and saving the
  link), boot reconcile still looks for a live session that belongs to the
  task and adopts it instead of starting a second worker.
- **A reset ends every live session first.** When a task is reset and
  relaunched, every live session of that task and of its worktree is ended
  before the new worker starts, so two workers never write to the same
  worktree. The task history records which sessions were ended.

chunks.heading: Orphan session sweep
chunks.body:
### Orphan session sweep

A periodic sweep looks for live task worker sessions that are bound to no
non-terminal task. A session is given a grace period before anything is done
to it; the period is `autonomous.orphan_grace_seconds` (default `300`; `0` or
unset uses the default). The sweep compares session ids in short form, the text after the last hyphen, so a worker bound to a task is never ended because of how its id is written.

1. **Report.** The first time a session is seen unbound, the sweep records a
   note in the Automaton's decision history and writes an audit entry
   (`autonomous_orphan_session_seen`).
2. **End.** If the session is still unbound after the grace period, the sweep
   ends it, records the outcome in the history and writes an audit entry
   (`autonomous_orphan_session_ended`).

A session that gets bound to a task again within the grace period is left
alone.

chunks.title: How-to: Recover a stuck, failed, or incorrectly-terminal Automaton
chunks.heading: Stuck-running watchdog
chunks.body:
### Stuck-running watchdog

An Automaton can sit in `running` with every task finished (completed, failed
or cancelled), no live worker, verifier or guardrail session, and no executor
holding it, for example when the completion rollup was lost. A periodic
watchdog, built like the orphan sweep, looks for that state. The bound is
`autonomous.stuck_running_seconds` (default `900`, 15 minutes; `0` or a negative
value uses the default). It is read on every pass, so a change applies without
a restart.

1. **Re-check.** The first pass that sees the Automaton in that state only
   starts the clock. After one full bound the watchdog records a
   `stuck_running_refire` note in the Automaton's decision history and re-runs
   the completion rollup once, the same way boot resume does. The clock
   restarts.
2. **Block.** If the Automaton is still in that state after a second full
   bound, the watchdog moves it to `blocked`. It records a
   `stuck_running_blocked` decision with the reason, writes an audit entry
   (`autonomous_stuck_running_blocked`, with the time stuck and the bound) and
   fires the usual status event, so the Automaton shows as blocked in the PWA
   and in notifications. If something else changed the Automaton at the same
   moment, that change wins and the watchdog leaves it alone.

The clock starts over whenever the state stops holding: a session starts, a
task is reset to pending, or the Automaton leaves `running`. To clear a blocked
Automaton, use `rejudge` (above) when every task completed, or `reset_task`
for a task that did not.

Set the bound on the PWA Settings Automata card ("Stuck Automaton timeout"),
with `datawatch config set autonomous.stuck_running_seconds <n>`, through
`PUT /api/config`, the MCP `config_set` tool, or `configure
autonomous.stuck_running_seconds=<n>` in a comm channel.

chunks.heading: Checking this against a sandbox daemon (opt-in live test)
chunks.body:
### Checking this against a sandbox daemon (opt-in live test)

The deterministic tests run with `go test ./internal/autonomous/`. The live
check starts a long worker, restarts the daemon mid-task, and asserts the
session id is unchanged, the worker was not killed, no second session was
spawned for the task, and the task reaches verification. It is skipped unless
`DW_LIVE_RESTART_TEST=1`, so normal test runs never touch a daemon. Run it
only against a sandbox daemon, never production, from the daemon's host with
the same `TMUX_TMPDIR` as that daemon:

```sh
env -u TMUX -u TMUX_TMPDIR \
DW_LIVE_RESTART_TEST=1 DW_BASE=https://127.0.0.1:18443 DW_BASE_TOKEN=... \
  DW_LIVE_RESTART_CMD='<command that restarts the sandbox daemon>' \
  go test -count=1 -timeout 25m -run TestDaemonRestartAdoptsLiveWorkerLive -v ./internal/session/
```

The same check for a claude-code worker is a separate test:

```sh
env -u TMUX -u TMUX_TMPDIR \
DW_LIVE_RESTART_TEST=1 DW_BASE=https://127.0.0.1:18443 DW_BASE_TOKEN=... \
  go test -count=1 -timeout 25m -run TestDaemonRestartAdoptsLiveClaudeCodeWorkerLive -v ./internal/session/
```

`DW_LIVE_RESTART_BACKEND` selects the worker backend for that test (default
`claude-code`); the default-backend test ignores it.

Leave `DW_LIVE_RESTART_CMD` unset to restart through the operator path
(`systemctl --user restart datawatch`, falling back to `datawatch restart`);
only do that when that unit is the daemon behind `DW_BASE`. Optional:
`DW_LIVE_RESTART_PROJECT_DIR` sets the probe's project directory.

chunks.heading: Task failed with `no matching files found` (docs-bm25-index) or "no new changes to verify"
chunks.body:
## Task failed with `no matching files found` (docs-bm25-index) or "no new changes to verify"

Symptom: a task is reported `failed` even though the worker's own work
was fine — either the verification build shows
`pattern assets/docs-bm25-index.json: no matching files found`, or the
task simply failed with "no new changes to verify".

**Cause.** The `internal/docsindex` package go:embeds
`assets/docs-bm25-index.json`, a git-ignored generated artifact. A
fresh git worktree checkout does not contain the file, so packages that
import it (`internal/server`, `cmd/datawatch`) cannot compile, the
build/verification step fails, and the task ends up reported failed
with nothing to verify.

**Fixed now — worktrees self-heal.** When the daemon creates or
reuses a PRD worktree it now prepares the tree: in repos with
`internal/docsindex` it writes the same `{}` placeholder `make
docs-index` writes, only if the file is missing (an existing index is
never touched), keeps it git-ignored (falling back to the worktree's
own `info/exclude` if the ignore rule is absent), and never stages or
commits it. Both new and reused worktrees get this, so this failure
should not recur for worktrees created by the current daemon.

**Manual fix for a worktree created by an older daemon.** Run `make
docs-index` inside the worktree, or create
`internal/docsindex/assets/docs-bm25-index.json` containing `{}` (the
placeholder `make docs-index` would seed). Then retry the task with
`reset_task` (above) if it was left `failed`.

chunks.title: How-to: Recover a stuck, failed, or incorrectly-terminal Automaton
chunks.heading: Worker finished a turn without the completion marker
chunks.body:
## Worker finished a turn without the completion marker

A claude-code worker sometimes finishes its turn, goes quiet at the prompt
and never prints `DATAWATCH_COMPLETE`. Instead of waiting for the longer
session idle timeout, datawatch sends the worker one nudge.

- **When it fires:** the worker session has been in `waiting_input` or
  `idle` with no new output for `autonomous.worker_idle_nudge_seconds`
  (default `180`), and no completion marker has appeared.
- **What it sends:** one message asking the worker to print its completion
  line, or to continue if it is not finished. Only one nudge is ever sent
  per task attempt.
- **No nudge while work is running:** only work children block a nudge. A
  work child is a process the worker's runner started, such as a build, a
  test run or a long command; while one is alive the worker is not idle, so
  no nudge is sent, and the idle clock restarts once it exits. The worker's
  own channel and MCP servers do not count as work, so a worker that has
  only those running is still nudged. The rule holds after a daemon restart:
  an adopted worker is nudged and blocked by the same work-child check.
- **What gets recorded:** each nudge is stored on the task as an event
  (`nudge_events`: time, count, `session_id` and outcome) and the task's
  `nudge_count` goes up. Both show in `autonomous_prd_get`. The `session_id`
  names the session the nudge was typed into, so a retry in a fresh session
  does not inherit the old nudge state.
- **Outcome values:** a new event is `sent` once the nudge is typed. It then
  becomes `answered` when the worker prints its completion marker or fresh
  output follows, or `stalled` when the worker stays silent past the stall
  window.
- **If the worker answers:** a completion marker or fresh output after the
  nudge ends the wait normally (outcome `answered`) and the task is verified
  like any other.
- **If it stays silent:** after `autonomous.worker_idle_nudge_stall_seconds`
  (default `600`, counted from the nudge) the worker is treated as stalled.
  It goes through the existing retry path (`auto_fix_retries`), the same as
  any other stalled worker; once that budget is spent the task fails.
- **Where the counts show:** `GET /api/autonomous/status` and the MCP
  `autonomous_status` tool report `nudges_total`, `nudge_tasks` (per-task
  counts) and `nudges_by_backend`. The fields are omitted when no nudge has
  been sent.
- **Setting them:** both keys are hot-applied, no restart. Use `config.yaml`,
  the web settings card, `PUT /api/config`, MCP `autonomous_config_set`, or
  the `configure` chat command. A value of `0` means "use the default".

```yaml
autonomous:
  worker_idle_nudge_seconds: 180
  worker_idle_nudge_stall_seconds: 600
```

chunks.heading: Confirming a nudge fired
chunks.body:
### Confirming a nudge fired

Three places show what the daemon did with a worker's nudge: the journal,
the task record and the config read.

1. **The wait-start line.** When a claude-code worker finishes its turn, the
   daemon logs one line as the wait for the completion marker begins:

   ```
   [autonomous] post-turn wait start: session <session> task <automaton>/<task>: backend family claude-code, nudge applies=yes, nudge window 3m0s, stall window 10m0s, session idle limit 15m0s, persisted nudge=false
   ```

   The second part of `task <automaton>/<task>` is the Automaton ID and the
   task ID. `nudge applies=yes` means the nudge owns this worker's idle clock.
   `pending` means the session was not visible yet; the daemon reads the
   backend family on each tick until it is, then logs
   `backend family resolved to claude-code; nudge applies=yes`. `no` means the
   worker is not claude-code and is never nudged. `persisted nudge=true` means
   a nudge for this session is already recorded on the task, so it is not sent
   again.

   If the nudge window is not shorter than the session idle limit, a
   `post-turn wait warning` line follows, once for that wait. The idle detector
   can then end the worker before the nudge is sent.

2. **The nudge and its outcome.** When the nudge is typed, the journal gets:

   ```
   [autonomous] idle worker <session> task <automaton>/<task>: nudge 1 sent after 3m0s idle
   ```

   The answer is logged the same way: `nudge answered by completion marker`,
   `nudge answered by new output` or `nudge answered by session completion`.
   A worker still silent after the stall window logs
   `still silent for <duration> after nudge; ending session for retry`.

3. **The task record.** `autonomous_prd_get` shows the task's `nudge_count`
   and `nudge_events`. Each event has `at`, `count`, `session_id` and
   `outcome`. Find the event whose `session_id` is the worker's session: its
   `outcome` is `sent` (typed, no answer yet), `answered` or `stalled`.

**Reading the effective windows.** Unset settings are not shown in
`config.yaml`, so read the windows the daemon actually applies. `GET /api/config`
has an `autonomous` section with two read-only keys:
`worker_idle_nudge_effective_seconds` (the nudge window) and
`worker_idle_nudge_stall_effective_seconds` (the stall window). With both
settings unset they read `180` and `600`. A setting of `0` or less also reads
as the default. The same section is returned by MCP `get_config` with
`section: autonomous`. The keys cannot be set; change the settings themselves.

**What the idle detector says now.** If the session idle detector ends a
worker, its end reason finishes with the nudge history for that session:

- `..., no nudge sent`: no nudge was recorded for the session.
- `..., nudge 1 sent at 2026-10-25T16:20:00Z, outcome answered`: the nudge
  came first. The outcome is `sent` when no answer was recorded.

**Which workers are nudged.** The nudge applies to every claude-code worker
waiting after its turn, whatever status the task shows, including a task in
`verifying` whose only lease is the worker's. A worker whose session was not
yet visible when its wait began is nudged from its first visible tick.

chunks.title: How-to: Recover a stuck, failed, or incorrectly-terminal Automaton
chunks.heading: Task failed with `session never started`
chunks.body:
## Task failed with `session never started`

A claude-code worker was handed its task and then sat in `waiting_input`
with no sign of work for longer than `autonomous.session_start_confirm_seconds`
(default `120`). The daemon ends that session and retries the task. After two
such start failures the task stays failed.

- **What counts as started:** an assistant turn; a tool call in progress or
  finished (a `⏺` tool line, a `⎿` result line or a spinner); a process the
  worker started; a change in the pane; or a channel event after the task was
  delivered. Delivering the task alone does not count.
- **A long silent tool call is not a failure:** a worker that is inside one
  long command keeps its tool line and spinner on screen, which keeps the clock
  running. Only silence longer than the bound ends a session.
- **After a daemon restart:** a worker that was adopted is measured from its
  last evidence of life, not from the adoption, so a live worker is not ended
  just because the daemon restarted.
- **Where the output is:** the last 20 pane lines are stored on the task as
  `start_failure_tail`. Read them with `autonomous_prd_get` to see where the
  worker stopped. A dialog nobody answered shows there; a bare shell prompt
  means the agent never launched.
- **If the bound is too short for your first step:** raise it with
  `datawatch config set autonomous.session_start_confirm_seconds 300`. A value
  of `0` means "use the default".

chunks.title: How-to: Recover a stuck, failed, or incorrectly-terminal Automaton
chunks.heading: Task failed with `descendant-only stall`
chunks.body:
## Task failed with `descendant-only stall`

A worker using a one-shot `pi` backend ended its own run, but has a still-running child process (build, test, long-running command), and for longer than `autonomous.descendant_stall_seconds` (default 2700 = 45 minutes) is not showing any other sign of life. The daemon terminates the attempt as an infrastructure failure and retries the task through the existing `auto_fix_retries` budget; as soon as that budget is exhausted, the task remains failed.

Symptom: the task is reported as `failed` (or is silently retrying), its
detail shows an error terminating with “worker was in descendant-only
silence for …”, and the worktree may still contain the working child
processes that attempt had been waiting for.

- **Why this exists:** a `pi` run writes nothing to the log until it finishes, so the usual log-based stall check does not reach it. Without the descendant-only check, an attempt with a running work child and no other output would wait forever with no safety net.
- **What counts as output:** a live working descendant process, a session log that is up to date, and files written to the working directory. If there is newer evidence, the clock resets.
- **What you see:** a `Task worker descendant-only stall` alert; the task's error ends with “worker was in descendant-only silence for …”; the session's termination reason reads `descendant-only stall detector: …`; and the pane tail and the surviving descendant process are recorded on the attempt.
- **Leftover process cleanup:** the surviving work child processes are signalled with real kernel signals, with a short grace period in between, only while they remain the recorded ones — recycled process IDs are never touched. Which ended, and which survived, are recorded.
- **If you want a different value:** `datawatch config set autonomous.descendant_stall_seconds 5400`. A value of `0` means “use the default 2700” — this setting can not be accidentally disabled.

chunks.title: How-to: Recover a stuck, failed, or incorrectly-terminal Automaton
chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Cancelling a story mid-run and not restarting it.** The rest of the
  Automaton keeps going — a sibling story that `depends_on` the cancelled
  one will still run against missing prerequisites unless you also fix
  `depends_on` (see above) or manually sequence the retries.
- **Forgetting the downstream redo.** Fixing the skipped story alone
  isn't enough — anything that already ran off its absence produced
  output without the real prerequisite content and needs `force`-reset
  too.
- **Reject vs Cancel vs reset_task.** Reject = the Automaton shouldn't
  exist. Cancel (story/task) = stop this piece; the Automaton is fine.
  `reset_task force=true` = bring a stopped or already-finished piece
  back to pending for a genuine retry.

chunks.title: How-to: Review and approve an Automaton
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

After `plan`, an Automaton sits in `needs_review` until the operator
acts. Three actions:

- **Approve** — promotes to `approved`, ready to run. Per-story
  approve is finer-grained: only approved stories run when you hit
  Run.
- **Reject** — terminal; the Automaton won't run. Use for "this isn't
  what I meant; throw it away".
- **Request revision** — bounces back to the LLM for re-planning
  with operator notes. Status returns to `planning`.

Every action is recorded in the Decisions tab + audit log.

chunks.heading: 4a. Happy path — CLI
chunks.body:
### 4a. Happy path — CLI

```sh
PRD_ID=abc123

# 1. Confirm status.
datawatch autonomous get $PRD_ID | jq .status
#  → "needs_review"

# 2. Skim the plan.
datawatch autonomous get $PRD_ID | jq '.stories[] | {title, n_tasks: (.tasks|length)}'
#  → {"title":"Audit current auth flow","n_tasks":3}
#  → {"title":"Implement JWT issuance","n_tasks":4}
#  → ...

# 3. Read a specific story / task in full.
datawatch autonomous get $PRD_ID --story 0 --task 1

# 4. Approve all stories + the Automaton.
datawatch autonomous approve $PRD_ID
#  → approved; ready to run

# 5. Or approve per-story (finer control).
datawatch autonomous approve $PRD_ID --story 0
datawatch autonomous approve $PRD_ID --story 1
datawatch autonomous reject  $PRD_ID --story 2 --reason "Out of scope; defer to a separate Automaton"

# 6. Or request revision.
datawatch autonomous request-revision $PRD_ID \
  --notes "Story 2 is too broad — split into 'Migrate sessions' + 'Migrate cookies' as two separate stories"
#  → status: planning; LLM re-planning

# 7. Read the audit trail.
datawatch autonomous decisions $PRD_ID
#  → 2026-05-06T14:23:01Z  approve_story  story=0  actor=operator
#    2026-05-06T14:23:18Z  approve_story  story=1  actor=operator
#    2026-05-06T14:23:30Z  reject_story   story=2  reason="Out of scope..."
#    2026-05-06T14:24:02Z  approve_prd    actor=operator
```

   `planning`.

   `rejected` from the Settings modal). Rejected Automata persist for
   audit; archive when ready.
7. **Decisions** tab shows every action with timestamp, actor, and
   reason. Click any row to expand the raw `details` payload.

### 5e. YAML

Per-Automaton state lives in the Automaton YAML at
`~/.datawatch/autonomous/prds/<id>.yaml`:

```yaml
status: needs_review
stories:
  - title: Audit current auth flow
    status: needs_review                  # → approved / rejected per-story
    approval_notes: ""
    tasks:
      - title: Map all uses of CookieAuthMiddleware
        status: pending
      ...
```

hand-edit story / task content between plan + approve to refine the
spec — the daemon picks up the changes on next run.

chunks.heading: 5f. Web UI
chunks.body:
### 5f. Web UI

- **Settings → Automata, Autonomous block**: *Failure escalation enabled*, *Failed attempts before the task is held for review* (default 3, minimum 1), and *Escalation steps* as compact text, for example `ollama:qwen3.8:27b@2,claude-code:claude-sonnet-5-5`. Each step covers its attempts and the last step covers the rest. A step written as `-` uses the task's normally resolved worker. The same fields are in the General settings list.
- **Automaton detail, task row**: a held task shows the *Held for review* chip and a flag badge. Expand the row to read the attempts (worker, time spent, outcome, files changed, verifier report) and the review report. Then choose *Retry*, *Edit spec and retry*, *Change worker*, *Narrow scope* or *Cancel task*.
- **Automaton detail, Overview**: *Failure escalation override* sets the Automaton's own policy. Each task's expanded row has the same editor for that task. An empty field inherits the next level up: the Automaton, then the global setting. *Clear override* removes every field at that level.
- **Automation view**: a member Automaton with held tasks shows a count badge, and the chain's strip header counts the held tasks across its members.

chunks.title: How-to: Review and approve an Automaton
chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Approving without reading.** Cheap; common. The Stories tab is
  there for a reason. Even a 30-second skim catches most "this is
  not what I meant" moments.
- **Per-story approve forgotten.** Run only fires approved stories;
  unapproved ones stay `needs_review` and the Automaton continues without
  them. May or may not be what you want.
- **Reject vs Cancel.** Reject = "this Automaton shouldn't exist"
  (terminal). Cancel = "stop this run; the Automaton itself is fine"
  (Automaton goes to `cancelled`; can be re-run).
- **Lost decisions trail.** Decisions are append-only and persist
  with the Automaton (not deleted on archive). To prune, hard-delete the
  Automaton.

chunks.title: How-to: Review and approve an Automaton
chunks.heading: Guided mode: per-task approval (v9.0.17+)
chunks.body:
## Guided mode: per-task approval (v9.0.17+)

Per-story approve/reject above gates whole stories. Guided mode gates
individual **tasks** instead — useful when you want to review each
task's spec right before it runs, not just each story up front.

1. Turn it on for the Automaton:
   ```sh
   curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"guided_mode":true}' \
     $BASE/api/autonomous/prds/$PRD_ID/set_guided_mode
   ```
   Or the PWA: Automaton → Settings → "Guided Mode" checkbox. Or on
   creation: the New-Automaton wizard's "Guided Mode" checkbox.
2. Approve the Automaton as usual (`.../approve`). Every pending task
   immediately lands in `awaiting_approval` instead of `pending`.
3. In the PWA, a gated task row shows a ⏸ glyph and a bright green
   "✓ Approve" button. Click it to let that one task run. Approving one
   task does **not** auto-approve the rest — each is reviewed
   individually.
4. CLI / comm / MCP equivalents:
   ```sh
   # CLI
   datawatch autonomous approve-task $PRD_ID $TASK_ID
   ```
   ```
   # Comm channel
   You: autonomous approve-task abc123 task-1a
   Bot: autonomous approve-task  {...}
   ```
   MCP tool: `autonomous_prd_approve_task` (args: `id`, `task_id`).
5. REST equivalent:
   ```sh
   curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"task_id":"'"$TASK_ID"'"}' \
     $BASE/api/autonomous/prds/$PRD_ID/approve_task
   ```

Independent of per-story approval — a PRD can use either, both, or
neither. See "Guided Mode and the Per-Task Approval Gate" in
[`../operations.md`](../operations.md) for the full writeup, including
the `scope_drift` project rule that pairs with it as an automated
detector for the same failure mode (a decomposer writing code tasks
into a doc-only PRD).

# How-to: Channel-Address Federation via Comms (BL331)

Channel-address federation lets you route inbound messages from a known
channel identity — a Telegram group, a Signal number, a Matrix room — to
a specific federation peer, with an optional automata type and default
project directory. Sessions and PRDs created through this routing carry an
`owner_peer` field that tracks which federated peer originated the request.

chunks.title: How-to: Channel-Address Federation via Comms (BL331)
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.body:
## Overview

```
Inbound message (Telegram group -1001234567890)
         │
         ▼
  channel_routing.json  ← PUT /api/channel/routing
         │  matches channel_pattern
         ▼
  federation peer "nas-peer"  ← has channel_identity set
         │
         ▼
  Session / PRD  ← owner_peer = "nas-peer"
```

When a message arrives on a comm channel, datawatch checks the routing
rules in order. The first rule whose `channel_pattern` matches the
inbound channel address wins. The daemon proxies or forwards the request
to the named federation peer, and any session or PRD created as a result
has `owner_peer` set to that peer's name.

This is useful when you want different Telegram groups (or Signal numbers)
to dispatch to different servers — a home server for personal projects,
a NAS peer for long-running builds, a cloud peer for GPU tasks.

## 3 — The comms-channel-agent capability group

This release adds a 14th builtin federation capability group: `comms-channel-agent`.
It grants `comm:read + comm:write` — the same surface as `comm-bridge` from
v8.2.0, but semantically distinct: use `comms-channel-agent` for peers that
act as channel-routing agents, and `comm-bridge` for generic push/notification
bridge peers.

```sh
# Verify the group is present (should be 14 entries).
curl -sk \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://datawatch.local:8443/api/federation/groups/builtins | jq 'length'
# 14

# Inspect what comms-channel-agent grants.
curl -sk \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://datawatch.local:8443/api/federation/groups/builtins \
  | jq '.[] | select(.name=="comms-channel-agent")'
```

chunks.heading: 4 — Example: Telegram group → federation peer routing
chunks.body:
## 4 — Example: Telegram group → federation peer routing

This end-to-end example routes messages from a Telegram group to a secondary
NAS peer that handles long-running builds.

```sh
# Step 1: Register the NAS peer.
curl -sk -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "nas-builds",
    "url": "https://192.168.1.50:8443",
    "token": "nas-secret-token",
    "capabilities": "comms-channel-agent",
    "channel_identity": ["telegram:group:-1009876543210"]
  }' \
  https://datawatch.local:8443/api/federation/peers

# Step 2: Set the routing rule.
curl -sk -X PUT \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "rules": [{
      "channel_pattern": "telegram:group:-1009876543210",
      "peer_name": "nas-builds",
      "automata_type": "feature",
      "default_project_dir": "/mnt/data/workspace/myapp"
    }]
  }' \
  https://datawatch.local:8443/api/channel/routing

# Step 3: Send a message to the Telegram group.
# Telegram → datawatch (via Telegram bot) → routing match → forwarded to nas-builds

# Step 4: Check sessions on the NAS peer — owner_peer will be set.
curl -sk \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://datawatch.local:8443/api/sessions \
  | jq '.[] | select(.owner_peer != null) | {id, owner_peer}'
```

chunks.heading: 5 — owner_peer on sessions and PRDs
chunks.body:
## 5 — owner_peer on sessions and PRDs

When a session or PRD is created via a channel routing match, the `owner_peer`
field records which federation peer originated the request. You can filter
sessions and PRDs by owner.

```sh
# List sessions, show owner_peer field.
curl -sk \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://datawatch.local:8443/api/sessions | jq '.[] | {id, name, owner_peer}'

# List PRDs, show owner_peer field.
curl -sk \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  https://datawatch.local:8443/api/autonomous/prds | jq '.[] | {id, title, owner_peer}'
```

The `owner_peer` field is `null` (or absent) for sessions created locally. It
is set to the `peer_name` from the matching routing rule when the session was
created via a routed channel message.
