chunks.title: Discussion Scopes
chunks.heading: Setting up participant sync
chunks.body:
## Setting up participant sync

Participant sync lets you fan-out every write to a list of registered federation peers.
When you add peers to a discussion's participant list, every future POST to that discussion
automatically triggers an asynchronous push to each participant.

chunks.title: Discussion Scopes
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.body:
### Prerequisites

Register the participant peers in your daemon before adding them to a discussion:

```sh
datawatch federation peer add \
  --name "peer-alpha" \
  --url "https://peer-alpha.internal:8080" \
  --token "<peer-alpha-bearer-token>"
```

chunks.title: Discussion Scopes
chunks.heading: Set the participant list
chunks.body:
### Set the participant list

**REST:**

```sh
dw -X PUT $DW_HOST/api/memory/discussion/my-topic/participants \
  -d '{"participants":["peer-alpha","peer-beta"]}' | jq .
# {"ok":true}

# Verify
dw $DW_HOST/api/memory/discussion/my-topic/participants | jq .
# {"id":"my-topic","participants":["peer-alpha","peer-beta"]}
```

**CLI:**

```sh
datawatch memory discussion participants my-topic --set peer-alpha,peer-beta
datawatch memory discussion participants my-topic
# peers: peer-alpha, peer-beta
```

**MCP:**

```
memory_discussion_participants(id="my-topic", participants=["peer-alpha","peer-beta"])
# → {"ok":true}
```

chunks.title: Discussion Scopes
chunks.heading: What happens on write
chunks.body:
### What happens on write

After a successful POST, the daemon fans out the entry to each participant peer
asynchronously. The sync uses the peer's registered URL and token. Each entry in the WAL
records `origin_peer` and `origin_wal_seq` so the receiving peer can detect and skip
re-syncing entries it originally produced.

---

chunks.title: Discussion Scopes
chunks.heading: Understanding the WAL and conflict resolution
chunks.body: ## Understanding the WAL and conflict resolution

chunks.title: Discussion Scopes
chunks.heading: The WAL
chunks.body:
### The WAL

Every write appends a record to `~/.datawatch/discussions/<id>/wal.jsonl`. Each record has:

| Field | Description |
|---|---|
| `seq` | Monotonically increasing sequence number within the discussion |
| `content` | The entry content |
| `ts` | RFC 3339 timestamp at write time |
| `origin_peer` | Peer that originally produced this entry (empty = local) |
| `origin_wal_seq` | Sequence number of the entry on the originating peer |

```sh
# View the WAL
datawatch memory discussion wal my-topic
# or via REST:
dw $DW_HOST/api/memory/discussion/my-topic/wal | jq .
```

chunks.title: Discussion Scopes
chunks.heading: Conflicts
chunks.body:
### Conflicts

A conflict occurs when two peers write to the same discussion concurrently without
coordination, producing entries with overlapping sequence windows. Conflicts are detected
when the daemon receives a sync push from a peer whose entries overlap with locally
committed entries.

**List conflicts:**

```sh
dw $DW_HOST/api/memory/discussion/my-topic/conflicts | jq .
# {"id":"my-topic","conflicts":[{"seq_a":3,"seq_b":3,"ts":"..."}]}
```

**Resolve a conflict:**

Identify which entry should be the canonical winner, then call the resolve endpoint:

```sh
dw -X POST $DW_HOST/api/memory/discussion/my-topic/conflicts/resolve \
  -d '{"winner_seq":3,"loser_seq":3}' | jq .
# {"ok":true}
```

The loser entry is tombstoned in the WAL; it will not be returned by subsequent reads or
sync operations.

---

chunks.title: Discussion Scopes
chunks.heading: The 60 ops/min throttle
chunks.body:
## The 60 ops/min throttle

To prevent sync storms, each federation peer is limited to **60 write operations per
minute** per discussion. This is a per-peer token bucket; local writes by the daemon
itself are not throttled.

When a peer exceeds the limit, the daemon returns `429 Too Many Requests`. The peer should
back off and retry after the bucket refills (approximately 1 second per token).

```sh
# Writing from a peer that exceeds 60/min:
# → HTTP 429 Too Many Requests
# Retry-After header indicates when the bucket refills
```

If you operate a high-throughput discussion (more than 60 writes per minute from a single
peer), consider batching entries into a single POST with a structured content block, or
splitting the workload across multiple discussion IDs.

---

chunks.title: Discussion Scopes
chunks.heading: Accessing via MCP
chunks.body:
## Accessing via MCP

The four MCP tools for discussion scopes are available in any MCP-connected client
(Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, etc.):

| Tool | Description |
|---|---|
| `memory_discussion_write` | Write an entry to a discussion scope |
| `memory_discussion_recall` | Read all entries for a discussion scope |
| `memory_discussion_wal` | Read the raw WAL for a discussion scope |
| `memory_discussion_participants` | Get or set the participant peer list |

All four tools require an active connection to the datawatch MCP server. Verify they appear
in the tool list:

```sh
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $DW_TOKEN" \
  "$DW_HOST/api/mcp/docs" | jq '[.tools[] | select(.name | startswith("memory_discussion"))] | map(.name)'
# ["memory_discussion_participants","memory_discussion_recall","memory_discussion_wal","memory_discussion_write"]
```

---

chunks.title: Discussion Scopes
chunks.heading: Security model
chunks.body:
## Security model

Discussion scope endpoints are gated on the `comm:*` capability surface:

| Action | Required cap |
|---|---|
| List discussions, read entries, read WAL, read participants, read conflicts | `comm:read` |
| Write entry, delete discussion, set participants, resolve conflicts | `comm:write` |

**Builtin groups and their access:**

| Group | Can read | Can write |
|---|---|---|
| `comm-bridge` | Yes | Yes |
| `read-only` | Yes | No |
| `full-control` | Yes | Yes |
| `config-admin` | No | No |
| `federation-peer` (default) | No | No |

To give a peer write access to discussion scopes, grant it the `comm-bridge` group or
explicitly add `comm:write` to its capabilities:

```sh
datawatch federation peer update peer-alpha --capabilities "comm:read,comm:write"

datawatch federation group add discussion-writers --caps "comm:read,comm:write"
datawatch federation peer update peer-alpha --capabilities "discussion-writers"
```

See [federation-cbac.md](federation-cbac.md) for the full capability reference.

chunks.title: How-to: Docs-as-MCP-Interface (the operator's AI-driven docs surface)
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

Four MCP tools, each mirrored across REST + CLI + comm + PWA:

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `docs_search` | Hybrid search (vector primary + BM25 fallback) over core + trusted skill + trusted plugin sources. Trust filtering applied. |
| `docs_read` | Read a specific chunk by `path` + `anchor`. The `path` parameter must use the full relative path including subdirectory prefix, e.g. `"path": "howto/daemon-operations.md"` — **not** just the filename or a bare howto name. |
| `docs_list_howtos` | List every howto in the index. `has_exec_steps:true` means the howto carries an authored MCP-call sequence; `false` means LLM-translation is required at apply time. |
| `docs_apply` | Plan-then-execute. `mode=plan` returns the resolved exec_steps + an `approval_token`. `mode=execute` consumes the token and runs each step via the in-process MCP dispatcher. `risk_gate=true` pauses before each mutating step and issues a continuation token. |

> **MCP `docs_read` path format**: Always pass the `path` parameter as a relative path with directory prefix. Example MCP call: `{"tool": "docs_read", "params": {"path": "howto/daemon-operations.md"}}`. Using `{"howto": "daemon-operations.md"}` or omitting the `howto/` prefix will not resolve correctly.

chunks.heading: Trust model (operator-controlled)
chunks.body:
## Trust model (operator-controlled)

Skills and plugins are isolated per-source (`skill:<name>` / `plugin:<name>`).
On first sight, the docsindex runtime adds an entry to the pending-trust
queue (`~/.datawatch/docs-trust-pending.json`); operator accepts via:

```sh
datawatch docs trust accept skill:test-first
# or via REST: POST /api/docs/trust {source:"skill:test-first", granted_by:"operator"}
# or via PWA: Settings → General → Docs Search → pending list → Trust
```

Once trusted, the source's docs land in the BM25 (and vector, if Ollama
is configured) index and surface through `docs_search`/`list_howtos`.

## Provenance

Every plan response includes a `provenance` field per step:

- **`authored`** — the howto carries hand-written `exec_steps:` front-matter.
- **`llm_translated`** — the howto has no front-matter; the configured
  LLM (Ollama default, OpenWebUI fallback) translated the prose into a
  step sequence at apply time. LLM-translated plans force `risk_gate=true`.

22 of 24 howtos under `docs/howto/` are curated `authored`. The remaining
two (`channel-state-engine`, `README`) are LLM-only by design.

chunks.heading: Hard constraints

- **No GPU required.** Vector layer falls back to BM25 when Ollama is
  unreachable; LLM-translation falls back to "no exec_steps" when no
  LLM backend is configured.

  plugins must be explicitly trusted before their docs index.

  `check-howto-coverage.sh`, `check-plugin-manifests.sh` to catch the
  three classes of silent breakage caught by the docs audit.

chunks.title: How-to: Evals — rubric-based grading
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

Suites of grader rules at `~/.datawatch/evals/<name>.yaml`. A suite has:

- A **name** (filename without extension).
- A **mode**:
  - `capability` (default 70% threshold) — exploring whether a backend
    or model can handle a task class.
  - `regression` (default 99% threshold) — gating CI / pre-deploy.
- An optional **threshold_pct** override.
- A list of **graders**, each with `type`, `weight`, and type-specific
  parameters.

Four grader types:

| Type | Does | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `string_match` | Output contains/equals a target string. | Confirm a specific token. |
| `regex_match` | Output matches a regex. | Pattern checks. |
| `binary_test` | Pipes output into a shell command; exit 0 = pass. | Real validators (`jq empty`, `pytest`). |
| `llm_rubric` | Second-pass LLM grades against a written rubric. | Subjective qualities. |

Score = `Σ(weight × pass) / Σ(weight) × 100`. Pass if score ≥ threshold.

chunks.title: How-to: Evals — rubric-based grading
chunks.heading: 4a. Happy path — CLI
chunks.body:
### 4a. Happy path — CLI

```sh
# 1. Author a suite.
cat > ~/.datawatch/evals/json-output.yaml <<'EOF'
name: json-output
mode: capability
threshold_pct: 70
graders:
  - type: regex_match
    pattern: '^\s*\{'
    weight: 1
    description: starts with an opening brace
  - type: binary_test
    command: jq empty
    weight: 2
    description: parses as JSON
  - type: llm_rubric
    rubric: |
      Does the output answer the prompt without trailing commentary,
      apologies, or markdown fences? Score 0-1.
    weight: 1
EOF

# 2. List configured suites.
datawatch evals list
#  → json-output  capability  70%  3 graders

# 3. Run the suite against an ad-hoc input.
datawatch evals run json-output --input "Give me a JSON object describing yourself"
#  → suite=json-output mode=capability threshold=70 score=83 PASS
#      ✓ regex_match (weight 1) — starts with an opening brace
#      ✓ binary_test (weight 2) — parses as JSON
#      ✗ llm_rubric (weight 1) — trailing apology detected

# 4. List + inspect runs (persisted at ~/.datawatch/evals/runs/).
datawatch evals runs --suite json-output --limit 10
datawatch evals get-run <run-id>

# 5. Compare across backends.
datawatch evals compare json-output --backends claude-code,opencode-acp,ollama
#  → claude-code      score=92  PASS
#    opencode-acp     score=83  PASS
#    ollama:llama3    score=58  FAIL (capability threshold 70)
```

### 4b. Happy path — PWA

1. PWA → Settings → Automate → **Evals** card.
2. Click **+ New Suite**. The editor opens with a starter YAML
   template. Fill in name, mode, threshold, graders. **Save**.

   count + last-run summary.
4. Click **Run** next to the suite. A modal asks for an input string
   (or a file). Type the prompt; click **Run**.
5. Result modal renders the per-grader pass/fail with explanations and
   the aggregate score in a colored badge (green PASS / red FAIL).
6. The **Recent Runs** section below the suite list shows the last
   ~20 runs across all suites; click any row to re-render the result
   modal.

chunks.title: How-to: Evals — rubric-based grading
chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Mixed-mode suites.** A capability suite that includes a brittle
  `regex_match` grader will keep tipping below threshold for cosmetic
  reasons. Either loosen the regex or split into a separate regression
  suite.
- **LLM rubric self-grading.** Using the same model for `llm_rubric`
  that produced the output biases the grade upward. Use a smaller /
  different backend for the grader where possible.
- **No description on graders.** When a suite fails 6 months later you
  won't remember why grader #3 exists. Always set `description:`.
- **Threshold gymnastics.** If you find yourself adjusting
  `threshold_pct` on a regression suite to make it pass, the
  regression already happened. Roll back.
- **Slow `binary_test` commands.** Each grader runs serially per
  invocation. `pytest -k some_slow_thing` makes the suite minutes-long.
  Move expensive validators to a separate suite you only run on demand.

chunks.title: How-to: Failure escalation
chunks.body:
# How-to: Failure escalation

A task that keeps failing should not burn retries on the same worker forever,
and it should not quietly fail either. Failure escalation does three things:

1. **Moves the task up a ladder of workers.** After each failed attempt the
   next attempt can run on a different worker, for example a local model first
   and then a stronger Claude model that reads the earlier failure reports.
2. **Counts the failures.** After a set number of failed attempts (3 by
   default, 4 or more if you want) the task stops.
3. **Asks you.** The task is held with the status `review_needed` and a report of
   every attempt. Nothing else is spent on it until you retry it, change it, or
   cancel it.

This is the decision the daemon used to make for you by failing the task. Now
you make it, with the evidence in front of you.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:

chunks.title: How-to: Failure escalation
chunks.heading: Why this exists
chunks.body:
## Why this exists

A worker that fails the same task three times usually fails the fourth time
too, for the same reason. Retrying it unchanged wastes time and tokens. A
different worker, or the same worker with the earlier failures in its prompt,
has a real chance of getting past the problem. When even that does not work,
the honest answer is "this needs a human," and the daemon should say so once,
clearly, rather than keep trying or silently marking the task failed.

chunks.title: How-to: Failure escalation
chunks.heading: The policy
chunks.body:
## The policy

The policy has three fields. Each can be set at three levels (see
[Override order](#override-order) below).

| Field | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` turns escalation on. `false` restores the old behaviour: retry up to `autonomous.auto_fix_retries`, then mark the task failed. | `true` |
| `max_failures` | Failed attempts after which the task is held for review. Minimum 1; 4 or more is allowed. | `3` |
| `steps` | The ladder of workers, in order. Empty means every attempt uses the task's normally resolved worker. | empty |

Each step has these fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `backend` | The worker backend, for example `pi-prompt` or `claude-code`. Empty means the task's normally resolved worker. |
| `model` | The model on that backend. Needs a backend. |
| `effort` | Effort level for this step only (JSON form only). Empty means the task's effort. |
| `attempts` | How many consecutive failed attempts this step covers. Default 1. |

chunks.title: How-to: Failure escalation
chunks.heading: How the ladder is walked
chunks.body:
### How the ladder is walked

Attempts are counted as failed attempts since the last operator action. Step 1
covers its `attempts` failed attempts, step 2 covers the next ones, and so on.
The **last step covers every remaining attempt**, so a one-step ladder means
"this worker for every attempt until the limit."

With `steps: pi-prompt:ollama/qwen3.8:27b@2,claude-code:claude-opus-5-5` and the
default `max_failures` of 3:

| Attempt | Failed attempts so far | Worker |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | `pi-prompt` / `ollama/qwen3.8:27b` |
| 2 | 1 | `pi-prompt` / `ollama/qwen3.8:27b` |
| 3 | 2 | `claude-code` / `claude-opus-5-5` |
| — | 3 | Held for review |

Raise `max_failures` to 4 and the Claude step gets two attempts instead of one.

Every time an attempt moves the task to a different worker, the Automaton's
decision log gets a `failure_escalation` entry naming the worker.

chunks.heading: Model names must fit the backend
chunks.body:
### Model names must fit the backend

The daemon checks each step before the Automaton starts. A step that cannot run
refuses the start and names the task and the step.

- `claude-code` takes bare Claude names such as `claude-opus-5-5` or
  `claude-sonnet-5-5`. It refuses provider-qualified names with a `/`.
- `pi-prompt` (and the other pi-based backends) takes provider-qualified names
  such as `ollama/qwen3.8:27b`. It refuses bare Claude names.

chunks.heading: Mixed: a local model, then a stronger Claude model
chunks.body:
### Mixed: a local model, then a stronger Claude model

The usual setup. Local models do the cheap first tries. The Claude step gets the
earlier failure reports in its prompt, so it starts from what went wrong
instead of from nothing. Use this on one Automaton, not the whole daemon, if
you only want it for risky work:

```sh
datawatch autonomous failure-escalation set <automaton-id> --max-failures 4 \
  --steps "pi-prompt:ollama/qwen3.8:27b@2,claude-code:claude-opus-5-5"
```

For a single task that needs a stronger worker from the start, put the same
steps on that task with `--task <task-id>`.

chunks.title: How-to: Failure escalation
chunks.heading: What the retry prompt contains
chunks.body:
## What the retry prompt contains

When a task has failed attempts on record, the next worker receives them before
it starts. The prompt begins with a line saying earlier attempts did not finish
successfully, then lists each attempt, oldest first:

- the attempt number and the worker it ran on
- how long it ran and how it ended (`failed`, `stalled` or `cancelled`)
- the verifier's summary and issues
- the files it changed

The prompt is capped at about 12,000 characters. When the reports would be
longer, the oldest attempts are shortened to one line each. If that is still
too long, the oldest are left out, and the prompt says which attempts were left
out. The worker is never silently missing a failure.

Any operator reset of the task, including a retry from review, starts the failure
count again from zero, so the ladder starts over at step 1. The exception is a
review retry that changes the worker: the worker you chose is kept for the
attempts after it, and the ladder does not replace it. A review retry without a
worker change lets the ladder apply again.

chunks.title: How-to: Failure escalation
chunks.heading: When a task needs review
chunks.body:
## When a task needs review

A task reaching `max_failures` is **held**, not failed. What you see:

- **Web UI.** The task row carries a "Held for review" badge. Expand the row for the attempt list, the full report and the
  action buttons. On the Automaton header, in the Automaton list rows and on the
  Automation strip, a count shows how many tasks are waiting.
- **Status output.** `datawatch autonomous status` lists each held task under
  `review_needed`, with the Automaton, the task, the failed-attempt count, the
  last worker and when it was held. The comm channel's `autonomous status`
  adds one line per held task and tells you the command to decide it. MCP
  `autonomous_status` and REST `GET /api/autonomous/status` carry the same
  `review_needed` array.
- **Alert.** One error-level alert, titled "Automaton task needs review", is raised
  when the task is held. Its body names the Automaton, the task, the failed-attempt
  count, the last worker and the ways to act. You get one alert per hold, not one
  per failed attempt.
- **The Automaton.** Other tasks that do not depend on the held one keep running.
  Tasks that depend on it wait. The Automaton shows as blocked until you act.
  You do not have to wait for the Automaton to go idle before you act. Retry
  and cancel work while it keeps running other tasks, and no second executor is
  started: the one that is running picks up your decision.
- **The report.** The task keeps every attempt, and its review report is a plain
  text summary of each one, with the total time spent.

chunks.title: How-to: Failure escalation
chunks.heading: The five operator actions
chunks.body:
## The five operator actions

Every action is available on every surface. The table gives the way in on each.

| Action | What it does | Web UI | CLI | REST (`resolve_task_review`) | MCP (`autonomous_prd_resolve_task_review`) | Comm channel |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Retry** | Requeues the task on its normally resolved worker, with the earlier reports in the prompt. | **Retry** button on the task | `datawatch autonomous resolve-review <automaton-id> --task <task-id> --action retry` | `{"task_id":"…","action":"retry"}` | `action=retry` | `autonomous review-task <automaton> <task> retry` |
| **Edit spec and retry** | Replaces the task spec, then retries. | **Edit spec and retry** (opens a form) | add `--spec "<new spec>"` to the retry | add `"spec":"…"` | `spec=…` | add `spec=…` to the retry |
| **Change worker** | Retries with a different backend, model and effort for this task. | **Change worker** (opens a form) | add `--backend`, `--model`, `--effort` | add `"backend"`, `"model"`, `"effort"` | `backend`, `model`, `effort` | add `backend=… model=… effort=…` |
| **Narrow scope** | Retries with the list of files the task may change cut down. | **Narrow scope** (opens a form) | add `--files a.go,b.go` | add `"files":["a.go","b.go"]` | `files` | add `files=a.go,b.go` |
| **Cancel** | Cancels the task. The Automaton can roll up without it. | **Cancel task** button on the task | `datawatch autonomous resolve-review <automaton-id> --task <task-id> --action cancel` | `{"task_id":"…","action":"cancel"}` | `action=cancel` | `autonomous review-task <automaton> <task> cancel` |

Notes on the actions:

- Retry and cancel work while the Automaton keeps running other tasks. The
  answer comes back at once, with no wait and no "try again shortly" error. No
  second executor is started. The executor that is already running is told about
  your decision and reads the Automaton again. A retried task runs next: when
  the Automaton runs one task at a time, right after the task now running
  finishes; when it runs tasks side by side, at once if a slot is free. A
  cancelled task is marked finished and the tasks that depend on it fail. Tasks
  already running are not interrupted. If the
  Automaton has no executor running at the moment, the decision starts one, as
  before.
- A retry can carry a spec, a worker and a file list in one go. Each change is
  checked before anything is written, so a refused change leaves the task held.
- A `--note` (REST and MCP `note`, comm `note=…`) is recorded on the decision log
  and given to the next attempt.
- Asking to act on a task that is not held answers **409** on REST and an error
  on the other surfaces. Nothing changes.

chunks.heading: Examples
chunks.body:
### Examples

```sh
# Retry with a changed worker and a narrowed file list, with a note
datawatch autonomous resolve-review <automaton-id> --task <task-id> --action retry \
  --backend claude-code --model claude-opus-5-5 --effort high \
  --files internal/parser/parse.go --note "the failure is in the parser only"

# Cancel
datawatch autonomous resolve-review <automaton-id> --task <task-id> --action cancel
```

```
You: autonomous review-task <automaton-id> <task-id> retry backend=claude-code model=claude-opus-5-5 note=narrowed to the parser
Bot: {"id":"<automaton-id>", ...}
```

```sh
# REST
curl -sk -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"task_id":"<task-id>","action":"retry","backend":"claude-code","model":"claude-opus-5-5","files":["internal/parser/parse.go"],"note":"narrowed to the parser"}' \
  https://localhost:8443/api/autonomous/prds/<automaton-id>/resolve_task_review
```

chunks.title: How-to: Failure escalation
chunks.heading: Override order
chunks.body:
## Override order

Each field is resolved on its own, from the most specific level that sets it:

1. **Task** override (`failure_escalation` on the task)
2. **Automaton** override (`failure_escalation` on the Automaton)
3. **Daemon default** (`autonomous.failure_escalation` in the config)

So a task can set only `max_failures` and still inherit the Automaton's
`steps`. The CLI `show` command prints the override at the level you ask about
next to the daemon default, so you can see what the level above supplies.

To remove an override, clear it at that level. Clearing a task or Automaton
override lets it inherit again.

chunks.title: How-to: Failure escalation
chunks.heading: Setting each level
chunks.body:
### Setting each level

**Daemon default**

| Surface | How |
|---|---|
| Web UI | Settings → Automata → Autonomous block: *Failure escalation enabled*, *Failed attempts before the task is held for review*, *Escalation steps* |
| CLI | `datawatch autonomous failure-escalation global --enabled true --max-failures 4 --steps "…"`; or `datawatch config set autonomous.failure_escalation.max_failures 4` |
| REST | `PUT /api/config` with `autonomous.failure_escalation.enabled`, `.max_failures` or `.steps` |
| MCP | `config_set` with `key` and `value`, using the same keys |
| Comm channel | `configure autonomous.failure_escalation.max_failures=4` |
| YAML | `autonomous.failure_escalation: {enabled: true, max_failures: 4, steps: [...]}` in `config.yaml` |

**Automaton override**

| Surface | How |
|---|---|
| Web UI | Automaton detail → Overview → *Failure escalation override*. Empty fields inherit. **Clear override** removes it. |
| CLI | `datawatch autonomous failure-escalation set <automaton-id> --max-failures 4`; `datawatch autonomous failure-escalation clear <automaton-id>` |
| REST | `POST /api/autonomous/prds/{id}/set_failure_escalation` with `{"policy":{"max_failures":4}}`; `"policy": null` clears |
| MCP | `autonomous_prd_set_failure_escalation` with `id` and `policy`; `clear=true` removes it |
| Comm channel | `autonomous set-failure-escalation <automaton-id> max_failures=4`; `autonomous set-failure-escalation <automaton-id> clear` |

**Task override**

| Surface | How |
|---|---|
| Web UI | Automaton detail → Stories → expand the task → the same editor, for that task |
| CLI | add `--task <task-id>` to `set`, `clear` or `show` |
| REST | the same `set_failure_escalation` call with `"task_id":"<task-id>"` |
| MCP | `autonomous_prd_set_failure_escalation` with `task_id` set |
| Comm channel | `autonomous set-failure-escalation <automaton-id> <task-id> max_failures=4` |

To see the effective value and where it comes from, run
`datawatch autonomous failure-escalation show <automaton-id> [--task <task-id>]`
or read the Automaton with `autonomous_prd_get` and the daemon default with
`autonomous_config_get`.

chunks.title: How-to: Failure escalation
chunks.heading: Upgrading from the old retry count
chunks.body:
## Upgrading from the old retry count

Before this policy, an attempt that failed was retried up to
`autonomous.auto_fix_retries` (default 1), which meant two attempts in all, and
then the task was marked failed.

With failure escalation on, which is the default, a task gets `max_failures`
attempts (default 3) and is then held for review instead of failed. An Automaton
with no settings of its own therefore gets one more attempt than before, and a
held task waits for you instead of ending as failed.

To keep the old behaviour:

```sh
datawatch config set autonomous.failure_escalation.enabled false
```

or, on one Automaton, `datawatch autonomous failure-escalation set <automaton-id> --enabled false`.
With escalation off, a task that fails its attempts is marked failed, and the
retry count is still `autonomous.auto_fix_retries`.

chunks.title: How-to: Federated observer
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

Each datawatch instance is identified by `name` + `shape`:

- **Shape A** = Agent — a worker pushing into a primary.
- **Shape B** = Standalone — a sibling primary that exchanges with
  others.
- **Shape C** = Cluster — a single representative for a whole
  Kubernetes cluster.

Peers register with each other via `datawatch observer peer-register`
(or auto-register from the agent fleet). Once registered, each pushes
periodic snapshots (process envelopes, system stats, optional memory
summaries) over the same Tailscale mesh used for agent workloads.

chunks.heading: Observer-to-ComputeNode binding (v7)
chunks.body:
### Observer-to-ComputeNode binding (v7)

Each observer peer can be explicitly bound to a Compute Node so that
LLM workloads on that node are attributed to the correct observer:

- `Node.observer_peer` — explicit binding field on a Compute Node.
  Auto-set on first datawatch-stats push via name-match; can be
  overridden manually.
- **Free peers** — peers with no bound Compute Node. Use
  `GET /api/observer/peers/free` to list them.
- **By-node view** — `GET /api/observer/peers/by-node` groups peers by
  their bound CN: `{by_node: {<cn-name>: [...peers]}, unbound: [...]}`.
  The PWA "Group by ComputeNode" toggle uses this endpoint.
- **Federation meta-peers** — `GET /api/federation/meta-peers` shows
  cross-instance observer attribution per node.

### datawatch-stats multi-parent (v7)

`datawatch-stats` can push to multiple daemon instances simultaneously:

```bash
datawatch-stats \
  --datawatch https://primary:8443,https://secondary:8443 \
  --insecure-tls
```

Each parent gets its own peer registration + per-parent token file
(`peer-primary_8443.token`, `peer-secondary_8443.token`). A slow parent
does not delay pushes to others.

chunks.title: How-to: Federated observer
chunks.heading: Base requirements
chunks.body:
## Base requirements

- `datawatch start` — daemon up on each host.
- Tailscale or Headscale mesh established between hosts (see
  [`tailscale-mesh.md`](tailscale-mesh.md)).
- Operator role on each host (peer-register is gated).
- **`observer.peers.allow_register: true`** must be set in `~/.datawatch/datawatch.yaml` on the **primary** host before any peer (including `datawatch-stats` sidecars and agent workers) can register. Without this flag, all inbound peer-register calls are rejected — no error is surfaced on the registering peer; it simply cannot push.

> **Pre-conditions for peer registration**: The primary daemon's config must include `observer.peers.allow_register: true` (see the Setup block below). This flag gates all inbound observer peer registrations. When automating or testing observer peer operations, confirm this flag is present before calling `observer_peer_register` or `compute_node_attach_observer`.

chunks.title: How-to: Federated observer
chunks.heading: Setup
chunks.body:
## Setup

On the **primary** (the host you'll log into):

```yaml
# ~/.datawatch/datawatch.yaml
observer:
  enabled: true
  peers:
    allow_register: true               # accept inbound registrations
    push_interval: 5s                  # default push cadence
```

On each **peer** that should push to the primary:

```yaml
observer:
  enabled: true
  peers:
    push_to:
      - name: primary-kona
        url: https://100.64.0.1:8443    # primary's tailnet IP
        token: ${secret:PRIMARY_TOKEN}
        shape: B                        # or A / C
```

`datawatch reload` on each.

chunks.title: How-to: Federated observer
chunks.heading: 4a. Happy path — CLI
chunks.body:
### 4a. Happy path — CLI

```sh
# On the PRIMARY:

# 1. Mint a peer-registration token + share with the peer.
datawatch observer peer-token-mint --name lab-east-peer
#  → token: ops_...
#    expires: 2026-05-13T14:00:00Z

# (Manually share with the peer's operator. On the PEER:)

# 2. Register.
datawatch secrets set PRIMARY_TOKEN "ops_..."
datawatch observer peer-register \
  --primary-url https://100.64.0.1:8443 \
  --name lab-east-peer \
  --shape B
#  → registered; pushing every 5s

# On the PEER — start datawatch-stats pushing to multiple primaries:
datawatch-stats \
  --datawatch https://100.64.0.1:8443,https://100.64.0.2:8443 \
  --insecure-tls

# Back on the PRIMARY:

# 3. Confirm peers are pushing (includes is_self:true entry for local daemon).
datawatch observer peers
#  → (self)           shape:A   is_self:true  ip:local
#    lab-east-peer    shape:B   last_push:3s ago   ip:100.64.0.42
#                                compute_node:datawatch-ollama

# 4. View free peers (not yet bound to a Compute Node).
datawatch compute node observer-free

# 5. Bind an observer peer to a Compute Node.
datawatch compute node attach-observer datawatch-ollama lab-east-peer

# 6. View peers grouped by Compute Node.
datawatch compute node observer-by-node
#  → datawatch-ollama: [lab-east-peer]
#    (unbound):        []

# 7. View envelopes from a specific peer.
datawatch observer envelopes --peer lab-east-peer
#  → backend:claude-docker  cpu_pct=4.2  rss_mb=512  ...

# 8. Cross-host envelope view (every peer).
datawatch observer envelopes --all-peers
#  → primary-kona      backend:claude-docker  cpu=2.1  ...
#    lab-east-peer     backend:claude-docker  cpu=4.2  ...

# 9. Remove a peer.
datawatch observer peer-remove lab-east-peer
```

chunks.title: How-to: Federated observer
chunks.heading: 4b. Happy path — PWA
chunks.body:
### 4b. Happy path — PWA

1. On the PRIMARY: bottom nav → **Observer** → scroll to **Federated
   Peers** card.
2. The list now always includes a **local self-peer** row (marked
   "(this daemon)") so you see the complete host picture in one table.
3. Empty remote-peers state shows the registration command. Click
   **Mint peer token** → modal with name + shape inputs → **Generate**
   → token copied to clipboard.
4. Hand the token to the peer's operator (private channel).
5. On the peer's PWA: Observer → Federated Peers → **+ Push to
   primary** → paste the primary's URL + token → **Save**.
6. Within ~5s the primary's Federated Peers card shows the new peer
   with a green health dot and the bound Compute Node name (or a
   "free" pill if not yet bound).
7. **Group by ComputeNode toggle** — a toggle in the card header
   switches between flat list and per-CN buckets. Persists in
   localStorage. Each bucket shows the peers observing that node;
   unbound peers appear below.
8. To bind a free peer: Compute Nodes panel → edit a node → select
   from the **Observer Peer** dropdown (pre-populated with free peers
   only).
9. Click into a peer row → drill-down modal: last snapshot, push
   history, per-envelope detail.
10. Cog-nav badge: when any peer goes stale (no push in >60s), the
    gear icon shows a numeric badge. Click → navigates to Federated
    Peers + flashes the offending row.

chunks.title: How-to: Federated observer
chunks.heading: 5b. REST
chunks.body:
### 5b. REST

```sh
# List (includes is_self:true entry for local daemon).
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $BASE/api/observer/peers
# Each entry now carries compute_node (bound CN name, or "" if free).

# Mint a registration token (primary).
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"lab-east-peer","shape":"B"}' \
  $BASE/api/observer/peer-token-mint

# Register (called by the peer).
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $PRIMARY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"lab-east-peer","shape":"B","url":"https://100.64.0.42:8443"}' \
  $PRIMARY_BASE/api/observer/peers

# Remove.
curl -sk -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  $BASE/api/observer/peers/lab-east-peer

# Envelopes.
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $BASE/api/observer/envelopes
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $BASE/api/observer/envelopes/all-peers

# Free peers (no bound Compute Node).
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $BASE/api/observer/peers/free

# By-node grouping.
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $BASE/api/observer/peers/by-node
# → {"by_node":{"datawatch-ollama":[...]}, "unbound":[...]}

# Federation meta-peers (cross-instance attribution).
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $BASE/api/federation/meta-peers

# Bind an observer peer to a Compute Node.
curl -sk -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"peer":"lab-east-peer"}' \
  $BASE/api/compute/nodes/datawatch-ollama/observer-peer

# Detach the binding.
curl -sk -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  $BASE/api/compute/nodes/datawatch-ollama/observer-peer
```

chunks.title: How-to: Federated observer
chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Peer can't reach primary.** Mesh is up but `push_to.url` wrong
  (probably `127.0.0.1` instead of the tailnet IP). Use the primary's
  100.x.y.z address.
- **Token expired.** Peer-mint tokens default to 7-day TTL. Mint a
  fresh one + re-register on the peer.
- **Stale peer in the list.** Peer crashed; daemon restarted but the
  push config got removed. Either re-register on the peer or
  `observer peer-remove` on the primary to clean up.
- **Memory summaries not flowing.** Opt-in: `push_memory_summaries:
  true` on the peer. Off by default to avoid leaking content across
  trust boundaries.
- **Cog badge stuck on N stale.** A registered peer hasn't pushed in
  >60s. Either bring it back or remove the peer record. Click the
  badge in the PWA to navigate to it.

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.body:
# Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide

Datawatch v7.3.0 introduces cross-host session federation with
capability-based access control (CBAC). A federated peer is an AI agent running
on a remote datawatch instance that can connect to your instance using its own
bearer token. Every action it takes is gated against the capabilities you grant.

---

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: Base requirements
chunks.body:
## Base requirements

- Two running datawatch instances (primary + secondary). See [federated-observer.md](federated-observer.md) for how to set up federation and configure `observer.peers.allow_register: true`.
- Remote Server entry on the primary pointing at the secondary. See [multi-servers.md](multi-servers.md).
- Token credentials for cross-instance calls stored as secrets. See [secrets-manager.md](secrets-manager.md).

> **Pre-conditions**: CBAC requires a working federated observer setup. Complete [federated-observer.md](federated-observer.md) first.

---

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: Quick start
chunks.body: ## Quick start

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: 1. Register a peer with limited capabilities
chunks.body:
### 1. Register a peer with limited capabilities

```bash
# Register a remote instance as a federation peer.
# Default capabilities: ["federation-peer"] — health check + read its own
# entry only (v9.0.0, SEC-009). Grant more explicitly below if this peer
# needs it — the default no longer includes session/agent/observer reads
# or the ability to list other peers.
datawatch federation peer add peer-alpha \
  --url http://198.51.100.2:8080 \
  --token tok-peer-alpha \
  --capabilities federation-peer

# Verify it was registered:
datawatch federation peer list
```

Via comm channel (Telegram, Signal, etc.):
```
federation peer add peer-alpha http://198.51.100.2:8080 token=tok-peer-alpha
```

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: 2. Grant specific capabilities
chunks.body:
### 2. Grant specific capabilities

```bash
# Grant read-only access across all surfaces:
datawatch federation peer update peer-alpha \
  --capabilities read-only

# Grant session-operator (can send input + start/kill sessions):
datawatch federation peer update peer-alpha \
  --capabilities session-operator

# Grant multiple capabilities (mix groups and individual caps):
datawatch federation peer update peer-alpha \
  --capabilities "session-operator,analytics:read,dashboard:read"
```

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: 3. Test connectivity
chunks.body:
### 3. Test connectivity

```bash
datawatch federation peer test peer-alpha
# → {"ok":true,"latency_ms":12,"version":"v7.3.0"}
```

---

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: Capability model
chunks.body: ## Capability model

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: Built-in groups
chunks.body:
### Built-in groups

| Group | Key capabilities |
|---|---|
| `monitor` | health:read, analytics:read, sessions/agents/alerts list, usage:read |
| `session-viewer` | sessions:list/read, agents:list/read |
| `session-operator` | session-viewer + write/kill/input + pipeline start/cancel |
| `inference-admin` | llms:*, compute:* |
| `config-reader` | config:read, docs:read |
| `config-admin` | config:read/write, usage:read/write |
| `analytics-viewer` | analytics:read, dashboard:read, audit:read, usage:read |
| `autonomous-operator` | autonomous:list/read/write/run |
| `council-operator` | council:list/read/run |
| `federation-peer` | health:read, federation:self, usage:read |
| `comm-bridge` | sessions:list/read/input, comm:read/write, alerts:list/read |
| `session-default` | Design A3's per-session scoped-credential default — sessions/agents, queue, results, memory, comm, docs, autonomous-read, pipelines, council, usage:read/write; NOT secrets/config-write/federation/tailscale/LLM-registry/plugin-install |
| `read-only` | all :read/:list caps across every surface, incl. usage:read |
| `full-control` | all 58 capabilities |

**`federation-peer` is intentionally minimal as of v9.0.0 (SEC-009, breaking
change)** — a newly registered peer can check daemon health and read its own
registered entry (`GET /api/federation/peers/self`, gated on `federation:self`,
distinct from `federation:list`/`federation:read` which can enumerate every
*other* peer too), nothing else. Earlier versions granted sessions/agents/
observers/alerts/dashboard reads and `federation:list/read` by default — if
you're upgrading and a peer integration breaks, it was almost certainly
relying on one of those; grant the specific capability or group it actually
needs (see "Grant specific capabilities" above).

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: Individual surface:action capabilities
chunks.body:
### Individual surface:action capabilities

58 individual capabilities across 22 surfaces:

```
sessions:list   sessions:read   sessions:write  sessions:kill  sessions:input
agents:list     agents:read     agents:spawn     agents:terminate
observers:list  observers:read  observers:write
llms:list       llms:read       llms:write
compute:list    compute:read    compute:write
analytics:read  health:read
config:read     config:write
secrets:list    secrets:read    secrets:write
pipelines:list  pipelines:read  pipelines:start  pipelines:cancel
autonomous:list autonomous:read autonomous:write autonomous:run
council:list    council:read    council:run
federation:list federation:read federation:write federation:self
docs:read       audit:read
comm:read       comm:write
alerts:list     alerts:read
dashboard:read  dashboard:write
queue:read      queue:write
results:list    results:read    results:write
memory:read     memory:write
usage:read      usage:write
```

`queue:*` and `results:*` were added in v8.39.24 (Design A2 audit) — the
durable work queue (`/api/queue*`) and structured agent result store
(`/api/result-store*`) had no capability check of any kind before then.

`memory:*` was added in v8.39.25 (Design A3) to scope the memory_* MCP
tools for the new `session-default` group.

`usage:*` adds the usage-calculator readings series federation: the daemon
named by `usage.calculator.keeper` keeps the series and answers
`GET`/`POST /api/usage/readings`, `DELETE /api/usage/readings/{id}` and
`PUT /api/usage/extra-credit` for peers; the other daemons read through the
keeper (hop-marked requests always serve the keeper's local store) and
forward writes to it. `usage:read` is granted to the read groups
(`monitor`, `analytics-viewer`, `federation-peer`, `session-default`,
`read-only`), `usage:write` to the config/admin groups
(`config-admin`, `session-default`, `full-control`). A peer with
`usage:read` cannot append or delete readings — grant `usage:write`
deliberately.

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: Design A3 — per-session scoped credential
chunks.body:
### Design A3 — per-session scoped credential

A spawned session's bridge used to hold the real admin token (HLLM-001/002's
root cause — a hostile/misaligned session was a full-admin principal). As of
v8.39.25, every spawned session gets its own scoped credential instead,
minted at spawn and revoked immediately when the session ends:

- Default grant: the `session-default` builtin group (see the table above).
  Override via `session.capabilities` in config (accepts the same values as
  a federation peer's `--capabilities`: builtin group names or individual
  `surface:action` strings).
- Enforced at the REST chokepoint the native Go channel bridge actually
  uses — `GET /api/mcp/tools` (filters the catalog to what the caller can
  call) and `POST /api/mcp/call` (403s a disallowed tool; an unknown tool
  name is 404 for every caller, including admin). Every one of the 374 MCP
  tools has an assigned capability (`internal/federation/mcp_tool_caps.go`);
  a new tool with no entry is admin-only until classified, never silently
  open.
- The token is persisted (0600, under `data_dir`) so an already-running
  session's bridge keeps working across a daemon restart, and revoked
  immediately on session kill — a killed session's token can never be
  reused.
- The standalone MCP SSE transport (direct IDE/Cursor connections, not the
  session-bridge path) still uses its own, separate, admin-vs-federation-peer
  gate (`mcpFedCap`) — Design A3 does not change that path; extending the
  same per-tool map there is tracked as its own follow-up.

---

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: Custom capability groups
chunks.body:
## Custom capability groups

Create reusable named groups with exactly the capabilities you need:

```bash
# Create a custom group for read-only analytics + session listing:
datawatch federation group add analytics-reader \
  --caps "analytics:read,dashboard:read,sessions:list,health:read"

# Apply it to a peer:
datawatch federation peer update peer-alpha --capabilities analytics-reader

# List all groups (builtins + custom):
datawatch federation group list

# Delete a custom group:
datawatch federation group delete analytics-reader
```

Via REST API:
```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/federation/groups \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"analytics-reader","caps":["analytics:read","dashboard:read","sessions:list","health:read"]}'
```

---

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: YAML-seeded federation peers
chunks.body:
## YAML-seeded federation peers

Declare federation peers in your config file for automatic registration at startup:

```yaml
servers:
  - name: peer-alpha
    url: http://198.51.100.2:8080
    token: tok-peer-alpha
    enabled: true
    federated: true
    auth_type: token
    capabilities:
      - federation-peer
      - analytics:read
```

YAML-seeded peers have `builtin: true` — they cannot be deleted or modified at
runtime (same protection as YAML-seeded plain servers). Runtime-registered peers
override YAML seeds with the same name.

---

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: Verify capability enforcement
chunks.body:
## Verify capability enforcement

Test that capability gates work correctly:

```bash
# Peer token with sessions:list should succeed (200):
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer tok-peer-alpha" \
  http://localhost:8080/api/sessions

# Peer token without sessions:write should fail (403):
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer tok-peer-alpha" \
  http://localhost:8080/api/sessions/start \
  -d '{"profile":"default"}'

# Unknown token should fail (401):
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer bad-token" \
  http://localhost:8080/api/sessions
```

---

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: Cross-host session input
chunks.body:
## Cross-host session input

A federation peer can send input to a session on your instance. From a remote
peer's perspective, the path format is:

```
POST /api/sessions/<peer_name>/<session_id>/input
{"text": "hello"}
```

The local daemon looks up `<peer_name>` in the server registry, resolves its URL,
and proxies the request with the peer's registered token.

From the comm channel:
```
send peer-alpha/sess-abc: hello world
```

---

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: Rotating a peer's token
chunks.body:
## Rotating a peer's token

`GET`/list responses never return a peer's real bearer token — only
`token_present` (a token is set) and `token_prefix` (its first 4 characters,
enough to recognize which token you're looking at, not enough to reconstruct
it). This means you can no longer read a token back out once it's set; keep
the value somewhere you control (a password manager, the secrets vault) when
you first register a peer.

To rotate a peer's token, `PUT` the new value explicitly — you cannot copy a
`GET` response and re-submit it to "refresh" the token, since that response
never contained one:

```bash
curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>" \
  http://localhost:8080/api/federation/peers/peer-alpha \
  -d '{"token": "new-token-value"}'
```

Any other field update (label, capabilities) that omits `token` from the
request body leaves the existing token untouched — the update handler only
overwrites fields actually present in the request.

---

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: Enforcement points (BL316 S1)
chunks.body:
## Enforcement points (BL316 S1)

| Entry point | Capability required |
|---|---|
| GET /api/sessions | sessions:list |
| POST /api/sessions/start | sessions:write |
| POST /api/sessions/{id}/input | sessions:input |
| DELETE/POST /api/sessions/kill | sessions:kill |
| POST /api/mcp/call | comm:write |
| WebSocket MsgCommand | sessions:input |
| WebSocket MsgNewSession | sessions:write |
| POST /api/federation/peers | federation:write (admin only) |
| GET /api/federation/peers/self | federation:self (in the default group) |

---

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: PWA Federation Peers panel
chunks.body:
## PWA Federation Peers panel

The Observer tab includes a **Federation Peers** card where you can:

- View all registered peers with their URL, enabled status, and capability pills
- Test connectivity (shows latency and remote version)
- Add new peers via a form
- Delete peers

If you are connected with a federated peer token, the Add/Delete buttons will
return 403 — the panel shows a "Read-only (peer token)" message.

---

chunks.title: Federation Peer CBAC — Operator Guide
chunks.heading: MCP tools (BL316 S2)
chunks.body:
## MCP tools (BL316 S2)

```
federation_peer_list         — list all registered peers
federation_peer_add          — register a new peer
federation_peer_get          — get one peer by name
federation_peer_update       — update peer config/capabilities
federation_peer_delete       — remove a peer
federation_peer_test         — ping peer /api/health

federation_group_list        — list builtin + custom groups
federation_group_list_builtins — list builtin groups only
federation_group_add         — create a custom group
federation_group_get         — get a group by name
federation_group_update      — update a custom group
federation_group_delete      — delete a custom group
```

chunks.title: Share-aware capacity across federated peers
chunks.body:
# Share-aware capacity across federated peers

Two datawatch daemons can quietly run the *same physical resource*: the
same GPU box reached through two addresses, or two LLM entries that bill
to the same cloud account. Without telling the daemons about it, each
daemon budgets that resource in full — two sessions on alpha, two on
beta, and the physical box (or the plan ceiling) gets double-booked.

The **resource fingerprint exchange** lets the two daemons detect that
they hold the same resource — without either side ever learning the
other's raw identity values, labels, or credentials — and surface each
candidate to you as a **pending match**. You confirm or reject each one.
Once confirmed, a shared compute node is treated as one shared pool
(peer usage counts against your local limit at admission), and a shared
billing group is surfaced so you can fold the peer's spend into your
budget decision (see *Billing groups*, below).

Everything is **opt-in in both directions and off by default**. With no
opted-in peers and no confirmed matches the daemon does nothing new: no
extra HTTP calls, no different admission behaviour.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [federation, capacity, queue, compute, budget, peers, security]
exec_steps:
  - tool: federation_fingerprint_matches
    description: List resource-fingerprint matches with federated peers (all states by default; filter optional)
    args:
      state: pending   # optional: pending | confirmed | rejected (omit for all)
    read_only: true
  - tool: federation_fingerprint_confirm
    description: Confirm a match - the two daemons hold the same underlying resource
    args:
      id: "{{params.match_id}}"
    read_only: false
  - tool: federation_fingerprint_reject
    description: Reject a match (also undoes a prior confirmation)
    args:
      id: "{{params.match_id}}"
    read_only: false
  - tool: federation_peer_update
    description: Enable the fingerprint exchange for one peer on this daemon
    args:
      name: "{{params.peer_name}}"
      fingerprint_sync: true
    read_only: false
  - tool: llm_update
    description: Label an LLM entry with the shared billing-group name (same label on both daemons)
    args:
      name: "{{params.llm_name}}"
      billing_group: "{{params.billing_group}}"
    read_only: false

chunks.title: Share-aware capacity across federated peers
chunks.heading: What gets fingerprinted
chunks.body:
## What gets fingerprinted

| Kind | Source value (never leaves the host) | Matched as |
|------|--------------------------------------|------------|
| `compute_node` | The node's own identity: its GPU UUIDs, else its disk-persisted node-instance ID — never the name or address you configured for it, so the same box is the same value under a LAN address and a tailnet address | A node whose identity both daemons resolve |
| `billing_group` | The operator-set label on an LLM entry (`billing_group`) that you choose to give to LLMs on both daemons that bill to one account | LLM entries that carry the *same* label on both sides |

A node with no identity source (no observer peer bound, host reported
neither GPU UUIDs nor an instance ID) is simply not fingerprinted —
that is not a failure.

chunks.title: Share-aware capacity across federated peers
chunks.heading: How detection works
chunks.body:
## How detection works

1. Each daemon derives a **pair key**: HMAC-SHA256 over the bearer token
   it uses for the pair, under a fixed message namespace. Both sides
   arrive at the same key independently — no new secret, no new channel.
2. Each daemon computes one **keyed hash per resource** —
   HMAC-SHA256 of `kind + value` under the pair key — and is ready to
   answer `GET /api/federation/fingerprints` with the list
   (`kind`, `name`, `hash`).
3. On a fixed **15-minute cadence** (a built-in constant, not a config
   key), each daemon pulls the fingerprint list of every peer it has
   opted in, and records a **pending match** for every hash that
   appears on both sides. The first exchange runs immediately when the
   daemon starts; a flag you flip at runtime is picked up on the next
   15-minute tick (the peer list is re-read on every pass).
4. Matches are **suggestions**, never auto-decisions. Your confirm/reject
   is persisted under `<data_dir>/autonomous/fingerprint/matches.json`
   and survives restarts. A rejected match **stays rejected** — a
   re-sync can never re-open it. A confirmation can later be undone with
   a reject. Every decision is written to the audit log.

chunks.title: Share-aware capacity across federated peers
chunks.heading: Effect of a confirmation
chunks.body:
## Effect of a confirmation

- **`compute_node`** — at admission time, the pool check for that node
  adds the peer's live usage of the same node (fetched from the peer's
  `/api/capacity` at check time) to your local in-flight count before
  comparing to your local limit. A task held by this shows the reason
  `shared node busy on peer …` in the wait queue. Only a *confirmed*
  match with an *opted-in* peer triggers a peer call; pending and
  rejected matches never do, and only `node:` pools are affected —
  never the `host`, `llm:` or external pools, and never
  operator-started interactive sessions.
- **`billing_group`** — the confirmation records that both LLMs bill to
  the same account, which feeds your budget decision: name the peer in
  the LLM budget's `peer_window` (CLI `--budget-peer-window`, MCP
  `llm_update`/`budget_set` `peer_window`, config, or the budget's own
  surfaces) and that peer's spend counts toward the ceiling. The
  exchange never modifies your budget by itself.

chunks.title: Share-aware capacity across federated peers
chunks.heading: Base requirements
chunks.body:
## Base requirements

- Two datawatch daemons that are already **federated peers of each
  other** (each registered on the other) with a peer-to-peer bearer
  token, and with a federated capability grant that includes the
  fingerprint surface (the full-control grant includes it).
- At least one shared resource of a fingerprinted kind:
  - a compute node reachable from **both** daemons with an identity
    source (observer peer bound on the node, or a local node whose host
    reports GPU UUIDs / node-instance ID), or
  - LLM entries on both daemons that you will give the **same
    `billing_group` label**.
- **Both** daemons must opt in: on each daemon, the peer entry that
  points at the other must have `fingerprint_sync: true`. A capability
  grant does not imply fingerprint trust — the serving daemon answers
  `403` to a peer that has not opted it in, and the pulling daemon
  never even calls a peer whose entry is off.

Enablement per channel (run on **both** daemons, with the *other*
daemon's name):

| Channel | Command / action |
|---------|------------------|
| CLI (new peer) | `datawatch federation peer add --name beta --url <url> --token <tok> --fingerprint-sync` |
| CLI (existing peer) | `datawatch federation peer update beta --fingerprint-sync` — turn it off again with `--fingerprint-sync=false` (the flag is only sent when you set it, so "unset" never resets a previous `true`) |
| Chat (any comm channel) | `federation peer fingerprint beta on` · `federation peer fingerprint beta off` |
| MCP | `federation_peer_add` / `federation_peer_update` with `"fingerprint_sync": true` |
| PWA | Settings → Comms → **Federation Peers** → per-peer **Resource fingerprint exchange** toggle (also a checkbox in the *Add Federation Peer* form) |
| Config (YAML `servers[]` entry) | `fingerprint_sync: true` (default `false`; requires a daemon restart) |

Labelling an LLM with a shared billing group (both daemons, same
label):

| Channel | Command / action |
|---------|------------------|
| CLI | `datawatch llm add … --billing-group shared-plan-a` · `datawatch llm update <name> --billing-group shared-plan-a` (empty value clears it) |
| Chat | `llm add <name> … billing_group=shared-plan-a` (kv-style on the llm verbs) |
| MCP | `llm_add` / `llm_update` with `"billing_group": "shared-plan-a"` |
| PWA | Settings → Compute → **LLM edit** → `billingGroup` field |
| REST | `PUT /api/llms/<name>` with `"billing_group": "shared-plan-a"` |

chunks.title: Share-aware capacity across federated peers
chunks.heading: Walkthrough: the same GPU box behind two daemons
chunks.body:
## Walkthrough: the same GPU box behind two daemons

1. **Opt in both directions.** On daemon `alpha`, enable the exchange
   for peer `beta`; on daemon `beta`, do the same for `alpha` (any
   channel above).
2. **Wait for the first tick** — it runs immediately on daemon start,
   or within 15 minutes of flipping the flag at runtime.
3. **Find the pending match.**
   - CLI: `datawatch fingerprint list --state pending`
   - Chat: `federation fingerprint list pending`
   - MCP: `federation_fingerprint_matches` with `"state": "pending"`
   - REST: `GET /api/federation/fingerprint-matches?state=pending`
   - PWA: Settings → Comms → Federation Peers → **Pending resource
     matches** panel

   Each row shows the id, state, kind, and the local and peer resource
   names — e.g. id `m-7f3a…`, `pending`, `compute_node`, local `rtx4090`,
   peer `beta`, peer name `rtx`.
4. **Decide.** You own the box and both daemons should share it:
   - CLI: `datawatch fingerprint confirm m-7f3a…`
   - Chat: `federation fingerprint confirm m-7f3a…`
   - MCP: `federation_fingerprint_confirm` with the match `id`
   - REST: `POST /api/federation/fingerprint-matches/m-7f3a…/confirm`
   - PWA: the **Confirm** button on the row

   (Same verbs with `rejected`/`reject` when the match is wrong — two
   different boxes that happen to share a name are *not* a match, and
   the identity value, not the name, is what was compared.)
5. **Share-aware admission is now active.** Watch
   `datawatch capacity` / the wait queue on `alpha`: while `beta`'s
   usage on the same box is in flight, `alpha`'s `node:rtx4090` pool
   limit is tested against *combined* usage, and tasks wait with the
   reason `shared node busy on peer beta: …` instead of overloading the
   hardware.

chunks.title: Share-aware capacity across federated peers
chunks.heading: When the peer is down
chunks.body:
## When the peer is down

The exchange is deliberately **slow and soft** — it answers *is this
the same resource?*, not *how busy is it right now*:

- **Pull failure.** A peer that does not answer a fingerprint pull
  (timeout, `403` not opted in on their side, malformed body) is logged
  **once per failure episode** (silent until it answers again) and the
  pass continues — one dead peer never blocks the others or the loop.
- **Admission failure.** When the gate checks a confirmed shared node,
  the peer's live usage is polled at that moment; if the peer cannot be
  reached, contributes a wrong status, or does not report the pool, it
  **contributes zero** and your local work is admitted against your own
  counts — admission **fails open** on peer errors. The failure is
  logged once per episode the same way.
- **Decisions are durable.** Peer down-ness never changes match
  records: a rejected match is never re-opened by a later sync, and a
  confirmed one stays confirmed until a reject undoes it.
- **Cadence.** The 15-minute tick is a fixed constant (open by design,
  not a config key): no new polling loop, one shared exchange pass. A
  single peer pull is capped at a 5-second timeout and a 64 KiB body,
  so a broken or hostile peer cannot hang the loop or stream memory.

chunks.title: Share-aware capacity across federated peers
chunks.heading: What actually crosses the wire
chunks.body:
## What actually crosses the wire

Only three fields per resource leave a daemon: `kind`, `name` (your
own local label for the resource — the only plain-text field) and
`hash`. The identity values themselves — GPU UUIDs, node-instance IDs,
the billing-group label, tokens, addresses, credentials — **never do**,
on either direction of the exchange:

- The hash is HMAC-SHA256 of `kind + value` keyed by the **per-pair
  key** (derived from the pair's bearer token under a fixed message
  namespace). Two different peers holding the same box get *different*
  hashes for it, so peers cannot cross-correlate, and a hash cannot be
  checked against a candidate value without the pair key (there is no
  unkeyed precompute to look up).
- `kind` is mixed into the MAC, so a node identity can never be
  mistaken for a billing-group label (or vice versa) even if the
  underlying strings coincide.
- `GET /api/federation/fingerprints` rejects the local admin token with
  `400` (it has no peer identity), missing bearer tokens with `401`,
  and peers that have not opted in with `403` — a capability grant
  alone is not enough, and both daemons must have opted in.
- Match confirmations and rejections are audit-logged
  (`fingerprint_match_confirmed` / `fingerprint_match_rejected`) with
  the kind, local name and peer name — not the identity values.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph alpha[daemon alpha]
    A1[identity / labels stay local] --> A2[keyed hashes]
  end
  subgraph beta[daemon beta]
    B1[identity / labels stay local] --> B2[keyed hashes]
  end
  A2 -- "GET /api/federation/fingerprints\n(kind, name, hash)" --> B2
  B2 -- "GET /api/federation/fingerprints\n(kind, name, hash)" --> A2
  A2 --> M[Pending match list]
  B2 --> M
  M -- "operator confirms or rejects\n(persisted + audited)" --> G[shared-node gate\nat admission / budget peer_window]
```
