chunks.title: How-to: Native ACME / Let's Encrypt Certificates (BL397)
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

- **Two validation methods.** HTTP-01 (default) — one A/AAAA record per
  hostname, port 80 reachable, no DNS management. DNS-01 — a zone-scoped
  provider API token (Cloudflare in this build), no port 80 needed, the
  only method that supports wildcard domains. Pick HTTP-01 unless you
  need a wildcard or genuinely can't open port 80.
- **Staging first.** `acme.endpoint` defaults to `staging` — Let's
  Encrypt's test directory, generous rate limits, but the issued cert
  isn't trusted by real browsers. Verify the whole flow works there,
  then flip to `production` for a real cert.
- **Apply mode.** By default, a successful issue or renewal writes the
  PEM, updates `server.tls_cert`/`tls_key`, and restarts the daemon so
  the TLS listener picks it up — one short window roughly every 90 days.
  Set `acme.apply.hot_swap: true` for zero-downtime renewals instead —
  the listener reloads the cert from disk on its next handshake, no
  restart (the first-ever switch to ACME still restarts once regardless,
  since the running listener isn't watching the new path yet).
- **Renews itself.** A background check runs on startup and every 6
  hours; a cert within `renewal_days` (default 30) of expiring is
  automatically re-ordered.

chunks.title: How-to: Native ACME / Let's Encrypt Certificates (BL397)
chunks.heading: Base requirements
chunks.body:
## Base requirements

- `datawatch` daemon running and reachable at its public hostname.
- A public DNS A/AAAA record for that hostname pointing at this host.
  **datawatch does not manage DNS** — create this record yourself before
  enabling ACME.
- **Inbound TCP/80 reachable from the public internet.** Let's Encrypt's
  validator connects to port 80 specifically — this is *not* the same as
  `server.port` (default `8080`; the existing dual-port model only
  redirects 8080→8443, it doesn't bind port 80). You need either:
  - `server.port: 80` directly, which on Linux requires root or
    `setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep <path-to-datawatch-binary>` if the
    daemon runs as an unprivileged user, or
  - an external port-forward from 80 to whatever `server.port` is.
- Firewall: open TCP/80 inbound (`ufw allow 80/tcp` or equivalent).

chunks.title: How-to: Native ACME / Let's Encrypt Certificates (BL397)
chunks.heading: Enable it
chunks.body:
## Enable it

1. Confirm the DNS record resolves:
   ```bash
   dig +short your-hostname.example.com A
   ```
2. Edit `config.yaml` (or use the PWA Settings → Web Server card's
   certificate-source selector — see below):
   ```yaml
   server:
     port: 80   # see "Base requirements" above
   acme:
     enabled: true
     endpoint: staging
     domains:
       - your-hostname.example.com
   ```
3. Restart the daemon. Watch the issuer log:
   ```bash
   datawatch acme status
   ```
   `issued: true` with a `not_after` date roughly 90 days out means it
   worked. `last_error` set and `consecutive_failures` climbing means
   something's wrong — check `acme verify` next.
4. Verify the pre-flight conditions directly:
   ```bash
   datawatch acme verify
   ```
   Reports whether every configured domain resolves and whether the
   configured ACME directory is reachable. Does not perform an order —
   safe to run anytime.
5. Once staging issues cleanly, flip to production:
   ```yaml
   acme:
     endpoint: production
   ```
   then force a renewal so it actually re-orders against the new
   directory (switching the config alone doesn't trigger a new order
   until the cert is actually due for renewal):
   ```bash
   datawatch acme renew
   ```
6. Confirm from outside with a real browser or `curl` **without** any
   `-k`/insecure flag — a clean connection with no certificate warning is
   the real acceptance test:
   ```bash
   curl https://your-hostname.example.com:8443/api/health
   ```

chunks.heading: Using DNS-01 instead (wildcards, or no port 80)
chunks.body:
## Using DNS-01 instead (wildcards, or no port 80)

1. Mint a **zone-scoped** API token — Cloudflare "Zone > DNS > Edit" on
   the ONE zone you're issuing for, never the account-global key.
2. Store it via the secrets manager:
   ```bash
   datawatch secret set cf-zone-edit-token "<your-token>"
   ```
3. Config:
   ```yaml
   acme:
     method: dns01
     dns01:
       provider: cloudflare
       token_secret: "${secret:cf-zone-edit-token}"
   ```
4. Restart — no port 80 / firewall changes needed for this path. The
   rest of the workflow (staging first, `acme verify`, flip to
   production) is identical to HTTP-01.

chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.body:
## Troubleshooting

- **`acme_status` shows `enabled: false` even though `acme.enabled: true`
  is set** — the subsystem failed to start at boot (check daemon logs for
  `[acme] startup failed`). Common cause: the account couldn't register
  (network blocked outbound 443, or a stale registration from switching
  staging↔production — the daemon re-registers automatically on an
  endpoint change, so this should self-heal on the next restart).
- **Order fails, `last_error` mentions a timeout or connection refused**
  — port 80 isn't actually reachable from the public internet. Check the
  firewall and that `server.port` is really `80` (not `8080`).
- **Switched to `production` but still see the old self-signed cert** —
  switching `acme.endpoint` doesn't force a new order by itself (the
  existing cert isn't due for renewal yet); run `datawatch acme renew`
  explicitly.

chunks.title: How-to: list endpoints, paging, and loading states
chunks.body:
# How-to: list endpoints, paging, and loading states

datawatch's list endpoints are deliberately small. A long-running daemon
accumulates tens of thousands of bytes of long text per record — task text,
prompts, responses, story and task data — and almost none of it is rendered
in a list. So every list endpoint sends one compact row per item, pages by
`limit`/`cursor`, and answers unchanged re-requests with **304 Not
Modified**. The full record is always one request away on the by-id route.

The difference in size, measured on the operator's daemon before and after:

| List | Before | After (raw / gzip) |
|---|---|---|
| Sessions | 32 MB | 16 KB / 2 KB |
| Automata (PRDs) | 339 MB (one record alone: 13 MB) | 57 KB / 3.5 KB |
| Automations | 1.6 GB | 9.2 KB / 1.3 KB |
| Alerts | 219 KB | 22 KB / 6.8 KB |

(On the seeded live-style data set: 3000 sessions, 300 Automata, 20
Automations, 500 alerts.)
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [sessions, automata, automations, api, pwa]

chunks.title: How-to: list endpoints, paging, and loading states
chunks.heading: The sessions list
chunks.body:
## The sessions list

`GET /api/sessions?view=summary` returns an array of rows. Each row carries
only what a list card renders — identity, state, backend, project, activity
times, a one-line `status_line` from the latest response (capped), token and
cost totals, and the parent id. No task text, no prompts, no transcripts.

By default the response holds every non-terminal session plus the 50 most
recently updated terminal ones; when the cap drops anything you get an
`X-Datawatch-Sessions-Omitted` count in the headers.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [sessions, automata, automations, api, pwa]

chunks.title: How-to: list endpoints, paging, and loading states
chunks.heading: Paging and filters
chunks.body:
### Paging and filters

| Param | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `view=summary` | select the row-only summary view |
| `limit` | rows per page — default 50, maximum 500; with `limit` or `cursor` the body becomes the envelope `{"sessions": [...], "next_cursor": "...", "total": N}` |
| `cursor` | opaque; pass back `next_cursor` to get the next page (newest-first, no repeats, no skips) |
| `status` | comma list of state names, or `active` for all non-terminal states |
| `active=1` | only non-terminal sessions |
| `q` | case-insensitive match on name, id or the first 256 chars of the task text |
| `since` | RFC3339 or unix seconds; only sessions updated after it |

Without `view` and without paging the legacy full array is returned
unchanged, so existing scripts keep working.

```bash
# Set DW to your daemon base URL (no trailing path):
export DW="http://<host>:<port>"

# First page: 50 rows, newest first.
curl -sS "$DW/api/sessions?view=summary&limit=50"

# Next page: use the next_cursor the first page returned.
curl -sS "$DW/api/sessions?view=summary&limit=50&cursor=$NEXT"

# Only running work, matched by name or task text.
curl -sS "$DW/api/sessions?view=summary&limit=20&active=1&q=release"
```

Headers on every summary response (both shapes):

```
ETag: "9f2c…"                     ← 32-hex sha of the body
Cache-Control: no-cache
X-Datawatch-Sessions-Total: 3654  ← filtered total, even though the body is one page
```

chunks.title: How-to: list endpoints, paging, and loading states
chunks.heading: The Automata list
chunks.body:
## The Automata list

`GET /api/autonomous/prds` (no params) returns the summary list:

```json
{ "prds": [ { "id": "…", "title": "…", "status": "running", "rev": 9,
              "story_count": 5, "task_count": 14,
              "task_status_counts": {"done": 9, "in_progress": 3} } ],
  "total": 273,
  "next_cursor": "eyJ1…" }
```

A row's size depends only on the PRD's identity fields and how many distinct
task statuses it has — never on how much story and task text it holds. Fields
include `id`, `title`, `status`, `rev`, timestamps, `decision_count`,
`story_count`, `task_count`, `task_status_counts`, cost totals, `tags`,
`type`, `backend`, `priority`, `automation_id`, `blocked_reason`,
`quality_gate_state` and `parent_prd_id`. Story-level detail (per-story
counts) is one more request away on by-id.

The same paging and filter params as the sessions list, plus:

- `status=queued,blocked` — comma list of PRD statuses,
- `tag=NAME` (or `tag_id=ID`) — only PRDs carrying that tag,
- `q=needle` — matches title and id.

One quirk worth knowing: on the **unfiltered** first page you get every
active PRD (running, queued, waiting, blocked, paused, …) plus the most
recent `limit` of the rest; the cursor then walks only the rest, so active
rows are never repeated or skipped as you page.

`?full=1` returns the legacy shape: every PRD, in full. That is the 339 MB
form — useful for export, wrong for a list UI.

```bash
curl -sS "$DW/api/autonomous/prds?limit=50&active=1"
# next page:
curl -sS "$DW/api/autonomous/prds?limit=50&cursor=$NEXT"
```

chunks.heading: Getting the full record
chunks.body:
## Getting the full record

| Want | Endpoint |
|---|---|
| One session in full | `GET /api/sessions/{id}` |
| One Automaton in full | `GET /api/autonomous/prds/{id}?full=1` |
| One Automaton, with the heavy text fields capped | `GET /api/autonomous/prds/{id}` |
| The heavy text of an Automaton (checks, results, outputs, verifier transcript) | `GET /api/autonomous/prds/{id}/outputs` |

The capped by-id form keeps each long text field under a 4 KB cap and marks
what it cut (`truncated` lists the field names; each cut field carries a ref
to the full copy), so the body stays small even on a 13 MB Automaton.

chunks.title: How-to: list endpoints, paging, and loading states
chunks.heading: Re-asking without re-downloading (ETag / 304)
chunks.body:
## Re-asking without re-downloading (ETag / 304)

Every list endpoint above sets an `ETag`. Send it back and an unchanged
list answers **304 Not Modified** with no body — nothing to parse, nearly
nothing to transfer. Browsers do this for you with `Cache-Control: no-cache`
semantics; manual clients must copy the header:

```bash
ETAG=$(curl -sSI "$DW/api/autonomous/prds?limit=50" \
          | tr -d '\r' | awk -F': ' '/^ETag:/{print $2}')
# unchanged → 304, empty body:
curl -sS -D - -o /dev/null "$DW/api/autonomous/prds?limit=50" \
     -H "If-None-Match: $ETAG" | grep -i '^HTTP\|^etag'
HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
```

A 304 means "your cached copy is still the latest"; the client keeps
whatever it last stored. That is what lets a tab show old data
instantly and refresh it in the background.

chunks.heading: Compression
chunks.body:
## Compression

JSON list responses larger than ~1 KB are served gzipped to clients that
ask (`Accept-Encoding: gzip`, so `curl --compressed` or any browser).
Small bodies, streams, WebSocket and the proxy paths are never compressed.
That is the gap between the two size columns in the table above — the
Automata list goes from 57 KB to 3.5 KB on the wire.

chunks.title: How-to: list endpoints, paging, and loading states
chunks.heading: How the web UI loads these lists
chunks.body:
## How the web UI loads these lists

Every list view in the web app (Sessions, Automata, Automation, Alerts)
behaves the same way:

1. **Instant skeleton + "Loading".** You never see a blank tab; the tab
   shows a placeholder row the moment you open it.
2. **Cached first paint.** If a previous response is in the tab's local
   storage it is rendered immediately and labelled *stale* / *cached —
   N s ago*, while the fresh request runs in the background.
3. **Stale is not failed.** A slow or timed-out refresh shows the stale
   copy with a warning ("data may be stale — last load N s ago"),
   never a blank screen.
4. **Failed has a Retry.** If there is no cached copy either, the error is
   shown with a Retry button that re-issues the same request.
5. **Hidden tabs stop polling.** List tabs you are not looking at do not
   keep re-fetching; opening one refetches in the background and updates
   the *stale* badge when it lands.

So the contract a tab can rely on is: **something on screen in 100 ms,
fresh data as soon as the network allows, a visible reason and a Retry
every time the network does not.** The nine slow-network scenarios (cold
load, empty list, failed load, stale revalidation, offline, and page-reload
patterns) exercise exactly this, throttled to a slow-4G profile — run them
with `cd scripts/test-stories/pwa && node run-all.mjs --group load`, or let
release smoke §79 run them against the smoke daemon.

chunks.title: How-to: list endpoints, paging, and loading states
chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.body:
## Troubleshooting

- **A list is blank with an error and a Retry button** — the request failed
  (network, timeout, 5xx). Retry, or hit the endpoint with curl to see the
  real status: `curl -sS "$DW/api/autonomous/prds?limit=10"`.
- **A list looks incomplete** — the summary view caps how many terminal
  sessions (or non-active PRDs on one page) it returns. Use `cursor` to
  page, `X-Datawatch-Sessions-Omitted` tells you how many terminal sessions
  the cap dropped.
- **A 304 keeps coming back** — good: your cached copy matches. Force a
  fresh body by omitting `If-None-Match`.
- **An endpoint still looks huge** — check you are not on the legacy form:
  no `view=summary`/`limit` on `/api/sessions`, or `full=1` on the Automata
  routes is exactly that.

chunks.title: How-to: LLM Registry (v7.0.0)
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

The LLM registry is the single source of truth for every language
model datawatch can reach. Each entry is a named definition:

```
name     — the identifier consumers use (sessions, Council, /api/ask, Automata)
kind     — the protocol adapter (ollama, openwebui, claude, claude-code, …)
models[] — per-node model assignments ({node, model} pairs)
compute_nodes — ordered failover list of Compute Node names
```

Before v7, every backend had its own config block (`cfg.ollama`,
`cfg.aider`, …) and separate mental model. In v7 they collapse here:
Settings → Compute → LLM Configuration.

> **Auto-registered LLMs**: The daemon automatically registers a `claude-code` entry (kind `claude-code`) at startup if the `claude` binary is on PATH. No manual `llm add` step is needed for Claude Code sessions. Other kinds (`ollama`, `claude`, `aider`, etc.) must be registered explicitly. Use `GET /api/llms` (plural) or `datawatch llm list` to see what is currently registered, including any auto-registered entries.

chunks.heading: LLM kinds
chunks.body:
### LLM kinds

| Kind | Protocol | Compute nodes needed | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ollama` | Ollama HTTP API | Yes | Local GPU / homelab inference |
| `openwebui` | OpenWebUI HTTP API | Yes | OpenWebUI front-end proxy |
| `opencode` | Ollama-compatible wrapper | Yes | opencode session backend |
| `claude` | Anthropic API (cloud) | No | Cloud inference, Council |
| `claude-code` | tmux session agent | No | AI coding assistant sessions |
| `opencode-acp` | tmux session agent | Optional | opencode ACP sessions |
| `opencode-prompt` | tmux session agent | Optional | opencode prompt sessions |
| `aider` | tmux session agent | Optional | aider coding assistant |
| `goose` | tmux session agent | Optional | goose coding assistant |
| `gemini` | tmux session agent | Optional | Gemini coding assistant |
| `shell` | tmux session / shell script | Optional | Custom shell automation |

**Inference kinds** (`ollama`, `openwebui`, `opencode`, `claude`) go
through the dispatcher for one-shot calls (Council debates, `/api/ask`,
agent spawning). **Session-backend kinds** (`claude-code`, `aider`,
`goose`, etc.) own a tmux session end-to-end; the registry holds their
binary path, model selection, and console preferences.

chunks.title: How-to: LLM Registry (v7.0.0)
chunks.heading: EnabledModel — per-node model pairs
chunks.body:
### EnabledModel — per-node model pairs

The `models[]` list on an LLM entry holds `{node, model}` pairs. Each
pair pins one model name to one Compute Node. The dispatcher consults
this list when routing a call: it picks the first reachable node that
has a matching pair. For SaaS kinds (`claude`, `gemini`) the `node`
field is empty — only `model` matters.

Example (multi-node Ollama):

```json
{
  "name": "my-ollama",
  "kind": "ollama",
  "compute_nodes": ["gpu-primary", "gpu-secondary"],
  "models": [
    {"node": "gpu-primary",   "model": "qwen3:32b"},
    {"node": "gpu-secondary", "model": "llama3.1:8b"}
  ]
}
```

If `gpu-primary` is unreachable, the dispatcher falls to
`gpu-secondary` and uses `llama3.1:8b` there.

chunks.heading: Tag roles on LLMs
chunks.body:
## Tag roles on LLMs

A role is a workload label on a registry entry, such as `planning` or
`verification`. It lets a call site ask for "the LLM that does planning" and
leaves the choice of entry to the registry. Roles are an open set of strings;
they are trimmed, lower-cased and de-duplicated, and an empty role is refused.

```sh
# Tag at creation.
datawatch llm add big-gpu --kind ollama --role planning --role verification

# Change later. Omitting --role keeps the stored roles.
datawatch llm update big-gpu --role planning

# A single empty value clears them.
datawatch llm update big-gpu --role ""
```

The same `roles` list is accepted by REST (`POST /api/llms`, `PUT
/api/llms/{name}`), MCP (`llm_add`, `llm_update`), the comm channel
(`llm add|update <name> roles=planning,verification`; `roles=` clears) and the
Settings → Compute → LLM edit form.

chunks.title: How-to: LLM Registry (v7.0.0)
chunks.heading: How a role resolves
chunks.body:
### How a role resolves

1. **An explicit override wins.** A call site that names a backend or model
   uses it, and the role lookup is skipped.
2. **Otherwise the role lookup runs.** Only enabled entries count. One
   claimant is used. Several claimants are ambiguous: the first by name is
   used and a warning is raised.
3. **No claimant** leaves the call site on its normal default.

chunks.title: How-to: LLM Registry (v7.0.0)
chunks.heading: The contention warning
chunks.body:
### The contention warning

The daemon checks roles every `autonomous.role_scan_interval_seconds` (300 by
default) and again on every LLM write. It warns when:

- two or more enabled entries claim one role (the warning names the role, the
  entries and the one being used), or
- roles that pointed at different entries at the previous check now resolve to
  the same one.

Warnings are advisory and are written to the audit log. Nothing is blocked.
`GET /api/llms` lists them under `status.role_warnings`, `GET /api/llms/{name}`
shows the ones that name that entry as `role_warnings`, and `GET /api/llm-roles`
returns the resolved table with them.

### Why it matters

A single `ollama-gpu-box` entry routes all workloads to the same node with the same model. A use-case entry lets you say: "coding requests go to a node with a coding-optimized model first; heavy reasoning goes to the highest-VRAM node only; fast triage uses the smallest model on the lowest-latency node."

chunks.heading: Pattern
chunks.body:
### Pattern

```json
{
  "name": "llm-coding",
  "kind": "ollama",
  "model": "codestral:22b-q5_k_m",
  "compute_nodes": ["gpu-primary", "gpu-secondary"],
  "models": [
    {"node": "gpu-primary",   "model": "codestral:22b-q5_k_m"},
    {"node": "gpu-primary",   "model": "devstral:latest"},
    {"node": "gpu-primary",   "model": "qwen3-coder:30b"},
    {"node": "gpu-secondary", "model": "codestral:22b-q5_k_m"},
    {"node": "gpu-secondary", "model": "devstral:latest"}
  ]
}
```

The dispatcher tries `gpu-primary` first (in model-list order); falls to `gpu-secondary` only if `gpu-primary` is unreachable or busy. Models are chosen by the `{node, model}` pair — only pairs listed here are eligible.

chunks.title: How-to: LLM Registry (v7.0.0)
chunks.heading: Recommended use-case entries
chunks.body:
### Recommended use-case entries

These names are conventions, not reserved identifiers. Adjust nodes and models to your hardware:

| Entry | Use case | Default model | Node order |
|---|---|---|---|
| `llm-coding` | Code generation, review | coding-optimized model (e.g. `codestral:22b`) | High-VRAM node → secondary |
| `llm-reasoning` | Deep analysis, architecture | largest available model | Highest-VRAM node only |
| `llm-chat` | General conversation | mid-size quality model (e.g. `mistral-small3:24b`) | Low-latency node → high-VRAM fallback |
| `llm-fast` | Quick responses, triage | smallest capable model (e.g. `qwen3:1.7b`) | Low-latency node → any fallback |
| `llm-embed` | Embeddings | embedding-specific model (e.g. `nomic-embed-text`) | Any node with the model |

chunks.title: How-to: LLM Registry (v7.0.0)
chunks.heading: Hardware budget considerations
chunks.body:
### Hardware budget considerations

When building the `models[]` list, exclude model+node combinations where the model exceeds the node's VRAM. A model that won't fit causes Ollama to CPU-offload layers silently, which is slower than using a different node that can run it fully on GPU. For example, a 65GB model should not appear in the `models[]` list for a 32GB node — put it only in the entry for your high-VRAM node.

```json
{
  "name": "llm-reasoning",
  "kind": "ollama",
  "model": "gpt-oss:120b",
  "compute_nodes": ["blackwell-128gb"],
  "models": [
    {"node": "blackwell-128gb", "model": "gpt-oss:120b"},
    {"node": "blackwell-128gb", "model": "llama3.3:70b-q4_k_m"},
    {"node": "blackwell-128gb", "model": "mixtral:8x22b-q4_k_m"}
  ]
}
```

The RTX 5090 (32GB) is intentionally absent from `llm-reasoning` — models that won't fit fully should fail over to a node that can run them, not partially offload to CPU.

chunks.title: How-to: LLM Registry (v7.0.0)
chunks.heading: Selecting a use-case entry in routing rules
chunks.body:
### Selecting a use-case entry in routing rules

Routing rules can match on session context and select the target LLM by name:

```yaml
routing_rules:
  - name: coding-sessions
    match:
      session_tags: [coding]
    target_llm: llm-coding

  - name: analysis-sessions
    match:
      session_tags: [analysis, architecture]
    target_llm: llm-reasoning
```

Use-case entries are otherwise identical to any other LLM entry — they appear in `datawatch llm list`, can be referenced in Council personas, Automata PRDs, and session start requests (`llm: llm-coding`).

---

chunks.title: How-to: LLM Registry (v7.0.0)
chunks.heading: 4a. Happy path — CLI
chunks.body:
### 4a. Happy path — CLI

```sh
# 1. List what's registered.
datawatch llm list
#  → name            kind         enabled  models
#    claude-api      claude       yes      claude-sonnet-5
#    my-ollama       ollama       yes      llama3.1:8b  (node: gpu-box)
#    claude-code     claude-code  yes      —

# 2. Fetch one entry.
datawatch llm get my-ollama

# 3. Add a second model on the same node.
datawatch llm models add my-ollama \
  --node gpu-box \
  --model qwen3:32b

# 4. Enable auto-model discovery.
datawatch llm update my-ollama \
  --kind ollama \
  --compute-nodes gpu-box \
  --auto-add-models

# 5. Refresh the model list now (instead of waiting for the next poll).
datawatch llm refresh-models my-ollama

# 6. See what's currently bound to this LLM.
datawatch llm in-use my-ollama
#  → sessions: 2, automata: 0, personas: 0

# 7. Disable an LLM while the GPU box is offline.
datawatch llm disable my-ollama

# 8. Re-enable — optionally run a probe first.
datawatch llm enable my-ollama --pretest

# 9. Delete (blocked if active sessions are using it).
datawatch llm delete my-ollama
#  → 409 Conflict: blocked_by: [{kind:session, id:ralfthewise-7a3c, ...}]

# 10. Safe path: reassign bindings first, then delete.
datawatch llm reassign my-ollama --to-llm claude-api
datawatch llm delete my-ollama   # now succeeds

# 11. Force path: cancel active work and delete in one shot (destructive).
datawatch llm force-delete my-ollama
```

chunks.body:
### 4b. Happy path — PWA

1. Settings → Compute → **LLM Configuration** card.

![LLM Configuration card — entries with kind badges, enabled toggles, action buttons](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmz006/datawatch/main/docs/howto/screenshots/settings-llm.png)

2. Click **+ Add LLM**. Fill in:
   - **Name** — unique identifier (`my-ollama`, `claude-api`, …)
   - **Kind** — dropdown of all supported kinds
   - **Compute Nodes** — ordered failover list (local kinds only; hidden for SaaS kinds)
   - **Model** — starting model (you can add more per-node later)
   - **API Key** — literal or `${secret:name}` (cloud kinds only)
   - **Timeout** — override the adapter default (local: 300 s, cloud: 60 s; 0 = use default)
   - **Tags** — optional operator labels

![Add LLM modal — Name, Kind, ComputeNodes, Enabled Models, API key, Test and Save buttons](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmz006/datawatch/main/docs/howto/screenshots/settings-llm-add.png)

3. Click **Save**. The entry appears in the list with an enabled toggle.

4. Click the toggle to enable or disable. When enabling, a one-shot
   reachability probe runs first; the toggle only flips if the probe
   succeeds. Probe result appears in the alert dock (bell icon).

![LLM list — aider disabled (grey toggle) alongside enabled (green) entries](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmz006/datawatch/main/docs/howto/screenshots/settings-llm-toggle.png)

5. Click the pencil icon to open the Edit LLM form. The **Enabled Models**
   section shows `{node, model}` pairs with × to remove and **+ Add model**
   to pin a new pair. Click **Save** to apply changes.

![Edit LLM form — Enabled Models section showing node/model pairs, + Add model, Auto-enable toggle](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmz006/datawatch/main/docs/howto/screenshots/settings-llm-detail.png)

6. **Delete** is blocked when active bindings exist. The modal shows active
   sessions/automata and a "Reassign to" dropdown. Pick the target LLM
   and click **Reassign + Delete**, or expand **Force delete** to terminate
   active work immediately.

![Delete blocked — active binding listed, Reassign to dropdown, Reassign + Delete button](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmz006/datawatch/main/docs/howto/screenshots/settings-llm-delete.png)

chunks.heading: 5b. REST
chunks.body:
### 5b. REST

```sh
BASE=https://localhost:8443
TOKEN=<your-auth-token>

# List all LLMs.
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $BASE/api/llms | jq .

# Fetch one.
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $BASE/api/llms/my-ollama | jq .

# Create.
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "my-ollama",
    "kind": "ollama",
    "compute_nodes": ["gpu-box"],
    "models": [{"node": "gpu-box", "model": "llama3.1:8b"}]
  }' $BASE/api/llms

# Update (full replace).
curl -sk -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"my-ollama","kind":"ollama","compute_nodes":["gpu-box"],
       "models":[{"node":"gpu-box","model":"qwen3:32b"}]}' \
  $BASE/api/llms/my-ollama

# Enable / disable.
curl -sk -X PATCH -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"enabled":true,"pretest":true}' \
  $BASE/api/llms/my-ollama/enabled

# Run a one-shot test call.
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"prompt":"Reply with OK to confirm reachability."}' \
  $BASE/api/llms/my-ollama/test | jq .

# Models — list, add, remove.
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $BASE/api/llms/my-ollama/models
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"node":"gpu-box","model":"qwen3:32b"}' \
  $BASE/api/llms/my-ollama/models
curl -sk -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"node":"gpu-box","model":"qwen3:32b"}' \
  $BASE/api/llms/my-ollama/models

# Trigger model-list refresh.
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  $BASE/api/llms/my-ollama/refresh_models

# In-use — see what's bound.
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "$BASE/api/llms/my-ollama/in_use?page=1&size=10&filter=running" | jq .

# Reassign all bindings to another LLM.
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"to_llm":"claude-api"}' \
  $BASE/api/llms/my-ollama/reassign

# Delete (409 if active bindings exist).
curl -sk -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  $BASE/api/llms/my-ollama

# Force delete (terminates active work).
curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"confirm":"yes I understand this terminates active work"}' \
  $BASE/api/llms/my-ollama/force_delete
```

chunks.heading: 5c. MCP
chunks.body:
### 5c. MCP

Tools available in every MCP host (Claude Code, Cursor, etc.):

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `llm_list` | List all LLMs |
| `llm_get` | Fetch one LLM by name |
| `llm_add` | Register a new LLM |
| `llm_update` | Replace an existing LLM |
| `llm_delete` | Remove an LLM (blocked if active bindings) |
| `llm_test` | Send a one-shot reachability probe |
| `llm_enable` | Enable an LLM (optional pretest) |
| `llm_disable` | Disable an LLM |
| `llm_in_use` | List sessions / Automata / personas bound to this LLM |
| `llm_add_model` | Add an enabled model (node + model pair) |
| `llm_remove_model` | Remove an enabled model |
| `llm_list_models` | List enabled models for an LLM |
| `llm_refresh_models` | Trigger model-list refresh from Compute Nodes |

Examples:

```
llm_list
llm_add  name=gpu-ollama kind=ollama compute_nodes=gpu-box model=llama3.1:8b
llm_test name=gpu-ollama
llm_enable name=gpu-ollama pretest=true
llm_in_use name=gpu-ollama filter=running page=1 size=10
llm_add_model llm=gpu-ollama node=gpu-box model=qwen3:32b
llm_remove_model llm=gpu-ollama node=gpu-box model=llama3.1:8b
llm_refresh_models name=gpu-ollama
```

chunks.heading: 5e. YAML
chunks.body:
### 5e. YAML

LLM entries live in `~/.datawatch/inference/llms.json` (managed by the
daemon — do not hand-edit while the daemon is running). To pre-seed
entries before first start or in a deployment, write the file before
launching:

```json
[
  {
    "name": "my-ollama",
    "kind": "ollama",
    "compute_nodes": ["gpu-box"],
    "models": [
      {"node": "gpu-box", "model": "llama3.1:8b"}
    ],
    "auto_add_models": true
  },
  {
    "name": "claude-api",
    "kind": "claude",
    "models": [{"model": "claude-sonnet-5"}],
    "api_key_ref": "${secret:ANTHROPIC_KEY}",
    "cost_per_1k_input": 0.003,
    "cost_per_1k_output": 0.015
  }
]
```

`${secret:name}` references in `api_key_ref` are resolved at call time
via the secrets store (never written to disk in resolved form).

chunks.title: How-to: LLM Registry (v7.0.0)
chunks.heading: Block-on-delete and the reassign flow
chunks.body:
## Block-on-delete and the reassign flow

Deleting an LLM that has active sessions, running Automata, or bound
personas returns `409 Conflict` with a `blocked_by` list:

```json
{
  "blocked_by": [
    {"kind":"session","id":"ralfthewise-7a3c","name":"my-session","state":"running"},
    {"kind":"automata","id":"prd-001","title":"Deploy feature X","state":"planning"}
  ]
}
```

Two resolution paths:

**Reassign (recommended)** — migrates all bindings to a different LLM.
Running sessions pick up the change on their next LLM call; sessions in
`waiting_input` or `planning` state switch immediately.

```sh
datawatch llm reassign my-ollama --to-llm claude-api
# optionally pin to a specific model in the target LLM:
datawatch llm reassign my-ollama --to-llm claude-api --to-model claude-haiku-3
```

**Force delete** — cancels all active work and deletes in one shot.
Requires an explicit confirmation string to prevent accidents:

```sh
datawatch llm force-delete my-ollama
# The CLI sends: {"confirm":"yes I understand this terminates active work"}
```

chunks.heading: Diagram
chunks.body:
## Diagram

```
  Consumer (Council / /api/ask / Session start / Automata)
                      │
                      │ resolve by LLM name
                      ▼
          ┌──────────────────────┐
          │    LLM Registry      │
          │  name / kind / models│
          │  compute_nodes[]     │
          └──────────┬───────────┘
                     │ first reachable node (left-to-right failover)
                     ▼
          ┌──────────────────────┐
          │   Dispatcher         │
          │   adapter per kind   │
          └──────────┬───────────┘
                     │
          ┌──────────┴───────────┐
          │                      │
          ▼                      ▼
  Compute Node A          Compute Node B
  (ollama/openwebui/…)    (fallback)
```

For session-backend kinds (`claude-code`, `aider`, …) the dispatcher
does not make a network call — it resolves the binary path and model
selection stored in the LLM entry, then the session manager spawns the
tmux process.

chunks.title: How-to: LLM Registry (v7.0.0)
chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **LLM disabled.** Trying to start a session with a disabled LLM
  returns `"llm <name> is disabled (toggle on in Settings → Compute →
  LLMs)"`. Enable it with `datawatch llm enable <name>`.
- **No Compute Nodes for a local kind.** Adding an `ollama` LLM with
  no `compute_nodes` means the dispatcher has nowhere to route. Add at
  least one Compute Node to `compute_nodes`.
- **Model not in `models[]`.** If the dispatcher finds the node but
  not the model, the call fails. Either add the pair with
  `llm models add` or enable `auto_add_models` and run
  `llm refresh-models`.
- **`api_key_ref` with wrong secret name.** The LLM will test as
  reachable if the network is OK, but calls fail at runtime when the
  secret can't resolve. Verify with `datawatch secrets get <name>`.
- **Delete blocked by stale session.** A session stuck in `running`
  after its tmux pane died will still show as a binding. Kill the
  stale session first (`datawatch sessions kill <id>`), then delete
  the LLM.
- **Auto-migration name collision.** If you manually added an entry
  named `ollama-default` before upgrading, the v6→v7 migration skips
  it. Check that your manual entry has the correct `kind` and
  `compute_nodes`. See [`v7-compute-migration.md`](v7-compute-migration.md).

# How-to: MCP Elicitation (BL302 S3)

**MCP Elicitation** lets the daemon prompt the operator for structured input
through whatever MCP-aware client is connected (Claude Code, Claude Desktop,
etc.) — returning a typed response without the operator leaving their AI tool.

Use it when an Automaton needs a decision, a plugin needs a parameter, or the
daemon needs operator confirmation before an irreversible action.

> **Pre-conditions**: MCP elicitation requires an MCP client (Claude Code or Claude Desktop) connected to the daemon. See [mcp-tools.md](mcp-tools.md) for MCP client connection setup.

chunks.title: How-to: MCP Elicitation (BL302 S3)
chunks.heading: REST
chunks.body:
### REST

```bash
# Approval
curl -X POST https://localhost:8443/api/mcp/elicit \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"schema":"approval","prompt":"Allow this Automaton to push to main?","context":{"automaton_id":"abc"}}'

# Choice
curl -X POST https://localhost:8443/api/mcp/elicit \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"schema":"choice","prompt":"Select effort level","options":["quick","normal","thorough"]}'
```

The call blocks until the operator responds or the timeout expires.
On timeout: `{"error": "elicitation timeout"}`

chunks.heading: How it appears to the operator
chunks.body:
## How it appears to the operator

When an elicitation fires, Claude Code (or the connected MCP host) surfaces
it as a native form — the form type depends on the schema:

- `approval` → a yes/no prompt with optional reason field
- `text_input` → an editable text box
- `choice` → a radio button or dropdown

The operator responds inside their AI tool; the response is sent back through
the bridge to the daemon, which unblocks the waiting handler.

chunks.title: How-to: MCP Resources (BL302 S1+S2)
chunks.heading: Channel bridge forwarding
chunks.body:
## Channel bridge forwarding

When a downstream MCP client connects via `datawatch-channel`, it
automatically discovers all resources (static + live) from the daemon
and forwards them. The bridge calls `GET /api/mcp/resources` and
`GET /api/mcp/resources/templates` at startup, then registers
forwarders that proxy `resources/read` calls to
`GET /api/mcp/resources/read?uri=<resolved-uri>`.

On startup, the bridge logs:
```
[datawatch-channel] discovered 21 resources
[datawatch-channel] discovered 8 resource templates
```

# How-to: MCP Sampling (BL302 S3)

Datawatch can request LLM completions from whichever Claude Code session is
currently connected — without spawning a new session. This is **MCP Sampling**:
the daemon sends a `sampling/createMessage` request through the channel bridge
to the MCP host (Claude Code / Claude Desktop) and gets a completion back.

### REST

```bash
# Built-in trigger (daemon fills template + live data)
curl -X POST https://localhost:8443/api/mcp/sample \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"trigger":"alert_triage","context":{"alert_id":"abc123"}}'

# Custom prompt
curl -X POST https://localhost:8443/api/mcp/sample \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"prompt":"What is the best backend to use for long-running code tasks?","max_tokens":512}'

# View last 50 results
curl https://localhost:8443/api/mcp/sampling-log \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

chunks.heading: Graceful degradation
chunks.body:
## Graceful degradation

When no Claude Code session with a connected MCP host is active,
`ErrSamplingNotSupported` is returned:

```json
{"error": "sampling not supported: no MCP host connected"}
```

The ring buffer still records the attempt. Callers should handle this
gracefully — it is not a daemon error, just a state condition.

# How-to: MCP tools — drive datawatch from Claude / Cursor / any MCP host

Datawatch exposes its operator surface as MCP tools — every REST

chunks.heading: Lifecycle event subscriptions (BL427)
chunks.body:
## Lifecycle event subscriptions (BL427)

`autonomous_subscribe`, `autonomous_unsubscribe` and
`autonomous_subscriptions` manage persisted Automaton (PRD/task)
lifecycle-event subscriptions: when an event fires, the daemon delivers it to
the subscription's sink.

| Tool | Proxies | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `autonomous_subscribe` | `POST /api/autonomous/subscriptions` | Register a subscription: `kinds` (e.g. `task.session_started,prd.blocked`) and/or `level` (`prd`|`task`), optional `prd_id`/`task_id` scope, `sink_type` + `sink_target` (`comm`, `session`, `topic`, `alert`), optional `action_text` (send_input into a session sink), `one_shot`, `coalesce`, `expires_in_seconds` |
| `autonomous_unsubscribe` | `DELETE /api/autonomous/subscriptions/{id}` | Remove one subscription by id (404 for unknown ids) |
| `autonomous_subscriptions` | `GET /api/autonomous/subscriptions` | List subscriptions, optional `owner` filter |

The same surface over CLI (handy for one-off setups from a shell):

```
datawatch autonomous subscribe --task <id> --on session_started \
  --send "Task started, build is running." --sink session --target <session-id> --one-shot
datawatch autonomous subscribe --on prd.blocked --sink comm --target my-router
datawatch autonomous subscriptions [--owner operator]
datawatch autonomous unsubscribe <id>
```

The CLI's `--on` shorthand words map to task kinds (`session_started` →
`task.session_started`); full kinds pass through. `--send` is the
send_input action (session sinks only) and is one-shot by default when `--task`
is given.

chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **MCP host can't find datawatch.** Verify `command` resolves to the
  binary on the host's PATH. `which datawatch` from the same shell
  the MCP host is started in.
- **Tool calls return 401.** `DATAWATCH_TOKEN` env var missing or
  wrong. Reset via `datawatch token rotate` and update the host config.
- **ACL denies a call.** Daemon returns the denied scope set; check
  `mcp.per_tool_acl` and adjust.
- **Tool not in catalogue but in the docs.** A new tool was added;
  restart the MCP host so it re-fetches the catalogue.
- **Rate-limit hits.** Bump `rate_limit_per_caller` for known-safe
  callers (e.g. an autonomous executor that legitimately needs to
  fire many calls per minute).

## Proxy mode (specific server)

When you select a named server chip, the PWA routes through the local
daemon's proxy:

```
GET /api/sessions  →  GET /api/proxy/{name}/sessions  →  remote /api/sessions
```

The proxy authenticates with the remote server's stored bearer token —
you never expose the remote token to the browser directly.

Runtime-registered servers (added via REST/MCP/CLI) are available for proxy
routing immediately. YAML-seeded servers are also proxy-reachable.

chunks.title: How-to: Multi-Server Management
chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.body:
## Troubleshooting

**Test button returns red / error toast**
- Verify the URL is reachable from the browser (not just from the daemon host).
- Check that the remote bearer token matches what the remote daemon is configured with.
- If TLS: ensure the remote's CA cert is trusted by the browser.

**[remote] badge missing on aggregated cards**
- The remote server may be offline; the aggregated endpoint skips unreachable
  servers and returns only what succeeded.

**Proxy 502 / 504**
- The daemon can reach the remote (test passes) but a specific API call is
  failing. Check the remote daemon's log: `datawatch logs --tail 50`.

**YAML-seeded servers show "read-only"**
- This is intentional. Builtin entries can't be deleted via the UI; remove
  them from `datawatch.yaml` and restart.

chunks.title: Navigation at phone widths
chunks.body:
# Navigation at phone widths

The bottom navigation bar of the web UI (the PWA) has to fit a phone screen: six buttons, each with an icon and a label, on a bar about 320 to 414 px wide. This page covers the check that proves it fits, how to run that check, where its report goes, how to read a finding, and what you see in the PWA now.

This is a test-runner check, not a feature you configure. Nothing here changes a setting, an API, an MCP tool, a CLI command or a comm-channel command. The surface is the PWA only.

chunks.title: Navigation at phone widths
chunks.heading: What the check measures
chunks.body:
## What the check measures

The check loads the PWA in a real headless Chrome, against an isolated daemon the test runner starts for itself. It sizes the window to each phone width and reads the bottom navigation bar. It runs in two themes, light and dark.

| Setting | Value |
|---------|-------|
| Widths gated | 320x568, 360x740, 390x844 (CSS px) |
| Themes gated | light and dark |
| Tabs measured | the bottom navigation bar only |
| Zoom | 100 percent only; text zoom is not measured |

It reports three kinds of finding. Any one of them fails the check.

| Check | What it means | Limit |
|-------|---------------|-------|
| `clipped-text` | A label runs past the visible navigation bar, so the bar cuts it off | the bar's own edges |
| `tap-target` | A navigation button is smaller than 44 by 44 CSS px | 44 x 44 px |
| `overlap` | A label or a button box intersects another navigation item | none |

A passing run measures six navigation items at each width and theme and finds no problems. The report also prints the bar's `scrollWidth` and `clientWidth` for each combination. The check records those two numbers but does not test them, so sideways scrolling in the bar does not fail the run by itself. Read them yourself: on a bar that fits, the two are equal (after the fix, 320, 360 and 390 px in both themes). A scroll width larger than the client width means the bar scrolls, even when the run passes.

The check does not look at the header or the tabs below the bar. Those are measured by a separate report-only pass, described under [Other modes](#other-modes).

chunks.title: Navigation at phone widths
chunks.heading: Base requirements
chunks.body:
## Base requirements

- **Node.js with npm**, on the `PATH`. The runner uses them for the story script.
- **Google Chrome** at `/usr/bin/google-chrome`, or the path in `DW_CHROME_PATH`. If no browser is found the check is skipped, not failed.
- **Go**, only if `bin/datawatch` is missing. The runner uses an existing `bin/datawatch` as it is, so rebuild it after any web change:

  ```bash
  go build -o bin/datawatch ./cmd/datawatch/
  ```

  The PWA files are compiled into the daemon (`internal/server/server.go` embeds the `web` directory). A stale binary serves the old navigation bar, and the check then measures the old bar.
- **A short `TMPDIR`.** Chrome keeps a Unix socket in `TMPDIR`, and the socket path must stay under 108 bytes. The default `/tmp` is fine. A long `TMPDIR` makes Chrome exit at once, and the runner then reports `chrome DevTools endpoint did not come up`.
- **Sandbox isolation.** Run the check with `env -u TMUX -u TMUX_TMPDIR` in front of the command. The daemon it starts must not reach your own tmux sessions.

chunks.title: Navigation at phone widths
chunks.heading: Run the check
chunks.body:
## Run the check

From the repository root:

```bash
env -u TMUX -u TMUX_TMPDIR make test-e2e-shared-nav
```

The target runs `scripts/e2e-pwa.sh group:shared-nav`. That script does the following:

1. Picks free loopback ports and writes a daemon config from `testdata/datawatch.yaml`, with the token `dw-e2e-pwa-token` (unless `TEST_TOKEN` is set).
2. Starts the daemon from `bin/datawatch` in the foreground and waits up to 60 seconds for `/api/health`.
3. Runs `npm ci` in `scripts/test-stories/pwa`. This replaces the tracked symlink `scripts/test-stories/pwa/node_modules` with a real directory, and `git status` then shows the symlink as a deleted file. Restore it after the run with `git checkout -- scripts/test-stories/pwa/node_modules`, and do not commit the deletion.
4. Runs `run-all.mjs --group shared-nav`, which runs `shared-nav-mobile-fit.mjs`. That file runs the probe `shared-nav-mobile-fit-probe.mjs` in gate mode.
5. Stops the daemon.

A run takes about half a minute on a development machine. The summary line at the end reads `summary: 1 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped, 1 total` on a pass.

Exit codes:

| Result | Make exit | Summary |
|--------|-----------|---------|
| Pass, no navigation finding | 0 | `shared-nav-mobile-fit PASS (exit 0)` |
| Fail, a finding or the probe could not run | 2 (from `make`) | `shared-nav-mobile-fit FAIL (exit 1)` |
| Skipped, no Chrome or no daemon | 0 | `shared-nav-mobile-fit ... skipped` |

A skip does not fail the target. Read the summary line before you call a run clean.

To run against a daemon you already have, set `TEST_HTTP`, `TEST_TLS` and `TEST_TOKEN` together. The runner then starts nothing and checks that daemon. Use a sandbox daemon, not your production one.

chunks.title: Navigation at phone widths
chunks.heading: Where the report is written
chunks.body:
## Where the report is written

The gate writes two files into the run's evidence folder:

- `shared-nav-mobile-fit/repro-report.txt`: the readable report, one block per theme and width.
- `shared-nav-mobile-fit/repro-report.json`: the same results as data, with each finding's fields.

In local mode the evidence folder is `dw-e2e-pwa-XXXXXX/evidence/` inside `${TMPDIR:-/tmp}`. The runner removes the whole `dw-e2e-pwa-XXXXXX` folder when the run passes, so the report is gone after a pass. When the run fails, the runner keeps the folder and prints its path, with the daemon log.

Setting `EVIDENCE_DIR` does not move the report in local mode: the runner resets it. To keep the report of a passing run, copy the two files out while the run is still going.

chunks.title: Navigation at phone widths
chunks.heading: Read a finding
chunks.body:
## Read a finding

A failed run prints one line per finding under its theme and width:

```text
Theme dark, viewport 320x568: 2 findings, 6 nav items, nav bar 320x60, scrollWidth 440, clientWidth 320
  [clipped-text] <selector> "<label text>" clipped <n>px left, <n>px right
  [tap-target] <selector> "<label text>" <w>x<h>
  [overlap] <selector> "<label text>" with <other item>
```

The placeholders above stand for the values the run prints. Read the fields in this order:

1. **Theme and width.** Which combination failed. A finding that appears at only one width usually comes from the bar's width at that size, not from the bar's design.
2. **Check.** Which of the three checks flagged it.
3. **Selector and text.** Which button or label. The selector is the element's CSS path. The text is its label.
4. **The measurement.** The overflow in pixels for `clipped-text`, the box size in CSS pixels for `tap-target`, or the other item for `overlap`.

What to do:

- **`clipped-text`.** The label is wider than the bar can show. The labels now truncate with an ellipsis, so a clipped label means the truncation has stopped working. Check that the label's CSS still sets `text-overflow: ellipsis`, `white-space: nowrap` and `overflow: hidden`, and that the button's `min-width` is still `0` or the flex share is still in place.
- **`tap-target`.** The button is smaller than 44 by 44 CSS px. Check the button's `min-width` and `min-height` in `internal/server/web/style.css`. The stylesheet sets a 40 px minimum width on the bottom buttons, which is 4 px below the check's 44 px line, so the stylesheet alone does not keep a button above the line. What keeps it above is the equal share of the bar: six buttons on a 320 px bar are each more than 44 px wide. A button between 40 and 43 px wide passes the stylesheet but fails the check, and it points at a change that shrank the button's share of the bar (padding, a fixed width, or a seventh item).
- **`overlap`.** A label or a button's box crosses a neighbour. Look for padding or a fixed width added to the button, or a badge placed over the label.

After a fix, rebuild `bin/datawatch` and run the check again. The report is evidence only for the binary it was run against. Through `make`, the report's `daemon_version` reads `unknown`, so record the version yourself with `bin/datawatch version`.

chunks.title: Navigation at phone widths
chunks.heading: What you see in the PWA now
chunks.body:
## What you see in the PWA now

- **Six equal buttons.** The bottom bar gives every button an equal share of its width, so the six buttons fit a 320 px phone without the bar scrolling sideways.
- **Labels truncate.** A long label ends with an ellipsis (`…`) inside its button and does not wrap onto a second line.
- **The full name.** Each bottom button carries its full name as a `title` attribute. On a desktop browser, hovering the button shows the name after the browser's usual delay. On a phone, a long press may show the name, depending on the browser. Some phone browsers show nothing, so the truncated label is all you see there.
- **Tap targets.** The stylesheet sets a 40 px minimum width on the bottom buttons; the check's line is 44 by 44 CSS px. The equal share of the bar is what keeps the buttons above 44 px. In the last run no bottom button fell under the line at 320, 360 or 390 px, in either theme.

What is not covered yet:

- Buttons in the header and in the tabs below the bar are not gated. Some are still under 44 px. The header search button and the Observer section toggle now reach 40 px.
- Text zoom above 100 percent is not measured.
- Sideways scrolling in the bar is recorded in the report, not tested (see above).
- The ellipsis and the `title` attribute are covered only by a small unit test, `internal/server/web/app-shared-nav.test.js`, which reads the stylesheet and `index.html`. It does not render the bar, and it does not test hover or long press. Run it by hand with `node --test internal/server/web/app-shared-nav.test.js`; `make test-e2e-shared-nav`, the other make targets and CI do not run it.
- The check runs on the PWA only. Android and iOS are not covered by this check.

chunks.title: Navigation at phone widths
chunks.heading: Other modes
chunks.body:
## Other modes

The probe has two more modes. Both run through the same environment variables as the gate, and both are run directly rather than through `make`:

- **Report-only** (the default mode of the probe). It audits every tab at six phone widths in one theme. It writes `report-only.json` and `occurrences.json` to `PROBE_OUT_DIR`. It never fails a run. Use it to see what the next fix has to cover.
- **Baseline** (`SHARED_NAV_MODE=baseline`). It records the bottom bar's boxes at 768x1024, 1024x768 and 1280x800, in both themes, to `nav-baseline.json`, with the tolerance (2 px or 1 percent) written into the file. The probe does not compare a later run against that file; the comparison is a separate step.

The probe's header comment, `scripts/test-stories/pwa/shared-nav-mobile-fit-probe.mjs`, lists the variables each mode reads.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

The Ollama Marketplace is a browseable, searchable catalog of curated
models (llama3.1, qwen3, gemma3, deepseek-r1, codellama, and more).
Each model entry shows available tag variants with their disk size,
minimum RAM, minimum VRAM, and a hardware-fit indicator that checks
whether your target node's declared capacity is sufficient.

Pulling a model is a background operation — the pull runs on the
Ollama host while the daemon tracks progress and surfaces it in the
alert dock. You can continue working while the download completes.
You can also delete models from a node through the same surface.

The embedded catalog is curated and ships with the daemon. It covers
the most commonly used open models. Live refresh from ollama.com is a
planned follow-up.

```
  PWA / CLI / REST / MCP / comm
          │
          ▼
  datawatch daemon
  POST /api/compute/nodes/<node>/models/pull
          │
          ▼   (background goroutine)
  Ollama host — /api/pull (streaming progress)
          │
          ▼
  PullTask in daemon memory
  alert dock: "Pulling llama3.1:8b (N%)"
```

## Happy path — CLI

```sh
# 1. Browse the embedded catalog.
datawatch marketplace catalog

# 2. Pull a model to a node (background; returns a task descriptor).
datawatch compute pull-model <node-name> llama3.1:8b
# Output: {"id":"pull-XXXX","node_name":"...","model":"llama3.1:8b","status":"pending",...}

# 3. Poll the pull task until status=done.
datawatch marketplace task <task-id>
# Output: {"id":"pull-XXXX","status":"in_progress","progress":0.42,...}
# ...repeat until "status":"done"

curl -sk http://<ollama-host>:11434/api/tags | jq '.models[].name'

# 5. Delete a model from the node when no longer needed.
datawatch compute remove-model <node-name> llama3.1:8b
```

chunks.heading: Happy path — PWA
chunks.body:
## Happy path — PWA

![Ollama Marketplace modal](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmz006/datawatch/main/docs/howto/screenshots/ollama-marketplace-modal.png)

1. Bottom nav → **Settings** → **Compute** tab → **Compute Nodes**.
2. Tap or click the Compute Node row for your Ollama node to open its
   edit panel.
3. In the edit panel, find the **Models** sub-section (visible only
   for `kind=ollama` nodes). The installed model list is shown here.
4. Click **Browse marketplace** to open the Ollama Marketplace modal.
5. The modal loads the embedded catalog. Use the **Search models...**
   field to filter by name or description (e.g. "coder", "embed",
   "reasoning").
6. Click **Pick variant →** on any model card to open the tag-grid.

![Tag-grid modal with hardware fit columns](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmz006/datawatch/main/docs/howto/screenshots/ollama-marketplace-tags.png)

7. The tag-grid shows every available size variant with:
   - **Tag** — the full `model:tag` string (e.g. `llama3.1:8b`)
   - **Size** — estimated disk footprint
   - **Min RAM** — floor RAM for inference
   - **Min VRAM** — floor GPU memory (blank = CPU-only is fine)
   - **Fit** — green checkmark if the node's declared capacity covers
     the variant; warning triangle if not
8. Click **Pull** on the row you want. If the variant exceeds the
   node's declared RAM or VRAM, a confirmation dialog asks you to
   confirm before proceeding.
9. The modal closes and a progress entry appears in the **alert dock**
   at the bottom of the screen: *"Pulling llama3.1:8b (0%)"*. It
   updates as the download progresses.

![Alert dock showing pull progress — "🔽 Pulling llama3.1:8b on datawatch-ollama (47%)"](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmz006/datawatch/main/docs/howto/screenshots/ollama-marketplace-pull-progress.png)

10. When the pull completes the dock entry shows *done*. Refresh the
    node edit panel to see the new model in the installed list.
11. To delete a model, click the **✕** button next to its name in the
    installed list. The deletion is immediate (no background task).

chunks.title: How-to: Ollama Model Marketplace
chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Model name must include a tag.** `llama3.1:8b` works; `llama3.1`
  alone will be rejected or pull the wrong default. Always specify the
  colon-separated tag.
- **Pull can take several minutes.** Large models (70b+) are 40–230 GB.
  The progress percentage in the alert dock reflects bytes transferred.
  Do not assume the node is broken if progress stalls briefly — Ollama
  downloads layer-by-layer and may pause between layers.
- **Node must be reachable from the daemon, not just from your browser.**
  If the node is on a remote host that your workstation can reach but
  the daemon cannot (e.g. different network), the pull request will
  succeed at the daemon (task is created) but then immediately fail
  with a connection error. Check `marketplace task <id>` to see the
  error field.
- **Fit warning is advisory.** The hardware-fit column compares the
  tag's minimum requirements against the node's *declared* capacity,
  not measured capacity. If you set `ram_gb` or `gpu_mem_gb` lower
  than actual hardware, the warning fires incorrectly. Update the
  node's declared capacity to reflect real hardware.
- **Delete is immediate and permanent.** There is no recycle bin. If
  you delete a model that a running session is using, that session
  will fail on its next inference call. Stop sessions that use the
  model before deleting it.
- **Pull task state is in-memory.** The daemon stores pull tasks in
  memory with 1-hour retention after completion. If the daemon
  restarts mid-pull the task record is lost, but the pull itself

chunks.title: How-to: getting notified when an Automaton asks you a question
chunks.body:
# How-to: getting notified when an Automaton asks you a question

An Automaton that runs under datawatch can stop and **ask the operator a
question**: a short decision statement, two to twenty numbered options, the
asker's recommendation, and the context it is being asked in. The question
is stored durably, appears in the PWA question list and in the REST
questions API — and in this step of the channel, it is also **announced**:

- a **WebSocket `question_raised` message** to every connected client
  (the PWA surfaces it the moment it lands);
- a **line in every configured messaging channel** (the comm router
  targets you have set up);
- an **alert** in the alert store (warning level, broadcast to
  connected clients) — high-priority questions only.

When you later **answer** the question — or it gets **withdrawn** — that
too is an event: `question.answered` and `question.withdrawn`, both
subscribable through the ordinary lifecycle subscription surface (REST,
MCP, CLI, comm channel, one-shot notify) with every ordinary sink (comm
route, session, topic, alert store, `mcp_queue`, webhook, peer).

Finally, an Automaton that asked the question gets it back on the path you
chose at raise time:

1. **The default path — event plus polled GET.** The answer is an event on
   the bus, and `GET /api/questions/{id}` carries the current answer's
   summary (chosen option, the verbatim quote, actor, when). This path
   needs nothing from the asker.
2. **The opt-in line — a single `DATAWATCH_ANSWER:` line dropped into the
   asker's session.** One per answer, only when the question was raised
   with `return_path: true` *and* the daemon's `autonomous.questions`
   switch and `return_path` toggle are both on. A session that has gone
   away by then simply gets nothing: the answer stays in the store, the
   asker can still read it back by polling.

> **The whole channel is off by default.** `autonomous.questions.enabled`
> starts `false`: none of the announce steps above runs, the REST question
> endpoints refuse with `503`, and no event fires. Questions **never
> expire** — an open one stays open and answerable until answered,
> withdrawn, or the store is removed.

This guide assumes the
[lifecycle subscriptions](automaton-lifecycle-subscriptions.md) and
[alerts and notifications](alerts-and-notifications.md) guides if you have
not read them — the question events ride exactly those rails.

chunks.heading: Base requirements
chunks.body:
## Base requirements

- A daemon with the **questions channel built in** (current datawatch
  builds; the channel is gated behind its switch, so builds without the
  channel simply never fire it).
- At least **one comm router backend** if you want the messaging group
  line (Telegram, Slack, or the console fallback). Without any router the
  messaging announcement has nowhere to go and is skipped silently; the
  WebSocket, alert and event paths are unaffected.
- Any of the ordinary ways to turn settings on and off — YAML config,
  the REST settings endpoint, the MCP `config_set`/`get_config` tools,
  `datawatch` CLI, a comm channel `configure` instruction, or the PWA
  settings card. All of them work; the PWA card is the only surface with a
  ready-made checkbox for this feature.
- For the return line: a **live datawatch session** to receive it (the
  question's `session_id`), and that session's input read for a
  line beginning `DATAWATCH_ANSWER:`.

chunks.heading: Setup: turning the channel on, and the three announces
chunks.body:
## Setup: turning the channel on, and the three announces

The four switches, in `autonomous.questions`:

| Key | Default (key absent) | Controls |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | **off** | the whole channel: REST endpoints, the raise-time announcement (WebSocket, messaging, alert), the `question.answered` / `question.withdrawn` events, and the opt-in line. Everything else in datawatch is untouched when it is off. |
| `notify_messaging` | **on** | adds/removes the messaging-group line on every raise. |
| `notify_alert` | **on** | adds/removes the alert on every **high-priority** raise. |
| `return_path` | **on** | whether a raise *may* ask for the single `DATAWATCH_ANSWER:` session line (the question still has to opt in per-question, see below). |

All four are read **live**: changing any of them takes effect from the
next question onwards, no restart, and the PWA settings card flips each
with a checkbox. Turning `enabled` on also attaches the answered and
withdrawn event sink at that moment (the config write calls it), so those
two events start without a restart too; turning it off drops the sink.

chunks.heading: All the ways to turn it on
chunks.body:
### All the ways to turn it on

YAML (under the `autonomous:` section of the daemon config):

```yaml
autonomous:
  questions:
    enabled: true          # the channel switch — off until this is true
    # the three toggles below default to true when the key is absent;
    # uncomment only to switch an announce off:
    # notify_messaging: false   # no messaging-group line on raise
    # notify_alert: false       # no high-priority alerts on raise
    # return_path: false        # refuse the per-question session line
```

| Surface | How to turn the channel on |
|---|---|
| YAML | as above, under `autonomous.questions` in the daemon config file. |
| REST | `curl -sk -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"autonomous.questions.enabled": true}' https://localhost:8443/api/config` |
| MCP | `config_set(key="autonomous.questions.enabled", value=true)` — then `get_config(section="autonomous")` reads the toggles back under `questions`. |
| CLI | `datawatch config set autonomous.questions.enabled true` — and, to quiet an announce, `datawatch config set autonomous.questions.notify_messaging false`; read either one back with `datawatch config get <key>`. |
| Comm channel | `configure autonomous.questions.enabled=true` (all three toggles are listed in the daemon's `configure` help text). |
| PWA | **Settings → Autonomous Automata planning**: the four checkboxes — *Operator questions for Automata (off by default)*, *Notify on question asked and answered (on by default)*, *Alert on high-priority questions (on by default)*, and *Allow the per-question session return line on top of the event plus polled answer path (on by default)*. Flip the first one and the channel starts announcing from the next raise. |

The REST, MCP, CLI, comm and PWA changes are all read live by the daemon
at the moment the next question matters — no restart.

chunks.title: How-to: getting notified when an Automaton asks you a question
chunks.heading: Turning the three announces off, independently
chunks.body:
### Turning the three announces off, independently

The toggles sit *under* the switch: with `enabled: false` nothing fires
regardless of the toggles, and with it `true` each announce runs unless
its own toggle says otherwise.

- **No messaging line?** `notify_messaging: false` (any surface above).
  The WebSocket and high-priority alert still fire.
- **No alert?** `notify_alert: false`. The WebSocket and messaging lines
  still fire; normal-priority questions never alerted in the first place.
- **No session line ever?** `return_path: false`. The default
  event-plus-polled path is untouched — an asker that does not ask for
  the line is never affected by this toggle.

Each toggle is read live at the moment it matters: messaging and alert at
raise time, `return_path` at answer time.

chunks.heading: Walkthrough: a question is raised
chunks.body:
## Walkthrough: a question is raised

Here is the full shape of a raise (REST, same fields everywhere):

```bash
curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/questions" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "label": "decision",
    "context": "task",
    "task_id": "task_9f3",
    "text": "Should the retry backoff cap at five minutes, or unbounded?",
    "options": [
      {"id": "cap",  "label": "Cap at five minutes"},
      {"id": "none", "label": "Leave it unbounded"}
    ],
    "default": "cap",
    "risk": "normal",
    "priority": "high",
    "return_path": true,
    "asked_by": "session-s1",
    "asker_kind": "session",
    "session_id": "s1"
  }'
# → 201, the stored question with its id
```

Two fields belong to this step of the channel:

- **`priority`** — `normal` (the default) or `high`. It changes nothing
  but the announces: a **high** question additionally raises an alert in
  the alert store. Both priorities get the WebSocket message and the
  messaging line (while their toggles are on).
- **`return_path`** — `true` asks for the opt-in session line on the way
  back (it still requires `session_id` and both switches). `false` or
  omitted keeps the default event-plus-polled path.

chunks.heading: What the daemon does with it, in order
chunks.body:
### What the daemon does with it, in order

```
POST /api/questions ──▶ 1. store the question (durable) ──▶ 201 back to the asker
                                              2. WebSocket `question_raised` to every connected client
                                              3. one messaging line per configured comm route
                                              4. alert in the alert store      (priority = high, toggle on)
```

The raise is already answered with `201` before any announcement runs —
a slow router never holds the raise hostage. Each of the three announces
has its own toggle under `autonomous.questions` (WebSocket rides the
switch itself).

chunks.heading: 2. The messaging group line
chunks.body:
### 2. The messaging group line

One line per active messaging route, built the same way, in the daemon
hostname style — for a question `q_7d21c9e8f43c`, label `decision`,
priority `high`:

```
[myhost] question q_7d21c9e8f43c — decision (high priority)
Should the retry backoff cap at five minutes, or unbounded?
Options:
1. Cap at five minutes
2. Leave it unbounded
Answer: POST /api/questions/q_7d21c9e8f43c/answer, or in the Automaton PWA.
```

The line names the hostname marker, the question id and label, a
`(high priority)` marker when set, the question text, the options as a
numbered list, and the two answer routes (the REST endpoint and the PWA).
It never carries anything the daemon would consider a secret, and a
question with no options (an open-ended one) simply leaves the options
block out. Suppress the line with `notify_messaging: false`; with no
messaging route configured at all it is skipped silently and the
WebSocket and alert parts are unaffected.

chunks.heading: 3. The alert (high priority only)
chunks.body:
### 3. The alert (high priority only)

A high-priority raise also lands in the
[alert store](alerts-and-notifications.md) at **warning level**: the title
is `Operator question raised (high priority): <question-id> — <label>`,
the body carries the question text plus the option labels, and the daemon
broadcasts the alert over the same WebSocket hub every connected client
is already watching (the PWA surfaces it like any other alert).
Normal-priority raises never alert. The alert is one-way (it says nothing
back to the asker), and `notify_alert: false` turns it off. Read the
alert store with the ordinary alert surface (`GET /api/alerts`).

chunks.title: How-to: getting notified when an Automaton asks you a question
chunks.heading: Walkthrough: the question gets answered — or withdrawn
chunks.body:
## Walkthrough: the question gets answered — or withdrawn

When you answer an open question — from the PWA, over REST, or from a
comm channel (the daemon records which surface carried it: `pwa`, `rest`,
`cli`, `mcp` or `comm:<channel>`) — the daemon records the answer first
and then fires **one** `question.answered` event. Answering a question
that already has an answer is a *supersede*: you name the answer the new
one replaces (`supersedes`), it fires `question.answered` for the **new**
answer, and the old one stays in the answer log. A withdrawal fires one
`question.withdrawn`.

```
answer lands ──▶ 1. the answer is recorded (durable, append-only) ──▶ 2xx to you
                               2. the question's state becomes answered
                               3. event `question.answered` → every matching subscription
                               4. (if this question opted in) one DATAWATCH_ANSWER: line → the asker's session
```

The operator's own words go on a single answer body:

```bash
curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/questions/q_7d21c9e8f43c/answer" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "chosen_option_id": "cap",
    "quote": "Cap it — unbounded backoff wedged the worker in prod",
    "actor": "operator"
  }'
# → 201, the recorded answer plus the question's new state
```

`chosen_option_id` names the option, `quote` is your verbatim text (the
daemon stores it byte-for-byte, up to the quote cap, and records its
SHA-256 so later copies can be checked against the record), `actor` names
who is answering (absent = the caller of record), and a superseding
answer must carry `supersedes: <answer id>`. An answer that trips the
daemon's secret-pattern check is refused with `422` naming only the rule,
never the text. Withdrawing:

```bash
curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/questions/q_7d21c9e8f43c/withdraw" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"actor": "operator", "reason": "duplicated"}'
```

chunks.title: How-to: getting notified when an Automaton asks you a question
chunks.heading: The two events
chunks.body:
### The two events

| Kind | Fired when | Carries |
|---|---|---|
| `question.answered` | an open question's state becomes `answered` — first answer or a superseding one | the question id, the answer id it names, the chosen option, the actor, one-line details ("question q_… answered, option cap, by operator"), and the Automaton and task ids when the question named them. |
| `question.withdrawn` | an open question's state becomes `withdrawn` | the question id, the actor, the reason (when given), one-line details. |

Both are regular lifecycle events: they ride the same per-subscriber queue
as `task.completed` and friends, and each fires **exactly once** even
across a daemon restart — the store keeps an emit marker per question (and
per answer), and a startup reconcile re-fires exactly the ones that were
recorded but never delivered. The event's `details` is one bounded line
(capped at 512 characters) naming the question, the answer's option and
actor; the event carries the Automaton and task ids when the question named
them, which is what routes it into the right scope. With the channel
switch off, neither event fires — though the answer and withdrawal are
still recorded either way, and readable by polling.

chunks.title: How-to: getting notified when an Automaton asks you a question
chunks.heading: Subscribing — every surface
chunks.body:
### Subscribing — every surface

**REST** (create a subscription that catches the two kinds, same shape as
any lifecycle subscription):

```bash
curl -s -X POST "$BASE/api/autonomous/subscriptions" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"filter": {"kinds": ["question.answered", "question.withdrawn"]},
       "sink": {"type": "comm", "target": "my-group"}}'
# → 201 + the stored record (with its id); list later with GET /api/autonomous/subscriptions
```

**MCP** (the ordinary `autonomous_subscribe`; the kinds accept the two
question kinds alongside the task and Automaton kinds):

```
autonomous_subscribe(kinds="question.answered,question.withdrawn", sink_type="comm", sink_target="my-group")
persistent: autonomous_subscribe(kinds="question.answered", sink_type="mcp_queue", sink_target="ops")
```

**CLI**:

```bash
datawatch autonomous subscribe \
  --on question.answered --on question.withdrawn \
  --sink comm --target my-group
# into a pollable queue instead:
datawatch autonomous subscribe --on question.answered --sink mcp_queue --target ops
# and read it later:
datawatch autonomous queue ops
```

**Comm channel** (a verb to the daemon):

```
autonomous subscribe question.answered question.withdrawn --sink comm --target my-group
```

`mcp_queue` subscribers get a line per event they can poll; `comm:<channel>`
surfaces see the same. Webhook and peer sinks work exactly as described
in the [lifecycle webhooks guide](automaton-lifecycle-webhooks.md) — the
question kinds are accepted by every sink type.

chunks.title: How-to: getting notified when an Automaton asks you a question
chunks.heading: Polling instead of subscribing: GET /api/questions/{id}
chunks.body:
### Polling instead of subscribing: GET /api/questions/{id}

An asker that cannot subscribe does not wait on the bus — it polls one
read. That read now carries the whole answer path: the question (state,
priority, return path, options, the asker's recommendation, answer count)
**plus, when the question is answered, the current answer's summary**:

```bash
curl -s "$BASE/api/questions/q_7d21c9e8f43c"
```

```json
{
  "question": {
    "id": "q_7d21c9e8f43c",
    "label": "decision",
    "context": "task",
    "task_id": "task_9f3",
    "text": "Should the retry backoff cap at five minutes, or unbounded?",
    "options": [
      {"id": "cap",  "label": "Cap at five minutes"},
      {"id": "none", "label": "Leave it unbounded"}
    ],
    "default": "cap",
    "priority": "high",
    "return_path": true,
    "asked_by": "session-s1",
    "asker_kind": "session",
    "session_id": "s1",
    "state": "answered"
  },
  "answer_count": 2,
  "current_answer_id": "a2",
  "answer": {
    "id": "a2",
    "chosen_option_id": "cap",
    "quote": "Cap it — unbounded backoff wedged the worker in prod",
    "actor": "operator",
    "surface": "pwa",
    "created_at": "2026-10-27T09:41:00Z"
  }
}
```

Read this one endpoint for the whole return path: `state` tells you the
question's state, `answer_count` every answer ever recorded (superseded
answers stay in the log — they are decided, never deleted),
`current_answer_id` which answer stands now, and `answer` the standing
answer's summary — its id, chosen option, the **verbatim quote** exactly
as received (never trimmed or re-encoded), who answered, on which
surface, and when. While the question has no answer, `answer` is
`null`. The full answer log of record is `GET /api/questions/{id}/answers`.

## Walkthrough: the opt-in session line (the single DATAWATCH_ANSWER)

This is for the one case where event-plus-polled is not enough: an
Automaton whose session must *see* the answer come back, without any
polling loop of its own. It is deliberately the narrowest path in the
channel and it is **off unless the question asked for it**.
