chunks.heading: Stage 2 — minimal setup: one backend, one session (opencode or claude)
chunks.body:
## Stage 2 — minimal setup: one backend, one session (opencode or claude)

The fastest path from a fresh install to a real AI session: no
messaging backend, no LLM registry, no MCP server required yet. Pick
whichever coding CLI you already have on your machine.

```sh
# opencode
datawatch config set llm.backends.opencode.enabled true
datawatch config set llm.backends.opencode.path "$(which opencode)"

# — or — claude-code
datawatch config set llm.backends.claude_code.enabled true
datawatch config set llm.backends.claude_code.path "$(which claude)"

datawatch reload

# Confirm backend is healthy.
datawatch backends list
#  → opencode | claude-code  ENABLED  reachable  models=[...]

# Spawn a smoke session.
SID=$(datawatch sessions start --llm opencode \
  --task "What model are you?" --project-dir /tmp 2>&1 \
  | grep -oP 'session \K[a-z0-9-]+')
# (swap --llm claude-code if that's the one you configured)
sleep 5
datawatch sessions tail $SID | head -20
datawatch sessions kill $SID
```

Or the same thing from the PWA instead of the CLI:

1. Open `https://localhost:8443` in your browser. Accept the
   self-signed cert (or trust the CA bundle from
   `~/.datawatch/tls/ca.pem`).
2. PWA prompts for the bearer token printed at `datawatch init` time.
   Paste + click **Save & Reconnect**.
3. PWA loads. Bottom nav: Sessions / Automata / Alerts / Observer /
   Settings.
4. Settings → LLM → pick opencode or claude-code → fill in the config
   card (binary path, etc.) → **Save**. The status row turns green
   when the daemon can reach the backend.
5. Bottom nav → **Sessions** → **+** FAB → backend dropdown → Task
   "Hello, what model are you?" → **Start**.
6. Watch the session detail open with xterm-streamed output. Confirm
   the LLM answers.

This is a complete, working datawatch install — everything in Stage 3
is additive, not required.

Later, to update: `datawatch update` (downloads the latest version if
one is available) then `datawatch restart` (graceful stop + start;
preserves running sessions via pipe-pane re-establish).

chunks.title: How-to: Setup + install
chunks.heading: MCP — set up and manage datawatch itself through natural-language prompts
chunks.body:
### MCP — set up and manage datawatch itself through natural-language prompts

MCP isn't just an API wrapper for *using* datawatch from your editor —
it's a way to let an AI assistant *configure and operate* datawatch
itself, so the rest of Stage 3 (and ongoing day-2 management) can be
driven by prompts instead of memorized CLI flags. Connect any MCP host
— Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, or a `claude-code`/`opencode`
session datawatch itself spawned in Stage 2 (it already has this same
MCP server wired in, so a session can configure the daemon it's
running inside):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "datawatch": {
      "command": "datawatch",
      "args": ["mcp"],
      "env": { "DATAWATCH_TOKEN": "<bearer>" }
    }
  }
}
```

Live tool catalogue (60+ tools) at `https://localhost:8443/api/mcp/docs`.

**Example prompts — setup.** Once connected, say these to your
assistant instead of running the equivalent CLI command yourself:

| You say | Tool(s) it calls |
|---|---|
| "What LLM backends and compute nodes do I have configured?" | `backends_list`, `llm_list`, `compute_node_list` |
| "Register my gaming PC at 192.168.1.50 running Ollama as a compute node, then pull llama3.1:8b on it" | `compute_node_add`, `compute_node_pull_model` |
| "Add a new LLM entry called 'fast' that fails over from my Ollama node to claude-code" | `llm_add`, `llm_add_model` |
| "Set my operator identity — I'm a backend engineer, prefer terse answers" | `set_identity` / `configure_identity` |
| "Register my home server at https://homelab.local:8443 as a federation peer, and skip TLS verification since it's self-signed" | `federation_peer_add` (`tls_skip_verify: true`) |
| "Enable the Telegram channel with this bot token" | `config_set` + `reload` |

**Example prompts — day-2 management.** The same connection keeps
working after setup, for ongoing operation:

| You say | Tool(s) it calls |
|---|---|
| "Start a claude-code session to refactor the auth module in ~/proj" | `start_session` |
| "Is anything stuck or unhealthy right now?" | `diagnose`, `get_stats`, `sessions_stale` |
| "Kill session abc123 and tell me what it was doing" | `session_output`, `kill_session` |
| "Create an alert rule that pages me when a session fails twice in a row" | `alert_rule_create` |
| "Reload the config, I just edited datawatch.yaml by hand" | `reload` |
| "Restart the daemon" | `restart_daemon` |

This is the same pattern Stage 2's minimal setup already demonstrated
in reverse — a datawatch-spawned coding session doing work *for* you —
except here the "work" is operating datawatch's own configuration. See
[`mcp-tools.md`](mcp-tools.md) for the full tool reference and
[`docs-as-mcp.md`](docs-as-mcp.md) for how an assistant can also search
and apply these how-tos directly through MCP.

chunks.title: How-to: Setup + install
chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Self-signed cert browser block.** First load shows a security
  warning. Either accept the exception OR install the CA bundle from
  `~/.datawatch/tls/ca.pem` to trust it permanently.
- **Bearer token lost.** Reset with `datawatch token rotate`; the
  PWA will prompt for the new one. Old sessions stay alive.
- **Backend binary not on PATH.** `datawatch backends list` shows
  `unreachable` for misconfigured backends. Set the absolute `path:`
  in the backend config card.
- **`tmux` version too old (< 3.0).** Some pipe-pane features used
  by datawatch require 3.0+. Upgrade via your package manager.
- **Port 8443 in use.** Edit `server.port` in `datawatch.yaml` and
  restart.

# How-to: Sync skills from PAI (or any git registry)

Skills are reusable markdown packages that influence how an AI session
does its work. Two registries ship preconfigured:

- **PAI** — [danielmiessler/Personal_AI_Infrastructure](https://github.com/danielmiessler/Personal_AI_Infrastructure) — upstream skills for coding, methodology, and general AI practice.
- **Community** — [dmz006/datawatch-community](https://github.com/dmz006/datawatch-community) — community-contributed skills and plugins for autonomous session patterns, identity, comms, and more. `sync_on_start: false` by default; opt in with `datawatch skills registry-sync community`.

Add your own registries to share team / company skills across hosts.

chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

A **skill** is a directory with:

- `manifest.yaml` (PAI format + 6 datawatch extensions).
- One or more markdown files (`SKILL.md`, examples, sub-skills).

A **registry** is a git repo containing many skills. `datawatch
skills` syncs configured registries; resolved skills are referenced
by name from sessions, profiles, and Automatons. At session spawn
time the daemon copies the synced files into
`<projectDir>/.datawatch/skills/<name>/` so the LLM can read them.

chunks.heading: 4a. Happy path — CLI
chunks.body:
### 4a. Happy path — CLI

```sh
# 1. Sync all configured registries.
datawatch skills registry-sync
#  → syncing pai...   42 skills (3 new, 39 unchanged)
#    syncing team...  8 skills (8 new)

# 2. List synced skills.
datawatch skills list
#  → go-style                pai     code-style
#    test-first               pai     methodology
#    rtk-cli-aware           team    code-style
#    secrets-scan            pai     security
#    sast                    team    security

# 3. Inspect a skill.
datawatch skills get test-first
#  → name: test-first
#    registry: pai
#    description: Write the test before the implementation
#    instructions: |
#      ...

# 4. Use a skill in a session at spawn.
datawatch sessions start \
  --backend claude-code \
  --skills test-first,rtk-cli-aware,secrets-scan \
  --task "Add a new endpoint to /api/sessions"
# Skills get copied into <project_dir>/.datawatch/skills/<name>/
# at spawn; the LLM can read them with the same tooling it uses for
# other context.

# 5. Reference skills in a Project Profile (so every spawn against
#    that profile gets them).
$EDITOR ~/.datawatch/profiles/projects/datawatch-dev.yaml
# Add:
#   skills: [test-first, rtk-cli-aware, go-style]
```

chunks.body:
### 4b. Happy path — PWA

1. Settings → Automate → **Skill Registries** card.
2. The PAI registry is pre-listed. Click **+ Connect** to add another.
   Modal asks for name + git URL + branch.
3. Click **Sync** next to a registry. Status spinner; on completion
   the count of synced skills updates.
4. Below the registry list, **Synced skills** lists every skill from
   every connected registry, with `tag`, `description`, and an
   inspect ▾ expander.
5. To use a skill, spawn a session via Sessions → + FAB → wizard:
   - **Advanced (collapsed)** → **Skills** → multi-select chip
     picker shows synced skills.
   - Select; **Start**. The chosen skills get installed at spawn.
6. Or attach skills to a Project Profile via Settings → Agents →
   Project Profiles → edit a profile → Skills field.

chunks.heading: 5e. YAML
chunks.body:
### 5e. YAML

Registry config at `~/.datawatch/skills-registries.yaml`:

```yaml
registries:
  - name: pai
    url: https://github.com/danielmiessler/Personal_AI_Infrastructure
    branch: main
    sync_on_start: true
    sync_interval: 24h
  - name: team
    url: https://github.com/your-org/datawatch-skills
    branch: main
    auth: ${secret:GITHUB_TOKEN}      # for private repos
```

Synced skills land at `~/.datawatch/skills/<name>/` (operator-readable
copies). Don't edit them — re-sync would overwrite. Fork the registry
or add to your team registry for permanent edits.

Per-skill manifest:

```yaml
name: test-first
description: Write the test before the implementation
tags: [methodology, testing]
instructions: |
  Before writing implementation code:
  ...

# datawatch extensions:
backends: [claude-code, opencode-acp]   # restrict to backends that benefit
prerequisites: []                        # other skills required
session_inject: true                     # auto-inject into session prompt
```

chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Skill not appearing in the picker after registry-add.** You forgot
  to sync. `datawatch skills registry-sync`.
- **Private registry sync fails with 401.** Set `auth: ${secret:GITHUB_TOKEN}`
  in the registry config; ensure the token has read access.
- **Skill referenced in profile but not synced.** Spawn fails with
  "skill not found". Sync first; confirm with `skills list`.
- **Editing the synced copy.** Lost on next sync. Fork the registry
  or maintain your team registry instead.
- **Skill manifest schema mismatch.** Older PAI skills predate the
  `session_inject` extension; daemon defaults to `true`. Inspect with
  `skills get <name>` to see the merged manifest.

# How-to: Tailscale Mesh — private overlay network for agents

Spawn container workers in a Kubernetes cluster and have them join a
private Tailscale (or Headscale) mesh automatically. Datawatch + the
agent fleet end up on the same private tailnet; no public exposure
required, no per-cluster VPN to set up.

chunks.title: How-to: Tailscale Mesh — private overlay network for agents
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

A Tailscale sidecar (Headscale-compatible) injected into agent worker
pods at spawn time. The pod's main process can reach the datawatch
host (and any other peer in the tailnet) on private 100.x.y.z IPs.
Operator sees the agent in `datawatch tailscale nodes`; agent sees
the host as another node in the mesh.

**Headscale vs commercial Tailscale.** Headscale is the recommended
self-hosted control plane (free, you own the keys); commercial
Tailscale is the hosted alternative (free tier generous; managed for
you). Both speak the same protocol.

chunks.heading: Base requirements
chunks.body:
## Base requirements

- `datawatch start` — daemon up.
- A Kubernetes cluster reachable from the daemon (a Cluster Profile in
  `~/.datawatch/profiles/clusters/` — see `profiles.md`).
- Headscale running OR a commercial Tailscale account.
- A pre-auth key from your control plane (Headscale: `headscale
  preauthkeys create --reusable --expiration 0`; Tailscale admin
  console → **Keys**). Store this key as a secret using `${secret:TS_PREAUTH_KEY}` — see [secrets-manager.md](secrets-manager.md) for secret storage.
- Outbound UDP 41641 from agent pods (Tailscale's preferred direct
  port; falls back to DERP relay if blocked).

chunks.title: How-to: Tailscale Mesh — private overlay network for agents
chunks.heading: Setup
chunks.body:
## Setup

```sh
# 1. Run Headscale (skip if using commercial Tailscale).
docker run -d --name headscale \
  -v $HOME/.headscale:/etc/headscale -p 8080:8080 \
  --restart=unless-stopped \
  headscale/headscale:latest headscale serve

# 2. Create user + reusable, non-expiring pre-auth key.
docker exec -it headscale headscale users create datawatch
docker exec -it headscale headscale preauthkeys create \
  --user datawatch --reusable --expiration 0
#  → tskey-...

# 3. Store the key in the secrets manager.
datawatch secrets set TS_PREAUTH_KEY "tskey-..."
```

Configure datawatch:

```yaml
# ~/.datawatch/datawatch.yaml
agents:
  tailscale:
    enabled: true
    control_plane_url: http://headscale.your.host:8080
    preauth_key: ${secret:TS_PREAUTH_KEY}
    hostname_prefix: dw-agent
    tags:
      - tag:datawatch-agent
      - tag:env:lab
```

Restart: `datawatch restart`.

chunks.heading: 4a. Happy path — CLI
chunks.body:
### 4a. Happy path — CLI

```sh
# 1. Confirm Tailscale is configured + the daemon node is healthy.
datawatch tailscale status
#  → node: dw-host-kona  ip: 100.64.0.1  status: connected
#    control plane: http://headscale.your.host:8080  reachable: yes

# 2. Spawn an agent worker — it auto-joins.
datawatch sessions start \
  --backend claude-code \
  --agent k8s \
  --cluster lab-east \
  --task "Run integration tests"
#  → spawned session ralfthewise-abcd; agent dw-agent-abcd joining mesh ...

# 3. List peers.
sleep 10
datawatch tailscale nodes
#  → dw-host-kona       100.64.0.1   self
#    dw-agent-abcd      100.64.0.42  online (1m ago)

# 4. Generate + push an ACL that locks down the fleet.
datawatch tailscale acl-generate > /tmp/acl-preview.json
datawatch tailscale acl-push --dry-run     # show diff vs current
datawatch tailscale acl-push               # actually push

# 5. Prune stale nodes (after sessions finish + pods terminate).
datawatch tailscale prune --older-than 24h
```

chunks.title: How-to: Tailscale Mesh — private overlay network for agents
chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Pre-auth key expired.** Headscale + commercial Tailscale both let
  you create non-expiring keys (`--expiration 0` for Headscale; admin
  console toggle for commercial). Use those for agent fleets.
- **UDP 41641 blocked.** Tailscale prefers direct UDP; falls back to
  DERP relay if blocked. Works but slower. Open UDP 41641 outbound on
  the agent cluster.
- **Operator-added ACL rules wiped by `acl-push`.** Wrap in the
  `#operator-rules` markers; the generator preserves anything between.
- **Two control planes on one host.** Can't run Headscale + point at
  commercial Tailscale at the same time. Pick one.
- **Node IP visible in logs.** The 100.x.y.z address is fine to log;
  it's only routable inside the tailnet. Don't paste publicly.

chunks.title: How-to: Testing Against a Running Daemon
chunks.body:
# How-to: Testing Against a Running Daemon

Datawatch's two test scripts — `scripts/release-smoke.sh` (functional
smoke) and `scripts/run-tests.sh` (E2E stories) — each default to
spinning up their own fresh, isolated daemon with a throwaway data
directory. Both also support pointing at a daemon you already have
running instead: a CI-deployed kind/k8s instance, a persistent dev
daemon, a remote sandbox. This is a reusable capability, not a
one-off CI hack — any script or app driving datawatch's test surface
can use the same variables.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [testing, ci, scripts, autonomous]

chunks.title: How-to: Testing Against a Running Daemon
chunks.heading: Why this exists
chunks.body:
## Why this exists

`scripts/release-smoke.sh`'s own `kind-smoke` CI job builds a Docker
image, loads it into a `kind` cluster, and waits for it to answer
`/api/health` through a port-forward — the whole point is to catch
chart/image regressions in that *real deployed instance*. But the
script always launched its own separate local daemon anyway, so the
in-kind daemon was never actually exercised; the job silently tested
nothing new. Fixed 2026-10-13 by teaching `release-smoke.sh` to run
its functional checks against the daemon that's actually already
running, when asked to.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [testing, ci, scripts, autonomous]

chunks.title: How-to: Testing Against a Running Daemon
chunks.heading: `release-smoke.sh`: `DW_BASE` / `DW_BASE_TOKEN` / `DW_BASE_INSECURE`
chunks.body:
## `release-smoke.sh`: `DW_BASE` / `DW_BASE_TOKEN` / `DW_BASE_INSECURE`

```sh
# Point at an already-running daemon instead of starting a new one.
DW_BASE=http://localhost:18080 bash scripts/release-smoke.sh

# With auth and a self-signed/untrusted cert (the common case for a
# test/sandbox/kind-cluster daemon):
DW_BASE=https://sandbox.example:8443 \
  DW_BASE_TOKEN=your-bearer-token \
  bash scripts/release-smoke.sh
```

| Variable | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `DW_BASE` | to enable this mode | Full base URL of the already-running daemon (`scheme://host:port`, no trailing slash). Unset = default behavior, spin up a fresh isolated daemon (unchanged). |
| `DW_BASE_TOKEN` | no | Bearer token for that daemon's REST API. Empty = no `Authorization` header (matches a daemon with `server.token: ""`). |
| `DW_BASE_INSECURE` | no (default **on** in this mode) | Whether the `datawatch` CLI's own `-u`/`--url` calls skip TLS certificate verification. Every REST/MCP check in this script already uses `curl -sk` (skip-verify) unconditionally regardless of mode, so this defaults to `1` to match that same posture — the common case (a self-signed test/sandbox/kind-cluster cert) just works. Set `DW_BASE_INSECURE=0` yourself if your external daemon has a real, CA-trusted cert and you want the CLI checks to actually verify it. |

**What's skipped in this mode, and why:** a few checks need to drop a
fixture file where the *daemon* will read it from its own local disk
(the managed-plugin discovery/lifecycle sections, and the evals-suite
smoke check) — that only works when the script and the daemon share
one filesystem, which isn't guaranteed for an external/remote/
in-cluster target. These report `SKIP` with an explicit reason in
this mode, not a false `FAIL`. Everything else — every REST/MCP
check, every CLI round-trip — runs identically against any
already-running daemon, local or external.

chunks.title: How-to: Testing Against a Running Daemon
chunks.heading: `run-tests.sh`: `DW_BASE` / `DW_BASE_TOKEN` / `DW_BASE_INSECURE`
chunks.body:
## `run-tests.sh`: `DW_BASE` / `DW_BASE_TOKEN` / `DW_BASE_INSECURE`

```sh
# Run E2E stories against a daemon you already have running, instead
# of starting a fresh one.
DW_BASE=https://127.0.0.1:18443 DW_BASE_TOKEN=your-bearer-token \
  bash scripts/run-tests.sh --story=TS-042
```

Same three variables and the same meaning as `release-smoke.sh`'s
above — this is one mechanism, not two. `--no-daemon` on its own still
works too (it means "skip the script's own daemon-start step," full
stop) but on its own it does **not** give you a way to point at an
arbitrary external daemon — it only reuses one on the exact ports
`TEST_PORT`/`TEST_TLS_PORT` would otherwise have picked, which is only
useful for resuming a daemon this *same* harness already started
earlier in the run (see `DATAWATCH_TEST_ID=... --resume-from=...` in
the script's own header). Pointing at a daemon on arbitrary ports —
anything you didn't start with `run-tests.sh` itself — needs `DW_BASE`.

**Corrected 2026-10-13, same day this doc was first written:** an
earlier version of this section documented `--no-daemon` + `TEST_BASE`
as a general external-daemon override. That was wrong, and the only
reason it's not still wrong in this doc is that it got tested, not
just read from the script: `TEST_PORT`/`TEST_TLS_PORT` are only
honored by the script's own port-picker when the given port is
currently *free* — which an already-running daemon's port never is —
so a pre-set `TEST_BASE` got silently recomputed and ignored, and the
run failed against nothing. `DW_BASE` was added to `run-tests.sh`
afterward, mirroring `release-smoke.sh`'s real, working mechanism
instead, and re-verified against a real external daemon before this
section was rewritten.

## Why one mechanism now, not two

Both scripts' daemon-lifecycle code predates this capability and each
had its own (in `run-tests.sh`'s case, non-functional) attempt at it.
`DW_BASE`/`DW_BASE_TOKEN`/`DW_BASE_INSECURE` is now the one shared
mechanism both use, so a new script or app that needs the same
"point me at a daemon I already have" capability should use the same
three names rather than inventing a fourth variant.

chunks.heading: Mobile-fit suite
chunks.body:
## Mobile-fit suite

The mobile-fit suite is a Playwright layout-fitness check for the datawatch PWA. For one view it installs seeded API states, sweeps viewport/theme/zoom matrices, drives the view in a live browser, runs the same five-check layout pass over the settled DOM, and reports grouped findings. It is what the datawatch Automaton runs for the Observer (System Statistics) mobile layout, and what the release-smoke and the guard stories below wrap.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [testing, ci, scripts, autonomous]

chunks.title: How-to: Testing Against a Running Daemon
chunks.heading: What the suite checks
chunks.body:
### What the suite checks

Per scenario the harness runs (in `scripts/test-stories/pwa/mobile-fit-lib.mjs`):

- **`page-scroll`** — the document is wider than the CSS viewport, i.e. the page scrolls horizontally at a fixed, non-scrollable viewport.
- **`edge-cross`** — an element whose bounding box crosses the left/right viewport edge and does not sit inside its own scroll container.
- **`clipped-text`** — an element owns a direct text node that clips (overflows), yet does not expose the full value: it lacks `text-overflow: ellipsis` and/or a tooltip (non-empty `title` or `aria-label` within three levels). Ellipsis *and* tooltip together make clipped text acceptable.
- **`tap-target`** — an interactive element (`a[href]`, `button`, `select`, `textarea`, labeled `input`, `[role]`, non-negative `tabindex`) with width **or** height under **40 CSS px** (`TAP_MIN = 40`). Checkbox/radio inputs are measured over their label.
- **`overlap`** — two elements that are siblings (in layout) and overlap.

On top of the static layout pass, the runner performs the view's **interaction checks** at the first matrix cell. For the Observer view: section collapse/expand (re-fit after each toggle), refresh, and re-render without duplicated timers. `--scope`/`MOBILE_FIT_SCOPE` (a comma-separated CSS selector list, e.g. `'#view'` or `'#settings-sec-stats'`) narrows the layout checks to the matching subtree for that run.

chunks.title: How-to: Testing Against a Running Daemon
chunks.heading: How to run it
chunks.body:
### How to run it

The suite lives in `scripts/test-stories/pwa/` and follows the PWA story conventions: `npm ci` in that directory, and `TEST_HTTP` / `TEST_TLS` / `TEST_TOKEN` telling it which daemon under test to drive.

**Guard stories via Make** — `e2e-pwa.sh` boots an isolated daemon on fresh 127.0.0.1 ports (or runs against an external daemon when `TEST_HTTP`/`TEST_TLS`/`TEST_TOKEN` are set) and executes the story:

```bash
make test-e2e-mobile-fit                     # TS-817 then TS-818
bash scripts/e2e-pwa.sh TS-817               # Observer regression guard only
TEST_HTTP=https://host:8443 TEST_TLS=1 TEST_TOKEN=... bash scripts/e2e-pwa.sh TS-817
```

**Direct harness** (from `scripts/test-stories/pwa/`, any running daemon):

```bash
node mobile-fit.mjs                                  # observer view, quick profile (default)
node mobile-fit.mjs --view observer --profile full
node mobile-fit.mjs --scope '#settings-sec-stats' --profile full
node mobile-fit.mjs --exhaustive                     # cross product (requires --profile full)
node mobile-fit.mjs --list                           # print the run plan, no browser needed
```

Every flag has an env-var twin:

| Flag | Env | Default | Meaning |
|------|-----|---------|---------|
| `--view` | `MOBILE_FIT_VIEW` | `observer` | PWA view to drive (only `observer` is wired today) |
| `--profile` | `MOBILE_FIT_PROFILE` | `quick` | `smoke` \| `quick` \| `full` |
| `--exhaustive` | `MOBILE_FIT_EXHAUSTIVE=1` | off | full viewport×theme×zoom×state cross product (requires `--profile full`) |
| `--out` | `MOBILE_FIT_OUT` | `$EVIDENCE_DIR/$CURRENT_STORY/mobile-fit` | report/screenshot output directory |
| `--report-only` | `MOBILE_FIT_REPORT_ONLY=1` | off | rebuild the report from a saved run; no browser |
| `--scope` | `MOBILE_FIT_SCOPE` | whole page | comma-separated CSS selectors scoping the layout checks |
| `--list` | — | — | print the run plan (states × profiles, named scenarios, interactions) and exit |

Exit codes: `0` pass (no findings), `1` findings or a harness failure, `2` browser unavailable or malformed flags.

`node mobile-fit-selftest.mjs` proves the detectors themselves on known-good/known-bad fixture pages at a 360×740 viewport (no daemon, no PWA): the `clean` fixture must yield zero findings and each known-bad fixture must yield exactly its expected checks.

chunks.title: How-to: Testing Against a Running Daemon
chunks.heading: Profiles and what each covers
chunks.body:
### Profiles and what each covers

The matrices come from `mobile-fit-matrix.mjs` — 12 viewports: portrait 320/360/375/390/412/600/768 and landscape 320/360/375/390/412 (e.g. 390×844, 768×1024); themes light and dark; zooms 100, 130, 200.

- **smoke** — one cell: 390×844 portrait, dark, 100% zoom, on the first seeded state. Fastest possible check that the harness can drive the view at all.
- **quick** (default) — per quick state (all states except `stats-empty` and `stats-slow`): portrait 320/360/390/768, dark, 100% zoom; plus 360-landscape dark, one 360-portrait light cell per state; and one 360-portrait cell at 200% zoom on the first quick state. (Seven cells per quick state.)
- **full** — three sweeps over every state: **A** all 12 viewports, dark, 100% zoom; **B** four reference cells (360 portrait, 390 portrait, 768 portrait, 360 landscape), light, 100% zoom; **C** 130% and 200% zoom over portrait 320/360/390/412, on the `three-peers` zoom state. The 2026-10-24 Observer post-fix full run was 284 scenario runs.
- **exhaustive** (with `--profile full`) — the full cross product: all 12 viewports × 2 themes × 3 zooms × every state. Use only when debugging a specific geometry; it is an order of magnitude larger than full.

Every profile also runs the view's **named scenarios** (Observer: `system-stats-phone` — `three-peers` at 360×740, dark, 100% zoom, scoped to `#settings-sec-stats`) and the three **interaction checks** at the first matrix cell.

chunks.title: How-to: Testing Against a Running Daemon
chunks.heading: Seeded data states
chunks.body:
### Seeded data states

States live in `scripts/test-stories/pwa/mobile-fit-seeds.mjs`. The module is pure data plus a Playwright route-handler factory: `buildSeed(state)` returns a fixed set of API responses keyed by route, and `installSeed(page, state)` intercepts `**/api/**` at the context level so **no live peers, no real stats, no timing** are involved. Bodies are deterministic (fixed reference clock, no randomness or timestamps) — the unit tests assert byte-identical rebuilds.

Observer states today:

| State | What the view sees |
|-------|--------------------|
| `no-peers` | no peers at all; every peer table empty |
| `one-peer` / `three-peers` | one / three peers; basic card population (three-peers doubles as the zoom-sweep state) |
| `ten-peers` | ten peers inside fixed-height cards (scrolling stress) |
| `long-hostname` | 70-char local hostname, 80- and 40-char peer names (ellipsis/layout) |
| `peer-errored` | one 502 peer, one never-pushed peer, one stale peer |
| `peer-no-gpu` / `peer-multi-gpu` | local without GPUs / local with a multi-GPU set |
| `ebpf-unavailable` / `ebpf-many-processes` / `ebpf-long-names` | eBPF off, large per-process tables, long process names |
| `sessions-empty` / `sessions-large` | no sessions / large session lists |
| `stats-slow` | stats endpoints delayed (the view is checked in **loading** and settled phases) |
| `stats-failed` | stats endpoints return long 5xx errors |
| `numbers-large` | petabyte/exabyte-scale counters (compact unit formatting) |

**Adding a new data state:**

1. Pick a descriptive kebab-case name — states are referenced by name in stories, reports, and this table.
2. Add it to `STATE_NAMES` in `mobile-fit-seeds.mjs` (the seed inventory test `mobile-fit-seeds.test.mjs` pins the exact list — update its expectation in the same change).
3. Add a builder under `STATE_BUILDERS`: start from `baseSeed({ peers, local })` and override individual `responses` entries where the state needs different payloads (see `stats-slow`/`stats-failed` for per-endpoint delay/error patterns). Reuse the `make*` builders; keep it deterministic — no `Math.random()`, no `Date.now()`.
4. Decide its matrix tier in the view provider (`mobile-fit-observer.mjs`): `states` (full sweeps, always), `quickStates` (quick profile), `zoomStates` (zoom sweep). Slow or empty-endpoint states are typically excluded from `quick`.
5. Cover the new state in `mobile-fit-seeds.test.mjs` (shape + determinism) and re-run `node mobile-fit-selftest.mjs` to keep the detector evidence current.

chunks.title: How-to: Testing Against a Running Daemon
chunks.heading: Desktop and tablet baseline (TS-818)
chunks.body:
### Desktop and tablet baseline (TS-818)

`mobile-fit-desktop.mjs` captures the bounding rectangles of the tracked Observer selectors at 1280×800, 1920×1080 and 768×1024 (dark, 100% zoom, `three-peers`) and records them in `scripts/test-stories/pwa/mobile-fit-desktop-baseline.json`. TS-818 re-captures the same document against a live daemon and passes when every tracked value is within `max(2px, 1% of the baseline value)`; a tracked selector that no longer exists on the page is always a failure.

**Re-recording rule.** The baseline is a lock, not a snapshot of the moment. Re-record it (`node mobile-fit-desktop.mjs --record`, which needs `TEST_HTTP`/`TEST_TOKEN` of a live daemon; `--compare` is the default mode and `--self-test` is the browser-free comparator check) only for a **deliberate, reviewed layout change** whose reason is recorded with the change that re-recorded it. The capture harness is read-only — it must not modify `app.js`/`style.css` or the tracked layout — so an unexplained drift against the baseline is exactly what the guard exists to fail.

chunks.title: How-to: Testing Against a Running Daemon
chunks.heading: Release-smoke integration
chunks.body:
### Release-smoke integration

`scripts/release-smoke-mobile-fit.sh` is the release-smoke entry point (invoked from `scripts/release-smoke.sh` as the mobile-fit view runner check). It derives `TEST_HTTP` / `TEST_TLS` / `TEST_TOKEN` from `DATAWATCH_BASE` + `DATAWATCH_TOKEN` and runs the observer view at the quick profile. The report lands in a fresh temp dir whose path the script prints — `$REPORT_DIR/mobile-fit/mobile-fit-report.json` and `-report.txt`, plus `screenshots/`. It skips (exit 2) when the daemon is unreachable at `DATAWATCH_BASE`, `node` is missing from PATH, or Playwright is not installed in `scripts/test-stories/pwa` (run `cd scripts/test-stories/pwa && npm ci` there first).

| Exit | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `0` | suite passed (no findings) |
| `1` | findings present — release failure |
| `2` | browser or environment unavailable — `SKIP:` line on stderr; the release smoke records this as a skip, not a failure |

chunks.title: Usage calculator
chunks.body:
# Usage calculator

The usage calculator answers two questions about your provider's weekly
allowance:

1. Are you **within or over budget for the week**?
2. What does **each lane count cost against the rest of the week**, so you can
   choose how many lanes to run?

It takes readings you type, adds the lanes that were running, and returns
advice. **It only advises. It never stops, slows or re-prioritises a lane.**
The lane count is always yours to set.

    args: {limit: 10}
    read_only: true

    description: Worked example, a state-changing call. Type a reading, 42 percent of the weekly allowance used with 2 lanes running. Use your own provider figure in real use

chunks.title: Usage calculator
chunks.heading: The three policies
chunks.body:
## The three policies

The policy is the target the advice aims at. **Which policy to follow is the
operator's choice**, and you can change it at any time.

| Policy | Name on screen | What the advice aims for |
|---|---|---|
| `use-all` (default) | Use it all | The largest lane count that still ends the week at or under 100 percent of the allowance (plus any extra credit). |
| `pace` | Pace to the week | The largest lane count that ends the week the safety margin below 100 percent, so the allowance lasts to the reset. |
| `finish-early` | Run flat out | All lanes run; the advice says when the remaining work finishes against when the allowance runs out. |

Set it with `usage.calculator.policy`. A single `usage_advice` call can also
pass `policy` to look at another policy without saving it.

chunks.heading: Typing a reading
chunks.body:
## Typing a reading

A reading is one look at your provider's usage page.

- **Percent** of the weekly allowance used (or the spend in dollars; give
  exactly one of the two).
- **Session percent** (optional). The share of the current session window used.
  It is shown as a secondary line only and **has no verdict of its own**; the
  weekly figure is what sets lane counts.
- **Lanes** (optional). How many lanes were running, so the burn per lane can
  be worked out.
- **At** (optional). When you read it; the default is now.

A mistyped reading can be deleted by its id (`usage_reading_delete`); the advice
recomputes from the rest.

chunks.title: Usage calculator
chunks.heading: The weekly reset
chunks.body:
## The weekly reset

The reset is **Sunday 08:00** in the configured reset zone, entered as a
weekday, a local clock time and a time zone name (the keys
`usage.calculator.reset_weekday`, `reset_time` and `reset_zone`; match them to
what your provider actually shows).

By default `reset_zone` is *empty*, which means **follow the zone the daemon
runs in** — an example being Sunday 08:00 in `America/New_York` on a daemon
whose zone is `America/New_York`. The zone is resolved when the reset runs,
in this order: the `TZ` environment variable, then the zone named in the
system local-time symlink (`/etc/localtime` into `zoneinfo/Area/City`), then
the Go runtime's local zone. The resolved zone is a proper IANA zone name,
so it follows the zone's own rules: a fixed offset such as `+05:00` is wrong
for half the year once daylight saving time starts or ends, but a zone name
keeps the countdown correct across the change.

If no zone can be resolved on the host, the reset **falls back to UTC**: the
reset runs in UTC and the advice carries a note saying the zone fell back to
UTC and pointing at `usage.calculator.reset_zone`, so you can pin it. That
note appears in every rendering (CLI, comm channel, JSON, PWA).

An **explicit zone name always wins**, a plain `UTC` included: whatever
IANA name you set is used as-is and is never rewritten to the server's zone.
`Local` is refused because it is just the server's zone under another name,
which is what the empty value already means.

**Where to see the effective zone.** When the config's zone is empty, the
surfaces show the *effective* zone marked as the server's zone, not a blank
value:

| Surface | What it shows |
|---|---|
| PWA (settings → “Usage calculator reset time zone”) | the input stays empty, the effective zone appears as placeholder text, and a note says the zone is the server's (empty in the config) |
| `GET /api/config` | `usage.calculator.reset_zone` = the effective zone, with `reset_zone_source` of `server` (or `configured` when you set it explicitly) and `reset_zone_fell_back` `true` on the UTC fallback |
| `datawatch config get usage.calculator.reset_zone` | the zone with a marker, e.g. `America/New_York (server zone)` when server-resolved, or just the zone name when set explicitly |
| Calculator advice (text + JSON) | the text forms put `(server zone)` on the reset time; the JSON carries `zone` plus `"server_zone": true` |

chunks.title: Usage calculator
chunks.heading: The 2-hour notice
chunks.body:
## The 2-hour notice

The recent burn is worked from your last two readings. If there is **no reading
in the last 2 hours**, the calculator falls back to the **week average** and
**says so on the screen**, so you know the figure is smoother than the real
recent burn. Type a fresh reading to get the recent burn back.

chunks.heading: Remaining work for run-flat-out
chunks.body:
## Remaining work for run-flat-out

The `finish-early` policy needs to know how much work is left. There are two
sources and the screen always shows which one is in use:

- **Computed estimate.** The queued Automata tasks times the cost-per-task
  setting (`usage.calculator.cost_per_task_points`, default 0.1), labelled as
  an estimate.
- **Typed figure.** Type a number with `usage_remaining_work_set` and it
  **overwrites** the estimate and is labelled as typed. Typing 0 removes it and
  the estimate is used again.

The number of queued tasks is shown beside both. Treat the cost per task as a
starting figure and calibrate it against real readings.

chunks.heading: Sharing across federated daemons
chunks.body:
## Sharing across federated daemons

A weekly allowance belongs to the account, not to one daemon, so the readings
are shared.

- One daemon is the **keeper** of the series. Set `usage.calculator.keeper` to
  the peer's name on the other daemons; empty means this daemon keeps it.
- Peers **read it over REST** with the `usage:read` federation capability.
- A **write on a peer goes to the keeper** (`usage:write`), so there is one
  series.
- If the keeper cannot be reached, a peer shows **its last copy, marked as
  such** (stale), rather than failing or hiding the figures.

chunks.title: Usage calculator
chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.body:
## Troubleshooting

- **"No reading in the last 2 hours" on the screen.** Expected. Type a fresh
  reading.
- **A reading is rejected.** Give exactly one of percent or spend, and a
  percent between 0 and 100.
- **The week ends at the wrong moment.** Check `reset_weekday`, `reset_time`
  and `reset_zone` against your provider; use a zone name, never an offset.
- **A zone is refused.** An unknown name or a fixed offset is rejected; the
  value is unchanged.
- **Run-flat-out shows an estimate you do not trust.** Type the remaining work,
  or calibrate `cost_per_task_points`.
- **A peer shows stale figures.** The keeper is unreachable; the peer is
  showing its last copy. Check the peer link and the `keeper` setting.
- **A peer is refused.** It needs the `usage:read` (and for writes
  `usage:write`) capability.
- **A setting snapped back to its default.** A saved value that is no longer
  allowed (for example a retired variant) falls back to the default and the
  daemon logs one line saying so.
- **Lanes did not change.** By design. The calculator advises only; change the
  lane count yourself.

chunks.title: How-to: v7 Compute Unification — what was migrated
chunks.body:
# How-to: v7 Compute Unification — what was migrated

When you first started a v7.0.0-alpha.15 (or later) daemon, it auto-migrated every populated `cfg.<Backend>` block from your v6 `config.yaml` into the new **LLM registry** entries. This page explains what changed, where things moved, and how to verify the migration succeeded.

> **Pre-conditions**: Migration requires the new Compute Nodes registry. See [compute-nodes.md](compute-nodes.md) for the v7 compute model and [llm-registry.md](llm-registry.md) for the unified LLM registry.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [v7, migration, compute, llm]

chunks.title: How-to: v7 Compute Unification — what was migrated
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

In v6, each LLM backend had its own top-level config block: `cfg.ollama`, `cfg.openwebui`, `cfg.aider`, `cfg.opencode`, `cfg.opencode_acp`, `cfg.goose`, `cfg.gemini`, `cfg.shell_backend`. Each held a binary path or URL plus per-backend tunables (model, console size, output mode).

In v7, **all of them collapse into one place**: the `LLM registry` (Settings → Compute → LLMs). Each LLM entry is `{name, kind, model, address, compute_nodes, …}`. Sessions and Council debates resolve LLMs by **name**, not by hard-coded backend type.

This eliminates the v6 dual-LLM-concept ambiguity (inference adapters vs session backends) and means every consumer (Council, /api/ask, automata, future agent-spawn) goes through the same dispatcher.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [v7, migration, compute, llm]

chunks.title: How-to: v7 Compute Unification — what was migrated
chunks.heading: What was migrated for you
chunks.body:
## What was migrated for you

On first v7 startup with this version, the daemon walks your `config.yaml` and creates one LLM registry entry per populated block, named `<backend>-default`:

| v6 block                | v7 LLM entry              | Kind            | Source field    |
|-------------------------|---------------------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| `cfg.ollama`            | `ollama-default`          | `ollama`        | `host` + `model`|
| `cfg.openwebui`         | `openwebui-default`       | `openwebui`     | `url` + `model` |
| `cfg.session.claude_bin`| `claude-code-default`     | `claude-code`   | binary path     |
| `cfg.opencode`          | `opencode-default`        | `opencode`      | binary path     |
| `cfg.opencode_acp`      | `opencode-acp-default`    | `opencode-acp`  | binary path     |
| `cfg.opencode_prompt`   | `opencode-prompt-default` | `opencode-prompt` | binary path |
| `cfg.aider`             | `aider-default`           | `aider`         | binary path     |
| `cfg.goose`             | `goose-default`           | `goose`         | binary path     |
| `cfg.gemini`            | `gemini-default`          | `gemini`        | binary path     |
| `cfg.shell_backend`     | `shell-default`           | `shell`         | script path     |

Migration is **idempotent** — re-runs skip any name that already exists, so editing the LLM entry in the PWA persists across restarts.

The migration is also **additive** — the v6 cfg blocks remain in `config.yaml` so external scripts that read them keep working through the v7.0.x window. Hard removal happens in v7.0.x patches once we confirm no broken consumers.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [v7, migration, compute, llm]

chunks.title: How-to: v7 Compute Unification — what was migrated
chunks.heading: How to verify
chunks.body:
## How to verify

1. **PWA**: Settings → Compute → **LLMs** card. You should see one entry per backend that was populated in your v6 config. Auto-created entries are tagged `auto`.
2. **CLI**: `datawatch llm list` lists every entry.
3. **REST**: `curl -sk $BASE/api/llms | jq '.llms[].name'`.
4. **Daemon log**: lines like `[inference] auto-migrated legacy cfg → llm/ollama-default` confirm what was created.
5. **Migration status**: `curl -sk $BASE/api/migration/status` returns the canonical list with timestamp.

docs:
  index: true
  topics: [v7, migration, compute, llm]

chunks.title: How-to: v7 Compute Unification — what was migrated
chunks.heading: What to do next
chunks.body:
## What to do next

- **Edit any auto-created entry** to set the right ComputeNode failover list, model, or API key. Use the ✏️ Edit button (Form/YAML toggle) and the 🧪 Test action to verify before saving.
- **Add new LLMs** for hosts the migration didn't know about (remote GPU boxes, cloud Anthropic API, etc.). Use the `+ Add LLM` form on the same card.
- **Dismiss the migration toast** by clicking ✕ on it (or `curl -sk -X DELETE $BASE/api/migration/status` from the CLI). It won't show again.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [v7, migration, compute, llm]

chunks.title: How-to: v7 Compute Unification — what was migrated
chunks.heading: Migration didn't pick up my backend
chunks.body:
## Migration didn't pick up my backend

Reasons a backend might not have migrated:

- **Block was empty.** Migration skips entries with no address/binary. Set the value in `config.yaml` and restart, or just add the LLM via the PWA `+ Add LLM` form.
- **Name already existed.** Migration is idempotent. If you previously added a manual LLM with the same name, the auto-migration didn't overwrite it. Edit the existing entry instead.
- **Reading the wrong config file.** `datawatch config show` confirms which file the daemon loaded.
chunks.frontmatter_raw:
docs:
  index: true
  topics: [v7, migration, compute, llm]

chunks.title: How-to: v7 Compute Unification — what was migrated
chunks.heading: Why v7 unification
chunks.body:
## Why v7 unification

Before v7, datawatch had **two parallel LLM concepts** that operators had to reason about separately: "inference adapters" (used by Council, /api/ask) and "session backends" (used by tmux-spawning sessions). They had different config blocks, different APIs, different mental models — and no single answer to "what models are available?".

v7 collapses these into one model: every LLM is in the registry; every consumer (inference, session, automata) uses the same name to refer to it. The dispatcher routes through ordered ComputeNode failover. The Compute tab in Settings is the single source of truth.

  topics: [v7, migration, compute, llm]

chunks.title: How-to: Voice input
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.body:
## What it is

Inbound voice notes (or PWA microphone audio) get transcribed by a
configured backend and routed into the session as if you'd typed the
text. Backends:

| Backend | Where it runs | Privacy | One-line summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| `whisper` | Local Python venv | private | Default; needs Python + the `whisper` model files. |
| `openai` | Cloud (api.openai.com) | sends audio to OpenAI | Easiest if you already pay for an OpenAI key. |
| `openai_compat` | Any OpenAI-compatible HTTPS endpoint | depends | faster-whisper-server, vLLM, custom. |
| `openwebui` | Your already-configured OpenWebUI | private | Reuses whatever model OpenWebUI is fronting. |
| `ollama` | Your already-configured Ollama | private | Reuses Ollama's transcribe endpoint. |

Non-local backends (`openai`, `openai_compat`, `openwebui`, `ollama`)
**inherit endpoint + API key from the matching LLM-backend config
block** — you don't enter them twice.

Bare Ollama has **no audio endpoint**. When you set `whisper.backend: ollama`, datawatch transparently routes the audio request through your configured `openwebui:` block (because OpenWebUI is the only thing that fronts Ollama with an audio API). You'll see this on startup:


The fallback chain (see below) takes over if OpenWebUI's whisper engine isn't reachable.

chunks.heading: OpenWebUI configuration
chunks.body:
## OpenWebUI configuration

OpenWebUI's audio API is at `/api/v1/audio/transcriptions` (the daemon handles this for you). What it does on the server side depends on **OpenWebUI Settings → Audio → Speech-to-Text Engine**. Pick one:

| Engine | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| `local` (CTranslate2 + faster-whisper) | Fast on CUDA x86_64 | **Broken on ARM unless CTranslate2 is built with CUDA-arm64.** Default install often returns `Error transcribing chunk: This CTranslate2 package was not compiled with CUDA support`. |
| `openai` | Uses OpenAI's API | Requires API key + sends audio to OpenAI |
| `whisper.cpp` (via the OpenWebUI extension) | Pure CPU works on any arch | Slower than CUDA, faster than venv |

chunks.heading: NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor / other ARM-with-GPU
chunks.body:
### NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor / other ARM-with-GPU

CTranslate2's published wheels are x86_64-only. On an ARM box (Jetson AGX Thor, NVIDIA Grace Hopper, generic Orin), the OpenWebUI default `local` engine will return "CTranslate2 not compiled with CUDA support" because the wheel pip pulled is a CPU-only ARM build.

Fix one of:

1. **Build CTranslate2 from source with CUDA-arm64**. Heavy; needs the JetPack CUDA toolchain. See the [CTranslate2 build docs](https://opennmt.net/CTranslate2/installation.html#install-from-sources). Pin a known-working commit.
2. **Switch OpenWebUI's audio engine to `whisper.cpp`** in Settings → Audio. whisper.cpp has good ARM CUDA support and the daemon doesn't care which engine the server picks.
3. **Switch OpenWebUI's audio engine to `openai`** if you have a key — sends audio off-box, defeats local-GPU goal but unblocks transcription.
4. **Skip OpenWebUI entirely on Thor and use the local whisper venv directly** (`whisper.backend: whisper`). The Python venv's `whisper` package builds against PyTorch, which has native ARM-CUDA wheels; works without CTranslate2.

The daemon **fast-fails** on CTranslate2/CUDA/engine-not-loaded errors and falls through the chain to the local whisper venv (if configured), so voice keeps working even when the server engine is broken — you just don't get the bigger GPU. Look for this footer on the transcript:

```
_(transcribe: openai-compat (...) failed (...); fell back to local-whisper (...))_
```

When you see that footer, fix the OpenWebUI engine — the chain saves you in the meantime.

chunks.body:
### 4c. Recording overlay (v8.1.0)

When you tap the microphone icon the PWA shows a modal overlay rather
than an inline recording indicator:

- **Animated waveform** — five bars bounce with staggered timing,
  making it obvious the mic is live.
- **Cancel** — discards the recording and closes the overlay without
  sending anything.
- **Send** — stops recording immediately and submits audio for
  transcription exactly as before.

The overlay also closes (and discards) if you click outside it. This
is a PWA-only UX feature; the mobile app uses the OS native audio
recorder (see § 5a).

as session input — exactly as if you'd typed it.

```
(You send a voice note in Signal: "Refactor the payment module")
Bot: [transcribed] Refactor the payment module
Bot: <LLM's response>
```

If the transcription confidence is low (< 0.6), the bot replies with
the transcript + a `?` so you can correct it before it acts.

chunks.heading: Auto-fallback chain (v7.0.0+)
chunks.body:
## Auto-fallback chain (v7.0.0+)

When `whisper.backend` is HTTP-shape (`openai`, `openai_compat`, `openwebui`, `ollama`) **and** the local whisper venv is also installed, the daemon builds a **chained transcriber** at startup:

```
primary   = openai-compat (e.g. OpenWebUI)
secondary = local whisper venv      (last-resort)
```

What happens at runtime:

1. Browser-mic blob (webm/opus) arrives at `/api/voice/transcribe`.
2. Daemon transcodes to 16-kHz mono WAV via `ffmpeg` (must be on PATH).
3. POST to primary. On 503/504 retry with exponential backoff up to 4×.
4. On 404 (model not found), the openai-compat client tries a hardcoded chain of known whisper names (`whisper-1` → `whisper` → `large-v3` → … → `tiny`) before giving up.
5. On primary failure (or fast-fail signatures: `ctranslate2` / `cuda` / `engine-not` / `import-error`), fall through to the local whisper venv.
6. Result returns with a footer telling you which leg of the chain handled it.

You can see the chain wiring at startup:

```
[voice] enabled (backend=ollama, model=base, language=en)
[voice] fall-back: local whisper venv (~/.datawatch/venv, model=base) chained as last resort
```

Disable the auto-chain by leaving `whisper.venv_path` empty (only the primary path remains; failures bubble up).

## Startup preflight

The daemon actively probes the configured backend on startup by POSTing a 1-second silent WAV. Outcomes logged:

- Silent success — model is reachable + loaded.
- `preflight: HTTP 400 (...format/audio/file...)` — endpoint is reachable but rejected the synthetic probe; treated as success since real audio works fine.
- `preflight: model "X" not found` — runtime will use the fallback chain. Fix your `whisper.model` value.
- `preflight: HTTP 503/504` — server is loading the model; not an error.

chunks.title: How-to: Voice input
chunks.heading: Long recordings (longer than 30 s)
chunks.body:
## Long recordings (longer than 30 s)

Whisper is trained on 30 s windows, and some OpenAI-compatible backends
(windowed whisper.cpp / faster-whisper servers, duration-capping proxies)
refuse anything longer with HTTP 400. Since v9.5.32 this is handled
transparently: the daemon uploads the full recording first (correct for
full-length backends like OpenAI and OpenWebUI), and only if the backend
refuses does it split the audio locally into ≤30 s chunks — cutting at
near-silence points inside the last quarter of each window so words are
not split mid-syllable — transcribe each chunk in order, and join the
texts without duplication or loss. The split is deterministic for a
given input. If a chunk is still refused by the backend, the error is
surfaced (chunked retry never swallows a refusal).

**Upload size and time limits** (enforced by the daemon, in
`internal/server/voice.go` / `internal/transcribe/openai_compat.go`):

- **Upload size cap: 25 MB** — larger voice uploads are rejected with
  HTTP 413 (the Whisper API's own cap + headroom for a minute or more of
  16 kHz mono opus).
- **Server read timeout for voice uploads: 180 s** — covers a 25 MB
  body arriving over a slow link; a slow-but-valid upload still
  completes and transcribes.
- **Audio duration cap: configurable** — `max_audio_seconds` (default
  120 s) rejects longer files at intake; raise it for longer notes.
- **Transcription deadline: scales with the audio.** The request gets 5
  minutes, or twice the audio length when that is longer, capped at 30
  minutes. A clip whose length cannot be read gets the 5-minute base.
  The ffmpeg transcode has its own flat 5-minute budget. HTTP backends
  also retry 503/504 up to 4 times (1 s / 2 s backoff). There is no
  resumable upload, so either the full transcript comes back or the
  caller gets an error (see "When transcription fails" above).
- **PWA mic recordings:** Chrome's MediaRecorder emits webm with no
duration metadata; the handler's ffmpeg transcode to 16 kHz mono WAV
  handles arbitrarily long streams (verified with a 65 s
  MediaRecorder-style file).

chunks.heading: Long recordings and memory (local whisper)
chunks.body:
## Long recordings and memory (local whisper)

The local `whisper` backend loads the whole model and the whole clip into
memory for each run. A long recording on a small host can push the machine
into swap or get the whisper process killed. To keep memory flat, the
daemon splits long audio before it reaches whisper.

Audio longer than `whisper.chunk_seconds` (default **120**, `0` disables) is
split into slices of at most that length. Each slice is transcribed in turn
and the slice texts are joined with a single space, so you still get one
transcript back. Audio that already fits in one slice is sent as is.

How the split is done:

- **PCM WAV** is split in pure Go, with no external tool.
- **Any other format** (webm/opus from the browser microphone, ogg, m4a, mp3)
  is split with `ffmpeg`. If `ffmpeg` is not on PATH the split is skipped, the
  daemon logs `[voice] chunking skipped: ...; sending the whole file`, and the
  whole file goes to whisper in one piece. That still works for short clips
  but brings back the memory problem for long ones, so install `ffmpeg`.
- A slice that fails stops the whole request. The error names the slice, for
  example `slice 3 of 5 failed`, and the cause is classified as described below.

Chunking applies only to the local `whisper` backend, including when it is the
fallback leg of the chain described above. The HTTP backends (`openai`,
`openai_compat`, `openwebui`, `ollama`) ignore it.

`whisper.chunk_seconds` must be `0` or at least `30`, because whisper's own
window is 30 s. A value from 1 to 29 sent through the API is ignored and the
old value stays.

chunks.heading: Memory envelope
chunks.body:
### Memory envelope

Model size decides how much RAM a run needs. `medium` needs about 1.5 GiB for
the weights plus several GiB at peak while it decodes. `small` and `base`
need far less.

**A host with 8 GiB of RAM or less should use `small` or `base`.** On such a
host `medium` can get the whisper process killed by the kernel (cause
`killed`, below) once a long clip is under way. Shorter slices lower the
peak too, so on a tight host you can also lower `whisper.chunk_seconds`
(for example to 60); do not set it below 30.

chunks.heading: The five ways to set `whisper.chunk_seconds`
chunks.body:
### The five ways to set `whisper.chunk_seconds`

| Method | How |
|--------|-----|
| **YAML** | `~/.datawatch/config.yaml` → `whisper:` → `chunk_seconds: 120` |
| **CLI** | `datawatch config set whisper.chunk_seconds 120`, then `datawatch reload` |
| **Web UI** | Settings → General → **Voice Input (Whisper)** card → *Longest audio slice per local whisper run* |
| **REST API** | `PUT /api/config` with `{"whisper.chunk_seconds": 120}`; `GET /api/config` returns it under `whisper.chunk_seconds` |
| **Comm channel** | `configure whisper.chunk_seconds=120` |

The value is read when the daemon builds the transcriber, so reload (or
restart) after changing it. At startup the daemon logs
`[voice] chunking: local whisper slices audio longer than 120s` when it is on.
During a long request it logs `[voice] chunked: 5 slices of <=120s`.

chunks.title: How-to: Voice input
chunks.heading: When transcription fails: error causes
chunks.body:
### When transcription fails: error causes

`POST /api/voice/transcribe` no longer returns a bare error string. A failure
is HTTP 502 with a JSON body:

```json
{
  "error": "transcribe: the whisper process was killed by SIGKILL, usually the kernel out-of-memory killer",
  "cause": "killed",
  "hint": "Use a smaller whisper.model such as small or base, or lower whisper.chunk_seconds.",
  "detail": "whisper failed: signal: killed",
  "latency_ms": 41873
}
```

`cause` is one of these values. The PWA shows a plain-language message for
each; the table gives what it means and what to do.

| `cause` | What it means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `timeout` | The request ran past its deadline, or the client went away. The deadline is 5 minutes, or twice the audio length when that is longer, capped at 30 minutes. | Record a shorter clip, use a smaller `whisper.model`, or lower `whisper.chunk_seconds`. |
| `killed` | The whisper process ended by SIGKILL. On Linux this is almost always the kernel out-of-memory killer; `dmesg` shows `Out of memory: Killed process`. | Use `small` or `base`, lower `whisper.chunk_seconds`, or add RAM. |
| `out_of_memory` | Whisper itself reported it ran out of memory (a Python `MemoryError`, `Cannot allocate memory`, or a GPU out-of-memory message). | Same as `killed`. |
| `ffmpeg_missing` | `ffmpeg` is not installed or not on the daemon's PATH, and whisper needs it to read the audio. | `apt install ffmpeg` (or your package manager's equivalent), then retry. |
| `backend_error` | Any other non-zero exit, or an HTTP error from a remote backend. | Read `detail` and the `[voice] transcribe failed:` log line, fix the backend, retry. |
| `unknown` | The error matched nothing above. | Read the daemon log for the full error. |

`hint` is one sentence of advice for that cause and `detail` is the raw backend
error cut to 500 bytes. A recording over the upload limit is a separate case:
HTTP 413 before any transcription starts.

chunks.title: How-to: Voice input
chunks.heading: Reading the voice log lines
chunks.body:
### Reading the voice log lines

A failed request, and any request slower than 30 s even when it succeeds, writes
one line to the daemon log. The transcript text is never logged.

```
[voice] transcribe failed: backend=whisper bytes=1843201 audio_seconds=312.4 elapsed_ms=41873 cause=killed exit=killed err=whisper failed: signal: killed
[voice] transcribe slow: backend=whisper bytes=402112 audio_seconds=48.0 elapsed_ms=36120 cause=none exit=n/a err=
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `failed` / `slow` | `failed` means the request returned an error. `slow` means it succeeded but took longer than 30 s. |
| `backend` | The configured `whisper.backend`. |
| `bytes` | Size of the uploaded audio file. |
| `audio_seconds` | Length of the audio, or `unknown` when it could not be read (not a PCM WAV and no `ffprobe`). |
| `elapsed_ms` | Time spent in the transcriber only, not upload or ffmpeg transcode. |
| `cause` | One of the causes above, or `none` on a slow success. |
| `exit` | The whisper process exit status, the signal name (`killed`) when it was stopped by a signal, or `n/a` when there was no child process. |
| `ffmpeg=missing` | Present only when the transcode step could not find `ffmpeg`. |
| `err` | The first line of the error text. |

A rule of thumb: if `elapsed_ms` is much larger than `audio_seconds` times 1000,
the host is slower than realtime for this model and long clips will time out;
pick a smaller model.

chunks.heading: Failed recordings are kept in the PWA
chunks.body:
### Failed recordings are kept in the PWA

When a transcription fails in the PWA (the session input bar, any other
microphone-enabled text field, and the Test transcription button in Settings),
the audio is
**kept in the browser** and a notice appears beside the input with the message
for the cause, the line "Recording kept, nothing is lost.", and two buttons:

- **Retry transcription** sends the same recording again, without re-speaking.
  The button shows "Retrying transcription…" while it runs. If it fails again
  the notice stays and you can retry as many times as you like.
- **Discard recording** throws the audio away.

The recording stays until you press one of them. It is held in the page's memory,
so reloading or closing the tab loses it; retry before you leave. A retry after
fixing the cause on the daemon (for example installing `ffmpeg` or choosing a
smaller model and reloading) works with no new recording.

chunks.heading: Common pitfalls
chunks.body:
## Common pitfalls

- **Whisper venv path wrong.** `datawatch voice test` returns
  "venv not found"; fix `whisper.venv_path` and reload.
- **Wrong language detection.** Set `whisper.language` explicitly if
  `auto` keeps misclassifying.
- **`openai` backend without API key in secrets.** Will fail with
  401. Confirm with `datawatch secrets get OPENAI_API_KEY`.
- **Audio too long.** Default cap is 120s. Raise `max_audio_seconds`
  for longer notes. Recordings longer than 30 s are transcribed in ≤30 s
  chunks automatically now — see "Long recordings (longer than 30 s)"
  above — so a windowed backend is no longer a failure mode. Local whisper
  also slices at `whisper.chunk_seconds`; see "Long recordings and memory".
- **Whisper process killed or out of memory.** The error cause is `killed` or
  `out_of_memory`. Use `whisper.model` `small` or `base` on hosts with 8 GiB of
  RAM or less, or lower `whisper.chunk_seconds`.
- **PWA mic permission denied.** Browser blocks mic access on
  non-HTTPS origins. Use `https://` (the daemon's default) — not
  `http://` redirect.
- **OpenWebUI returns 400 "file format not supported".** Almost always actually masks a server-side engine error. Hit the endpoint with `curl` + your API key to see the real response. On ARM/Thor: it'll be the CTranslate2/CUDA error described in the OpenWebUI section above.
- **`ffmpeg` missing.** Daemon falls back to sending the original webm/opus blob to the primary; OpenWebUI usually rejects this. Install ffmpeg (`apt install ffmpeg`) so the WAV-transcode step runs. Without it,
  long non-WAV recordings also cannot be sliced, and a request whisper cannot read
  fails with cause `ffmpeg_missing`.

**Operator-directed 2026-05-10:** screenshots are NOT packaged with the
single-binary daemon. Embedded howto pages reference images from this

chunks.title: Howto screenshots — convention
chunks.heading: Add a screenshot
chunks.body: ## Add a screenshot 1. Drop the PNG into this directory (`docs/img/.png`). 2. Commit + push to `main`. The raw URL becomes: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmz006/datawatch/main/docs/img/.png` 3. Reference it in the howto markdown: ```markdown ![Caption that reads fine without the image](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmz006/datawatch/main/docs/img/.png) ``` The markdown→HTML pipeline (and the PWA's docs viewer) renders the above as `` — when the image fails to load (offline, GitHub blocked, or yet-uncommitted), the alt text shows in place. The surrounding caption already reads as full content.

chunks.title: Howto screenshots — convention
chunks.heading: Rules
chunks.body:
## Rules

- **No `embed.FS` of image files.** The Go embed list stays text-only
  (HTML / CSS / JS / JSON / Markdown).
- **Caption = the content.** Image is enrichment. The page must
  read fine without it.
- **No third-party hosts** (imgur, etc.). Screenshots live in this
  repo so they version with the docs.
- Refresh-only changes (replace image, keep filename + caption) need
  no daemon rebuild — push to GitHub and the reference resolves.
