chunks.title: Installing datawatch-stats on a remote Ollama / GPU host
chunks.body:
# Installing datawatch-stats on a remote Ollama / GPU host

This guide covers the **Shape B** standalone observer daemon — the
right deployment for an Ollama box, GPU inference host, or any node
that should report per-process stats to a primary datawatch without
running the full parent.

For the cluster sidecar (Shape C — DaemonSet, eBPF, DCGM scrape, k8s
metrics) see [`docs/api/observer.md#shape-c`](api/observer.md#shape-c)
and the Helm chart's `observer.shapeC.*` values.

chunks.title: Installing datawatch-stats on a remote Ollama / GPU host
chunks.heading: Two install paths
chunks.body:
## Two install paths

1. **Static binary on the host** — fastest, smallest footprint.
2. **Docker container** — easier for operators who already manage
   everything via compose / portainer.

Both paths push to the same `/api/observer/peers/{name}/stats`
endpoint; the parent doesn't care which you pick.

**Which path if Ollama itself is in Docker?** Use **Path 2 (Docker)** —
ride the same compose / pod as Ollama so they share lifecycle + network
namespace + restart policy. Sidecar pattern: one healthcheck, one
update path, one place to look in `docker ps`. The static-binary path
adds a host-OS dependency you've already containerized away.

---

chunks.title: Installing datawatch-stats on a remote Ollama / GPU host
chunks.heading: Path 1 — Static binary + systemd
chunks.body: ## Path 1 — Static binary + systemd

chunks.title: Installing datawatch-stats on a remote Ollama / GPU host
chunks.heading: 1. Download the binary
chunks.body:
### 1. Download the binary

```bash
OS=$(uname -s | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')   # linux | darwin
ARCH=$(uname -m | sed 's/x86_64/amd64/;s/aarch64/arm64/')

# Resolve the latest release tag from GitHub (no jq required).
VER=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/dmz006/datawatch/releases/latest \
        | grep -oE '"tag_name":\s*"[^"]+"' | head -1 | cut -d'"' -f4)
echo "Installing datawatch-stats $VER"

curl -L -o /tmp/datawatch-stats \
  "https://github.com/dmz006/datawatch/releases/download/${VER}/datawatch-stats-${OS}-${ARCH}"
# /tmp is often mounted noexec, so move to the final dest first, then chmod.
sudo mv /tmp/datawatch-stats /usr/local/bin/
sudo chmod +x /usr/local/bin/datawatch-stats
datawatch-stats --version
```

To pin a specific release instead, set `VER=v6.16.0` (or any other tag) before running `curl`.

chunks.title: Installing datawatch-stats on a remote Ollama / GPU host
chunks.heading: 2. Register the peer with your primary datawatch
chunks.body:
### 2. Register the peer with your primary datawatch

This mints a bearer token. The token is returned **once**; capture it
into the unit-file env or a config file before continuing.

```bash
# Option A — from any host with curl and the parent reachable:
curl -k -X POST https://primary:8443/api/observer/peers \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"ollama-box","shape":"B"}'
# → {"name":"ollama-box","shape":"B","token":"…long-base64…"}

# Option B — if you have the primary's CLI installed somewhere:
datawatch observer peer register ollama-box B "$(uname -r)"

# Option C — over chat (Signal / Telegram, after BL172 v4.5.1):
peers register ollama-box B
```

chunks.title: Installing datawatch-stats on a remote Ollama / GPU host
chunks.heading: 3. Persist the token
chunks.body:
### 3. Persist the token

The state directory must be owned by the user the systemd unit
runs as (default `datawatch`). Order matters: create → chown → chmod
→ write the token (so the file inherits the right owner).

```bash
# Create the system user if it doesn't exist:
id datawatch || sudo useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin datawatch

# Create + own + lock the state dir:
sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/datawatch-stats
sudo chown -R datawatch:datawatch /var/lib/datawatch-stats
sudo chmod 700 /var/lib/datawatch-stats

# Write the token AS the datawatch user so it inherits the right owner:
echo "<token-from-step-2>" | sudo -u datawatch tee /var/lib/datawatch-stats/peer.token
sudo chmod 0600 /var/lib/datawatch-stats/peer.token
```

chunks.title: Installing datawatch-stats on a remote Ollama / GPU host
chunks.heading: 4. Drop the systemd unit + start
chunks.body:
### 4. Drop the systemd unit + start

```bash
# Pull the unit file from the release source tree:
curl -L -o /tmp/datawatch-stats.service \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dmz006/datawatch/main/deploy/systemd/datawatch-stats.service
sudo mv /tmp/datawatch-stats.service /etc/systemd/system/

# Edit the Environment lines to point at YOUR primary + name:
sudoedit /etc/systemd/system/datawatch-stats.service
#   Environment="DATAWATCH_PARENT=https://primary:8443"
#   Environment="DATAWATCH_PEER_NAME=ollama-box"

# Tell the unit where to read the token:
sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/datawatch-stats.service.d
cat <<'EOF' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/datawatch-stats.service.d/token.conf
[Service]
ExecStart=
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/datawatch-stats \
    --datawatch ${DATAWATCH_PARENT} \
    --name     ${DATAWATCH_PEER_NAME} \
    --token-file /var/lib/datawatch-stats/peer.token \
    --push-interval 5s \
    --listen 127.0.0.1:9001
EOF

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now datawatch-stats
sudo systemctl status datawatch-stats --no-pager | head -20
```

chunks.title: Installing datawatch-stats on a remote Ollama / GPU host
chunks.heading: 5. Verify the round-trip
chunks.body:
### 5. Verify the round-trip

From the primary datawatch:

```bash
curl -ks https://primary:8443/api/observer/peers \
  | jq '.peers[] | select(.name=="ollama-box") | {last_push_at, version, host_info}'

# Or in the PWA: Settings → Monitor → Federated peers
# Or over chat: peers ollama-box stats
```

A green health dot + recent `last_push_at` means it's working.

chunks.title: Installing datawatch-stats on a remote Ollama / GPU host
chunks.heading: 6. (Optional) Enable per-process eBPF net
chunks.body:
### 6. (Optional) Enable per-process eBPF net

Runs cleanly on Linux ≥ 5.10 with `CAP_BPF` + `CAP_PERFMON`. The
unit file ships with `AmbientCapabilities` commented out (least
privilege by default); the setup helper edits the drop-in for you:

```bash
sudo datawatch setup ebpf --target stats
sudo systemctl restart datawatch-stats
# Verify host.ebpf.kprobes_loaded=true on the next push:
curl -ks https://primary:8443/api/observer/peers/ollama-box/stats | jq .host.ebpf
```

---

chunks.title: Installing datawatch-stats on a remote Ollama / GPU host
chunks.heading: Path 2 — Docker container
chunks.body:
## Path 2 — Docker container

Docker doesn't need the systemd unit; the binary is the entrypoint.

```bash
# Pull the matching binary into a slim base. (No prebuilt image is
# published for Shape B today — Shape C ships as ghcr.io/dmz006/
# datawatch-stats-cluster but it's distroless + privileged. For
# Shape B a plain alpine wrapper is enough.)

# Resolve latest release tag (or override VER on the buildx command).
VER=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/dmz006/datawatch/releases/latest \
        | grep -oE '"tag_name":\s*"[^"]+"' | head -1 | cut -d'"' -f4)

cat > Dockerfile.stats <<EOF
FROM alpine:3.20
RUN apk add --no-cache ca-certificates curl tzdata
ARG TARGETARCH
ARG VER=${VER}
RUN curl -L -o /usr/local/bin/datawatch-stats \\
      "https://github.com/dmz006/datawatch/releases/download/\${VER}/datawatch-stats-linux-\${TARGETARCH}" \\
    && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/datawatch-stats
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/datawatch-stats"]
EOF

docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
    --build-arg VER=${VER} \
    -f Dockerfile.stats -t local/datawatch-stats:${VER} .
```

Or skip the buildx + run the host binary inside a one-off container:

```bash
TOKEN=$(cat /var/lib/datawatch-stats/peer.token)
docker run -d --name datawatch-stats \
  --restart unless-stopped \
  --network host \
  -v /var/lib/datawatch-stats:/data:ro \
  -v /proc:/host/proc:ro \
  -v /sys:/sys:ro \
  -e DATAWATCH_PARENT=https://primary:8443 \
  local/datawatch-stats:${VER} \
    --datawatch ${DATAWATCH_PARENT} \
    --name ollama-box-docker \
    --token-file /data/peer.token \
    --insecure-tls \
    --push-interval 5s
```

`--network host` is needed so the daemon's `/proc` walk + GPU
detection see the host (not the container) namespace. `/proc` and
`/sys` mounts are read-only and only used for the observer's
collector.

For per-process eBPF inside Docker, add:
```
--cap-add BPF --cap-add PERFMON
```

---

chunks.title: Installing datawatch-stats on a remote Ollama / GPU host
chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.body:
## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Peer never appears in `peers` list | Token file missing / wrong | re-run step 2 + 3; check `journalctl -u datawatch-stats` |
| `last_push_at` stuck in the past | Network blocked or parent down | curl the parent from the box; check firewall |
| `host.ebpf.kprobes_loaded: false` after `setup ebpf --target stats` | Kernel < 5.10 or missing BTF | accept /proc-only mode; document kernel rev |
| Push fails with 401 every tick | Token rotated on parent | peer auto-re-registers if writable token file; otherwise re-seed |
| TLS verify error against self-signed parent | No CA trust | `--insecure-tls` flag (dev only) |

chunks.heading: Datawatch features that USE Ollama (and what happens without it)
chunks.body:
## Datawatch features that USE Ollama (and what happens without it)

**Hard rule:** datawatch never *requires* Ollama. Every feature listed below
has a documented degraded-mode fallback when `cfg.Ollama.Host` is empty
or the host is unreachable. Operators on a no-GPU box stay fully functional;
only the GPU-accelerated path opts into Ollama.

| Feature | Ollama endpoint hit | What GPU buys you | Degraded mode (no Ollama / unreachable) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Memory embedder** (`internal/memory`) | `/api/embeddings` (model: `cfg.Memory.embedder_model`, default `nomic-embed-text`) | 100-1000× faster batch embed of session output → richer cross-session recall | Embedder skipped; memory recall uses keyword + recency only. No errors. |
| **BL274 vector index** (`internal/docsindex/vector.go`) | Same embedder as above (reused) | Sub-100ms semantic docs_search across the corpus | Falls back to BM25 (`internal/docsindex/bm25.go`) — keyword search keeps every operator surface working. The fallback is the test harness for the rule. |
| **`/api/ask` endpoint** (`internal/server/ask.go`, BL34) | `/api/generate` (model: `cfg.Ollama.Model`) | Single-shot LLM Q&A from the chat surface; instant answers without spawning a session | Returns `503 ollama not configured` with clear remediation. PWA hides the card; CLI `datawatch ask` errors with the same text. OpenWebUI is the documented alternate backend. |
| **BL274 Sprint 4 LLM-translation fallback** (`internal/server/docs_translator.go`) | Same `/api/generate` as `ask` | Translates non-curated howto prose into MCP-call sequences | `LLMTranslator` is nil; `docs_apply` against an unauthored howto returns `501` with explicit message. Curated howtos (22/22 today) work without Ollama. |
| **Council Mode synthesis** (`internal/council`) | `/api/generate` (model from council config) | Multi-persona debate synthesis | Returns each persona's raw output; synthesis step skipped, operator reviews manually. |
| **Eval llm_rubric grader** (`internal/evals/graders`) | `/api/generate` per grading rule | Auto-scores LLM output against rubric | Grader marked `skipped`; suite still runs the deterministic rules (regex/contains/etc.) |
| **Autonomous decompose** (`internal/autonomous`) | `/api/generate` | Splits a PRD into stories | Returns 503 with explicit message; operator decomposes manually or switches PRD backend to claude-code/openwebui. |

**Sidecar pattern.** All seven features read `cfg.Ollama.Host` — set it once
in `~/.datawatch/config.yaml` and every feature follows. Pointing
multiple datawatch hosts at one shared Ollama box (e.g. dedicated GPU
on Tailscale) is the recommended deployment.

**Verify the rule.** `bash scripts/release-smoke.sh` runs against the
local daemon with whatever Ollama config you have. To verify the
no-GPU path: `unset` the Ollama host, restart, run the smoke — it
must still pass (BL274 vector layer, /api/ask fail-soft, etc. all
have fallbacks).

chunks.title: Installing datawatch-stats on a remote Ollama / GPU host
chunks.heading: Model host settings for datawatch builds
chunks.body:
## Model host settings for datawatch builds

A host that serves local models to datawatch (planning, execution, verification) needs a
64k context and resident models. Add a systemd drop-in, for example
`/etc/systemd/system/ollama.service.d/64k.conf`:

```
[Service]
Environment="OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=65536"
Environment="OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1"
```

Then `sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart ollama`. Keep one large model
per node. Do not set `OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS=1`, because small helper models would evict
the large one. Other tools that share the host (web UIs, scheduled jobs) can load their own
models; plan for that. Restarting Ollama interrupts running sessions on the host, so do it
between runs. Details: `docs/plans/2026-10-18-model-host-requirements.md`.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.body:
# LLM Backends

datawatch supports multiple AI coding backends. The active backend is selected via
`session.llm_backend`. Each backend runs inside a tmux session so you can attach and
interact with it directly.

---

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Selecting a Backend
chunks.body:
## Selecting a Backend

| Method | How |
|--------|-----|
| **YAML** | `session.llm_backend: claude-code` in `~/.datawatch/config.yaml` |
| **CLI** | `datawatch setup llm` (interactive wizard) |
| **Web UI** | Settings tab → General → **Datawatch** card → Default LLM backend dropdown |
| **REST API** | `PUT /api/config` with `{"session.llm_backend": "aider"}` |
| **Comm channel** | `configure session.llm_backend=aider` |

Per-backend settings (binary path, console size, output/input mode) are configurable via:
- **Web UI**: Settings tab → **LLM** tab → click any backend to expand its config popup
- **REST API**: `PUT /api/config` with e.g. `{"aider.binary": "/usr/local/bin/aider"}`
- **Comm channel**: `configure aider.binary=/usr/local/bin/aider`

Available backends: `claude-code`, `aider`, `goose`, `gemini`, `opencode`, `opencode-acp`, `opencode-prompt`, `ollama`, `openwebui`, `shell`

---

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Backend Comparison
chunks.body:
## Backend Comparison

> Interactive input here means: while a session is running, the operator
> can reply via `send <id>: <text>` (CLI / chat / MCP) or the PWA input
> bar, and the backend picks the message up. Backends marked **No** run
> a single non-interactive task and exit; you control them via
> scheduled commands and output filters instead. Some backends ship
> **two variants** (regular task launcher *and* an interactive
> chat/conversation mode); the table flags both.

| Backend | Name | Interactive input | External service | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `claude-code` | **Yes** | Anthropic API | Default; agentic coding loop. Channel mode (MCP bridge) wires structured tool callbacks + permission relay. |
| Shell | `shell` | **Yes** | Custom command | Bring-your-own; tmux pane stays attached so anything that reads stdin works. |
| opencode-acp | `opencode-acp` | **Yes** | Configurable (anthropic / openai / others via opencode) | opencode driven over the Agent Coding Protocol (HTTP/SSE). Thinking + structured replies render in the chat panel. |
| OpenWebUI (chat) | `openwebui` (chat mode) | **Yes** | OpenWebUI instance | The `InteractiveBackend` variant uses the OpenAI-compatible chat completions API; pure Go, no tmux. Picked when you start a session with the chat input mode. |
| Ollama (chat) | `ollama` (chat mode) | **Yes** | Local Ollama server | `LaunchChat` mode streams replies into the PWA chat panel; tmux not used. Fully local, no API key. |
| aider | `aider` | No | Configurable (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) | Single-shot batch task; finishes when the prompt completes. Use schedules + filters for follow-ups. |
| goose | `goose` | No | Configurable | Block's open-source agent. Single-shot. |
| Gemini CLI | `gemini` | No | Google AI | Google's official CLI. Single-shot. |
| opencode | `opencode` (TUI mode) | No | Configurable | SST's TUI agent run inside tmux. The interactive variant is **opencode-acp** (above). |
| OpenWebUI (task) | `openwebui` (default) | No | OpenWebUI instance | Default `Backend` variant runs a single-shot OpenAI-compatible completion. |
| Ollama (task) | `ollama` (default) | No | Local Ollama server | Default `Backend` variant runs a single-shot completion. |

---

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Command and Filter Support
chunks.body:
## Command and Filter Support

datawatch's saved command library and output filter engine work with any LLM backend.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Saved Commands
chunks.body:
### Saved Commands

Named commands from the library (`datawatch cmd add <name> <text>`) can be:
- Sent via any messaging backend: `send <id>: approve` (where `approve` is a saved command)
- Scheduled: `datawatch session schedule add <id> approve`
- Applied automatically via output filters

Seed useful defaults with `datawatch seed`:

| Name | Value | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| `approve` | `yes` | Approve a permission or prompt |
| `reject` | `no` | Decline a prompt |
| `enter` | `\n` | Send a blank Enter |
| `continue` | `continue` | Resume a paused session |
| `skip` | `skip` | Skip current step |
| `abort` | `Ctrl-C` | Interrupt the running session |

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Output Filters
chunks.body:
### Output Filters

Output filters (`datawatch cmd filter add`) watch session output for regex patterns and trigger actions automatically. Useful for hands-free operation:

| Filter trigger | Suggested action | Example pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Permission dialog | `alert` | `Do you want to proceed\?` |
| Rate limit hit | `alert` | `rate.limit` |
| Task complete | `alert` | `(All done|DATAWATCH_COMPLETE)` |
| Recurring prompt | `schedule approve` | `Overwrite existing file\?` |

Filters are configured per backend but apply to all sessions regardless of which LLM runs them.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Interactive Input Support
chunks.body:
### Interactive Input Support

Five backends accept interactive input from datawatch (the
`send <id>: <msg>` command, the PWA input bar, and chat / Signal /
Telegram replies):

- **`claude-code`** — full agentic loop, plus channel mode for
  structured tool callbacks.
- **`shell`** — anything you can drive over stdin in a tmux pane.
- **`opencode-acp`** — opencode over the Agent Coding Protocol,
  with thinking blocks rendered in the chat panel.
- **`openwebui` (chat mode)** — `InteractiveBackend` variant using
  the OpenAI-compatible chat completions API.
- **`ollama` (chat mode)** — `LaunchChat` variant streaming replies
  into the PWA chat panel.

The other backends (`aider`, `goose`, `gemini`, `opencode` TUI,
`openwebui` default, `ollama` default) run a single non-interactive
task and exit when complete. For these:

- The session moves to `complete` or `failed` when the process exits
- Output filters and scheduled commands still fire normally
- You can still view output with `status <id>` and `tail <id> [n]`

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: One-shot (`one_shot`) sessions
chunks.body:
### One-shot (`one_shot`) sessions

All backends named `*-prompt` (`pi-prompt`, `goose-prompt`, `opencode-prompt`, …)
are one-shot: the `one_shot` flag is recorded on the session at creation, even
when the session is started by hand (PWA, REST, MCP) without a `one_shot` field
in the request. Interactive backends (`claude-code`, `pi`, `aider`, `goose` TUI,
`gemini`, `opencode`, `opencode-acp`, `shell`, chat-mode backends) are **not**
flagged one-shot by default — `one_shot` only appears if a start request
explicitly asks for it. The decision is made once, at session creation; existing
session records are never rewritten retroactively.

The PWA session list and detail views do not read the `one_shot` flag on a
session: input boxes, reply prompts, and waiting-for-input affordances are
offered only while the session is in a running or waiting state, so a finished
prompt-style session renders as any other completed session (state badge,
output viewable, no input affordances).

---

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Model/backend pairing
chunks.body:
## Model/backend pairing

A model name must be one the chosen backend can serve. datawatch checks each
model against its backend when the model is set, and refuses a mismatched
pair. The refusal names the model and the backend.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: The pairing rule
chunks.body:
### The pairing rule

- A bare Claude alias such as `claude-haiku-5-5` is refused on the `pi` and
  `pi-prompt` backends. pi resolves a bare alias across providers and exits
  with no output. Use a provider-qualified name such as
  `anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5` on pi, or use the `claude-code` backend with a
  bare name.
- A provider-tagged model such as `ollama/qwen3.8:27b` is refused on
  `claude-code`, which takes only bare Claude model names. Use a bare name on
  `claude-code`.

The check runs when a PRD, story, task, or verification or guardrail model is
set. It applies to REST, MCP, and the comm channel alike. A refused set leaves
the record unchanged; REST returns `400` with the mismatch text, and MCP returns
a tool error.

The check runs again before a PRD runs. A PRD that contains a mismatched task is
not started, and the error names each offending task. This means records written
before the check existed are also refused, instead of spawning a session that
exits with no output.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: pi-prompt failure marker
chunks.body:
### pi-prompt failure marker

On the `pi-prompt` backend, a run that fails no longer reports success. A
non-zero exit from pi, or a run that produces no output, prints
`DATAWATCH_PI_FAILED` and does not print `DATAWATCH_COMPLETE`. The failure line
names the exit status and the model, for example:

```
DATAWATCH_PI_FAILED: pi exited with status 3 (model ollama/qwen3.8:27b)
DATAWATCH_PI_FAILED: pi produced no output
```

When you see `DATAWATCH_PI_FAILED`, check these two things:

1. **The model name.** Confirm it is provider-qualified (`provider/model`) and
   matches the `pi_prompt.model` setting, or the model set on the PRD, story,
   or task.
2. **The pi provider.** Run `pi` by hand in the project directory with the same
   model. Confirm the provider is configured (`pi auth`, or pi's
   `~/.pi/agent/models.json`) and that its endpoint is reachable. For Ollama,
   check that the server is running and has the model pulled.

Fix the cause, then run the task again.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Judge and planning model resolution (Automata)
chunks.body:
## Judge and planning model resolution (Automata)

Every guardrail **judge** session and every decompose (planning) session
launched by the autonomous runner must carry a model **you configured**.
datawatch never falls back to `pi`'s — or any other backend's — built-in
default model for these sessions: a judge running on an unpinned model would
evict the model you pinned on the node, and a decompose session would spend
its whole run on a model you may not want or pay for.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Guardrail judge resolution order
chunks.body:
### Guardrail judge resolution order

Every guardrail judge — `rules-review`, `ci-watch`, the per-task and
per-story guardrail verdicts (what the verify step judges), and the rejudge
action — resolves its model through a single resolver with a five-tier
precedence chain. The first tier that is set **and** that the judge's
backend can serve wins:

| Tier | Source | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | PRD `guardrail_model` | the Automaton's own guardrail judge pin |
| 2 | task `guardrail_model` | the override on the specific task being judged |
| 3 | `autonomous.guardrail_model` | the global guardrail judge model |
| 4 | `autonomous.verification_model` | the global verification model |
| 5 | `autonomous.planning_model` | the global planning model |

Tiers 1–2 are explicit pins for the resolved judge backend.
Tiers 3–5 are global defaults configured for the global pi-family backend;
when a judge resolves to the `claude-code` backend they are skipped (they
are pi-style model names that backend would reject), and only the explicit
PRD/task pins may win. Every tier is validated against the judge's resolved
backend with the [pairing rule](#the-pairing-rule) above — a provider-tagged
model is refused on `claude-code`, a bare Claude alias is refused on `pi`
and `pi-prompt` — so a tier that the backend cannot serve is skipped with a
recorded reason, never launched.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Loud failure when no tier resolves
chunks.body:
### Loud failure when no tier resolves

If no tier yields a model the backend can serve — either nothing is
configured, or every configured tier is unpairable for the judge's backend —
the judge is **not launched at all**. The guardrail record gets a loud,
non-retried infrastructure-category block instead, and the message names
exactly which keys to set:

- the PRD's `guardrail_model` pin, or
- the task's `guardrail_model` override, or
- `autonomous.guardrail_model`, or
- `autonomous.verification_model`, or
- `autonomous.planning_model`.

`pi`'s built-in default model is never used, and the model handed to `pi`
is never empty. The guardrail model setters (`set_prd_guardrail_llm` /
`set_task_guardrail_llm`, on REST, MCP and the comm channel) validate the
model/backend pair — and, when a model is pinned, the full resolution —
before accepting the change, so a pin that would leave the unit with no
resolvable model is refused at set time rather than failing at judge time.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Decompose (planning) sessions
chunks.body:
### Decompose (planning) sessions

Decompose sessions follow the same no-built-in-default rule. Their model
resolves as the PRD's `decomposition_model`, then `autonomous.planning_model`
(when it belongs to the resolved planning backend), then the PRD's own
model, then `autonomous.verification_model` — with each tier checked against
the resolved backend. When no tier resolves and the backend is pi-family,
the decompose attempt fails immediately (without consuming infrastructure
retry budget) with a message naming the same set of keys. A decompose
session is therefore never launched on the backend's built-in default.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Coverage
chunks.body:
### Coverage

This rule covers the `rules-review` judgment, the `ci-watch` guardrail, the
per-task and per-story guardrail verdicts, the rejudge action, and the
decompose (planning) session. The verifier's own model is a separate pin
(task → story → PRD → `autonomous.verification_model`), but a guardrail
judge that cannot resolve one of the tiers above always fails loudly
rather than borrowing the backend default.

---

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: claude-code (default)
chunks.body:
## claude-code (default)

**Name:** `claude-code`

Anthropic's official Claude Code CLI. This is the default backend. It supports full
interactive input — datawatch can detect when claude-code is waiting for your response
and route replies from your messaging app or MCP client directly to it.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.body:
### Prerequisites

- `claude` CLI installed and authenticated (`claude auth login`)
- Anthropic API access

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Installation
chunks.body:
### Installation

```bash
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
# or follow https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code
```

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Configuration
chunks.body:
### Configuration

```yaml
session:
  llm_backend: claude-code
  claude_code_bin: claude          # path to the claude binary; default: "claude" (claude-code only)
```

When claude-code outputs a prompt ending with `?`, `[y/N]`, `>`, or similar patterns,
datawatch marks the session as `waiting_input` and notifies you via your messaging
backend. Reply with `send <id>: <your answer>` to route input back to the session.

chunks.heading: Channel mode (MCP channel)
chunks.body:
### Channel mode (MCP channel)

claude-code supports an optional MCP channel (`channel_enabled: true`) that adds a
second, structured communication path alongside the tmux console. Tool output and
Claude's replies flow over the channel as clean text; folder-trust and consent prompts
still require console interaction.

See [docs/claude-channel.md](claude-channel.md) for a full breakdown of what is

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Session naming
chunks.body:
### Session naming

When a datawatch session has a name (set in the New Session form or via API), Claude is
launched with `--name <session-name>`. This tags the Claude conversation for easy
identification in Claude's `/resume` picker.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Session resume
chunks.body:
### Session resume

claude-code stores conversation history keyed by a session ID. To resume a previous
conversation, select it from the **Resume previous session** dropdown in the New Session
form (web UI), or pass it via API. The session is launched with `--resume <ID>`.

The web UI **Restart** button automatically pre-fills the form with the finished
session's details (name, task, directory, backend) and selects it in the resume dropdown.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Rate limit detection
chunks.body:
### Rate limit detection

claude-code is the only backend with captured throttle lines. The built-in
phrases are the usage-limit lines of its own limit messages and usage dialog
(the hard-limit lines, the extra-usage line, the approaching-limit warning, the
reset-time announcements and the stop-and-wait menu option). Every one is
recorded verbatim, with its in-tree source, in the fixtures under
`testdata/rate_limit_lines/` and the directory README.

Before a line is matched, the detector trims surrounding whitespace and
lowercases it, and strips ANSI cursor escapes it would otherwise misread; all
matches are line-start anchored, so a line that merely quotes one of these
phrases inside ordinary output does not match. The `⎿` gutter glyph plus two
spaces that claude-code prints before secondary lines, and the numbered menu
rows of its usage dialog (with or without the `❯` cursor), are tolerated as
that family's own prefixes. Table phrases are only checked on lines under 2048
characters; the shared protocol line is not subject to that length gate.

On top of the tool's own lines, the session carries two plain protocol lines
the detector recognizes line-start on every backend: `DATAWATCH_RATE_LIMITED:`
when the session reports a throttle (claude-code also writes `PAUSED.md` with
a progress summary while paused), and `DATAWATCH_COMPLETE:` when it finishes.
A rate-limited claude-code session is held in a paused `rate_limited` state and
resumed on retry, not failed — it still completes normally.

If you set `detection.rate_limit_patterns`, your list replaces these built-in
matches and is applied as before: a flat substring, anywhere on the line, for
all backends.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Which node a pi worker uses
chunks.body:
### Which node a pi worker uses

A pi or pi-prompt worker runs on the compute node its capacity lease holds.
When the node is known, the daemon points pi at that node for the launch. The
node is the one the entry's pool chose, or the entry's only node (see
[Compute-node pools and slots](howto/automata-capacity.md#compute-node-pools-and-slots)).

- The daemon writes a per-session pi configuration directory. Every entry of
  the source directory is linked into it, so credentials and sessions stay the
  source's own. Only `models.json` is rewritten: the `baseUrl` of the model's
  provider becomes the node's address with `/v1` appended. An address with no
  `http://` or `https://` scheme gets `http://` first.
- The launch command sets `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` to that directory for the pi
  process alone. The directory is removed when pi exits, or at once when the
  launch fails.
- The source directory is the daemon's own `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` when that is
  set, otherwise `~/.pi/agent`. Every other provider keeps the value the source
  wrote.
- A session keeps the node address it started on, so a resume reuses the same
  host.

A queued request picks its node again on each admission pass and whenever any
node frees an engine. A waiting request therefore moves to a node with a free
engine, least loaded first and then by node priority, rather than staying on the
node it first tried. A change to an LLM entry's `compute_nodes` list reaches
waiting work without a daemon restart. The limit of one engine per node still
applies.

The entry's `compute_nodes` list decides which nodes a local-model worker,
verifier and judge may run on. Each listed node that is known and serves the
model is a candidate. The request goes to the least loaded candidate;
`scheduling_priority` only breaks a tie, then list order. A node that does not
serve the model is skipped, and a one-entry list behaves as before.

The provider is the part of the model name before the first `/`; for
`ollama/qwen3.8:27b` it is `ollama`. The launch fails with an error, and nothing
starts, when the model has no provider prefix, or when the source `models.json`
has no entry for that provider or the entry is not a full provider object. A
bare `baseUrl` is not enough: pi needs the entry's api, key and models. A node
with an empty address gets no override at all.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: When a worker connects to the wrong host
chunks.body:
#### When a worker connects to the wrong host

Check these in order:

1. **The node it holds.** `datawatch capacity` prints the node beside each
   holder when the pool spans two or more nodes. If that node is not the one
   you expect, the problem is placement, not pi. See
   [automata capacity](howto/automata-capacity.md).
2. **The node's address.** `datawatch compute node get <name>` must show the
   address the daemon can reach. An empty address means no override, and pi
   uses its own provider table, which is usually the local host.
3. **The provider entry.** The model must be written `<provider>/<model>`, and
   that provider must be a full entry in the source `models.json`. Look at the
   source the daemon reads: its own `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR`, or `~/.pi/agent`. A
   daemon started by a service manager may not have the variable you set in an
   interactive shell.
4. **The node answers at the override address.** The provider's `baseUrl` is
   `<address>/v1`. The node must answer there; an Ollama node serves its model
   list at `/v1/models`, so `curl http://<address>/v1/models` should list the
   models it holds.
5. **The directory was not left behind.** The per-session directory is removed
   when pi exits, so check the source table and the node address rather than
   looking for the directory.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Notes
chunks.body:
### Notes

- `pi` backend is interactive (real TUI, stays open for follow-up input);
  `pi-prompt` is one-shot (`--print`), blocks until pi is genuinely done,
  then exits — same low-risk, no-async-completion-signal shape as `aider`.
- Session resume on the `pi` backend uses pi's own `--session-id`, which
  both creates and resumes a session by an arbitrary caller-supplied ID —
  unlike opencode's own ID format, no translation is needed between
  datawatch's session IDs and pi's.
- A third variant analogous to `opencode-acp` (pi's own `--mode rpc`) is
  planned but not yet implemented — see
  `docs/plans/2026-10-16-pi-opencode-evaluation.md`. Building it now would
  reintroduce the async completion-detection race class that `opencode-acp`
  had to fix when it was added.
- Known upstream caveat: pi issue [#9216](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/9216)
  describes Ollama + `qwen3.8:27b` stream-termination errors under heavy
  tool use — confirmed on datawatch's own exact model/stack. Live-tested
  tasks (3- and 4-tool-call chains, both one-shot and via a standalone
  smoke test with a real git commit) completed cleanly; a full multi-task
  PRD pilot under sustained heavy tool use has not yet been run.

chunks.body:

There is no captured pi throttle line in `testdata/rate_limit_lines/` — no

built-in detection for `pi` and `pi-prompt` is the shared `DATAWATCH_RATE_LIMITED:`
protocol line the session itself prints, matched line-start after trimming.
An operator-configured `detection.rate_limit_patterns` (flat substring, all
backends) is the escape hatch if pi starts printing a specific throttle line.

chunks.heading: Model Selection (v8.7.0)

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: SSE stalls on local models (B89)
chunks.body:
#### SSE stalls on local models (B89)

Large local models (30B+ params, or "thinking"/reasoning-enabled models like qwen3) can go several minutes with zero streamed output — either loading into VRAM on a cold start (`headerTimeout`) or reasoning silently before the first output token (`chunkTimeout`). OpenCode's own defaults for both are 300s (5 min), which is routinely too short: a stalled request aborts client-side and opencode prints `SSE read timed out` (or `SSE error` / `provider response headers`, depending on which timeout tripped and the opencode/ai-sdk version) into the TUI, then sits idle forever waiting for output that will never arrive because the underlying HTTP request is already dead.

Two layers of defense:

1. **Prevention** — `opencode.ollama_chunk_timeout_sec` / `opencode.ollama_header_timeout_sec` (config-accessible via YAML/REST/MCP/comm/PWA per the Configuration Accessibility Rule) raise opencode's own timeouts past the pauses observed on locally-hosted models, so the request doesn't get killed in the first place.
2. **Detection fallback** — the autonomous PRD executor's built-in stall detectors (`cmd/datawatch/sse_stall.go`): the verifier wait loop scans one-shot opencode session scrollback every ~30s and the automata watchdog every 60s, both through the one shared scan in that file. The scan applies only to the opencode family (decided from the session's backend — claude-code, pi, openwebui, ollama and the rest are never scanned for this and keep their own silence and activity detectors), and counts only a line that IS a known provider error as opencode prints it: a short line beginning with the phrase (optionally after an `Error:` or `AI_APICallError:` prefix), compared case-insensitively, that is new relative to the session's previous scan, and not inside a tool result or code block. On a match the session is ended so the executor's retry path fires (e.g. a genuine network/provider outage), with the matched line, the backend family and the scan source (verifier wait loop or automata watchdog) recorded in the end reason. If opencode ever prints a stall message not on the list, it will not be caught automatically — check `docs/plans/README.md` for the current bug if you hit this.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Language Server Protocol — LSP (v8.7.0)
chunks.body:
### Language Server Protocol — LSP (v8.7.0)

LSP gives OpenCode real-time language intelligence: type errors, completions, and diagnostics from the language server installed on your host. This is especially valuable when working with LLMs whose training data predates the current version of a library or language.

**How it works:**
1. Select the programming language in the **New Session** form (Go, TypeScript, Python, Rust, C++)
2. Datawatch writes `<projectDir>/opencode.json` with the server config at session start
3. OpenCode launches the configured LSP binary and uses its output during the session

**Prerequisites:** The language server binary must be installed:
```bash
go install golang.org/x/tools/gopls@latest          # Go
npm install -g typescript-language-server typescript  # TypeScript/JS
pip install pyright                                  # Python
rustup component add rust-analyzer                   # Rust
# clangd ships with clang-tools on most distros      # C/C++
```

**Daemon config** (`~/.datawatch/config.yaml`) — customize server commands:
```yaml
lsp:
  servers:
    go:
      command: ["gopls"]
      extensions: [".go"]
    typescript:
      command: ["typescript-language-server", "--stdio"]
      extensions: [".ts", ".tsx", ".js", ".jsx"]
    python:
      command: ["pyright-langserver", "--stdio"]
      extensions: [".py"]
    rust:
      command: ["rust-analyzer"]
      extensions: [".rs"]
    cpp:
      command: ["clangd"]
      extensions: [".cpp", ".cc", ".c", ".h", ".hpp"]
```

**Note:** Claude Code does not support native LSP. For claude-code sessions, use shell commands for diagnostics: `gopls check ./...`, `tsc --noEmit`, `pyright .`.

- **Rate limit detection** — there is no captured opencode throttle line in
  `testdata/rate_limit_lines/` (this covers `opencode`, `opencode-acp` and
  `opencode-prompt`). The opencode-specific lines recorded in-tree
  (`SSE read timed out`, `SSE error`, …) are network/SSE stall diagnostics,
  not throttle messages, so they are not fixtures. The only built-in
  detection for this family is the shared `DATAWATCH_RATE_LIMITED:` protocol
  line the session prints, matched line-start after trimming, with the same
  quoted-phrase rule: a line that only mentions a throttle phrase in ordinary
  output does not pause the backend.

chunks.heading: ACP vs tmux: what goes where
chunks.body:
### ACP vs tmux: what goes where

| Interaction | tmux | ACP (HTTP/SSE) |
|---|---|---|
| Initial task delivery | No | **Yes — POST /session/<id>/message** |
| Follow-up messages (`send <id>: …`) | No | **Yes — POST /session/<id>/message** |
| AI text replies | In tmux TUI | **Also here (channel_reply, amber)** |
| Tool execution output | In tmux TUI | Via SSE events → log |
| Session output log | tmux pane | SSE events written to log file |
| Folder trust / first-run prompts | N/A (no claude CLI) | N/A |
| Rate-limit / complete detection | Log pattern | Log pattern |

> ACP mode uses **no tmux input paths** — all user messages and AI replies flow
> through the HTTP API. The tmux window exists so you can attach and watch live,
> but all datawatch interaction bypasses it.

chunks.heading: Notes
chunks.body:
### Notes

- Does not require tmux interaction for input — ACP uses the HTTP API
- Output filter engine watches log lines written from SSE events

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Ollama (local models)
chunks.body:
## Ollama (local models)

**Name:** `ollama`

[Ollama](https://ollama.ai) runs large language models locally. No API key required —
models run entirely on your hardware.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.body:
### Prerequisites

- Ollama installed and running (`ollama serve`)
- At least one model pulled (e.g. `ollama pull llama3`)

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Installation
chunks.body:
### Installation

```bash
# Linux
curl -fsSL https://ollama.ai/install.sh | sh

# macOS
brew install ollama

# Start Ollama server
ollama serve

# Pull a model
ollama pull llama3
ollama pull codellama
ollama pull deepseek-coder

# Verify
ollama list
```

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Configuration
chunks.body:
### Configuration

```yaml
session:
  llm_backend: ollama

ollama:
  enabled: true
  model: llama3                    # model name; default: "llama3"
  host: http://localhost:11434     # Ollama server URL; default: "http://localhost:11434"
```

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: How it runs
chunks.body:
### How it runs

```bash
cd <project_dir> && ollama run <model> '<task>'
```

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Notes
chunks.body:
### Notes

- Ollama runs locally — no internet connection required after model download
- Model quality varies; `codellama`, `deepseek-coder`, or `qwen2.5-coder` are good for coding tasks
- **Remote Ollama**: set `host` to your server URL (e.g. `http://203.0.113.100:11434`). The `ollama` binary does not need to be installed on the datawatch host — availability is checked via `GET /api/tags` on the remote server, not by running `ollama --version`
- Interactive input is not supported via datawatch

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Recommended models
chunks.body:
### Recommended models

| Model | Size | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| `llama3` | 4.7 GB | General tasks |
| `codellama` | 3.8 GB | Code generation |
| `deepseek-coder` | 776 MB | Code-focused, lightweight |
| `qwen2.5-coder` | 4.7 GB | Strong coding performance |

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Rate limit detection
chunks.body:
### Rate limit detection

There is no captured Ollama throttle line in `testdata/rate_limit_lines/` —
nothing in-tree quotes one, and Ollama serves local models, so it rarely
rate-limits at all. The only built-in detection for `ollama` is the shared
`DATAWATCH_RATE_LIMITED:` protocol line the session prints, matched line-start
after trimming; a line that only quotes a throttle phrase in ordinary output
does not pause the backend. An operator-configured `detection.rate_limit_patterns`
(flat substring, all backends) is the escape hatch.

---

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: OpenWebUI
chunks.body:
## OpenWebUI

**Name:** `openwebui`

Calls an [OpenWebUI](https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui) instance via its
OpenAI-compatible API. OpenWebUI is a self-hosted UI for local and remote LLMs.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.body:
### Prerequisites

- OpenWebUI running (locally or on your network)
- API key if auth is enabled on your OpenWebUI instance

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Configuration
chunks.body:
### Configuration

```yaml
session:
  llm_backend: openwebui

openwebui:
  enabled: true
  url: http://localhost:3000      # OpenWebUI base URL; default: "http://localhost:3000"
  model: llama3                   # model name as shown in OpenWebUI; default: "llama3"
  api_key: ""                     # API key if OpenWebUI auth is enabled
```

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: How it runs
chunks.body:
### How it runs

The backend uses a native Go HTTP client to communicate with the OpenAI-compatible
chat completions API. It maintains conversation history in memory, enabling multi-turn
interactive sessions with follow-up messages. Responses are streamed via SSE and
displayed in the tmux session in real time.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Rich Chat UI
chunks.body:
### Rich Chat UI

OpenWebUI, Ollama, and OpenCode-ACP default to `output_mode: chat` which activates
the rich chat interface in the web UI:

- **Message bubbles** — rounded, with user (right-aligned, blue) and assistant
  (left-aligned, green) layout
- **Avatars** — U (user), AI (assistant), S (system) with colored backgrounds
- **Timestamps** — HH:MM on every message
- **Markdown rendering** — code blocks with syntax styling, bold, italic, bullet lists
- **Streaming** — animated typing dots during response generation
- **Thinking overlay** — collapsible "Thinking..." section for reasoning models
- **Hover actions** — Copy to clipboard, Remember (save assistant response to memory)
- **Memory command quick bar** — buttons for memories, recall, kg query, research
- **Memory commands in chat** — type `remember:`, `recall:`, `kg query`, `research:`
  directly in the chat input; commands are intercepted and processed locally
- **Prompt debounce** — configurable delay (default 3s) before alerting on detected prompts
- **Notification cooldown** — minimum 15s between repeated alerts per session

Backends that default to chat mode:
| Backend | Default `output_mode` | Conversation Manager |
|---------|----------------------|---------------------|
| OpenWebUI | `chat` | Go HTTP (`/api/chat/completions`) |
| Ollama | `chat` | Go HTTP (`/api/chat`) |
| OpenCode-ACP | `chat` | SSE event stream (`/event`) |
| Claude Code | `terminal` | N/A (TUI) |
| OpenCode | `terminal` | N/A (TUI) |

To override for any backend:
```yaml
ollama:
  output_mode: terminal  # disable chat, use raw terminal view
opencode_acp:
  output_mode: log       # disable chat, use log view
```

Any backend that supports interactive input can use the chat interface.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Notes
chunks.body:
### Notes

- Requires OpenWebUI v0.3+ with the OpenAI-compatible API enabled
- Supports any model available in your OpenWebUI instance (local Ollama models, OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.)
- **Interactive mode supported** — send follow-up messages via the web UI, CLI (`session send`), or messaging channels. Conversation context is maintained across messages.
- No external dependencies (curl, python3) needed — all API communication is handled in Go
- The API key can also be set via the `OPENWEBUI_API_KEY` environment variable

---

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Shell (custom script)
chunks.body:
## Shell (custom script)

**Name:** `shell`

Run any program or script as the AI backend. Your script receives the task and project
directory as arguments and is responsible for running the AI and producing output.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Configuration
chunks.body:
### Configuration

```yaml
session:
  llm_backend: shell

shell_backend:
  enabled: true
  script_path: ~/scripts/my-ai.sh   # path to your script
```

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Script interface
chunks.body:
### Script interface

Your script is called with:

```bash
/path/to/your/script '<task>' '<project_dir>'
```

- `$1` — task description (the text sent in `new: <task>`)
- `$2` — absolute path to the project directory

Output is captured in the tmux session. When your script exits, the session is marked
complete.

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Example script
chunks.body:
### Example script

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# my-ai.sh — custom AI backend example
set -euo pipefail

TASK="$1"
PROJECT_DIR="$2"

cd "$PROJECT_DIR"

# Call any AI tool you like
my-custom-ai-tool --task "$TASK" --dir "$PROJECT_DIR"
```

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Notes
chunks.body:
### Notes

- The script must be executable: `chmod +x ~/scripts/my-ai.sh`
- Use this to integrate with any AI tool not directly supported by datawatch
- Interactive input is not supported; the script runs to completion
- The completion marker `DATAWATCH_COMPLETE: shell done` is emitted automatically after the script exits

---

chunks.title: LLM Backends
chunks.heading: Adding a New LLM Backend
chunks.body:
## Adding a New LLM Backend

To add a new backend:

1. Create `internal/llm/backends/<name>/backend.go` implementing the `llm.Backend` interface:

```go
type Backend interface {
    Name() string
    Launch(ctx context.Context, task, tmuxSession, projectDir, logFile string) error
    SupportsInteractiveInput() bool
    Version() string
}
```

2. Register it in `internal/llm/registry.go`
3. Add config fields to `internal/config/config.go`
4. Wire it up in `cmd/datawatch/main.go`
5. **Document it in this file** (`docs/llm-backends.md`) with full config and usage details
6. Update `docs/backends.md` summary table
7. Update `CHANGELOG.md` under `[Unreleased]`

chunks.title: MCP Server
chunks.body:
# MCP Server

datawatch exposes a [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) (MCP)
server, enabling Cursor, Claude Desktop, VS Code, and remote AI agents to manage AI
coding sessions directly — without leaving the IDE or chat app.

---

chunks.title: MCP Server
chunks.heading: Daemon Mode Compatibility
chunks.body:
## Daemon Mode Compatibility

Since v0.2.0, `datawatch start` daemonizes by default.

- **Stdio transport** (`datawatch mcp`): unaffected — this is a separate foreground command invoked directly by the IDE. The daemon mode of `datawatch start` does not affect it.
- **SSE transport**: runs as a goroutine inside the daemon process. It starts and stops with the daemon regardless of whether the daemon is foreground or daemonized.

To run MCP SSE on a daemonized server, set `mcp.sse_enabled: true` in config and run `datawatch start` as usual.

---

chunks.title: MCP Server
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.body:
## Overview

MCP is an open protocol for connecting AI models to tools and data sources. When you
configure datawatch as an MCP server, your IDE's AI assistant can:

- List active sessions on any connected machine
- Start new sessions for coding tasks
- Read live session output
- Send input to sessions waiting for a reply
- Terminate sessions

Two transport modes are supported:

| Mode | When to use |
|---|---|
| **stdio** | Local IDE clients (Cursor, Claude Desktop, VS Code) — no port required |
| **HTTP/SSE** | Remote AI agents, autonomous workflows, cross-machine access |

---

chunks.title: MCP Server
chunks.heading: Local Setup (stdio)
chunks.body:
## Local Setup (stdio)

The stdio transport runs datawatch as a subprocess. Your IDE starts it on demand and
communicates over stdin/stdout. No port, no network, no TLS needed.

chunks.title: MCP Server
chunks.heading: Remote Setup (HTTP/SSE)
chunks.body:
## Remote Setup (HTTP/SSE)

The SSE transport starts an HTTP server that remote AI agents connect to. This enables:

- Remote AI agents (running in cloud functions, other machines, etc.) to manage sessions
- Multi-machine datawatch orchestration
- Programmatic access from scripts and CI systems

chunks.title: MCP Server
chunks.heading: Enable in config
chunks.body:
### Enable in config

```yaml
mcp:
  enabled: true
  sse_enabled: true
  sse_host: "0.0.0.0"     # bind address; default: 0.0.0.0
  sse_port: 8081           # port; default: 8081
  token: "your-secret"    # bearer token — required for remote connections
  tls_enabled: true
  tls_auto_generate: true  # auto-generate self-signed cert in ~/.datawatch/tls/mcp/
```

Start datawatch normally — the SSE server starts alongside all other backends:

```bash
datawatch start
```

Or run standalone:

```bash
datawatch mcp --sse
```

chunks.title: MCP Server
chunks.heading: Remote AI client config

chunks.title: MCP Server
chunks.heading: TLS
chunks.body:
### TLS

When `tls_enabled: true`:

- TLS 1.3 is enforced (TLS 1.2 and below are rejected)
- Post-quantum hybrid key exchange (X25519Kyber768) is negotiated automatically by
  Go 1.23+ when the client supports it — no extra config needed
- `tls_auto_generate: true` (default) generates a self-signed certificate at
  `~/.datawatch/tls/mcp/cert.pem` (valid 10 years, persisted across restarts)
- To use a CA-signed certificate, set `tls_cert` and `tls_key`:

```yaml
mcp:
  tls_enabled: true
  tls_auto_generate: false
  tls_cert: /etc/ssl/certs/datawatch.crt
  tls_key: /etc/ssl/private/datawatch.key
```

chunks.title: MCP Server
chunks.heading: Trusting self-signed certificates
chunks.body:
### Trusting self-signed certificates

When using `tls_auto_generate: true`, MCP clients need to trust the self-signed cert:

**Download the certificate:**
- Web UI: Settings > Comms > Web Server > Download CA Certificate
- API: `GET /api/cert?format=der` (.crt) or `GET /api/cert` (.pem)
- File: `~/.datawatch/tls/mcp/cert.pem`

**For Cursor / VS Code MCP clients:**
- Most MCP clients over SSE use HTTPS. Set `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` in the
  client environment, or install the CA cert system-wide.

**For Claude Desktop:**
- Claude Desktop uses stdio transport (not SSE), so TLS is not needed for local use.
- For remote SSE access, configure the cert in the OS certificate store.

**System-wide cert install:**
```bash
# Linux (Debian/Ubuntu)
sudo cp ~/.datawatch/tls/mcp/cert.pem /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/datawatch.crt
sudo update-ca-certificates

# macOS
sudo security add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain ~/.datawatch/tls/mcp/cert.pem
```

**For mobile PWA (Android/iPhone):**
See the operations guide for device-specific cert install instructions.

---

chunks.title: MCP Server
chunks.heading: Available Tools
chunks.body:
## Available Tools

The MCP server exposes **150+ tools** across the surfaces below
(v8.10.16 count — includes BL356–BL362 additions). The authoritative live list is served at
`GET /api/mcp/docs` (HTML) or `GET /api/mcp/docs?format=json` (JSON)
— `claude mcp list` queries this on connect, and the PWA Settings →
About → "MCP tools" link opens it. The selected tools below are
documented inline; the rest follow the same parameter-table-and-example
shape.

**Failure responses** (v9.5.29, BL463): a failed tool call returns an
`isError:true` result named after the tool (e.g.
`template_delete: HTTP 404: template not found`) — tools mirroring a REST
route also carry the upstream HTTP status and the daemon's error body
(truncated where long), holding MCP to REST's reliability bar. In stdio mode
`datawatch mcp` logs to **stderr only**; stdout is the JSON-RPC channel and
must stay strict JSON-RPC (release-smoke §7r asserts all of this).

chunks.title: MCP Server
chunks.heading: Tool families (high-level)
chunks.body:
### Tool families (high-level)

| Family | Tools |
|--------|-------|
| Sessions | `list_sessions`, `start_session`, `send_input`, `copy_response`, `kill_session`, `delete_session`, `restart_session`, `rename_session`, `session_output`, `session_timeline`, `session_bind_agent`, `session_import`, `session_reconcile`, `session_rollback`, `sessions_stale`, `stop_all_sessions`, `session_children`, `reply_to_parent`, `get_my_session_id`, `get_my_scope` |
| Vision | `vision_describe` |
| Web Search | `websearch_providers_list/get/add/update/delete/enable/disable/test`, `websearch_stats`, `websearch_history`, `web_search_stats` (deprecated alias) |
| Exit Hooks | `exit_hook_list`, `exit_hook_add`, `exit_hook_delete`, `exit_hook_enable`, `exit_hook_disable` |
| Work Queue | `queue_push`, `queue_claim`, `queue_complete`, `queue_fail`, `queue_list` |
| Discussion Subscribe | `discussion_subscribe`, `discussion_unsubscribe`, `discussion_subscriptions` |
| Result Store | `result_put`, `result_get`, `result_list`, `result_delete` |
| Scheduled Job Results | `post_result`, `schedule_results_list` |
| Autonomous PRDs | `autonomous_status`, `autonomous_config_get/set`, `autonomous_prd_list/create/get/decompose/approve/resume/reject/request_revision/edit_task/instantiate/run/cancel/rejudge/set_kind/set_llm/set_task_llm/set_task_verification_llm/set_story_verification_llm/set_verification_llm/children`, `autonomous_learnings`, `autonomous_progress`, `autonomous_progress_trend`, `autonomous_lane_fill_status`, `autonomous_triage`, `autonomous_prd_set_lane_preference`, `capacity_status` |
| Usage back-off | `usage_backoff_status`, `usage_backoff_set`, `usage_backoff_clear`, `usage_backoff_recheck` |
| Usage calculator | `usage_advice`, `usage_readings`, `usage_reading_add`, `usage_reading_delete`, `usage_extra_credit_set`, `usage_remaining_work_set` |
| Lifecycle subscriptions (BL427) | `autonomous_subscribe`, `autonomous_unsubscribe`, `autonomous_subscriptions`, `autonomous_subscription_update`, `autonomous_subscription_test`, `autonomous_events_pending` |
| Orchestrator | `orchestrator_graph_create/plan/run/get/list/cancel`, `orchestrator_verdicts`, `orchestrator_config_get/set` |
| Pipelines | `pipeline_start/list/status/cancel` |
| Memory + KG | `memory_remember/recall/list/forget/export/import/reindex/stats/learnings`, `kg_add/query/timeline/stats/invalidate`, `research_sessions`, `get_prompt`, `copy_response` |
| Observer | `observer_stats`, `observer_envelopes`, `observer_envelopes_all_peers` (BL180 cross-host), `observer_envelope`, `observer_peers_list/get/register/delete`, `observer_peer_stats`, `observer_agent_list/stats`, `observer_config_get/set`, `ollama_stats` |
| Agents | `agent_list/get/spawn/terminate/logs/audit` |
| Plugins | `plugins_list/reload`, `plugin_get/test/enable/disable` |
| Profiles + projects | `profile_list/get/create/update/delete/smoke`, `project_list/summary/upsert`, `project_alias_delete` |
| Templates / scheduling / cooldown | `template_list/upsert/delete`, `schedule_list/add/cancel`, `cooldown_status/set/clear` |
| Devices + routing | `device_alias_list/upsert/delete`, `routing_rules_list/test` |
| Channel bridge | `channel_info`, `channel_diagnostics` |
| Cost + audit + config + alerts | `cost_summary/usage/rates`, `analytics`, `audit_query`, `audit_access_query`, `get_config`, `config_set`, `get_stats`, `get_version`, `diagnose`, `reload`, `restart_daemon`, `splash_info`, `get_alerts`, `create_alert`, `mark_alert_read` |
| Saved commands | `list_saved_commands`, `send_saved_command` |
| Ask / assist | `ask`, `assist` |
| Voice | (no MCP tools — REST `/api/voice/transcribe` + chat-channel auto-handle) |

Autonomous PRD reads and writes:

- **`autonomous_prd_get`** — takes an optional `detail` argument that sets how much comes back. The default is `summary`. Any other value is rejected with an error.
  - `summary` returns the Automaton's ids, titles, statuses and counts, and the same for its stories and tasks.
  - `tasks` returns everything in `summary`, plus each task's status, error and verification summary.
  - `full` returns everything, including task specs and logs, and the `foreign_file_drift` field on tasks.
- **Behaviour change for PRD write tools.** `autonomous_prd_reset_task`, `autonomous_prd_run`, `autonomous_prd_approve`, `autonomous_prd_cancel`, and the set, add and edit tools no longer return the whole Automaton. Each write reply is now a small object with the Automaton's `id`, its `status` and `rev`, the id and status of the task or story that changed, and a `message`. To read the full Automaton after a write, call `autonomous_prd_get` with `detail` set to `full`.

Tools added in v5.9 → v5.26 (catch-up since the last doc sweep):

- **`autonomous_prd_resume`** — resume a PRD the boot-resume gate parked after a daemon restart (also resumes a paused PRD). Takes `id` and an optional `note`; errors if the PRD is in neither state.
- **`autonomous_prd_children`** (v5.9.0, BL191 Q4) — list child PRDs spawned from a parent's `Task.SpawnPRD` shortcuts.
- **`autonomous_prd_edit_task`** (v5.9.0+) — edit a task's `spec` while a PRD is in `needs_review`, `revisions_asked`, `cancelled`, or `blocked` (per-task `backend` / `effort` / `model` go through `autonomous_prd_set_task_llm`). On a `blocked` PRD only the `failed`/`blocked` task that halted it can be edited, and a `completed` task's spec is immutable in every status. Recovery flow for a stuck task: `autonomous_prd_edit_task` to fix the spec, then `autonomous_prd_reset_task` to retry it — completed sibling tasks are left untouched, no re-decompose needed.
- **`autonomous_prd_edit_story`** — rewrite a story's `title`/`description` while a PRD is in `needs_review` or `revisions_asked`.
- **`autonomous_prd_add_story`** / **`autonomous_prd_remove_story`** — add a new, empty story, or remove a story (and its tasks), without re-running decompose. Only allowed pre-approval.
- **`autonomous_prd_add_task`** / **`autonomous_prd_remove_task`** — add a new task to an existing story, or remove one, without re-running decompose. Only allowed pre-approval. `remove_task` is distinct from `autonomous_prd_cancel_task`, which stops a running/queued task without deleting it from the PRD.
- **`autonomous_prd_cancel`** — cancel a PRD (proxies bare `DELETE /api/autonomous/prds/{id}`) and best-effort kill its worker sessions. Response: `id`, `status` (`"cancelled"`), `killed_sessions` (count of session slots recorded on the PRD's tasks), and `killed_session_ids` (array of the session IDs a kill was actually attempted on — always an array, `[]` when none). A `kill_errors` map (`{"<id>": "<error>"}`) is added only when a kill failed. Use `killed_session_ids` to verify no unrelated session was stopped.
- **`autonomous_prd_set_llm`** (v5.4.0; v8.20.0 extended; v8.33.9 priority fix) — operator-pinned LLM override at the PRD level. Parameters: `backend` (task-execution backend — opencode, claude-code, goose, etc.), `effort`, `model`, and `decomposition_profile` (planning/decompose backend — any configured LLM; opencode/claude-code spawn a full session with codebase tool access, ollama/openwebui run headless; empty = use global `autonomous.planning_backend`). Per-PRD `decomposition_profile` takes priority over the global setting. Optional `guardrail_backend` / `guardrail_model` set the guardrail/verification judge LLM override; it inherits task → Automaton → global `autonomous.verification_backend` / `verification_model`. Only the guardrail params you pass are sent (omitted = unchanged, `""` = clear), and a call with only guardrail params leaves the worker LLM untouched.
- **`autonomous_prd_set_task_llm`** (v5.4.0) — operator-pinned LLM override at the task level (overrides the Automaton-level execution backend for that specific task). Accepts the same optional `guardrail_backend` / `guardrail_model` params with the same absent-vs-empty semantics, scoped to the one task. Acceptance is governed by `autonomous.task_override_statuses` (default `needs_review` / `revisions_asked` / `cancelled` / `blocked`).
- **`autonomous_prd_set_failure_escalation`** — set the failure escalation override on an Automaton (leave `task_id` empty) or on one task. `policy` is an object with `enabled` (boolean), `max_failures` (1 or more) and `steps` (an array of `{backend, model, effort, attempts}`); fields left out inherit from the next level up. `clear=true` removes the override at that level. Requires the autonomous-write capability for federation peers; a missing policy and no `clear` is refused before anything is sent.
- **`autonomous_prd_resolve_task_review`** — the operator's decision on a task held for review. `action` is `retry` (requeue it, optionally with a replaced `spec`, a worker `backend`/`model`/`effort` for the task, a narrowed `files` list, and a `note` the next attempt reads) or `cancel`. It works while the Automaton is running and other tasks are live: it answers at once and starts no second executor, and the running executor picks the decision up. A task that is not held answers 409, and an unknown Automaton or task answers 404.
- **`autonomous_prd_set_task_verification_llm`** / **`autonomous_prd_set_story_verification_llm`** / **`autonomous_prd_set_verification_llm`** (v9.0.69) — pick which LLM *verifies* (judges) the work of one task, every task in one story, or a whole Automaton. Precedence, most specific wins: task → story → Automaton → Automation → global `autonomous.verification_backend` / `verification_model` / `verification_effort`. Backend and model come from the same level (a less specific level's model never leaks past a more specific backend override); effort resolves independently. A backend set at any of these levels also bypasses the global `autonomous.verification_backends` capacity pool; a model or effort set without a backend at any per-unit level leaves the verifier on the global path. Effort is applied when the verifier runs as a session. Accepted while the Automaton is `needs_review`, `revisions_asked`, `cancelled` or `blocked`: acceptance is governed by `autonomous.task_override_statuses` (default `needs_review` / `revisions_asked` / `cancelled` / `blocked`). Each verification result records what actually ran as `verifier_backend` / `verifier_model` / `verifier_effort` / `verifier_source` (`task` | `story` | `prd` | `automation` | `global` | `pool`) on the task's `verification` object in `autonomous_prd_get`. The task itself records `executor_source` (`task` | `story` | `prd` | `automation` | `global`), the level that supplied its execution backend. `automation` is the default set on the Automation the Automaton belongs to (see `automation_set_llm` and `automation_set_verification_llm` below); it sits between the Automaton and the global default.

  | Parameter | Tools | Required | Description |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `id` | all three | yes | Automaton ID |
  | `task_id` | `..._set_task_verification_llm` | yes | Task to override |
  | `story_id` | `..._set_story_verification_llm` | yes | Story to override (a task-level override still wins) |
  | `verification_backend` | all three | no | Any configured LLM name (unknown → error). `""` clears (inherit the next level); omit to leave unchanged |
  | `verification_model` | all three | no | Model for the verifier. `""` clears; omit = unchanged |
  | `verification_effort` | all three | no | `low` / `medium` / `high` / `max` / `quick` / `normal` / `thorough`. `""` clears; omit = unchanged |
  | `actor` | all three | no | Who made the change (default `operator`) |

  ```
  autonomous_prd_set_task_verification_llm(id="a1b2c3d4", task_id="t7", verification_backend="claude-code", verification_model="opus", verification_effort="high")
  autonomous_prd_set_story_verification_llm(id="a1b2c3d4", story_id="s2", verification_backend="ollama", verification_model="qwen3:8b")
  autonomous_prd_set_verification_llm(id="a1b2c3d4", verification_model="")   # clear the Automaton-level model only
  ```

  Returns the write reply described above (a small summary, not the whole Automaton). These overrides are separate from `guardrail_backend` / `guardrail_model` on `autonomous_prd_set_llm` / `autonomous_prd_set_task_llm`, which pick the guardrail judge.

Takes `id` and `kind`; an empty `kind` clears the setting so the kind is derived again from the title and spec. An unknown kind is refused. `autonomous_prd_create` takes the same optional `kind`. Proxies `POST /api/autonomous/prds/{id}/set_kind`.
- **`autonomous_progress`** — read the progress metrics: counts by kind (feature, bug, other) and in total, throughput per active day, worker utilization, lead time per stage, the inactive windows left out of every rate, the remaining work split into known records and estimated work, and the completion range in days with the method behind each figure. Read-only; returns the same object as `GET /api/autonomous/progress`. All parameters are optional.

  | Parameter | Required | Description |
  |---|---|---|
  | `automation_id` | no | Count only the Automata of this Automation |
  | `tag_id` | no | Count only the Automata carrying this tag |
  | `since` | no | First day counted, `YYYY-MM-DD` (default: the configured date, else the first record's creation date) |
  | `until` | no | Last day counted, `YYYY-MM-DD`, inclusive (default: now) |

  ```
  autonomous_progress()
  autonomous_progress(tag_id="t-ui", since="2026-10-10")
  ```

  A missing backlog file is not an error: the reply carries `backlog_available: false`. A bad date, or `until` before `since`, is refused. Needs the autonomous read capability when called by a federated peer.

Read-only; returns the same body as `GET /api/autonomous/progress/trend`: `days`, `points` (one per snapshot, oldest first: `date`, `reason`, `completion_low_days`, `completion_high_days`, `known_tasks`, `estimated_tasks`, `throughput_3d`, `utilization`, `completed_prds`) and `direction` (`converging`, `widening`, `flat` or `unknown`).

  | Parameter | Required | Description |
  |---|---|---|
  | `days` | no | How many days back to read, a whole number from 1 to 365 (default 30) |

  ```
  autonomous_progress_trend()
  autonomous_progress_trend(days=90)
  ```

  Without saved snapshots `points` is empty and `direction` is `unknown`. A `days` value outside 1 to 365 is refused.

  | Parameter | Required | Description |
  |---|---|---|
  | `limit` | no | How many decisions to return, a whole number from 1 to 1000 (default 50) |

  ```
  autonomous_lane_fill_status()
  autonomous_lane_fill_status(limit=200)
  ```

  A `limit` outside 1 to 1000 is refused with the daemon's message. Needs the autonomous read capability when called by a federated peer.

Read-only: listing never starts, retries or edits anything. Returns the same object as `GET /api/autonomous/triage`.

  | Parameter | Required | Description |
  |---|---|---|
  | `automation_id` | no | only records in this automation |
  | `prd_id` | no | the record of one Automaton |
  | `status` | no | `failed` or `blocked` (case-sensitive; anything else is refused) |

  ```
  autonomous_triage()
  autonomous_triage(status="failed")
  autonomous_triage(automation_id="aut_01", status="blocked")
  ```

  A wrong `status` comes back as a tool error with the daemon's message. Needs the autonomous read capability when called by a federated peer.
