chunks.body:
## Prompt injection mitigations — v8.18.0

User-controlled text flowing into LLM prompts is a class of vulnerability not covered by gosec or Trivy. The following controls were added:

| Call site | File | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| `decomposeFn` — PRD spec sent to planning LLM | `cmd/datawatch/main.go` | Security preamble + `<user_data>` wrap |
| `autonomousVerify` — task spec sent to verifier LLM | `cmd/datawatch/main.go` | Security preamble (spec already tagged) |
| `autonomousGuardrail` — unit title+spec sent to guardrail LLM | `cmd/datawatch/main.go` | Security preamble + `<user_data>` wrap on both fields |

Input scanner: `ScanForInjection(text)` in `internal/autonomous/security.go` checks PRD/task specs at create and edit boundaries against 11 known injection patterns. Enabled via `autonomous.injection_guard: true`; blocking via `autonomous.block_on_injection: true`.

**Residual risk:**
- Memory retrieval: learnings injected into decompose context are not yet scanned (scanner only runs at create/edit boundaries; stored memories can grow stale)
- Memory retrieval injection: conversation history retrieved from memory is not yet scanned before injection into LLM context
- Council persona descriptions: user-controlled and injected into debate prompts; not yet covered by the scanner

**Procedural addition:** Any new LLM prompt site that interpolates user-supplied text (spec, title, description) must add a security preamble and `<user_data>` tag. Reviewers: grep for `fmt.Sprintf` calls in `cmd/datawatch/main.go` that interpolate `req.Spec`, `task.Spec`, or user-facing string fields.

chunks.title: Security review — pre-v6.0
chunks.heading: gosec baseline-diff refresh — SEC-026, 2026-10-08
chunks.body:
## gosec baseline-diff refresh — SEC-026, 2026-10-08

`.gosec-baseline.json` had drifted out of sync with reality: `total: 60` against a measured live count of 63 (`by_rule` was last taken 2026-05-19, v8.4.0-era). Every one of the 63 live findings is one of the six rule IDs the baseline file's own `_comment` already blanket-accepts (G118, G122, G123, G702, G703, G704) — no new rule category appeared, so this is a bookkeeping refresh to the measured true count, not a loosening of what's actually accepted:

| Rule | Old baseline | Live (2026-10-08) |
|---|---|---|
| G118 | 2 | 2 |
| G122 | 6 | 6 |
| G123 | 1 | 1 |
| G702 | 3 | 3 |
| G703 | 29 | 32 |
| G704 | 19 | 19 |
| **Total** | **60** | **63** |

`.gosec-baseline.json` updated to `total: 63` / `by_rule.G703: 32` so future *actual* regressions (a new rule category, or a count above 63) get caught, instead of a gate that was already 3 over and about to pass anything up to the next bump regardless.

**Separate gap, not fixed here:** `.github/workflows/security-scan.yaml` only triggers on `pull_request` to `main`, never on a direct push — so this drift went uncaught through roughly 5 months of main-branch commits (2026-05-19 → 2026-10-08), none of which went through a PR. Whether to also run this gate on push (and how that interacts with the release pipeline's own `gosec` step in `release.yaml`) is a CI-workflow-trigger decision, not a baseline-number change — flagged for a deliberate call, not decided unilaterally here.

chunks.title: Security review — pre-v6.0
chunks.heading: Code-scanning triage
chunks.body:
## Code-scanning triage

Open code-scanning alerts for Go path injection, disabled certificate validation and the JavaScript sanitization rules in test files were triaged one by one; the per-alert reasons are in `docs/plans/path-injection-alert-decisions.md`.

| Outcome | Count | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed in code | 9 | 6 path-injection alerts (project directory containment and cleaning, pack directory containment, test-run directory cleaning), 2 certificate-check alerts in the PWA story scripts, and the Go node-usage client, which now verifies certificates unless the node sets `tls_insecure_skip_verify` |
| Dismissed | 16 | 5 path-injection alerts on sanitized or fixed-name paths, 3 certificate-check alerts in test-only scripts against local listeners, and 8 sanitization alerts in test files |

Each dismissed alert has a `code-scanning/<alert number>` entry in `security/accepted-risks.yml` with the traced evidence; alerts fixed in code have none. The GitHub dismissals are applied by the operator using the commands listed in the decision list.

chunks.title: Security review — pre-v6.0
chunks.heading: Procedural changes
chunks.body:
## Procedural changes

- Run `gosec -severity high -confidence medium ./...` and `govulncheck ./...` before every patch. The audit doc is updated only when triage changes (new findings or new mitigations).
- Run `trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignorefile .trivyignore --exit-code 1` on the agent-base image before every release. CI enforces this automatically.
- New `//#nosec` annotations must include the rule ID *and* a one-line reason. PRs adding bare `//#nosec` get rejected by review.
- New `InsecureSkipVerify=true` sites must be paired with pinning (`VerifyPeerCertificate` + a fingerprint check) or get an entry in the G402 table above with an "accept (documented)" verdict and a config gate.
- New `.trivyignore` entries require a one-line rationale in this document. PRs adding bare CVE IDs without rationale get rejected.

chunks.title: Security review — pre-v6.0
chunks.heading: CodeQL workflow and alert gate
chunks.body:
## CodeQL workflow and alert gate

CodeQL runs from `.github/workflows/codeql.yaml` (go, javascript-typescript, actions and python; one `/language:<name>` category each, `upload: always`, `security-events: write` only on the analyze job). A final `alert-gate` job queries open code-scanning alerts for the ref and fails when any are high or critical, printing the counts and a list of rule, path and alert number. Only alerts in state `open` count, so an alert dismissed in code scanning does not. The gate does not read `security/accepted-risks.yml`; that registry records the reason for each dismissal, which the operator applies in GitHub.

The workflow replaces GitHub default setup, which must be disabled by the operator in the repository settings first; the two cannot upload the same categories. Background and the investigation of the earlier Analyze failures are in `docs/plans/codeql-analyze-upload-failure-findings.md`.

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.body:
# Session Tracking

Every datawatch session has a dedicated git-tracked folder that records the complete
history of the session: task, output, conversation, state changes, and git commits.

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.heading: Folder Location
chunks.body:
## Folder Location

```
~/.datawatch/sessions/<hostname>-<id>/
```

Example: `~/.datawatch/sessions/hal9000-a3f2/`

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.heading: Folder Contents
chunks.body:
## Folder Contents

| File | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `.git/` | Git repository — every event is a commit |
| `README.md` | Auto-updated session overview (task, status, timestamps, tmux name) |
| `task.md` | Original task description and any amendments |
| `output.log` | Full raw claude-code output, streamed live by tmux pipe-pane. Kept on disk only: it is listed in `.git/info/exclude` and is **not** committed to the folder's git history (nor are `output.log.enc` / `output.log.pipe`). |
| `conversation.md` | Human-readable history of prompts received and inputs sent |
| `timeline.md` | Append-only timestamped event log |
| `session.json` | Machine-readable session state snapshot |
| `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENT.md` | Session guardrails (auto-generated from templates). `CLAUDE.md` is used for claude-code sessions; `AGENT.md` is used for all other backends (opencode, aider, goose, etc.) |
| `PAUSED.md` | Written by claude-code when it hits a rate limit (auto-deleted on resume) |

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.heading: Git Commit Timeline
chunks.body:
## Git Commit Timeline

Every significant event creates a git commit in the session folder:

```
$ git -C ~/.datawatch/sessions/hal9000-a3f2 log --oneline

d8f3c2a session: complete
b7e1f90 session: input sent
a3d4c81 session: waiting for input — Should I add tests?
9c2b7e3 session: state running→waiting_input
4f8a1e2 session: start — refactor the authentication module to use JWT
```

This gives you a full audit trail of every interaction.

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.heading: Project Directory Git Tracking
chunks.body:
## Project Directory Git Tracking

For a one-shot task session, datawatch snapshots the project directory
before the worker starts and commits automatically the moment the worker
signals it's done — before verification looks at the result. The
worker's own one-line summary becomes the commit message (the task
title if there isn't one); workers never run `git commit` themselves.
This is unconditional for task sessions.
`session.auto_git_commit` is **deprecated and ignored** — it no longer
changes this behavior; it is kept only so old config files still load.

This makes it trivial to see exactly what claude changed:

```bash
# In the project directory:
git log --oneline
# a8f3c12 session[a3f2](complete): refactor auth module
# 7b2e9d1 pre-session[a3f2]: refactor auth module

# Diff of everything claude did:
git diff HEAD~2 HEAD~1..HEAD
```

If something went wrong, roll back:
```bash
git reset --hard HEAD~1   # undo claude's changes, keep pre-session state
```

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.heading: Accessing Session History
chunks.body: ## Accessing Session History

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.heading: Via CLI
chunks.body:
### Via CLI
```bash
# Navigate to session tracking folder
cd $(datawatch session log a3f2)

# View git history
datawatch session history a3f2

# Follow live output
datawatch session tail a3f2 --lines 50

# Pi sessions: tail also prints one status line (e.g.
# "progress: turns=5 tools=bash:3,edit:1,read:1 last=bash idle=42s");
# --follow keeps re-emitting it every --status-interval (default 60s).
# Non-pi sessions print no status line.
datawatch session tail a3f2 --lines 50 --follow --status-interval 30s

# Read the conversation
cat conversation.md

# See full timeline
cat timeline.md
```

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.heading: Via PWA
chunks.body:
### Via PWA
The session detail view in the PWA shows live output. The session tracking folder
path is shown in the session info panel.

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.heading: Via Signal
chunks.body:
### Via Signal
```
tail a3f2 30     — last 30 lines of output
status a3f2      — current state + recent output
```

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.heading: Rate Limit Handling
chunks.body:
## Rate Limit Handling

When claude-code hits an API quota or rate limit, the session transitions to a
`rate_limited` state instead of failing:

1. claude-code writes `PAUSED.md` with a progress summary
2. The daemon detects the `DATAWATCH_RATE_LIMITED:` output line
3. State changes to `rate_limited` — you receive a Signal/PWA notification
4. The daemon schedules a retry after the reset time
5. On retry: the session resumes, `PAUSED.md` is used as context, and the session
   continues from where it left off

A couple of rules about how a line counts as a rate limit:

- A line that only quotes a throttle phrase inside ordinary output — a doc
  sentence, an echoed command, a file listing — does not pause a backend.
  The built-in matches are per backend (each backend family recognises only
  the phrases captured from its own output) and they are anchored to the
  start of the line, after surrounding whitespace is trimmed.
- The `DATAWATCH_RATE_LIMITED:` protocol line is the shared exception: it is
  recognised line-start on every backend, including backends with no captured
  throttle line of their own.
- If you set `detection.rate_limit_patterns`, your list replaces the built-in
  matches and is applied as before: a flat substring, anywhere on the line,
  for all backends.
- After an upgrade, the usage back-off status reports the patterns as stale
  until an operator rechecks them: `POST /api/usage-backoff/recheck`
  records the current pattern fingerprint and clears the stale flag.

You can also manually resume a paused session:
```
send a3f2: continue from where you left off, see PAUSED.md for context
```

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.heading: Session Guardrails (CLAUDE.md / AGENT.md)
chunks.body:
## Session Guardrails (CLAUDE.md / AGENT.md)

Each session has a guardrails file auto-generated from templates and placed in both the
session tracking folder and the project directory:

- **claude-code sessions** use `CLAUDE.md` (generated from `templates/session-CLAUDE.md`)
- **All other backends** (opencode, aider, goose, etc.) use `AGENT.md` (generated from `templates/session-AGENT.md`)

This file gives the LLM operating constraints for the session:

- **Scope**: constrained to the project directory tree
- **Git**: required to commit frequently with conventional messages
- **Rate limits**: wait and write a pause note, do not fail
- **Input protocol**: `DATAWATCH_NEEDS_INPUT:` line for async input requests
- **Completion protocol**: `DATAWATCH_COMPLETE:` line when done
- **Safety**: no deletes without confirmation, no secrets in commits

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.heading: Disabling Tracking
chunks.body:
## Disabling Tracking

The session folder is always created — it's how the daemon tracks state.
`auto_git_commit` no longer has any effect; project-directory commits
for a task session are unconditional and cannot be disabled.
`auto_git_init` still controls whether datawatch initializes a git repo
in the project directory if one doesn't exist:

```yaml
session:
  auto_git_init: false
```

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.heading: Storage
chunks.body:
## Storage

Session folders accumulate over time. Each folder is small (text files + git objects).
To clean up old completed sessions:

```bash
# List sessions older than 30 days
find ~/.datawatch/sessions -maxdepth 1 -mtime +30 -type d

# Archive or remove
datawatch session purge --older-than 30d
```

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.heading: Repository size & maintenance
chunks.body:
### Repository size & maintenance

Each session folder's git repo only records the small text files (`task.md`,
`timeline.md`, `conversation.md`, `session.json`, `README.md`, guardrail files).
The live `output.log` (and `output.log.enc` / `output.log.pipe`) stays on disk and is
never committed. Repos created before this change had `output.log` tracked; the
daemon untracks it automatically (`git rm --cached`, the file itself is kept) on the
first commit it makes to that repo after a restart.

When the daemon creates or resumes a session repo it also sets these git options on it:

| Option | Value | Why |
|--------|-------|-----|
| `gc.auto` | `0` | Turns off git's implicit auto-gc. Without this, an ordinary `git commit` made by the daemon can start a full repack in the background. |
| `gc.autoDetach` | `false` | If a gc does run, it does not detach and keep running unseen. |
| `pack.windowMemory` | `64m` | Caps the delta-search memory per pack thread. |
| `pack.threads` | `1` | One pack thread, so the cap above is the total. |
| `core.bigFileThreshold` | `16m` | Files over 16MB are stored without delta compression, which is where repack memory goes. |

Why this matters: the daemon makes these commits from inside its own process and
systemd cgroup. Any git work they trigger counts against the daemon's memory, so an
implicit auto-gc on a large repo can exhaust host memory and the OOM killer then takes
down the whole daemon, not just that git process. With auto-gc off, session repos are
never repacked by the daemon. They stay small because `output.log` is no longer in
history.

Repos that grew large before this change keep their old history until you shrink them.
Use `scripts/shrink-session-repo.sh` (below), which runs outside the daemon under a
memory cap. `scripts/repro-tracker-git-growth.sh` reproduces the growth in a scratch
directory and prints a size table, before and after the fix.

chunks.title: Session Tracking
chunks.heading: Shrinking a bloated session repo
chunks.body:
### Shrinking a bloated session repo

Session folders created before `output.log` was excluded from git history can grow
to many gigabytes, because every commit stored a full copy of the growing log. Do not
run `git gc` or `git repack` on one of these repos from inside the daemon, and do not
run them by hand either. On 2026-10-13 a repack of such a repo used over 100GB of
memory and the OOM killer took down the whole datawatch service.

Use `scripts/shrink-session-repo.sh` instead. It deletes `output.log` and
`output.log.enc` from the repo's git **history** only. The on-disk `output.log` is
moved aside during the rewrite and then put back, and the script verifies that its
size and inode are unchanged. The heavy git steps (history rewrite, `gc --prune=now`,
`fsck`) run in a transient `systemd-run --user` scope with `MemoryMax=4G` and
`MemorySwapMax=0`, at nice 19 and idle I/O priority. If they overrun, only that scope is
killed, never `datawatch.service`. The script prints the scope's peak memory. Without a
systemd user manager it falls back to `nice`/`ionice` plus `ulimit -v`.

When to run it: when `du -sh ~/.datawatch/sessions/*/.git` shows a session repo far
larger than its text files. Run it on completed sessions. It refuses a session whose
`session.json` state is `running`/`waiting_input`, a repo that committed within the
last 2 minutes, and a repo with a `.git/index.lock`.

```bash
# See what would happen (changes nothing)
scripts/shrink-session-repo.sh --dry-run ~/.datawatch/sessions/<session-dir>

# Shrink one or more session repos
scripts/shrink-session-repo.sh ~/.datawatch/sessions/<dir1> ~/.datawatch/sessions/<dir2>

# Cheap, non-destructive sweep: apply only the git hygiene settings
# (gc.auto=0, bounded pack memory, output.log in .git/info/exclude) to every session repo
scripts/shrink-session-repo.sh --all-hygiene ~/.datawatch/sessions
```

Options and environment:

| Setting | Effect |
|---------|--------|
| `--allow-active` | Rewrite even if the session looks active. `.git/index.lock` is still re-checked just before rewriting. |
| `SHRINK_MEMORY_MAX=8G` | Raise the memory cap. If the scope is killed, the script says so, restores `output.log`, and leaves history intact, so you can retry with a higher cap. |
| `SHRINK_FILTER_TOOL=filter-branch` | Force `git filter-branch` even if `git-filter-repo` is installed (the default is filter-repo when available). |
| `SHRINK_NO_SCOPE=1` | Skip `systemd-run` and use the `ulimit -v` fallback. |

The rewrite changes commit hashes in the session repo, so anything that recorded a
session-repo commit hash (not the project repo's) will no longer resolve. History of
`timeline.md` and `conversation.md` is kept: the script checks that their commit counts
are unchanged. If a run is interrupted hard (e.g. `kill -9`), the live file is left in
`<session-dir>/.git/shrink-backup/`. The script refuses to run again until you move it
back.

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.body:
# Setup Guide

Step-by-step instructions for getting `datawatch` running from scratch.

---

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Messaging Backends
chunks.body:
## Messaging Backends

datawatch supports many messaging backends. You don't need Signal — pick whichever you use:

| Backend | Setup command | Prerequisites |
|---------|--------------|---------------|
| **Signal** | `datawatch link` or `datawatch setup signal` | Java 17+, signal-cli, phone number |
| **Telegram** | `datawatch setup telegram` | Telegram bot token (from @BotFather) |
| **Discord** | `datawatch setup discord` | Discord bot token and channel ID |
| **Slack** | `datawatch setup slack` | Slack bot token and channel ID |
| **Matrix** | `datawatch setup matrix` | Matrix homeserver URL, user, token, room ID |
| **Twilio SMS** | `datawatch setup twilio` | Twilio account SID, auth token, phone numbers |
| **ntfy** | `datawatch setup ntfy` | ntfy server URL and topic (push notifications only) |
| **Email** | `datawatch setup email` | SMTP server details (outbound alerts only) |
| **Webhooks** | `datawatch setup webhook` | Webhook URL for incoming/outgoing |
| **GitHub** | `datawatch setup github` | GitHub webhook secret |
| **Web UI only** | `datawatch setup web` | No external service needed |

All backends can also be configured via the **web UI** (Settings tab), the **REST API** (`/api/config`), or by editing `~/.datawatch/config.yaml` directly. See [messaging-backends.md](messaging-backends.md) for detailed configuration of each backend.

You can enable multiple backends simultaneously — messages are routed to all active channels.

---

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Prerequisites
chunks.body:
## Prerequisites

- Linux or macOS (WSL2 also works)
- tmux
- An LLM backend CLI installed and authenticated (e.g. `claude` for claude-code)
- For Signal: Java 17+, signal-cli, phone number (see below)
- For voice input (optional): Python 3, ffmpeg, and `openai-whisper` in a venv (see [messaging-backends.md](messaging-backends.md#voice-input-whisper-transcription))

---

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Step 1: Install signal-cli
chunks.body:
## Step 1: Install signal-cli

signal-cli is a command-line interface for the Signal messenger. It wraps the official Signal library (libsignal) with Java bindings.

**Download the latest release:**

```bash
# Check https://github.com/AsamK/signal-cli/releases for the latest version
VERSION=0.13.7
wget https://github.com/AsamK/signal-cli/releases/download/v${VERSION}/signal-cli-${VERSION}-Linux.tar.gz
tar xf signal-cli-${VERSION}-Linux.tar.gz
sudo mv signal-cli-${VERSION}/bin/signal-cli /usr/local/bin/
sudo mv signal-cli-${VERSION}/lib /usr/local/lib/signal-cli
```

**Verify installation:**

```bash
signal-cli --version
```

> **Note:** signal-cli requires Java 17+. Install with `sudo apt install openjdk-17-jre` (Debian/Ubuntu) or `brew install openjdk@17` (macOS).

---

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Step 2: Install datawatch
chunks.body:
## Step 2: Install datawatch

```bash
go install github.com/dmz006/datawatch/cmd/datawatch@latest
```

Or build from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/dmz006/datawatch.git
cd datawatch
make install
```

---

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Step 3: Set up a messaging backend
chunks.body: ## Step 3: Set up a messaging backend

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Option A: Interactive setup wizard (any backend)
chunks.body:
### Option A: Interactive setup wizard (any backend)

```bash
datawatch setup telegram   # or discord, slack, matrix, web, etc.
```

The wizard prompts for the required credentials and writes them to `~/.datawatch/config.yaml`.

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Option B: Signal — link and set up the control group (one command)
chunks.body:
### Option B: Signal — link and set up the control group (one command)

```bash
datawatch link
```

You'll be prompted for your Signal phone number, then a QR code is displayed.

**Scan the QR code** with your Signal app: **Settings → Linked Devices → Link New Device**

After you scan, datawatch automatically:
- Confirms the link
- Creates a Signal group called `datawatch-<hostname>`
- Saves the group ID to `~/.datawatch/config.yaml`
- Prints: `datawatch start`

That's it — no manual group creation, no `listGroups`, no `config init` needed.

**Example output:**

```
Linking device 'my-server' to Signal account +12125551234...
Scan the QR code with your Signal app:
  Settings → Linked Devices → Link New Device

[QR code displayed here]

Waiting for you to scan the QR code...

Device linked successfully!

Creating Signal control group 'datawatch-my-server'...
Group created: datawatch-my-server (ID: aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ=)

Setup complete! Start the daemon with:
  datawatch start

Send 'help' in the 'datawatch-my-server' group on Signal to verify.
```

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: If auto-group creation fails
chunks.body:
### If auto-group creation fails

If the group creation step fails (rare — usually a signal-cli startup timing issue), fall
back to manual setup:

```bash
# Option A: create the group from your phone
# Open Signal → new group → add yourself → name it "datawatch control"
# Then get the group ID:
signal-cli -u +12125551234 listGroups
# Copy the base64 Id and run:
datawatch config init

# Option B: create via signal-cli directly
signal-cli -u +12125551234 updateGroup -n "datawatch control" -m +12125551234
# Copy the returned group ID, then:
datawatch config init
```

---

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Optional: Set up Voice Input (Whisper)
chunks.body:
## Optional: Set up Voice Input (Whisper)

Voice messages sent via Telegram or Signal can be automatically transcribed to text. This requires OpenAI Whisper running locally.

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Install dependencies
chunks.body:
### Install dependencies

```bash
# ffmpeg is required for audio decoding
sudo apt install ffmpeg        # Debian/Ubuntu
brew install ffmpeg             # macOS

# Create a Python virtual environment and install Whisper
cd /path/to/datawatch          # or wherever you run datawatch from
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install openai-whisper
```

> **Note:** On systems without a GPU, pip will install CPU-only PyTorch automatically. If you have a CUDA GPU and want faster transcription, install the CUDA version of PyTorch first: `.venv/bin/pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121` before installing whisper.

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Configure
chunks.body:
### Configure

All configuration methods:

| Method | How |
|--------|-----|
| **YAML** | Edit `~/.datawatch/config.yaml` → `whisper:` section (see below) |
| **Web UI** | Settings tab → General → **Voice Input (Whisper)** card |
| **REST API** | `PUT /api/config` with `{"whisper.enabled": true, "whisper.model": "base"}` |
| **Comm channel** | `configure whisper.enabled=true`, `configure whisper.model=small` |
| **Test endpoint** | `POST /api/test/message` with `{"text": "configure whisper.enabled=true"}` |

```yaml
whisper:
  enabled: true
  model: base          # tiny, base, small, medium, large
  language: en         # ISO 639-1 code, or "auto" for detection
  venv_path: .venv     # path to the Python venv (relative or absolute)
```

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Model selection
chunks.body:
### Model selection

| Model | Size | Speed | Best for |
|-------|------|-------|----------|
| tiny | 39 MB | fastest | Quick commands, low-resource servers |
| base | 74 MB | fast | General use (default) |
| small | 244 MB | moderate | Mixed languages, accented speech |
| medium | 769 MB | slow | High accuracy |
| large | 1.5 GB | slowest | Maximum accuracy, all languages |

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Supported languages
chunks.body:
### Supported languages

99 languages supported. Common codes: `en` (English), `es` (Spanish), `de` (German), `fr` (French), `ja` (Japanese), `zh` (Chinese), `ko` (Korean), `pt` (Portuguese), `ru` (Russian), `ar` (Arabic), `hi` (Hindi).

Set `language: auto` for automatic detection (slower, may be less accurate for short messages).

Full list: [Whisper language support](https://github.com/openai/whisper#available-models-and-languages)

> **Multi-user note:** Currently a single default language is configured globally. Per-user language preferences are planned as part of the multi-user access control feature.

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.body:
### How it works

1. Send a voice message via Telegram or Signal
2. The backend downloads the audio to a temp file
3. Whisper transcribes the audio to text
4. The router echoes `Voice: <transcribed text>` back to the channel
5. The transcribed text is processed as a normal command (`new`, `send`, implicit send, etc.)
6. Temp audio files are cleaned up after transcription

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Verify
chunks.body:
### Verify

Send a voice message in your Telegram or Signal group. You should see:

```
[myhost] Voice: your spoken words here
[myhost][a1b2] Input sent.
```

chunks.body:
## Optional: Set up RTK (Token Savings)

[RTK (Rust Token Killer)](https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk) is a Rust CLI proxy that compresses AI coding agent output, reducing token consumption by 60-90%.

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Install RTK
chunks.body:
### Install RTK

```bash
# Download the latest release
curl -fsSL https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk/releases/latest/download/rtk-linux-amd64 \
  -o ~/.local/bin/rtk && chmod +x ~/.local/bin/rtk

# Initialize hooks for your AI coding tool
rtk init -g
```

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Configure in datawatch
chunks.body:
### Configure in datawatch

All configuration methods:

| Method | How |
|--------|-----|
| **CLI** | `datawatch setup rtk` (interactive wizard) |
| **YAML** | Edit `~/.datawatch/config.yaml` → `rtk:` section (see below) |
| **Web UI** | Settings tab → General → **RTK (Token Savings)** card |
| **REST API** | `PUT /api/config` with `{"rtk.enabled": true}` |
| **Comm channel** | `configure rtk.enabled=true`, `configure rtk.auto_init=true` |

```yaml
rtk:
  enabled: true
  binary: rtk              # path to RTK binary
  show_savings: true       # show savings in stats dashboard
  auto_init: true          # auto-run 'rtk init -g' if hooks missing
  discover_interval: 0     # seconds between optimization checks (0 = disabled)
```

RTK only activates for supported backends: **claude-code**, **gemini**, **aider**.

chunks.body:
## Optional: Set up Backend Profiles and Fallback Chains

Profiles allow multiple accounts or API keys for the same LLM backend. Fallback chains auto-switch to the next profile when the primary hits a rate limit.

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Configure profiles
chunks.body:
### Configure profiles

```yaml
profiles:
  claude-work:
    backend: claude-code
    # Uses default claude auth (e.g. Max subscription)
  claude-personal:
    backend: claude-code
    env:
      ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: "sk-ant-..."
  gemini-fallback:
    backend: gemini
    env:
      GEMINI_API_KEY: "AIza..."
```

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Set up a fallback chain
chunks.body:
### Set up a fallback chain

```yaml
session:
  fallback_chain:
    - claude-personal
    - gemini-fallback
```

When the primary backend hits a rate limit, datawatch automatically starts a new session with the next profile in the chain, copying the task and project directory.

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Manage profiles
chunks.body:
### Manage profiles

All configuration methods:

| Method | How |
|--------|-----|
| **YAML** | Edit `~/.datawatch/config.yaml` → `profiles:` and `session.fallback_chain:` sections |
| **Web UI** | Settings tab → General → **Profiles & Fallback** card (fallback chain); New Session form → **Profile dropdown** |
| **REST API** | `GET /api/profiles` (list), `POST /api/profiles` (create), `DELETE /api/profiles?name=X` (remove) |
| **Comm channel** | `configure session.fallback_chain=claude-personal,gemini-backup` |
| **New session with profile** | `new claude-personal: <task>` (from any comm channel) |

chunks.heading: Optional: Set up Proxy Mode (Multi-Machine)
chunks.body:
## Optional: Set up Proxy Mode (Multi-Machine)

Proxy mode lets one datawatch instance manage sessions on multiple remote machines.
Commands from Signal/Telegram are auto-routed to the correct machine.

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Add a remote server
chunks.body:
### Add a remote server

| Method | How |
|--------|-----|
| **CLI** | `datawatch setup server` (interactive wizard) |
| **YAML** | `servers:` list in `~/.datawatch/config.yaml` (see below) |
| **Web UI** | Settings tab → Comms → **Servers** section |
| **REST API** | N/A (edit config directly — servers require daemon restart) |
| **Comm channel** | N/A |

```yaml
servers:
  - name: prod               # short name used in commands
    url: http://203.0.113.10:8080   # remote datawatch URL
    token: "bearer-token"     # must match remote server.token
    enabled: true
  - name: pi
    url: http://203.0.113.50:8080
    token: "another-token"
    enabled: true
```

Restart the daemon after adding servers.

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Usage
chunks.body:
### Usage

From any messaging channel or the test endpoint:

```
list                          — shows sessions from ALL servers
status a3f2                   — auto-finds which server has session a3f2
send a3f2: yes                — routes to the correct remote
kill a3f2                     — kills on the owning remote
new: @prod: deploy pipeline   — starts session on specific remote
new: @pi: run backups         — starts on the pi server
```

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Web UI
chunks.body:
### Web UI

In Settings → Comms → Servers, click a remote server to switch the web UI to that
instance. All session views, terminal output, and input are proxied through the local
instance — no direct network access to the remote is needed.

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Where to see aggregated sessions
chunks.body:
### Where to see aggregated sessions

| Location | What you see |
|----------|-------------|
| **Web UI** | Server badges on session cards; server indicator in toolbar |
| **REST API** | `GET /api/sessions/aggregated` — all servers, tagged with `server` field |
| **Comm channel** | `list` shows `[local]`, `[prod]`, `[pi]` sections |
| **CLI** | `datawatch --server prod session list` (targets one remote) |

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Network requirements
chunks.body:
### Network requirements

- The proxy instance must be able to reach each remote's HTTP port
- Remote instances must have `server.token` set (the proxy injects it as Bearer auth)
- WebSocket relay requires persistent TCP connection to each remote
- No inbound connections from remotes to proxy are needed

See [architecture.md](architecture.md#proxy-mode-architecture) for flow diagrams.

### Using systemd (recommended for servers)

Create `/etc/systemd/system/datawatch.service`:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=datawatch daemon
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=youruser
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/datawatch start
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

```bash
sudo systemctl enable --now datawatch
sudo journalctl -u datawatch -f
```

```bash
configure memory.enabled=true
```

```yaml
  enabled: true
```

### Memory commands

```
remember: always run go mod tidy before committing
recall: how to commit
memories                    # list recent
memories reindex            # re-embed after model change

kg add Alice works_on myapp # knowledge graph
```

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: PostgreSQL backend (enterprise)
chunks.body:
### PostgreSQL backend (enterprise)

For team deployments or large memory stores, use PostgreSQL instead of SQLite:

```bash
# Prerequisites: PostgreSQL 14+ with pgvector
sudo apt install postgresql-17 postgresql-17-pgvector

# Create database
sudo -u postgres psql -c "CREATE USER datawatch WITH PASSWORD 'datawatch';"
sudo -u postgres psql -c "CREATE DATABASE datawatch OWNER datawatch;"
sudo -u postgres psql -d datawatch -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;"

# Configure
configure memory.backend=postgres
configure memory.postgres_url=postgres://datawatch:datawatch@127.0.0.1/datawatch
```

See [memory.md](memory.md) for full PostgreSQL setup and migration instructions.

See [encryption.md](encryption.md) for details.

chunks.heading: Troubleshooting
chunks.body: ## Troubleshooting

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: signal-cli fails to start
chunks.body:
### signal-cli fails to start

**Symptom:** `datawatch start` fails with "start signal-cli: ..."

**Solutions:**
- Verify `signal-cli` is in your PATH: `which signal-cli`
- Verify Java 17+ is installed: `java --version`
- Check signal-cli works directly: `signal-cli --version`
- Verify the account is linked: `signal-cli -u +<number> listAccounts`

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: QR code scan not detected
chunks.body:
### QR code scan not detected

**Symptom:** Scanned QR code but signal-cli link never completes

**Solutions:**
- Make sure you're scanning with the correct Signal account
- Try re-running `datawatch link` — the QR code expires
- Ensure the Signal app on your phone is up to date

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Messages not received
chunks.body:
### Messages not received

**Symptom:** Daemon is running but doesn't respond to Signal messages

**Solutions:**
- Confirm the `group_id` in config matches the output of `signal-cli listGroups`
- Ensure the linked device is still active: check Signal → Settings → Linked Devices
- Check signal-cli can receive: `signal-cli -u +<number> receive`

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Session stays in `running` state forever
chunks.body:
### Session stays in `running` state forever

**Symptom:** A session never transitions to `waiting_input` or `complete`

**Solutions:**
- Check the log file: `cat ~/.datawatch/logs/<hostname>-<id>.log`
- Verify tmux session exists: `tmux list-sessions`
- Attach to the session to see what claude-code is doing: `tmux attach -t cs-<hostname>-<id>`
- Adjust `input_idle_timeout` in config if claude-code takes a long time to produce output

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: "session not found" error
chunks.body:
### "session not found" error

**Symptom:** `status a3f2` returns "not found"

**Solutions:**
- Run `list` to see current session IDs
- Session IDs are 4 hex characters — check for typos
- Sessions are scoped per-host; `status` on a different machine won't find the session

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Config File Security
chunks.body:
## Config File Security

The config file at `~/.datawatch/config.yaml` contains sensitive credentials (bot tokens, API keys, phone numbers). By default it is stored in plaintext with `0600` permissions (readable only by your user).

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Encrypting the Config File
chunks.body:
### Encrypting the Config File

Encryption can be enabled **at any time** — you do not need to start with encryption. Existing plaintext data files are automatically migrated to encrypted on the first `--secure` start.

```bash
# Option A: Enable encryption on an existing installation
# Just add --secure to your start command — plaintext files are migrated automatically
datawatch --secure start --foreground

# Option B: Start fresh with encryption from the beginning
datawatch --secure config init
datawatch --secure start --foreground

# Option C: Non-interactive (for systemd / background use)
export DATAWATCH_SECURE_PASSWORD="your-passphrase"
datawatch --secure start
```

When `--secure` is set, **all data files** in `~/.datawatch/` are encrypted, not just `config.yaml`:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `config.yaml` | Bot tokens, API keys, credentials |
| `sessions.json` | Session metadata and task descriptions |
| `schedule.json` | Scheduled commands |
| `commands.json` | Saved command library |
| `filters.json` | Output filter rules |
| `alerts.json` | System alert history |

**How it works:**
- The config file is encrypted with XChaCha20-Poly1305 using Argon2id key derivation (64 MB, 4 threads, run once). The salt is embedded in the config file header.
- A 32-byte data key is derived from the same password + salt — this avoids re-running the expensive KDF on every session state update.
- All data store writes use XChaCha20-Poly1305 with a fresh random nonce per write.
- Session output logs use streaming block encryption (DWLOG1 format) via FIFO.
- On first `--secure` start, existing plaintext files are automatically migrated to encrypted.

chunks.title: Setup Guide
chunks.heading: Important Warnings
chunks.body:
### Important Warnings

> **If you lose the encryption password, all data files cannot be recovered.**
> Back up your bot tokens, API keys, and session data before enabling encryption.

- The password is never stored or cached — you must enter it each time the daemon starts.
- Encrypted config is not compatible with daemon mode (background daemonize requires interactive password input). Use `--foreground` with `--secure`, or set `DATAWATCH_SECURE_PASSWORD` environment variable.

chunks.title: Skills (BL255, v6.7.0)
chunks.body:
# Skills (BL255, v6.7.0)

A **skill** is a self-contained markdown-and-scripts package that influences how an AI session does its work. Skills come from registries (built-in PAI by default; operator can add others), get sync'd selectively into `~/.datawatch/skills/`, and resolve at session spawn either as files in the working directory or via the `skill_load` MCP tool.

chunks.title: Skills (BL255, v6.7.0)
chunks.heading: Why skills
chunks.body:
## Why skills

- **Reuse a body of practice.** Hand-craft a skill once (e.g., "review-go-changes"), commit it to a git repo, every session that spawns with `skills: [review-go-changes]` gets the practice.
- **Share registries across teams.** Operators can point at internal git repos with team-authored skills.
- **PAI compatibility.** danielmiessler/Personal_AI_Infrastructure ships ~45 skill packs in this same shape; datawatch uses PAI's `SKILL.md` + YAML frontmatter format directly, plus 6 datawatch-specific extensions.
- **Survives sessions.** Skills follow the BL219 lifecycle pattern: injected on session start, cleaned up on session end (when `cleanup_artifacts_on_end=true`), `.datawatch/` added to `.gitignore` so the operator's repo isn't polluted.

chunks.title: Skills (BL255, v6.7.0)
chunks.heading: Architecture
chunks.body:
## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph operator["Operator surfaces"] PWA[PWA Settings → Automata → Skill Registries] CLI[CLI: datawatch skills registry add/connect/sync/...] MCP[MCP: skills_registry_* / skill_load] COMM[Comm: skills registry add-default / sync ...] YAML[(datawatch.yaml
skills:)] end subgraph daemon["datawatch daemon"] REST[REST: /api/skills/registries/* + /api/skills/*] MGR[skills.Manager] STORE[(skills.json index
~/.datawatch/skills.json)] CACHE[(shallow-clone cache
~/.datawatch/.skills-cache/<reg>/)] SYNCED[(synced content
~/.datawatch/skills/<reg>/<name>/)] end subgraph external["External git registries"] PAI[(PAI default
github.com/danielmiessler/
Personal_AI_Infrastructure)] OWN[(operator-added
git repos)] end subgraph runtime["Session spawn (option C + D)"] INJ[Inject files
<projectDir>/.datawatch/skills/<name>/] LOAD[skill_load MCP tool
agent reads on demand] end PWA --> REST CLI --> REST MCP --> REST COMM --> REST YAML -. seed registries .-> MGR REST --> MGR MGR --> STORE MGR --> CACHE MGR --> SYNCED CACHE -- git clone --> PAI CACHE -- git clone --> OWN SYNCED -. session start .-> INJ SYNCED -. on demand .-> LOAD ```

chunks.title: Skills (BL255, v6.7.0)
chunks.heading: Lifecycle
chunks.body:
## Lifecycle

1. **Add a registry.** Either:
   - `datawatch skills registry add-default` (idempotent — adds PAI), or
   - `datawatch skills registry add <name> <git-url>` (your own)
2. **Connect.** Daemon does a `git clone --depth=1` into `~/.datawatch/.skills-cache/<reg>/` and walks the tree for `SKILL.md` files. Each becomes an *available* skill.
3. **Browse.** Inspect what's available before committing disk space. PWA shows a checkbox table; CLI: `datawatch skills registry browse <name>`.
4. **Sync.** Pick the skills you want. The daemon copies each selected skill's directory into `~/.datawatch/skills/<reg>/<name>/`. Only synced skills consume real disk + appear in the resolution path.
5. **Use.** Spawn a session with `Skills: ["my-skill"]` (set on PRD, or directly on `/api/sessions/start`). Daemon copies the skill's files into `<projectDir>/.datawatch/skills/<name>/` and the `skill_load` MCP tool can read them on demand.
6. **Cleanup.** When the session ends and `cleanup_artifacts_on_end=true`, the `<projectDir>/.datawatch/skills/` directory is removed. The synced copy at `~/.datawatch/skills/` stays for reuse.

chunks.title: Skills (BL255, v6.7.0)
chunks.heading: Manifest format
chunks.body:
## Manifest format

Each skill ships a `SKILL.md` (or `skill.md` / `skill.yaml`) with a YAML frontmatter block:

```yaml
---
# PAI base format (compatible with danielmiessler/Personal_AI_Infrastructure)
name: review-go-changes
description: Review staged Go changes for tests, error handling, and AGENT.md compliance.
version: 1.2.0
tags: [code-review, go]
entrypoint: ./run.sh

# datawatch v1 extensions (all six are optional and additive)
compatible_with: [datawatch>=6.7.0]   # (a) compatibility hints
requires: [test-runner-go]             # (b) dependency declarations
applies_to:                            # (c) routing / applicability
  agents: [claude-code, opencode]
  session_types: [coding]
  comm_channels: []                    # empty = any
cost_hint: medium                      # (d) resource hints
disk_mb: 12
verify: ./verify.sh                    # (e) verification command (post-sync)
provides_mcp_tools: [scan_for_test_gaps]  # (f) MCP-tool declarations
accepts_images: false                  # (g) true if skill accepts [image: <desc>] vision context
---

# Review Go Changes

A walk-through of how to inspect a Go diff for the patterns we care about…
```

The parser is **tolerant of unknown fields** (per the [Skills-Awareness Rule](../AGENT.md#skills-awareness-rule-bl255-v670)): future extensions land in the `Extra` map and round-trip through sync without loss. PWA / CLI surfaces render unknown fields as raw key/value rather than hiding them. Known extension fields to date: `(a)` `compatible_with`, `(b)` `requires`, `(c)` `applies_to`, `(d)` `cost_hint`/`disk_mb`, `(e)` `verify`, `(f)` `provides_mcp_tools`, `(g)` `accepts_images` (vision context flag — skill can receive `[image: <desc>]` in task text).

chunks.title: Skills (BL255, v6.7.0)
chunks.heading: Resolution at session spawn (options C + D)
chunks.body:
## Resolution at session spawn (options C + D)

When a session spawns with `Skills: ["foo", "bar"]`:

| Option | Behavior | Always-on? |
|---|---|---|
| **C — File injection** | Daemon copies each synced skill's directory into `<projectDir>/.datawatch/skills/<name>/`. Agent process reads the markdown from disk. | Yes for v1 (per BL255 design Q3). |
| **D — `skill_load` MCP tool** | The agent calls `skill_load <name>` over MCP and gets the skill's markdown returned as text. Avoids prompt bloat when many skills are configured but only one is needed. | Yes — the tool is registered unconditionally. |

`.datawatch/` is auto-added to `.gitignore` (and `.cfignore`/`.dockerignore` when present) on session start, mirroring the BL219 backend-artifact hygiene pattern.

chunks.title: Skills (BL255, v6.7.0)
chunks.heading: Configuration
chunks.body:
## Configuration

YAML — declarative seeding (operator-edited registries persist in `skills.json` and survive YAML edits):

```yaml
skills:
  add_default_on_start: true              # idempotently add PAI on every daemon start
  auto_ignore_on_session_start: true      # default true — adds .datawatch/ to .gitignore
  registries:
    - name: my-team
      kind: git
      url: https://gitea.example.com/team/skills
      branch: main
      auth_secret_ref: ${secret:gitea-skills-token}   # MUST be a secret-ref per Secrets-Store Rule
      description: Internal team skill catalog
      enabled: true
```

chunks.title: Skills (BL255, v6.7.0)
chunks.heading: Operator commands (cheat sheet)
chunks.body:
## Operator commands (cheat sheet)

| What | Comm channel | CLI | REST |
|---|---|---|---|
| List registries | `skills registry list` | `datawatch skills registry list` | `GET /api/skills/registries` |
| Add a registry | `skills registry add <n> <url>` | `datawatch skills registry add <n> <url>` | `POST /api/skills/registries` |

chunks.heading: Running E2E

### Running E2E

```bash
# Parallel mode (default) — starts isolated daemon, cleans up after
make test-e2e

# Serial mode
bash scripts/run-tests.sh --serial

# Single story
bash scripts/run-tests.sh --filter TS-065
```

runs all stories, then kills the daemon and removes the temp dir. Artifacts
(evidence, logs) land in a dated work dir outside the repo.

chunks.title: Test Coverage
chunks.heading: PWA Playwright Suite
chunks.body:
### PWA Playwright Suite

Browser-level PWA stories live in `scripts/test-stories/pwa`. Each `TS-*.mjs`
story drives the PWA with Playwright, `lib.mjs` holds the shared helpers, and
`run-all.mjs` runs every story in sorted order, printing a PASS/FAIL line per
story and exiting 1 if any story fails.

```bash
# Run every PWA story
make test-e2e-pwa

# Point the path check at a different suite directory
make test-e2e-pwa PWA_SUITE_DIR=path/to/suite
```

`make test-e2e-pwa` first checks the suite directory. It stops with an error
naming the path if the directory, its `package.json`, or any `TS-*.mjs` story
is missing. It then starts the `datawatch` service from
`docs/testing/docker-compose.test.yml`, waits for it to report healthy, and runs
`node run-all.mjs` inside the `playwright` compose service. That service reaches
the daemon at `http://datawatch:8080` on the internal compose network, so the
suite does not depend on host ports.

`PWA_SUITE_DIR` defaults to `scripts/test-stories/pwa`. The `playwright` service
mounts that directory at `/tests/pwa` in the compose file, so the mount itself
does not follow `PWA_SUITE_DIR`.

## Pi-prompt descendant-only stall bound (autonomous.descendant_stall_seconds)

chunks.title: Testing Tracker
chunks.heading: Voice transcription errors and chunking
chunks.body:
## Voice transcription errors and chunking

`POST /api/voice/transcribe` changed its error contract. A failed transcription is HTTP 502 with a JSON body `{error, cause, hint, detail, latency_ms}`, where `cause` is `timeout`, `killed`, `out_of_memory`, `ffmpeg_missing`, `backend_error` or `unknown`. The deadline now scales with the audio (5 minutes, or twice the audio length, capped at 30 minutes). Local whisper splits audio longer than the new `whisper.chunk_seconds` (default 120, 0 disables). The PWA keeps a failed recording with Retry and Discard. A failed or slow request writes one `[voice] transcribe failed:` or `transcribe slow:` log line. The how-to is `docs/howto/voice-input.md` and the flow is `docs/flow/voice-transcribe-flow.md`.

Test conditions for every row below: no model download, no real ffmpeg and no network. ## Autonomous triage — records, pass, alert, and the read on every surface

The engine keeps one triage record per failed or blocked Automaton and serves it on every surface: REST (`GET /api/autonomous/triage`), MCP (`autonomous_triage`), CLI (`datawatch autonomous triage`), comm (`autonomous triage …`) and a triage card in the PWA's Automaton detail view. A triage pass runs on every coordinator tick, filling, refreshing and clearing records; once a record has sat for `autonomous.automation.triage_alert_minutes` (default 30; `0` = off), one triage alert per episode goes through the existing alert sink. The record is a read: nothing on this list starts, retries or edits anything. The operator reference is `docs/operations.md` (section *Triage records*), the API contract `docs/api/autonomous.md` (section *Triage records*), the mobile contract `docs/api/mobile-surface.md` (section *Triage records (Automata surface)*) and the how-to pointer `docs/howto/automation-tab.md`.

Every Tested row below was run on 2026-10-27 with Go 1.27.2 (linux/amd64) or Node 24.15.0, from the repository root, with `env -u TMUX -u TMUX_TMPDIR` in front of each command. All tests use fakes only: a spy store, fake Automata, fake HTTP servers, and the alert clock advanced with fake time. No test starts a live daemon or a real worker, so **no row is Validated**.

Run everything at once:

```sh
env -u TMUX -u TMUX_TMPDIR go test ./internal/autonomous/ ./internal/server/ ./internal/mcp/ ./internal/router/ ./cmd/datawatch/ -run 'Triage' -count=1
env -u TMUX -u TMUX_TMPDIR node --test internal/server/web/app-triage.test.js
```

chunks.title: Testing Tracker
chunks.heading: Monitoring and observability
chunks.body:
### Monitoring and observability

What exists today for the triage feature:

- **The triage record read.** `GET /api/autonomous/triage` (REST) and `autonomous_triage` (MCP) return every stored record plus the effective `alert_minutes`, newest first, with the same filters on both. The CLI and the chat verb read the same route. An operator or an agent can poll it to see what is stuck, why, and whether the alert has already fired (`alerted_at`).
- **The alert on the poll pass.** Once a failed or blocked Automaton has sat for `autonomous.automation.triage_alert_minutes` (default 30, 0 = off), the coordinator's triage pass raises one `warn` alert for that episode and stamps `alerted_at` on the record. It reaches the same alert sinks as the other coordinator alerts.
- **Audit entries.** The triage pass writes no operator audit entry of its own: it fills, refreshes and clears records in the store and raises the alert. Each read of the route does appear in the HTTP access log (`GET /api/audit/access`, MCP `audit_access_query`) like any other request, with its principal. A record that fails to save or clear is written to the daemon log.

Why no new stats field, Monitor card or Prometheus counter yet: the record read and the alert already answer "what is stuck" and "was I told", and the only candidate numbers (records by status, alerts raised) are derived from that same read. A counter or card added now would be a second source that can disagree with the record. Nothing has run against a live daemon over a wall-clock episode (see the pending live checks below), so there is no observed load or failure pattern to size a metric around. When a live run shows one (for example alerts being missed, or the pass running slowly), the first addition would be a count of records by status in the stats payload, with the Monitor card and the Prometheus counter following from it.

## Shared navigation mobile fit

The bottom navigation bar of the PWA now fits 320 to 414 px phones: six equal buttons, labels that truncate with an ellipsis, and a 40 px minimum tap width. The how-to is `docs/howto/navigation-mobile-fit.md`, the plan is `docs/plans/2026-10-25-shared-nav-mobile-fit.md`, and the run records are in `docs/testing/runs/shared-nav-mobile-fit/`. The detailed check steps are in `docs/testing.md` under "Shared navigation mobile fit — phone widths".

Test conditions for every row below, unless a row says otherwise:

- **Daemon:** `Version` 9.11.0 in `cmd/datawatch/main.go` (line 119). The binary was built from the branch with `go build -o bin/datawatch ./cmd/datawatch/`. The code under test is the post-fix tree, `a7cc30e4`, and nothing under `internal/` has changed since (`git diff --stat a7cc30e4 HEAD -- internal/` is empty).
- **Sandbox:** an isolated local daemon started by `scripts/e2e-pwa.sh` on loopback, from `testdata/datawatch.yaml`. No production daemon was used. Runs used `env -u TMUX -u TMUX_TMPDIR`.
- **Browser:** headless Chrome at `/usr/bin/google-chrome`, 100 percent zoom only.
- **Viewports:** gate 320x568, 360x740 and 390x844 in light and dark; baseline 768x1024, 1024x768 and 1280x800 in light and dark; report-only 320x568, 360x740, 375x667, 390x844, 414x896 and 768x1024 in dark.
- **Named checker:** `scripts/test-stories/pwa/shared-nav-mobile-fit.mjs` now exists (commit `cccbd9f0`) but is a wrapper around the probe `shared-nav-mobile-fit-probe.mjs`. Its findings are the probe's, not the spec's.

Tested is Yes only where the node unit test `internal/server/web/app-shared-nav.test.js` covers the row: it checks the `title` attribute on each nav button and the `.nav-label` ellipsis rule in `style.css`, by reading `index.html` and `style.css` (2 of 2 passed under `node --test` on 2026-10-25). Nothing in the Makefile, the scripts or CI runs that test, so it is run by hand. No Go test covers the bar. The gate is an end-to-end browser test, so it is recorded as Validated, not Tested. Tested and Validated are set only from runs that happened on 2026-10-25.

| Feature | Test Name | Test Conditions | Description | Test Type | Tested? | Pass/Fail? | Validated? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bottom bar at phone widths (gate) | `shared-nav-mobile-fit.mjs` → probe gate mode; `make test-e2e-shared-nav` | Daemon 9.11.0; sandbox; headless Chrome; 320x568, 360x740, 390x844; light and dark; 100% zoom | No clipped label, no bottom button under 44x44 CSS px, no overlap, in all six width and theme combinations. | E2E (browser, sandbox daemon) | **No** — the node unit test does not measure the rendered bar | PASS, 2026-10-25 13:51, 0 findings, `make` exit 0 | **Yes** — real Chrome against a live sandbox daemon, at the three phone widths in both themes | Before the fix the same gate FAILED with 4 findings (dark theme; Dashboard and Settings labels clipped; scroll width 440 px at 320, 360 and 390). The report's `daemon_version` reads `unknown` because the runner does not pass it. The probe's measures are not the spec's named measures. |
| Bottom bar fits without sideways scrolling | Same run as the gate row; the probe prints `scrollWidth` and `clientWidth` | Same as the gate row | The bar's scroll width equals its visible width, so six equal buttons fit 320 px without scrolling. | Observation in an E2E run (not a gate assertion) | **No** — nothing asserts it | Observed equal at 320, 360 and 390 px in both themes; not a pass/fail result | **No** — recorded, not asserted | The probe records the two widths in the report but never makes them a finding, so a scroll regression would not fail the gate. Before the fix the scroll width was 440 px at each phone width. Making it a finding is a change to the probe, not done here. |
| Bottom bar geometry at desktop and tablet widths | Probe `SHARED_NAV_MODE=baseline`, compared with `post-fix/nav-baseline.json` | Daemon 9.11.0 post-fix tree `a7cc30e4`; sandbox; 768x1024, 1024x768, 1280x800; light and dark | 456 boxes (nav, button, icon, label) compared with the pre-fix baseline, tolerance 2 px or 1 percent. The fix must not move them. | E2E (browser, sandbox daemon) | **No** — no Go or node unit test | PASS, maximum delta 0 px, 0 rows with a delta | **Yes** — live run against the sandbox daemon | The probe writes the baseline but does not compare; the comparison was a separate step, recorded in `post-fix-report.txt`. |
| Tap targets on the bottom bar | Gate row (44x44 CSS px line) and the 40 px `min-width` on `.nav-btn` in `style.css` | Same as the gate row | No bottom button under 44 by 44 CSS px at the phone widths. | E2E (browser, sandbox daemon) | **No** — CSS only | PASS, no bottom button flagged | **Yes** — same live run | The 40 px minimum in CSS is the stylesheet floor; the gate's line is 44 px. ## Tag change events — `tag_update` WebSocket message

| Item | Status |
|---|---|
| Tested | Yes — `TestTagEvent*` in `internal/autonomous` (one event per registry or assignment operation, refused operations emit nothing, id-only payload, not a lifecycle event, `prd_update` once per blocked / needs_review / paused transition) and `internal/server` (frame shape for every kind, delivery to every client, session route emits `session_assigned` and a refused tag emits nothing) |
| Validated | No — not yet checked against a running daemon with a WebSocket client |

Contract change: new WebSocket message `tag_update` (`{kind, tag_id?, prd_id?, session_id?}`), documented in `docs/api/autonomous.md`. Every Automaton status change now also sends `prd_update`, which previously only some status paths did.

## Usage calculator MCP tools — unreleased

The MCP surface of the account usage calculator: six tools that proxy this daemon's loopback REST surface (the REST surface's own tracking lives with the calculator's other sections). Design: `docs/plans/2026-10-23-usage-calculator-design.md`; decisions: `docs/plans/2026-10-25-usage-calculator-decisions.md`. Unit/integration run 2026-10-26: `go test ./internal/mcp/ ./internal/federation/ ./internal/server/ -count=1` — all pass (`-run 'TestUsageCalc'` covers the six tools).

| Interface / Endpoint | Tested | Validated | Test Conditions | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MCP `usage_advice` (one advice result; optional `variant`/`policy`/`lanes`/`cost` override the stored settings for this call only) | **Yes** (`internal/mcp/usage_calculator_test.go`: `TestUsageCalcAdviceProxiesGetWithQuery`, `TestUsageCalcAdviceOmitsOmittedArguments`) | **No** | Live: call the tool on a sandbox daemon's MCP endpoint and confirm the result matches `GET /api/usage/advice` with the same query parameters | Proxies `GET /api/usage/advice`; reads `usage:read`; omitted arguments are left off the query so the stored settings apply |
| MCP `usage_readings` (shared readings series, extra credit, per-policy remaining work) | **Yes** (`TestUsageCalcReadingsProxiesGet`) | **No** | Live: call the tool and confirm the series matches `GET /api/usage/readings` | Proxies `GET /api/usage/readings`; reads `usage:read`; stale-marker semantics are the REST layer's |
| MCP `usage_reading_add` / `usage_reading_delete` (one figure per reading — `percent` 0–100 or `spend_usd` >= 0, plus optional `at`/`session_percent`/`lanes`; delete by id) | **Yes** (`TestUsageCalcReadingAdd`, `TestUsageCalcReadingAddRejectsBadInput`, `TestUsageCalcReadingDelete`) | **No** | Live: add a reading, confirm it appears in `usage_readings`, delete it by id, confirm it is gone; confirm a 404 on an unknown id | Proxies `POST /api/usage/readings` and `DELETE /api/usage/readings/<id>`; writes `usage:write`; both-together / neither-together and negative ranges rejected before the request is sent |
| MCP `usage_extra_credit_set` / `usage_remaining_work_set` (points >= 0; extra credit shared, remaining work daemon-local) | **Yes** (`TestUsageCalcExtraCreditSet`, `TestUsageCalcRemainingWorkSet`) | **No** | Live: set extra credit (`points: 0` is valid), confirm the advice ceiling moves; set the typed remaining work, confirm the finish-early estimate compares against it | Proxies `PUT /api/usage/extra-credit` and `PUT /api/usage/remaining-work`; writes `usage:write`; negative or missing points rejected before the request is sent |

## Usage calculator comm-channel commands — unreleased

The comm-channel surface of the account usage calculator: the `usage` grammar in `internal/router/commands.go` (parse) and `internal/router/usage_calculator.go` (handler). The handler proxies this daemon's REST loopback, the same way the budget, cost and stale handlers do, so the reply shows the exact data the other surfaces show. Design: `docs/plans/2026-10-23-usage-calculator-design.md`; decisions: `docs/plans/2026-10-25-usage-calculator-decisions.md`. Run: `go test ./internal/router/ -count=1 -run 'TestUsageCalc'` — all pass (2026-10-26).

| Interface / Endpoint | Tested | Validated | Test Conditions | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parse: `usage`, `usage advice [variant=V] [policy=P] [lanes=N]` | **Yes** (`TestUsageCalcParseAdvice` — bare form, per-call overrides, case-folding of verbs/keys with verbatim values; `TestUsageCalcParseNotUsage` keeps `usagebackoff` and lookalikes on their own commands) | **No** | Live: send `usage` and `usage advice variant=lane-planner lanes=3` in a comm channel and confirm the advice arrives with the per-call overrides and no stored change | Bare `usage` and `usage advice` are the same read (`GET /api/usage/advice`); per-call `variant=`/`policy=`/`lanes=` override the stored settings for this call only; keys are case-insensitive, values pass verbatim |
| Parse: `usage reading <pct> [lanes=N] [session=N]` | **Yes** (`TestUsageCalcParseReading`; invalid tails in `TestUsageCalcParseInvalid`) | **No** | Live: send `usage reading 72.5 lanes=3 session=41` and confirm `POST /api/usage/readings` receives the percent, lanes and session_percent, and the reply shows the refreshed advice | Typed percent is non-negative; `session` belongs only to the reading verb; a malformed figure keeps the verb `invalid`, so no request goes out |
| Parse: `usage extra <points>`, `usage work <points\|clear>`, and every bad form | **Yes** (`TestUsageCalcParseExtraWork`; `TestUsageCalcParseInvalid` — 22 bad forms incl. `usage extra clear`, `usage advice session=3`, duplicate keys in any case) | **No** | Live: send `usage extra 20`, `usage work 15.5` and `usage work clear` and confirm `PUT /api/usage/extra-credit`, `PUT`/`DELETE /api/usage/remaining-work` respectively, each followed by the refreshed advice | `clear` is valid only on `work`; points are non-negative; unknown verbs and duplicate or unknown keys answer the usage lines |
| Handler: advice read via REST loopback, per-call overrides on the query, 50-column reply ending in the reply hint | **Yes** (`TestUsageCalcAdviceHandler`, `TestUsageCalcAdviceOverrides`, `TestUsageCalcReplyWidth`) | **No** | Live: send `usage advice` on a live daemon and confirm the reply matches the PWA/CLI read of the same stored state, at most 50 columns per line, closing with the reply hint | `usagecalc.FormatComm` renders the text; the reply hint is one form per line; field order matches the shared text layer |
| Handler: write verbs — ack line then refreshed advice; invalid form sends nothing; error path answers the failure | **Yes** (`TestUsageCalcReadingHandler`, `TestUsageCalcReadingBare`, `TestUsageCalcExtraHandler`, `TestUsageCalcWorkHandler`, `TestUsageCalcWorkClear`, `TestUsageCalcInvalidFormNoRequest`) | **No** | Live: run the write verbs against a sandbox daemon and confirm the acknowledgement figure matches the stored value (`GET /api/usage/readings`) | `reading`/`extra`/`work` write first, then show the advice after the write; `work clear` DELETEs the remaining-work and the per-task estimate stands in; an `httptest` stand-in plays the daemon loopback — no socket, no real daemon, no wall clock |
| `configure usage.calculator.variant=…` / `policy=` path untouched by the comm surface | **Yes** (`TestUsageCalcConfigureThroughRouter`) | **No** | Live: set the variant through `configure` on a live daemon and confirm the next `usage` shows the configured variant | The settings path is the existing `configure` handler; the per-call overrides never write settings |

## Lane fill — shadow mode first (automatic lane filling)

Lane fill runs the planner on every coordinator poll and records what it would start on each idle lane. In `shadow` mode (the default) it starts nothing; in `on` mode it starts work through the existing admission path; in `off` it does nothing. The rules are in `docs/plans/2026-10-24-lane-fill-shadow-mode.md` and the operator procedure is in `docs/howto/automation-lane-fill.md`.

The Go tests use fakes only: a fake starter that records calls, a fake pool evidence source, a fake session lister and host lister, a fixed clock, and temporary directories for the decision records. No test starts a live daemon, a real model host or a real worker. The PWA rows are Node tests of the rendering and escaping functions in `internal/server/web/app.js`, not a browser session.

The Shadow mode test `TestLaneFillShadowLoopPollsOnItsOwn` was intermittent before the final gate; its row gives the cause and the fix. After the fix every Go and node group passes in the final gate run.

**No row is Validated.** Every live check is still pending: the one-day shadow comparison against the supervisor's own lane fill (the criteria are in the how-to) has not been run, no sandbox daemon has been run in each mode, and nobody has looked at the Lane fill card in a running PWA. ## Start evidence and busy probe — next patch above main

A claude-code worker in a long silent first tool call now counts as started. The start-confirm tracker takes a tool line, a running or result line, a spinner, a new child process of the runner, a pane change or a channel event after delivery as evidence of work, and measures the silence from the last such evidence. An adopted session is measured from its last evidence of life, not from adoption. The busy probe keeps a delivered claude-code one-shot worker in Running while its pane shows work.

## Orphan sweep session id comparison — next patch above main

The orphan sweep, the reset that ends a task's live sessions, boot adoption and the task lookup by session id now compare session ids by their short form (the text after the last hyphen) on both sides.
